(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42274595)\nThyroid hormones (THs) critically regulate metabolism and the central nervous system (CNS) functions, acting as key factors in neuronal differentiation, synaptogenesis and myelination. Furthermore, they play a central role in regulation of cognitive process and behavior. Therefore, compromised TH signaling can interfere with normal brain function and promote neurodegenerative progression and dementia. This review explores the role of THs from embryonic development through adulthood, with particular emphasis on their crucial role in neurogenesis. We discuss key components of TH metabolism and signaling, highlighting their neuroprotective functions in maintaining cellular homeostasis. Furthermore, we address how disruptions in TH signaling contribute to cognitive decline observed in dementia\n\n[WEB:europepmc] The type 2 deiodinase Thr92Ala polymorphism and cognitive aging: current evidence and biological context. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42137609)\nType 2 iodothyronine deiodinase (DIO2) plays a central role in regulating thyroid hormone (TH) metabolism in the brain by catalyzing the conversion of thyroxine (T4) to the active triiodothyronine (T3), thereby ensuring adequate local TH signaling in neural tissues. Among DIO2 genetic variants, the Thr92Ala (rs225014) polymorphism has been extensively investigated in relation to TH homeostasis and diverse clinical phenotypes. Accumulating evidence suggests a potential association between the Thr92Ala variant and cognitive aging; however, findings across studies remain inconsistent. Proposed mechanisms include altered local TH availability, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cerebrovascular regulation, although the relative contribution of these pathways has not been fully cla\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Treatment of Hypothyroidism That Contains Liothyronine is Associated With Reduced Risk of Dementia and Mortality. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40579157)\nIntroduction Standard levothyroxine (LT4) therapy may not fully address all risks associated with hypothyroidism-especially cognitive decline, dementia, and mortality-even when TSH levels are normalized. Observational studies link hypothyroidism to higher dementia rates; the role of LT4 plus T3 therapies remains uncertain. Methods This retrospective cohort study analyzed TriNetX data, comparing 1.26 million patients with hypothyroidism (on LT4, LT4 + T3, or desiccated thyroid extract) to 3.32 million controls. Outcomes included dementia, atrial fibrillation, and mortality over 20 years of follow-up. Propensity score matching was used to balance covariates for age, sex, and comorbidities. Adjusted hazard ratios were obtained via Cox proportional hazard modeling. A parallel systematic review"}

This type of drug works by\n\n...Answer: The best treatment for dementia depends on what is causing it. In most cases, dementia is caused by Alzheimer's disease. Thankfully, there are several different treatment options available for Alzheimer's. The first type of treatment that is usually used is medication that helps to increase the levels of a chemical called acetylcholine. This can include medications like Donepezil (Aricept), Rivastigmine (Exelon), and Galantamine. These medications work by boosting up the levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Another medication that can be helpful is called Memantine (Namenda). This medication works by modulating two other chemicals in the brain, glutamate and dopamine. It can be especially helpful for individuals who are becoming apathetic and lack energy and motivation. Memantine is typically used in people with moderate to severe stages of Alzheimer's who are experiencing these difficulties. Lastly, for Alzheimer's, there is a new class of medications that can remove amyloid plaques from the brain and slow down the progression of the disease. These medications are still relatively new, but they show promise in treating Alzheimer's. It's important to note that these treatments are specifically for Alzheimer's, which is the most common cause of dementia....\n\n...● Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).\n● Depression.\nDementias that aren't reversible may still partially respond to medications that treat memory loss\nor behavior problems. In Alzheimer's, certain disease processes cause too much\nglutamate activity. Excess glutamate causes irregular activity and damage in nerve cells\nthat interact with the chemical messenger....\n\n...Answer: If someone has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, it's important to understand that we can't stop the disease from progressing. However, there are steps we can take to help slow down its progression. Firstly, there are non-pharmacologic interventions that have shown to be beneficial. These include engaging in aerobic exercise, following a Mediterranean diet, staying socially active, participating in cognitively stimulating activities, maintaining a positive mindset, and avoiding a sedentary lifestyle. These activities can help slow down the progression of the disease, especially in the early stage known as mild cognitive impairment. Secondly, there are symptomatic therapies available that can turn back the clock on Alzheimer's by six to 12 months. These medications work by raising levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Examples of such medications include Donepezil (Aricept), Rivastigmine (Exelon), and Galantamine. Finally, there are medications that have been recently approved to slow down the progression of Alzheimer's. These medications, such as Lecanemab and soon Donanemab, are designed to remove amyloid plaques from the brain. This type of drug works by regulating the activity of glutamate, a different chemical messenger that helps the brain process information. This drug is known as:\nMemantine (Namenda®): approved for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. Can cause side effects, including headache, constipation, confusion and dizziness.\nCholinesterase inhibitor + glutamate regulator...\n\n...Treatments to Address Cognitive and Behavioral Symptoms\nFive of the FDA-approved drugs for Alzheimer's disease\n— donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine, memantine and\nmemantine combined with donepezil — are aimed at\ntreating cognitive symptoms. They do not slow, stop or\nreverse the underlying brain changes that cause\nAlzheimer's, nor do they slow or stop the course of the\ndisease. Instead, they help compensate for the brain\nchanges of Alzheimer's by altering neurotransmitter\nlevels. Neurotransmitters are chemicals that brain cells\nuse to communicate with each other. Memantine\nprotects the brain from excessive levels of a\nneurotransmitter called glutamate, which overstimulates\nneurons and can damage them, while the remaining\ndrugs increase the amount of the neurotransmitter\nacetylcholine.\nThese five drugs may have side effects, such as\nheadaches and nausea. These are not all the possible\nside effects. As with lecanemab and donanemab,\nindividuals should talk with their doctors to develop a\ntreatment plan that is right for them, including weighing\nthe benefits and risks of all therapies....\n\n...due to Alzheimer's disease.\n● Donepezil (Aricept®): approved for mild-to-severe dementia due to\nAlzhiemer's disease.\n● Galantamine (Razadyne®): approved for mild-to-moderate dementia\ndue to Alzheimer's disease.\n● Rivastigmine (Exelon®): approved for mild-to-moderate dementia due to\nAlzheimer's disease as well as mild-to-moderate dementia due to\nParkinson's disease.\nThough generally well-tolerated, if side effects occur, they commonly include\ndiarrhea, dizziness, headache, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite and\nincreased frequency of bowel movements.  \nGlutamate regulators\nGlutamate regulators are prescribed to improve memory, attention, reason,\nlanguage and the ability to perform simple tasks. This type of drug works by\n\n...Answer: The best treatment for dementia depends on what is causing it. In most cases, dementia is caused by Alzheimer's disease. Thankfully, there are several different treatment options available for Alzheimer's. The first type of treatment that is usually used is medication that helps to increase the levels of a chemical called acetylcholine. This can include medications like Donepezil (Aricept), Rivastigmine (Exelon), and Galantamine. These medications work by boosting up the levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Another medication that can be helpful is called Memantine (Namenda). This medication works by modulating two other chemicals in the brain, glutamate and dopamine. It can be especially helpful for individuals who are becoming apathetic and lack energy and motivation. Memantine is typically used in people with moderate to severe stages of Alzheimer's who are experiencing these difficulties. Lastly, for Alzheimer's, there is a new class of medications that can remove amyloid plaques from the brain and slow down the progression of the disease. These medications are still relatively new, but they show promise in treating Alzheimer's. It's important to note that these treatments are specifically for Alzheimer's, which is the most common cause of dementia....\n\n...● Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).\n● Depression.\nDementias that aren't reversible may still partially respond to medications that treat memory loss\nor behavior problems. These dementias include:\n● Alzheimer's disease.\n● Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia.\n● Dementias associated with Parkinson's disease and similar disorders.\n● AIDS dementia complex.\n● Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.\nWhat medications are available to manage dementia?\nDrugs approved for the most common form of dementia, Alzheimer's disease, include:\n● Cholinesterase inhibitors, including donepezil (Aricept®), rivastigmine (Exelon®) and\ngalantamine (Razadyne®).\n● NMDA receptor antagonist memantine (Namenda®).\n● Anti-amyloid antibody aducanumab (Aduhelm®).\nHealthcare providers use these drugs to treat people with some of the other forms of dementia.\nCholinesterase inhibitors and the NMDA receptor antagonist affect different chemical processes\nin your brain. Both drug classes have been shown to provide some benefit in improving or...\n\ndose can help lessen side effects. Taking these medicines with food also might help\nlessen some side effects.\nPeople with certain conditions that cause irregular heartbeats can't take cholinesterase\ninhibitors.\nThree cholinesterase inhibitors are commonly prescribed:\n● Donepezil (Aricept) is approved to treat all stages of the disease. It's taken\nonce a day as a pill.\n● Galantamine is approved to treat mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. It's\ntaken as an extended-release pill once a day or as a pill or liquid twice a day.\n● Rivastigmine is approved for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. It's\ntaken as a pill twice a day. A rivastigmine skin patch (Exelon) that's approved\nto treat all stages of Alzheimer's disease is changed daily.\nMemantine\nGlutamate is a chemical messenger that is important for many brain functions, including\nlearning and memory. In Alzheimer's, certain disease processes cause too much\nglutamate activity. Excess glutamate causes irregular activity and damage in nerve cells\nthat interact with the chemical messenger....\n\n...Answer: If someone has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, it's important to understand that we can't stop the disease from progressing. However, there are steps we can take to help slow down its progression. Firstly, there are non-pharmacologic interventions that have shown to be beneficial. These include engaging in aerobic exercise, following a Mediterranean diet, staying socially active, participating in cognitively stimulating activities, maintaining a positive mindset, and avoiding a sedentary lifestyle. These activities can help slow down the progression of the disease, especially in the early stage known as mild cognitive impairment. Secondly, there are symptomatic therapies available that can turn back the clock on Alzheimer's by six to 12 months. These medications work by raising levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Examples of such medications include Donepezil (Aricept), Rivastigmine (Exelon), and Galantamine. Finally, there are medications that have been recently approved to slow down the progression of Alzheimer's. These medications, such as Lecanemab and soon Donanemab, are designed to remove amyloid plaques from the brain. While we cannot halt Alzheimer's disease, these interventions and medications can help in managing its symptoms and potentially slow down its progression....\n\nDementia\n(Stage 5)\nSevere\nDementia\n(Stage 6)\n1996 Donepezil (Aricept®)\n2000 Rivastigmine (Excelon®)\n2001 Galantamine (Razadyne®)\n2003 Memantine (Namenda®)\n2014 Memantine + Donepezil (Namzaric®)\n2020 Suvorexant* (Belsomra®)\n2023 Lecanemab (Leqembi®)\n2023 Brexpiprazole (Rexulti®)\n2024 Donanemab (Kisunla\nTM)\nTreatment\nFIGURE 1\n*Approved for insomnia, not Alzheimer's, but safe and effective in people living with Alzheimer's."}

The frequency of aggression tends to increase as the disease progresses. Understanding the triggers for this behavior is crucial in managing it effectively. Disorientation can trigger agitation and aggression, even when individuals are in their own homes. Most of the causes of delirium\nare treatable, such as constipation, dehydration or infections.\nDelirium can cause people to have hallucinations or delusions,\nbecome confused, drowsy, or distressed. For more information\ngo to alzheimers.org.uk/delirium\nWhat is perception?\nInformation from the sense organs, for example the eyes or\nears, travels to the brain. The brain processes this information,\nto understand it. The brain then analyses it alongside other\ninformation already in the brain, such as thoughts and memories\nand their associated emotions. Then the person becomes aware\nof what has been sensed (perceived).\nMy 93-yearold mother has\nbeen having\nfalse memories.\nNo matter what\nevidence is shown\nto her to prove\nthat what she is\nclaiming never\nhappened, she\nwill not back down\nand begins to get\nangry.\nFamily member\nof a person with\ndementia\n\nTell the doctor immediately if the person seems suddenly worse or different. Medical problems such as fever, infection, medication side effects,\nand dehydration can cause delirium, a state of extreme confusion and disorientation.\nAsk friends and family to make calls, or use email or online tools to keep others informed about the person's progress.\nHelp the person fill out menu requests. One condition to watch out for is an acute stroke, which occurs suddenly and can cause difficulty speaking, moving a body part, or slurred speech. Another condition is delirium, which develops more quickly than dementia and can come and go. But sometimes, it's just not possible. Dementia is a complex disease that requires a lot of time, attention, and specialized skills to provide proper care. As a caregiver, you might find that you have other responsibilities or limitations that prevent you from being able to care for your loved one exclusively. It's important to understand that \"family takes care of family\" doesn't always mean you have to do it all by yourself. Caring for your family member may involve bringing in specialists, home health aides, or other nurses who have the skills and expertise to best meet their needs. In some cases, it may even mean considering a facility where they can receive round-the-clock care. Taking care of someone with dementia is not an easy task, and it's essential to prioritize their safety and well-being. Sometimes, that means reaching out for additional support and resources. Remember, caring for your family member doesn't always have to be limited to just family. By allowing others to help, you can ensure that your loved one receives the best care while also taking care of your own health and well-being....\n\n...to understand and communicate effectively. Family\ncaregivers must often help people with dementia manage\nthese issues. The personality and behavior of a person with\ndementia are affected as well, and these changes are often\namong the most challenging for family caregivers.587-589\nIndividuals with dementia also require increasing levels of\nsupervision and personal care as the disease progresses.\nAs the person with dementia's symptoms worsen,\ncaregivers can experience increased emotional stress and\ndepression; neglect of their own health due to caregiving\npriorities;590, 591 new or exacerbated health problems; and\ndepleted income and finances due in part to disruptions\nin employment and paying for health care or other\nservices for both themselves and the person living\n\nQuestion: How can I continue to care for myself while caring for someone living with dementia?\nAnswer: When caring for someone with dementia, it's crucial to also take care of yourself. Your own well-being is directly linked to your ability to provide effective care. Taking care of yourself means getting enough rest, eating nourishing meals, and maintaining your overall health. It's important to schedule regular check-ups with your primary care physician and take any prescribed medications. Joining a caregiver support group can provide valuable support and give you permission to take breaks and prioritize your own needs. It may also be helpful to have your own mental health provider to guide you through the different stages of caregiving and offer a safe outlet for difficult emotions. Couples counseling or counseling with your loved one who has dementia can also be beneficial for a period of time. Remember, every step you take to protect your own health and well-being will contribute to a higher quality of life for both you and the person you are caring for.\nQuestion: Are there any safety concerns I should be aware of after a diagnosis of dementia?...\n\nOne of the biggest emotional burdens of caregiving is the sense of loss that\ncaregivers experience. Dementia, particularly Alzheimer's disease, gradually\nerodes a person's cognitive functions. This leaves caregivers mourning the\nloss of the person they once knew. Even though the individual is physically\npresent, the emotional connection may be diminished or completely lost as\nthe disease progresses.\nMany caregivers also struggle with feelings of guilt. They may feel guilty for\nfeeling frustrated or angry with their loved one, or they may question whether\nthey're doing enough to care for them. These emotions can exacerbate\nfeelings of isolation, making it more difficult for caregivers to seek the support\nthey need.\nFinancial Strain on Caregivers\nAnother significant impact of dementia on caregivers and family members is\nfinancial strain. Caregiving for dementia often requires a substantial\ninvestment of time, and it can become a full-time job, especially as the person\nwith dementia enters the later stages of the disease.\nMany family caregivers face financial challenges when they are forced to\nreduce their working hours or quit their jobs entirely to care for a loved one.\nAdditionally, the costs of caregiving can be high. It's important for caregivers to recognize the toll that this role can take on their mental and emotional well-being. Often, caregivers find themselves overwhelmed by the behavioral symptoms of dementia and may feel like they are constantly on duty, 24/7, with no respite. One way to cope with these behavioral symptoms is to consider how much time is being devoted to caregiving. If you are the sole caregiver and are with the person with dementia all the time, it's crucial to understand that you are asking your brain to do the impossible with inadequate support. It's okay to acknowledge that you need a break and cannot do it all alone. Limiting the amount of time spent caregiving can have a positive impact on both you and the person with dementia. By acknowledging that you need help, you can become more of a partner in their care instead of solely shouldering the responsibility. Seeking out support from others who are experienced in dementia care can provide the hands-on assistance that is needed. Lastly, it's important to remember to see the person behind the dementia. When the behaviors and symptoms become overwhelming, it can be easy to forget the things you still like about the person you are caring for....\n\n...Answer: To be an effective caregiver for someone with dementia, there are several important things to keep in mind. First, you need to have a good understanding of the disease itself. This means learning about both the physical and emotional aspects of caring for someone with dementia. It's crucial to prioritize safety for both the person with dementia and yourself. This means making sure the environment is safe and secure and taking measures to prevent accidents or injuries. It's also important to prioritize your own mental well-being and find ways to cope with the challenges of caregiving. Rather than arguing or trying to convince the person with dementia against their desires, it's best to find ways to redirect their attention or provide alternatives that are safer or more suitable. For example, if they want to go skydiving, you could suggest going for ice cream instead. In order to effectively care for someone with dementia, it's important to understand their world and learn about their experiences and needs. Reading about dementia and joining support groups can provide valuable insights and strategies. Being an effective caregiver often requires a lot of repetition, so it's important to learn and prepare for the specific tasks involved in their care. Attending caregiver classes and seeking information from local agencies can be helpful resources. However, it's crucial to always keep the person with dementia at the center of your care and to respect their dignity and autonomy....\n\nQuestion: How can I support my loved one?\nAnswer: To support a loved one with dementia, it is important to understand that you need to enter their world rather than expect them to live in yours. Your main responsibilities are to keep them safe and to preserve your own sanity during this journey. It is essential that you do not fight against dementia, as you will not win that battle. Instead, when they ask about someone who is no longer present or make false statements, it is best to go along with it and validate their feelings. For example, if they ask about Mary who has been gone for a long time, you can respond by saying that you are not sure what happened to her, even though you know the truth. Similarly, if they become angry and say hurtful things, it is important to remain calm and respond with kindness. Acknowledge their feelings, apologize if necessary, and assure them of your love. By keeping the temperature down and not engaging in arguments, you can create a supportive environment. Remember that safety and sanity are the two crucial aspects to keep in mind. "tf_final_answer_source": "", "tf_answer_llm_locked": false}, "final_answer": "C", "base_context_chars": 9622, "final_context_chars": 9622, "base_context": "...Question: What are the most common emotions faced by caregivers of someone with dementia?\nAnswer: Caregivers of people with dementia often experience a range of emotions, with grief being the most common. The grief starts even before the person passes away, as the diagnosis itself brings a lot of sadness. Caregivers may feel angry at the world for what has happened to their loved one, and it'sa difficult thing to come to terms with. Alongside grief, caregivers may also feel scared, as they are unsure of how to properly care for someone whose condition can change rapidly. The overwhelming amount of work involved in caregiving can lead to burnout and feeling overwhelmed. Caregivers want to do everything they can, but they also recognize the importance of taking care of themselves. This balance can be challenging and may result in feelings of guilt. It's important for caregivers to remember that they are doing their best and not to feel guilty about taking time for themselves or when things don't go perfectly.\nQuestion: How do I think about my own mortality?...\n\n...Answer: Caring for someone with dementia can be incredibly challenging and stressful. It's important for caregivers to recognize the toll that this role can take on their mental and emotional well-being. Often, caregivers find themselves overwhelmed by the behavioral symptoms of dementia and may feel like they are constantly on duty, 24/7, with no respite. One way to cope with these behavioral symptoms is to consider how much time is being devoted to caregiving. If you are the sole caregiver and are with the person with dementia all the time, it's crucial to understand that you are asking your brain to do the impossible with inadequate support. It's okay to acknowledge that you need a break and cannot do it all alone. Limiting the amount of time spent caregiving can have a positive impact on both you and the person with dementia. By acknowledging that you need help, you can become more of a partner in their care instead of solely shouldering the responsibility. Seeking out support from others who are experienced in dementia care can provide the hands-on assistance that is needed. Lastly, it's important to remember to see the person behind the dementia. When the behaviors and symptoms become overwhelming, it can be easy to forget the things you still like about the person you are caring for....\n\n...A person with dementia may not express many emotions through their facial expression, particularly happiness or sadness. Activities or events that generally entertain them may create little to no response. The lack of motivation and the low energy levels may cause a lack of effort and planning in carrying out activities they usually like.\nIn the long term, apathy may affect a person's ability to maintain personal relationships, which in turn can increase isolation. When apathy is one of the first signs of dementia – especially when it appears before a formal diagnosis – friends and family members may become frustrated by their loved one's indifference, and not realize the underlying cause.\nTips for caregivers\nIf you're caring for someone with dementia, their lack of interest and unwillingness to engage in everyday life activities can be a source of distress.\nIt's common for family members and caregivers to feel overloaded with every minute of their loved one's life. Making some changes in how you approach caring for your loved one can promote their autonomy and independence.\nFor example, it is essential to minimize your loved one's weaknesses. Reassure and involve them in simple and rewarding activities to maintain their self-esteem....\n\n...• Admitting a relative to a residential care facility has\nmixed effects on the emotional and psychological\nwell-being of dementia family caregivers. Some\nstudies suggest that distress remains unchanged\nor even increases for some caregivers (such as\nspouses), but other studies have found that\ndistress decreases.578, 633-635\n• The demands of caregiving may intensify as people\nwith dementia approach the end of life.636 In the year\nbefore the death of the person living with dementia,\n59% of caregivers felt they were “on duty” 24 hours a\nday, and many felt that caregiving during this time\nwas extremely stressful.637 The same study found that\n72% of family caregivers experienced relief when the\nperson with Alzheimer's or another dementia died.637\n• In the last 12 months of life, people with dementia\nrelied on more hours of family care (64.5 hours per\nweek) than people with cancer (39.3 hours per week).638\nCaregiver Physical Health and Health Conditions\nFor some caregivers, the demands of caregiving may\ncause declines in their own health. Evidence suggests that...\n\n...Attend carefully to what the person is saying and doing,\nto understand their reality. Acknowledge their worry, and\nexplain you will try to help. They are more likely to be gently\ndistracted, once they feel heard.\nNot contradicting their experience. They shouldn't be told\nwhat is or is not true in a confrontational manner. They may\nbecome frightened or upset.\nRemembering that emotional memories are often easier\nto retrieve. Staying open, calm and friendly can help the\nperson with dementia to associate a carer with positive\nemotions, even if they struggle to understand who you are\nin the present.\nRemaining calm. If a carer becomes frustrated that the person\nis struggling with the present, they should take themselves\nout of the situation until they feel calmer, perhaps making a\ndrink for them both to take some time out of the room.\nRemembering the positive difference they make to the\nperson with dementia. The person with dementia does not\nneed to fully understand your reality for them to feel happy,\nso continue to try and do what makes them feel content.\n\n...caregiver, even for a moment. For example, if the person with dementia cannot see or hear\ntheir caregiver, they might wander away looking for them and get lost.\n• People with dementia often become more sensitive to changes in the environment or\nroutine; try to provide a consistent and predictable routine.\n• Simplify the environment; reduce clutter and background noise.\n• People with dementia may use your emotions as cues for their own. For example, if you are\nanxious and worried, they may become anxious and worried. Take a deep breath and try to\nstay calm and relaxed.\n• Ask yourself whether you are expecting too much from the person with dementia. For\nexample, are you expecting them to remember information that they really cannot\nremember? Adjust your expectations and support the person to function at a level that is\nmost successful for them.\n• Consider the emotion the person may be expressing with their behavior. For example, are\nthey afraid of a noise or unfamiliar person? Are they not understanding the conversation and\nreacting with anger or embarrassment?\n• If the person is resistant and uncooperative, stop and try again later with a different\napproach....\n\n...Answer: Caring for a loved one with dementia can be incredibly challenging, especially when others don't understand the realities you face on a daily basis. It can be disheartening when your loved one seems perfectly normal around other people, making it difficult for others to believe or comprehend the challenges you experience. This can happen during doctor visits or when interacting with friends and acquaintances who don't witness the unusual behaviors firsthand. It's important to remember that dementia affects individuals in different ways, and their behavior can vary depending on the environment and situation. Even if your loved one appears fine to others, it's crucial to trust your own observations and instincts. It can be frustrating and hurtful when others question your reality or dismiss your concerns. As a caregiver, it can feel like living in two different worlds – your own and your loved one's world. The key is to try to understand and adapt to their perspective, even though it can be overwhelming and confusing. While it's natural to hope that your loved one's challenging behavior remains hidden, it's important to acknowledge that it may worsen over time, allowing others to eventually see the difficulties you face. In the meantime, it can be helpful to let go of your ego and appreciate the times when your loved one engages in seemingly normal conversations with others....\n\nCaregiving for dementia can have profound effects on both the individual\nwith dementia and their loved ones. While dementia may affect the person\ndiagnosed, the emotional, financial, and physical burden on family members\nand caregivers is often overwhelming. Caregivers of individuals with\ndementia are at risk of mental and physical health challenges, isolation,\nfinancial strain, and emotional stress. In this blog post, we will explore the\nimpact of dementia on caregivers and family members, including strategies\nto mitigate these challenges.\nThe Daily Challenges of Caregiving for Dementia\nCaring for someone with dementia is a multifaceted task, and the demands\ncan vary greatly depending on the stage of the disease. Tasks like assisting with personal hygiene,\npreparing meals, managing medications, and scheduling medical\nappointments often become full-time jobs.\nDementia can also lead to behavioral changes, which can be particularly\nchallenging to manage. In addition,...", "final_context": "...Question: What are the most common emotions faced by caregivers of someone with dementia?\nAnswer: Caregivers of people with dementia often experience a range of emotions, with grief being the most common. The grief starts even before the person passes away, as the diagnosis itself brings a lot of sadness. Caregivers may feel angry at the world for what has happened to their loved one, and it'sa difficult thing to come to terms with. Alongside grief, caregivers may also feel scared, as they are unsure of how to properly care for someone whose condition can change rapidly. The overwhelming amount of work involved in caregiving can lead to burnout and feeling overwhelmed. Caregivers want to do everything they can, but they also recognize the importance of taking care of themselves. This balance can be challenging and may result in feelings of guilt. It's important for caregivers to remember that they are doing their best and not to feel guilty about taking time for themselves or when things don't go perfectly.\nQuestion: How do I think about my own mortality?...\n\n...Answer: Caring for someone with dementia can be incredibly challenging and stressful. It's important for caregivers to recognize the toll that this role can take on their mental and emotional well-being. Often, caregivers find themselves overwhelmed by the behavioral symptoms of dementia and may feel like they are constantly on duty, 24/7, with no respite. One way to cope with these behavioral symptoms is to consider how much time is being devoted to caregiving. If you are the sole caregiver and are with the person with dementia all the time, it's crucial to understand that you are asking your brain to do the impossible with inadequate support. It's okay to acknowledge that you need a break and cannot do it all alone. Limiting the amount of time spent caregiving can have a positive impact on both you and the person with dementia. By acknowledging that you need help, you can become more of a partner in their care instead of solely shouldering the responsibility. Seeking out support from others who are experienced in dementia care can provide the hands-on assistance that is needed. Lastly, it's important to remember to see the person behind the dementia. When the behaviors and symptoms become overwhelming, it can be easy to forget the things you still like about the person you are caring for....\n\n...A person with dementia may not express many emotions through their facial expression, particularly happiness or sadness. Here are a few tips to help you choose:\n● Timing must be right: To achieve the most success when carrying out activities,\ncaregivers need to consider the time of the day when the patient is most alert.\nFor example, some patients will enjoy going for a walk first thing in the morning,\nwhile others may prefer to stay at home with a cup of tea, reminiscing and\nlooking through old photo albums. It's also important to make sure the patient\nisn't worried about something. If they are, they will not be able to concentrate on\nthe task.\n● Activities must be enjoyable and engaging: Activities that are fun and engaging\ncan reduce disruptive behaviors, such as frustration or agitation. Activities such\nas music, arts and crafts, or sensory stimulation are ideal. Also, patients with\ndementia may enjoy going out for the day, even if they later don't remember\nwhere they were. Try to redirect the individual's energy\ntoward manageable, supervised activities.\n• Restraining a person with dementia in response to agitation is NEVER advised.\nPhysical restraints disregard the individual's dignity and increase the level of\nagitation.\n• Community services such as adult day services can provide a structured\nenvironment for activities.\n• While a non-pharmacological approach is preferable, medication can have a\nsignificant role in reducing agitation. Unless monitored, adverse reactions can occur.\nRepetition...\n\nQuestion: How can I include someone with advanced dementia in activities?\nAnswer: People with advanced dementia can still participate in activities that bring them joy and improve their overall well-being. It's important for us, as caregivers, to let go of our expectations about how these activities should look. Even if someone with dementia doesn't follow the rules or seems to be doing something that doesn't make sense, it's okay. What matters is if they are enjoying themselves. Let them read a book upside down or hold cards the wrong way. Even coloring outside the lines is fine. You can also introduce new activities that they haven't tried before. Remember to tap into their past and bring activities they used to enjoy into their current life. For example, if they were a golfer, they may enjoy looking at golf magazines, watching golf on TV, or playing a putting game at home. The following are strategies that can be used for the\nperson with dementia and the family caregiver.\nSet the Right Environment\nMedications for Sleep\n• Keep a regular schedule: go to bed and get up at the same time every day.\n• Try to exercise daily but not within three hours of bedtime.\n• Make sure the temperature in the bedroom is comfortable (not too hot and not too cold).\n• Reduce liquid intake before bedtime.\n• Try not to nap during the day; if you do nap, try to do so before 3 p.m. and try to keep the\nnap short (about 20 minutes).\n• Keep the bedroom as dark and quiet as possible; use a nightlight if needed, but be\naware that bright light disrupts sleep/wake patterns.\n• Calm activities at the end of the day and before bedtime may help with sleep.\n• Avoid violent movies or TV shows; strong content and images can be upsetting and can\nmake it hard to relax.\n• Be aware that changes in your environment, such as moving to a new home or having\nunexpected visitors can be disruptive and confusing for the person with dementia....\n\n...Answer: There may come a point when a person with dementia realizes they have symptoms, but not everyone experiences this. In the case of the narrator's husband, who had behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (FTD), he had a condition called anosognosia, which means he lacked awareness and understanding of his symptoms and limitations. This may have been a gift for him, considering his brilliant mind and academic achievements. It would have been devastating for him to know that he was losing the ability to read, write, and speak. However, as the caregiver, the narrator had to find unique ways to navigate challenges. For example, when it was no longer safe for the husband to drive, the narrator had to give alternate reasons for him to stop, such as insurance coverage issues. On the other hand, the narrator's father, who is living with Alzheimer's disease, has expressed frustration and fear due to his memory loss. Over time, he has mentioned these concerns less often. The narrator reassures him that it's okay to forget certain things and emphasizes that he remembers the important things like family and loved ones. This reassurance seems to bring him some calmness. Plan activities the person with dementia enjoys and can\ndo. Dancing, painting, gardening, cooking, singing and other activities can\nhelp you connect with your loved one. The activities also can help people\nwith dementia focus on what they can still do.\n● Establish a nighttime routine. Behavior is often worse at night. Try to\nestablish going-to-bed routines. Aim for a calming routine away from the\nnoise of television, meal cleanup and active family members. Leave night\nlights on in the bedroom, hall and bathroom to prevent disorientation.\nLimiting caffeine, discouraging napping and offering opportunities for\nexercise during the day might ease nighttime restlessness.\n● Keep a calendar. A calendar might help your loved one remember\nupcoming events, daily activities and medicine schedules. Consider sharing\na calendar with your loved one.\n● Plan for the future. Develop a plan while your loved one is still able to\nparticipate. The plan can state goals for future care. Support groups, legal\nadvisers, family members and others might be able to help....\n\nchance of falls and other risk factors. The following are strategies that can be used for the\nperson with dementia and the family caregiver.\nSet the Right Environment\nMedications for Sleep\n• Keep a regular schedule: go to bed and get up at the same time every day.\n• Try to exercise daily but not within three hours of bedtime.\n• Make sure the temperature in the bedroom is comfortable (not too hot and not too cold).\n• Reduce liquid intake before bedtime.\n• Try not to nap during the day; if you do nap, try to do so before 3 p.m. and try to keep the\nnap short (about 20 minutes).\n• Keep the bedroom as dark and quiet as possible; use a nightlight if needed, but be\naware that bright light disrupts sleep/wake patterns.\n• Calm activities at the end of the day and before bedtime may help with sleep.\n• Avoid violent movies or TV shows; strong content and images can be upsetting and can\nmake it hard to relax.\n• Be aware that changes in your environment, such as moving to a new home or having\nunexpected visitors can be disruptive and confusing for the person with dementia....\n\n...Answer: There may come a point when a person with dementia realizes they have symptoms, but not everyone experiences this. In the case of the narrator's husband, who had behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (FTD), he had a condition called anosognosia, which means he lacked awareness and understanding of his symptoms and limitations. This may have been a gift for him, considering his brilliant mind and academic achievements. It would have been devastating for him to know that he was losing the ability to read, write, and speak. However, as the caregiver, the narrator had to find unique ways to navigate challenges. For example, when it was no longer safe for the husband to drive, the narrator had to give alternate reasons for him to stop, such as insurance coverage issues. On the other hand, the narrator's father, who is living with Alzheimer's disease, has expressed frustration and fear due to his memory loss. Over time, he has mentioned these concerns less often. The narrator reassures him that it's okay to forget certain things and emphasizes that he remembers the important things like family and loved ones. This reassurance seems to bring him some calmness. Being understanding and providing reassurance can be helpful for both the person with dementia and their loved ones....\n\ntime — activities and exercise may help reduce anxiety,\nagitation and restlessness.\n● Ensure all basic needs are met, including toileting, nutrition\nand hydration. Consider reducing — but not eliminating —\nliquids up to two hours before bedtime so the person\ndoesn't have to use and find the bathroom during the night.\n● Involve the person in daily activities, such as folding\nlaundry or preparing dinner. Learn about creating a daily\nplan.\n● Reassure the person if he or she feels lost, abandoned or\ndisoriented.\n● If the person is still safely able to drive, consider using a\nGPS device to help if they get lost.\n● If the person is no longer driving, remove access to car\nkeys — a person living with dementia may not just wander\nby foot. The person may forget that he or she can no\nlonger drive.\n● Avoid busy places that are confusing and can cause\ndisorientation, such as shopping malls.\n● Assess the person's response to new surroundings. Do not\nleave someone with dementia unsupervised if new\nsurroundings may cause confusion, disorientation or\nagitation....\n\nTips and strategies\nResponding to depression\n● Encourage pleasant activities that the person can still\nenjoy, such as short walks or outings.\n● Set realistic expectations. If you expect too much from a\nperson, they may feel frustrated and discouraged.\n● Establish a consistent daily routine. This will help\nreassure the person as well as reduce confusion.\n● Counselling, cognitive behavioural therapy, and group\ntherapy may be helpful.\n● Antidepressant medications may help. Talk to the\nperson's doctor about the options.\nResponding to apathy\n● Try to engage the person with dementia in activities that\nthey enjoy.\n● Make sure that they can participate at all levels and that\nthey are not overwhelmed.\n● Try introducing a small amount of the activity at a time.\n● Choose flexible activities that can be changed to suit the\nperson's needs.\n● Emphasize more on the process of doing things and not\nthe results.\n● Avoid activities where the person may not be able to\ncomplete the task."}

It's recommended to administer the medication about 30 minutes before bath time. Using visual and auditory cues can also be helpful, like turning on the shower, creating steam, or feeling the moisture in the air. These cues can signal to the person that it's time to bathe and potentially reduce resistance. Sometimes, accepting that bathing is a challenging issue and seeking help from others may be the best solution. This could involve finding a caregiver, whether through natural connections or someone who is paid to assist. It's important to recognize that this may not be an option for everyone, but if possible, getting help can make the process easier and more pleasant for both the person with dementia and the caregiver....\n\n...Answer: If your loved one is resistant to taking a bath, there are some things you can consider. Firstly, think about whether a bath is absolutely necessary or if a different form of hygiene care could be used, such as a shower or sponge bath. Modifying the personal hygiene routine to make it less disruptive or time-consuming may be helpful. Some people have found alternative solutions for showering, like using a kitty pool and shower chair in the kitchen. They set up tarps and use a handheld shower attachment connected to the faucet. This avoids the bathroom, which might be overwhelming or unsafe for the person with dementia. Others have given up on showers and baths altogether and focus on sponge baths instead. It's important to recognize that the resistance might not be solely related to logistics but also to a strong desire to avoid bathing. This resistance can persist for a long time. If the resistance becomes intense, violent, or dangerous, it might be necessary to explore medication options that can help reduce anxiety before bath time. This can make the experience less distressing for the person with dementia. It's recommended to administer the medication about 30 minutes before bath time. Using visual and auditory cues can also be helpful, like turning on the shower, creating steam, or feeling the moisture in the air....\n\n● Be sure the person has a role in the bathing process. For\nexample, have the person hold a washcloth, sponge or\nshampoo bottle.\n● Be aware that the person may perceive bathing to be\nthreatening. If the person is resistant, distract him or her\nand try again later.\n● Have activities ready in case the person becomes agitated.\nFor example, play soothing music or sing together.\n● Always protect the person's dignity, privacy and comfort.\nConsider covering the person with a bath towel while\nundressing to decrease feelings of vulnerability.\n● Try having a familiar person of the same sex help with\nbathing if that is more comfortable for the person living with\ndementia.\n● Try different approaches to coax the person into the tub or\nshower. For instance, allow the person to get into the tub\nor shower with a towel on to reduce embarrassment or to\nhelp the person feel warmer.\nAdapt the bathing process\n● Try bathing at the same time of day the person is used to.\nIf the person is usually a morning bather, a bath in the\nevening may be confusing....\n\n...Question: What should I do when someone with dementia fights with me during showers or baths?\nAnswer: If someone with dementia resists or fights during shower or bath, there are a few strategies that can help. This is more common in the advanced stages of dementia, but it can happen earlier too. One approach is to make the journey to the bathroom or shower more enjoyable. You can try playing music, using music therapy, or walking together to the bathroom. Singing while going to the bathroom can also make it more engaging. Once you're in the shower, you can turn on the water and use the music as a distraction. It can be helpful to laugh and use humor to lighten the mood. Knowing the person's routine and finding a time of day when they are calmer can also make bathing and showering easier. By following these tips, you can make the experience more positive for both the person with dementia and the caregiver.\nQuestion: What do I do if someone with dementia won't get out of the shower?\n\nEncourage the person\nto do as much as possible, but be ready to assist when needed.\nIn the earlier stages, the person may only need a reminder to\nbathe. As dementia progresses, he or she will require more\nassistance. Prepare the bathroom in advance:\n● Gather bathing supplies. Have large towels (that you can\ncompletely wrap around the person for privacy and\nwarmth), shampoo, soap and a bath stool/bench ready\nbefore you tell the person that it's time to bathe.\n● Make the room comfortable. Pad the shower seat and\nother cold or uncomfortable surfaces with towels. Check\nthat the room temperature is pleasant.\n● Place soap, shampoo and other supplies within reach. Try\nusing hotel-sized plastic containers of shampoo, and have\na washcloth ready to cover the person's eyes to prevent\nstinging.\n● Monitor water temperature. The person may not sense\nwhen the water is dangerously hot or may resist bathing if\nthe water is too cool. Always check the water temperature,\neven if the person draws his or her own bath.\n\nQuestion: What do I do if someone with dementia refuses to take a bath or shower?...\n\n● Arrange to have another individual, with whom the\nperson with dementia is comfortable, help with bathing.\n● Talk to other caregivers who have faced the same\nchallenge.\n● Consider leaving in a hearing aid or leaving on glasses.\nYou will need to be careful not to get water in a hearing\naid, and will have to remove it if you are washing her hair.\nKeep her busy with washing and then take out the\nhearing aid when it is time.\nAlternatives to bathing\n● Try bath and shower to see what she prefers. A\nhand-held shower may be less frightening than the\nregular showerhead.\n● Try a sponge bath at the sink. This might work if he has\nmobility problems. With a sponge bath, try uncovering\nonly the part of the body being washed, for greater\nprivacy.\n● Try washing one part of the body each day of the week.\n● If regular bathing is difficult, fill in between baths with the\nnecessities, i.e., washing hands before eating or handling\nfood, and after using the toilet; washing bottom and\ngenitals daily to prevent infection; and washing face to\nprevent skin problems....\n\nBathing can be a challenge because people living with\nAlzheimer's may be uncomfortable receiving assistance with\nsuch an intimate activity. They may also have depth perception\nproblems that make it scary to step into water. They may not\nperceive a need to bathe or may find it a cold, uncomfortable\nexperience. If people regard bathing as scary, embarrassing,\nunpleasant or uncomfortable, they may communicate their\ndiscomfort by verbally and/or physically resisting attempts to\nbathe. In some cases, this can escalate and become be unsafe\nand upsetting for all who are involved.  \nThere are ways to make bathing easier and more comfortable\n— however, each situation is unique, and finding what works is\noften the result of trial and error. For more bathing ideas, join\nALZConnected, our online support community where caregivers\nlike you share tips on bathing a person living with dementia.\n● Prepare the bathroom in advance\n● Help the person feel in control\n● Adapt the bathing process\n● Consider bathing alternatives\n● After-bath care\nPrepare the bathroom in advance", "final_context": "...This can make the experience less distressing for the person with dementia. It's recommended to administer the medication about 30 minutes before bath time. Using visual and auditory cues can also be helpful, like turning on the shower, creating steam, or feeling the moisture in the air. These cues can signal to the person that it's time to bathe and potentially reduce resistance. Sometimes, accepting that bathing is a challenging issue and seeking help from others may be the best solution. This could involve finding a caregiver, whether through natural connections or someone who is paid to assist. It's important to recognize that this may not be an option for everyone, but if possible, getting help can make the process easier and more pleasant for both the person with dementia and the caregiver....\n\n...Answer: If your loved one is resistant to taking a bath, there are some things you can consider. Firstly, think about whether a bath is absolutely necessary or if a different form of hygiene care could be used, such as a shower or sponge bath. Modifying the personal hygiene routine to make it less disruptive or time-consuming may be helpful. Some people have found alternative solutions for showering, like using a kitty pool and shower chair in the kitchen. They set up tarps and use a handheld shower attachment connected to the faucet. This avoids the bathroom, which might be overwhelming or unsafe for the person with dementia. Others have given up on showers and baths altogether and focus on sponge baths instead. It's important to recognize that the resistance might not be solely related to logistics but also to a strong desire to avoid bathing. This resistance can persist for a long time. If the resistance becomes intense, violent, or dangerous, it might be necessary to explore medication options that can help reduce anxiety before bath time. This can make the experience less distressing for the person with dementia. It's recommended to administer the medication about 30 minutes before bath time. Using visual and auditory cues can also be helpful, like turning on the shower, creating steam, or feeling the moisture in the air....\n\n● Be sure the person has a role in the bathing process. For\nexample, have the person hold a washcloth, sponge or\nshampoo bottle.\n● Be aware that the person may perceive bathing to be\nthreatening. If the person is resistant, distract him or her\nand try again later.\n● Have activities ready in case the person becomes agitated.\nFor example, play soothing music or sing together.\n● Always protect the person's dignity, privacy and comfort.\nConsider covering the person with a bath towel while\nundressing to decrease feelings of vulnerability.\n● Try having a familiar person of the same sex help with\nbathing if that is more comfortable for the person living with\ndementia.\n● Try different approaches to coax the person into the tub or\nshower. For instance, allow the person to get into the tub\nor shower with a towel on to reduce embarrassment or to\nhelp the person feel warmer.\nAdapt the bathing process\n● Try bathing at the same time of day the person is used to.\nIf the person is usually a morning bather, a bath in the\nevening may be confusing....\n\n...Question: What should I do when someone with dementia fights with me during showers or baths?\nAnswer: If someone with dementia resists or fights during shower or bath, there are a few strategies that can help. This is more common in the advanced stages of dementia, but it can happen earlier too. One approach is to make the journey to the bathroom or shower more enjoyable. You can try playing music, using music therapy, or walking together to the bathroom. Singing while going to the bathroom can also make it more engaging. Once you're in the shower, you can turn on the water and use the music as a distraction. It can be helpful to laugh and use humor to lighten the mood. Knowing the person's routine and finding a time of day when they are calmer can also make bathing and showering easier. By following these tips, you can make the experience more positive for both the person with dementia and the caregiver.\nQuestion: What do I do if someone with dementia won't get out of the shower?\n\nEncourage the person\nto do as much as possible, but be ready to assist when needed.\nIn the earlier stages, the person may only need a reminder to\nbathe. As dementia progresses, he or she will require more\nassistance. Prepare the bathroom in advance:\n● Gather bathing supplies. Have large towels (that you can\ncompletely wrap around the person for privacy and\nwarmth), shampoo, soap and a bath stool/bench ready\nbefore you tell the person that it's time to bathe.\n● Make the room comfortable. Pad the shower seat and\nother cold or uncomfortable surfaces with towels. Check\nthat the room temperature is pleasant.\n● Place soap, shampoo and other supplies within reach. Try\nusing hotel-sized plastic containers of shampoo, and have\na washcloth ready to cover the person's eyes to prevent\nstinging.\n● Monitor water temperature. The person may not sense\nwhen the water is dangerously hot or may resist bathing if\nthe water is too cool. Always check the water temperature,\neven if the person draws his or her own bath.\n\nQuestion: What do I do if someone with dementia refuses to take a bath or shower?...\n\n● Arrange to have another individual, with whom the\nperson with dementia is comfortable, help with bathing.\n● Talk to other caregivers who have faced the same\nchallenge.\n● Consider leaving in a hearing aid or leaving on glasses.\nYou will need to be careful not to get water in a hearing\naid, and will have to remove it if you are washing her hair.\nKeep her busy with washing and then take out the\nhearing aid when it is time.\nAlternatives to bathing\n● Try bath and shower to see what she prefers. A\nhand-held shower may be less frightening than the\nregular showerhead.\n● Try a sponge bath at the sink. This might work if he has\nmobility problems. With a sponge bath, try uncovering\nonly the part of the body being washed, for greater\nprivacy.\n● Try washing one part of the body each day of the week.\n● If regular bathing is difficult, fill in between baths with the\nnecessities, i.e., washing hands before eating or handling\nfood, and after using the toilet; washing bottom and\ngenitals daily to prevent infection; and washing face to\nprevent skin problems....\n\nBathing can be a challenge because people living with\nAlzheimer's may be uncomfortable receiving assistance with\nsuch an intimate activity. They may also have depth perception\nproblems that make it scary to step into water. They may not\nperceive a need to bathe or may find it a cold, uncomfortable\nexperience. If people regard bathing as scary, embarrassing,\nunpleasant or uncomfortable, they may communicate their\ndiscomfort by verbally and/or physically resisting attempts to\nbathe. In some cases, this can escalate and become be unsafe\nand upsetting for all who are involved.  \nThere are ways to make bathing easier and more comfortable\n— however, each situation is unique, and finding what works is\noften the result of trial and error. For more bathing ideas, join\nALZConnected, our online support community where caregivers\nlike you share tips on bathing a person living with dementia.\n● Prepare the bathroom in advance\n● Help the person feel in control\n● Adapt the bathing process\n● Consider bathing alternatives\n● After-bath care\nPrepare the bathroom in advance"}

things may interfere with both interest in\neating, and the ability to eat. Sequencing the steps involved in eating might be hard, or\ninterest in food may have diminished. Encourage and support your loved one to\nparticipate as fully and enjoyably as possible in mealtimes. Keeping to a routine, eating\nat the same time every day, and in the same place, is reassuring and provides a\nstructured, safe and predictable environment. If the individual lives alone, make sure\nthere are reminders to eat. You can check out The Apartment: A Guide to Creating a\nDementia-Friendly Home, for suggestions on devices that provide these reminders.\n2. Make it appealing\nMake the food preparation a social event. Invite your person into the kitchen while you\nare cooking. The aromas are a powerful appetite stimulator and socializing is interactive\nand comforting. If possible, create a small task for the individual- setting the table,\ncutting up vegetables, folding napkins- all reinforce a sense of autonomy and belonging.\nTry to create nutritious menus that incorporate all the food groups to ensure health and...\n\nFeeding\nEating can be hard for people with dementia. They may forget to eat, not recognize food, have difficulty utilizing utensils or breaking food into bite-sized portions or get distracted. Some have trouble chewing or swallowing, which can be dangerous. They might lose their appetite or want only sweet foods. Pain from teeth or dentures and side effects from medicine can also make eating harder. These problems can lead to weight loss and not getting enough water or nutrients.\nThings to try:\nCreate a routine and stick to it. Offer meals at regular times and allow enough time to eat.\nKeep it simple by trying one food, one bowl, and one utensil at a time. Don't use plastic utensils. Serve finger foods. Remove distractions from the table. Serve foods your loved one likes.\nAvoid messes by using a plastic tablecloth or placemat. Put a smock over your loved one's clothing. Use bowls (rather than plates) and spill-proof cups.\nAllow your loved one to feed themselves as able. Give one instruction at a time (open your mouth, chew your food, have another bite, drink the water). Help more when the time comes....\n\n...a series of complex skills, such as\ncutting up food, moving a utensil or\nhand towards the mouth, chewing\nand swallowing. This requires a\nlevel of concentration someone\nwith dementia may not be able to\nmaintain.\nHaving distractions around may\nalso cause the person to lose their\nconcentration.\n• Limit distractions: Serve meals in a quiet place so that the\nperson can focus on eating. Turn off the television, radio,\ntelephone ringer and mobile notifications.\n• Simplify the setting. Remove flowers, centrepieces and\ncondiments. Use only the utensils needed for the meal.\n• Serve the meal one course at a time. This prevents the person\nfrom getting overwhelmed.\n• Try to keep the environment as calm and relaxing as\npossible.\n• Try to be flexible. If the person does not want to be with\nother people while eating, don't force them to eat with\nothers.\n• If they want to stay in a different room where they are\ncomfortable, allow this. It may be difficult for them to\nchange routines. Use a tray as needed to help with clean up....\n\n...bowls with a contrasting color place mat. Always test the\ntemperature of foods and beverages before serving.\n● Offer one food item at a time. The person may be unable to decide\namong the foods on his or her plate. Serve only one or two items at a\ntime. For example, serve mashed potatoes followed by the main entree.\n● Be flexible with food preferences. It is possible the person may suddenly\ndevelop certain food preferences or reject foods he or she may have\nliked in the past.\n● Allow plenty of time to eat. Keep in mind that it can take an hour or more\nfor\nthe person to finish.\n● Eat together. Give the person the opportunity to eat with others.\nKeeping mealtimes social can encourage the person to eat.\n\nDuring the middle stages of Alzheimer's, distractions, too many choices, and\nchanges in perception, taste and smell can make eating more difficult. The\nfollowing tips can help:\n● Limit distractions. Serve meals in quiet surroundings, away from the\ntelevision and other distractions.\n● Keep the table setting simple. Avoid patterned plates, tablecloths and\nplacemats that might confuse the person. Using color to contrast plates\nagainst\na tablecloth or placemat can make it easier for the person to distinguish\nthe\nfood from the plate or table. Consider using a plastic tablecloth, napkins\nor\naprons to make cleanup easier. Provide only the utensils needed for the\nmeal to avoid confusion.\n● Distinguish food from the plate. Changes in visual and spatial abilities\nmay make it tough for someone with dementia to distinguish food from\nthe plate or the plate from the table. It can help to use white plates or\nbowls with a contrasting color place mat. Avoid patterned dishes,\ntablecloths and place mats.\n● Check the food temperature. For each abnormal behavior, the authors derived a\nproduct of frequency times severity in keeping with the\nmethod applied in the NPI.10\nManagement. As with many areas of intimate care, such as\nbathing and attending to toilet needs, there is relatively little\nresearch on individualized interventions about eating in persons with dementia, particularly when it is carried out at\nhome.105 Some of the conventional intervention methods\ninclude caregiver assistance and the use of finger foods, texture\nmodification, and supplementation. Both food and fluid intake\ncould follow a schedule, which ensures that eating and drinking\nare not forgotten.\nMaintaining eating independence in patients with dementia\ncan be facilitated by identifying factors that interfere with\nbeginning a meal by providing multidisciplinary care, eliminating environmental factors, and providing assistance that promotes beginning a meal.43 Within these broad environmental\nchanges are suggestions that meals may need to be familiar,\nattractive, and enticing.105 Interventions in the form of physical\nassistance emphasize the movement inherent in helping people...\n\n...Question: What are some important communication strategies for when it's time for someone with dementia to eat?\nAnswer: When it comes to mealtime for someone living with dementia, there are important communication strategies that can help. It's crucial to understand both the person's preferences and the brain changes that are contributing to their behavior. People with dementia may have difficulty recognizing objects (agnosia) or carrying out movements (apraxia), making it challenging for them to acknowledge and eat their meals. Other factors like confusion, visual clutter, noise, or even dental pain may also impact their ability to eat. To create a conducive environment, it's helpful to minimize distractions by reducing clutter and noise. Orienting the person to the situation and helping them initiate the eating process can be beneficial. Additionally, it's crucial to respect and understand their preferences, as past experiences or trauma related to food scarcity may influence their behavior. affect gait and walking?\nAnswer: Alzheimer's disease can affect a person's ability to walk. People with dementia may walk more slowly, shuffle their feet, or have difficulty picking up their feet when walking. Their walking may also become erratic, with quick and slow steps mixed together. Additionally, their stride length may change, and they may be unsure of where they are walking to. It is important to inform your healthcare provider if you notice any changes in their walking. Physical therapy or occupational therapy can help address these issues and prevent falls. It is also important to make adjustments to the environment to ensure safety, such as removing area rugs or toys that could cause tripping. It's worth considering that walking changes may not be solely caused by dementia, but other physical symptoms as well. Discussing with healthcare providers about suitable shoes can also be helpful. The goal is to keep the person as active as possible while ensuring their safety. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42111639)\nHospital discharge is a pivotal stage in the continuum of care, marking the transition from the acute clinical episode to subsequent therapeutic management. Rather than being a purely administrative procedure, discharge is a multifaceted process that requires structured planning, clear communication, and the coordinated participation of all healthcare stakeholders, with the patient playing a central role. Inadequate discharge processes may adversely affect clinical outcomes and increase hospital readmission rates, resulting in sub-optimal utilization of healthcare resources. This issue is particularly relevant in the context of an ageing and increasingly frail population, characterized by a high burden of comorbidities and complex clinical needs. In this setting, discharge planning should\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Exploring patient-centered care delivery in outpatient settings for older adults: a scoping review and recommendations for implementation in countries with low and middle income. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41272495)\nBackground Patient-centered care (PCC) has emerged as a crucial approach in healthcare delivery for older adults, given the aging population and the unique challenges they face. Long-term management and patient involvement are particularly relevant in outpatient settings. This scoping review aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of existing evidence on PCC for older adults in outpatient settings by mapping definitions, core elements, stakeholder perspectives, barriers to implementation, and practical models of PCC adaptation, as well as their outcomes. Additionally, it offers actionable recommendations for integrating PCC into healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar o\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Psychotropic medications versus non-pharmacologic approaches for managing behavioural and psychological symptoms in Australian aged care residents with dementia: general practitioners' and physicians' perspectives. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41179336)\nBackground Psychotropic medications are often inappropriately prescribed for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), posing significant risks such as falls, stroke and death. Although non-pharmacological interventions (NPIs) are the first-line treatment for BPSD, their use in practice remains limited. Objectives This study explored general practitioners' (GPs') and physicians' perspectives on using psychotropic medications compared to NPIs for managing BPSD in Australian residential aged care homes (RACHs). Design Semi-structured online in-depth interviews were conducted with GPs and physicians managing BPSD in Australian RACHs. Methods The interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed and analysed using inductive thematic analysis, with transcripts coded using NVivo 14 to"}

For someone with dementia, it can be easy to forget things like putting toothpaste on the toothbrush and actually brushing their teeth. One helpful strategy is to have a list of the steps involved in brushing their teeth. For example, you can post a picture of a toothbrush next to toothpaste and say that the first step is to pick out a toothbrush and toothpaste. Then, the second step is to apply the toothpaste to the toothbrush. If the person is a visual learner, you can include pictures instead of just written instructions. The third step could be taking the toothbrush with the toothpaste and wetting it under the sink. This sets them up for the actual act of brushing their teeth, which is where the type of toothbrush becomes important. Some toothbrushes vibrate and will automatically stop after two minutes to indicate that the brushing is done. This feature can help with sequencing and alerting the person when they have finished brushing their teeth. After brushing, the next step would be to clean off the toothbrush....\n\n...Answer: If you're finding it difficult to provide mouth care, toothbrushing, or flossing for someone living with dementia, there are several factors you can consider. It might not be about the person themselves, but rather about how you're introducing the activity, how you're asking them to do it, the timing, the tools you're using, the situation you're in, or even their sensory experience. Instead of assuming the problem lies with the person, let's try to modify different aspects and see if we get a better outcome. For example, if mouth activities become overwhelming, you may notice changes in their appetite and food preferences. In this case, you can try using a washcloth on your finger to clean their teeth instead of a toothbrush, or even consider using diluted mouthwash or alternative devices that don't require finger use for flossing. If you're feeling overwhelmed, it's okay to ask for help. Seek out someone with knowledge and experience in providing mouth care for individuals with dementia, such as a dental hygienist or an occupational therapist. Avoid using force, as it's generally unhelpful and may make the person resistant to any form of mouth care....\n\n...Answer: Taking care of someone with dementia can be challenging, especially when it comes to getting them to brush their teeth. It's important to address this issue because bad breath and bacteria buildup can affect their overall health. There may be several reasons why they refuse to brush their teeth, such as difficulty sequencing through the task or sensory discomfort. To overcome this, it's helpful to understand what's getting in the way of mouth care. If sequencing is the problem, you can try scheduling a reminder and have the toothbrush ready to use. Using visual cues, like showing them the toothbrush, can also prompt them to brush their teeth. However, it's crucial not to leave the toothbrush out all the time since they may skip it thinking they've already done it. If they need help starting, you can provide hand-under-hand assistance to guide them through the process. If they reach their limit, take a break and come back to it later. In more severe cases, where they are unable to perform mouth care on their own, you may need to assist them or substitute for what they are unable to do. Remember, maintaining good oral hygiene is essential for their overall wellbeing, and it's crucial to adapt your approach to their needs and abilities....\n\n...Answer: Brushing the teeth of someone living with dementia can be a distressing experience for both the caregiver and the person with dementia. It's important to understand what might be causing difficulties during this task. Variables such as the environment, props used, or the approach taken can all play a role in how the person with dementia responds. One approach is to involve the person with dementia in the task. By allowing them to participate, they may be more likely to engage in the actual act of brushing. For example, you can have the person hold a toothbrush while you guide their hand through the motions. It's also important to be observant and evaluate the person's response. Are they refusing to participate or simply not understanding what you're asking? Non-verbal cues, like handshakes or hand-under-hand gestures, can help trigger muscle memory and assist the person in getting started with the action. Remember, every situation is unique and what works for one person may not work for another. If you're having difficulties, it may be helpful to reach out to a healthcare professional or support group for guidance and assistance. They can help you identify any potential barriers and find solutions to make teeth brushing a more manageable task....\n\n...Some toothbrushes vibrate and will automatically stop after two minutes to indicate that the brushing is done. This feature can help with sequencing and alerting the person when they have finished brushing their teeth. After brushing, the next step would be to clean off the toothbrush. By following this step-by-step approach and using toothbrushes with helpful features, we can support individuals with dementia in maintaining good oral health....\n\n...Question: Can mouthwash be a replacement for brushing the teeth of someone with dementia?\nAnswer: Mouthwash is not a suitable replacement for brushing teeth for individuals with dementia. Mouthwash can dry the mouth and lacks the ability to clean properly like a toothbrush does. It doesn't massage the gums, clean along the gum line, or thoroughly clean between teeth. As dementia progresses, we may need to dilute the strength of the mouthwash. If a person has no teeth, it's crucial to consider if mouthwash is necessary. Bad breath, often due to a dry mouth or poor hygiene, could be the root issue. It's essential to prioritize assisting with brushing teeth over relying solely on mouthwash. If a person is averse to mouth care, an occupational or speech therapist can offer tailored support to ensure proper oral hygiene. It's crucial to ensure that the mouthwash is being used effectively and not just for comfort.\nQuestion: What can we do about teeth grinding?...\n\nShe couldn't withstand surgery to have them removed, and, even if operating was an option, her advanced dementia would have\nprevented her from understanding how and why to use dentures. So, we did what we could. Moving forward, her routine dental care\nconsisted of minimizing tooth pain and keeping her mouth as clean and as comfortable as possible.\nMany people without dementia experience anxiety about going to the dentist, if not outright dread. According to the Alzheimer's\nAssociation ( caregivers should prioritize dentist appointments\nand preventative dental care throughout the early stages of the disease to prevent more serious problems from arising. Establishing a\ndaily oral hygiene routine early on may help your loved one retain their habits longer, even as they require more help over time.\nRead: Oral Care Tips for Dementia Caregivers (/articles/oral-health-tips-for-dementia-caregivers-203144.htm)\nAs a loved one's dementia progresses, regular check-ups may no longer be feasible. It becomes even more important for caregivers to\nassist with daily oral care and keep an eye out for changes in eating habits, oral sores, and signs that their loved ones are experiencing...\n\nHygiene\nDay-to-day tasks like washing, brushing our teeth and going to the\ntoilet help keep us healthy and comfortable. But if someone you care\nabout lives with dementia, they might find it hard to maintain their\npersonal hygiene.\nHere are some ways to help. These are intimate and sometimes\nembarrassing tasks, though, so they might need time to adjust. Stay\ncalm and patient, and offer reassurance as you go.\nSupporting personal\ncare\nWe all have our own preferences and habits when it comes to our\npersonal care. For example, you might like to have a shower before\nyou go to bed each night, but dislike baths. Ask your loved one about\ntheir routine and try to continue it, even if their habits are different to\nyours.\nEncourage the person to do as much as they can themselves. These\ncan be complex activities with multiple steps, so you might need to\nsupport them through the process.
