(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/39776243)\nMaintaining good oral hygiene is essential for preventing and managing oral health problems. This systematic review aimed to identify and assess clinical practice guidelines on oral hygiene, focusing on quality and key areas. A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Cochrane, and organizational websites. Guidelines from health organizations that focused on oral health, hygiene education, and disease prevention were included. Guidelines based on expert opinions and those focusing on specific pathologies were excluded. The AGREE II tool was used to evaluate quality, and a narrative synthesis summarized recommendations across pediatric, adult, and senior age groups. Nine studies were reviewed. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41095775)\nThe link between oral health and Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained increasing attention in recent years. Emerging evidence suggests that this association is bidirectional, involving both biological mechanisms and behavioral consequences that reinforce one another over time.  Literature Review : A narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and scoping reviews published between January 2010 and March 2024 was conducted. Searching was performed in four electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, the Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library), using a combination of MeSH terms and free-text keywords related to dementia and oral health. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40322846)\nBackground The oral health status of older people living in residential aged care facilities (RACFs) is found to be very poor. Many oral health promotion interventions have been tested in RACF settings around the world with varying degrees of success. Aim The aim of this systematic review is to analyse the health promotion strategies used in oral health promotion interventions in RACF settings and map the behaviour change techniques (BCTs) used in interventions to the Behaviour Change Techniques Taxonomy Version 1 (BCTTV1). "tf_final_answer_source": "", "tf_answer_llm_locked": false}, "final_answer": "E", "base_context_chars": 8386, "final_context_chars": 8386, "base_context": "...Question: What is modified clothing for people with dementia?\nAnswer: Modified clothing for people with dementia refers to clothing that is designed to be easy to put on and take off, while also preventing the person from undressing at inappropriate times. While not everyone with dementia experiences this issue, some individuals may disrobe in public. To address this concern, there are clothing companies that offer modified clothing with velcro closures in the back, as well as pants or shorts with easy fasteners. These modifications aim to make dressing and undressing easier for both the caregiver and the person with dementia. Additionally, slip-on shoes can be a convenient option for individuals with dementia. If regular clothing is becoming challenging to manage, it may be worth considering modified clothing as an alternative solution.\nQuestion: What kind of clothing should I buy for someone with dementia?\n\n...the evenings, and front fastening bras can be easier to put on.\nWhile comfortable, slippers shouldn't be worn for more than a\nfew hours, as they may not support the person's feet enough.\nSlippers also encourage shuffling, which doesn't allow the leg\nmuscles and joints to work correctly.\nWhen helping a person with dementia choose comfortable\nclothing, you should:\nmake sure that items are not inside out, and that buttons, zips\nand fasteners are done up\ntry well-fitting slip-on shoes, or shoes with Velcro fastenings,\nor replace regular shoelaces with elastic ones. Shoes with\nlaces may be difficult for someone with dementia to manage\ntry buckle-free belts, which fasten with Velcro, and clip-on\nties, which are safer and easier to use\ntry several thin layers of clothing, particularly in cold weather,\nrather than one thick layer. The person can then remove a\nlayer if it gets too warm\navoid self-supporting stockings, as they can cause\ncirculation problems\ntry specially designed trousers, with a drop-down front, to\nmake using the toilet easier for men....\n\n...Question: What companies make modified clothing for people with dementia?\nAnswer: If you're looking for modified clothing for people with dementia, you can find a variety of options on Amazon. One company that specializes in modified clothing is Silverts. You can visit their website, silverts.com, and search for \"modified clothing.\" They offer options for both men and women, with features like back closures to prevent undressing in public, easy-to-put-on shoes, and stretchy socks designed for diabetics, which make it easier to put them on. Sometimes, individuals may prefer clothing that doesn't look like a traditional bib. In that case, you can find modified clothing that resembles shirts or blouses, offering a more appealing and discreet option. So, depending on the specific needs and preferences, modified clothing can help with preventing challenging situations and making dressing easier in the morning.\nQuestion: What is modified clothing for people with dementia?...\n\n● Choose clothing that is easy to wear and care for.\nZippers and Velcro™ are easier to fasten than buttons.\nSkirts and pants with elastic bands are easier to put on.\n● Soft, stretchy materials are often the most comfortable,\nand shouldn't be too tight.\n● For women, a front-closing bra may be easier to put on\nherself; for men, boxer shorts may be easier to manage\nthan fitted underwear.\n● Slippers are comfortable, though they may not offer\nenough support to be worn all the time.\nShopping for clothes\n● If possible, involve the person with dementia in shopping\nfor clothes. If you do the shopping, check his size\nregularly, as he may have lost or gained weight.\n● Choose clothing that is comfortable, easy to put on and\neasy to wash.\n● Remember that she may need to wear new clothes often\nbefore they become familiar to her, and she may think\nany new clothing doesn't belong to her.\n● Buy several of the same, favourite outfits, so she\nbelieves she is wearing the same familiar clothes.\n\nAccommodating Clothing\nConsider orthoses, wheelchairs, and other equipment. For example, if they wear ankle-foot orthoses,\nyou may need to buy pants with a stretchy hem so that the orthoses will fit under them.\nIf your care recipient has injuries or paralysis, contact an occupational therapist or another\nhealthcare provider for tips on clothing types.\nSituation Specific\nThe way a person with dementia looks will help them understand what they're doing. For example, if\nthey're dressed for work, they may think they need to go to work. If they're dressed in the clothes they\nusually relax in, this will remind them that they're not at work.\nAdditional Tips\nConsider the environment. Make sure the room is warm enough to get dressed in.\nUse layers. If they wear several thin layers of clothing, it makes it easier for them to remove one if they\nget warm throughout the day.\nEnsure your care recipient changes clothing regularly.\nRemove the dirty clothes and put clean clothes in their place when they're showering.\nEncourage them to change because someone is coming to visit or they're going out....\n\n...plan.\nDressing and undressing\nHere are some tips for a safe and pleasant dressing and undressing experience for a resident living with\ndementia:\n•\nDressing includes considering a person's style, sensory and mobility needs (hearing aids, glasses,\nmake-up, jewellery etc). Ensure you ask the resident about their style and needs.\n•\nThink of the steps you take to dress yourself daily and remember they are likely the same steps\nthis resident might take.\n•\nAsk what activities they plan to do that day. Is there an activity going on that day that would\nrequire a change of time for getting dressed (i.e. bath day)/undressed (later evening program)\nor an event that would requires a more formal attire?\n•\nOffer the resident the opportunity to go to the washroom and/or brush their teeth before\ngetting dressed/undressed.\n•\nProvide choice, and limit options to make it easier for the resident (maybe provide two options).\n•\nCheck the label on the clothing to ensure it belongs to the resident.\n\nDEMENTIA CAREGIVING\nDressing\nThe individual may have difficulty with buttons, snaps or zippers; he/she may not\nremember the order of putting on clothes, or recognize seasonal changes; and\nsometimes he/she may not want to change clothes at all.\nHelping the person you're providing care to dress appropriately helps him or her\nmaintain dignity and self-esteem.\n• For as long as possible, allow the individual to dress him/herself.\n• Reduce the number of choices. Empty the closet of unnecessary or\nimpractical clothing.\n• When self-selection become difficult, offer a choice between 2 outfits.\n• Allow enough time to dress.\n• Sneakers or crepe-soled shoes can help prevent falls.\n• Velcro closings and elastic waistband are easier to manage than buttons and\nzippers. Cardigans and front-buttoning shirts are easier than pullovers.\n• It may become necessary, to assist in dressing by handing the articles of\nclothing, one at a time.\nBathing and Grooming\nBathing can be frightening, or become a time of confrontation. Refusal to bathe is\nnot unusual....\n\n...Answer: When helping someone with dementia who doesn't want assistance with dressing, it's important to remember their need for autonomy and control. All individuals have a natural desire to make their own decisions and not have others making choices for them. This need for control can be especially prominent when it comes to dressing. To help address this situation, it is suggested to give the person as much control and autonomy as possible. This can be done by allowing them to choose their own outfit. For example, you can present them with two shirts from their closet and let them decide which one to wear. By giving them a sense of choice, they may be more likely to be compliant during the dressing process. Another technique that can be effective is the hand-over-hand technique, which involves two people working together to dress the individual. This approach allows the person with dementia to feel like they have more control over the situation. It also helps the caregiver or the person assisting in dressing to handle the task more smoothly. By implementing these strategies of providing choice and using the hand-over-hand technique, caregivers can help individuals with dementia feel more empowered and comfortable during the dressing process....", "final_context": "...Question: What is modified clothing for people with dementia?\nAnswer: Modified clothing for people with dementia refers to clothing that is designed to be easy to put on and take off, while also preventing the person from undressing at inappropriate times. While not everyone with dementia experiences this issue, some individuals may disrobe in public. To address this concern, there are clothing companies that offer modified clothing with velcro closures in the back, as well as pants or shorts with easy fasteners. These modifications aim to make dressing and undressing easier for both the caregiver and the person with dementia. Additionally, slip-on shoes can be a convenient option for individuals with dementia. If regular clothing is becoming challenging to manage, it may be worth considering modified clothing as an alternative solution.\nQuestion: What kind of clothing should I buy for someone with dementia?\n\n...the evenings, and front fastening bras can be easier to put on.\nWhile comfortable, slippers shouldn't be worn for more than a\nfew hours, as they may not support the person's feet enough.\nSlippers also encourage shuffling, which doesn't allow the leg\nmuscles and joints to work correctly.\nWhen helping a person with dementia choose comfortable\nclothing, you should:\nmake sure that items are not inside out, and that buttons, zips\nand fasteners are done up\ntry well-fitting slip-on shoes, or shoes with Velcro fastenings,\nor replace regular shoelaces with elastic ones. Shoes with\nlaces may be difficult for someone with dementia to manage\ntry buckle-free belts, which fasten with Velcro, and clip-on\nties, which are safer and easier to use\ntry several thin layers of clothing, particularly in cold weather,\nrather than one thick layer. The person can then remove a\nlayer if it gets too warm\navoid self-supporting stockings, as they can cause\ncirculation problems\ntry specially designed trousers, with a drop-down front, to\nmake using the toilet easier for men....\n\n...Question: What companies make modified clothing for people with dementia?\nAnswer: If you're looking for modified clothing for people with dementia, you can find a variety of options on Amazon. One company that specializes in modified clothing is Silverts. You can visit their website, silverts.com, and search for \"modified clothing.\" They offer options for both men and women, with features like back closures to prevent undressing in public, easy-to-put-on shoes, and stretchy socks designed for diabetics, which make it easier to put them on. Sometimes, individuals may prefer clothing that doesn't look like a traditional bib. In that case, you can find modified clothing that resembles shirts or blouses, offering a more appealing and discreet option. So, depending on the specific needs and preferences, modified clothing can help with preventing challenging situations and making dressing easier in the morning.\nQuestion: What is modified clothing for people with dementia?...\n\n● Choose clothing that is easy to wear and care for.\nZippers and Velcro™ are easier to fasten than buttons.\nSkirts and pants with elastic bands are easier to put on.\n● Soft, stretchy materials are often the most comfortable,\nand shouldn't be too tight.\n● For women, a front-closing bra may be easier to put on\nherself; for men, boxer shorts may be easier to manage\nthan fitted underwear.\n● Slippers are comfortable, though they may not offer\nenough support to be worn all the time.\nShopping for clothes\n● If possible, involve the person with dementia in shopping\nfor clothes. If you do the shopping, check his size\nregularly, as he may have lost or gained weight.\n● Choose clothing that is comfortable, easy to put on and\neasy to wash.\n● Remember that she may need to wear new clothes often\nbefore they become familiar to her, and she may think\nany new clothing doesn't belong to her.\n● Buy several of the same, favourite outfits, so she\nbelieves she is wearing the same familiar clothes.\n\nAccommodating Clothing\nConsider orthoses, wheelchairs, and other equipment. For example, if they wear ankle-foot orthoses,\nyou may need to buy pants with a stretchy hem so that the orthoses will fit under them.\nIf your care recipient has injuries or paralysis, contact an occupational therapist or another\nhealthcare provider for tips on clothing types.\nSituation Specific\nThe way a person with dementia looks will help them understand what they're doing. For example, if\nthey're dressed for work, they may think they need to go to work. If they're dressed in the clothes they\nusually relax in, this will remind them that they're not at work.\nAdditional Tips\nConsider the environment. Make sure the room is warm enough to get dressed in.\nUse layers. If they wear several thin layers of clothing, it makes it easier for them to remove one if they\nget warm throughout the day.\nEnsure your care recipient changes clothing regularly.\nRemove the dirty clothes and put clean clothes in their place when they're showering.\nEncourage them to change because someone is coming to visit or they're going out....\n\n...plan.\nDressing and undressing\nHere are some tips for a safe and pleasant dressing and undressing experience for a resident living with\ndementia:\n•\nDressing includes considering a person's style, sensory and mobility needs (hearing aids, glasses,\nmake-up, jewellery etc). Ensure you ask the resident about their style and needs.\n•\nThink of the steps you take to dress yourself daily and remember they are likely the same steps\nthis resident might take.\n•\nAsk what activities they plan to do that day. Is there an activity going on that day that would\nrequire a change of time for getting dressed (i.e. bath day)/undressed (later evening program)\nor an event that would requires a more formal attire?\n•\nOffer the resident the opportunity to go to the washroom and/or brush their teeth before\ngetting dressed/undressed.\n•\nProvide choice, and limit options to make it easier for the resident (maybe provide two options).\n•\nCheck the label on the clothing to ensure it belongs to the resident.\n\nDEMENTIA CAREGIVING\nDressing\nThe individual may have difficulty with buttons, snaps or zippers; he/she may not\nremember the order of putting on clothes, or recognize seasonal changes; and\nsometimes he/she may not want to change clothes at all.\nHelping the person you're providing care to dress appropriately helps him or her\nmaintain dignity and self-esteem.\n• For as long as possible, allow the individual to dress him/herself.\n• Reduce the number of choices. Empty the closet of unnecessary or\nimpractical clothing.\n• When self-selection become difficult, offer a choice between 2 outfits.\n• Allow enough time to dress.\n• Sneakers or crepe-soled shoes can help prevent falls.\n• Velcro closings and elastic waistband are easier to manage than buttons and\nzippers. Cardigans and front-buttoning shirts are easier than pullovers.\n• It may become necessary, to assist in dressing by handing the articles of\nclothing, one at a time.\nBathing and Grooming\nBathing can be frightening, or become a time of confrontation. Refusal to bathe is\nnot unusual....\n\n...Answer: When helping someone with dementia who doesn't want assistance with dressing, it's important to remember their need for autonomy and control. All individuals have a natural desire to make their own decisions and not have others making choices for them. This need for control can be especially prominent when it comes to dressing. To help address this situation, it is suggested to give the person as much control and autonomy as possible. This can be done by allowing them to choose their own outfit. For example, you can present them with two shirts from their closet and let them decide which one to wear. By giving them a sense of choice, they may be more likely to be compliant during the dressing process. Another technique that can be effective is the hand-over-hand technique, which involves two people working together to dress the individual. This approach allows the person with dementia to feel like they have more control over the situation. It also helps the caregiver or the person assisting in dressing to handle the task more smoothly. By implementing these strategies of providing choice and using the hand-over-hand technique, caregivers can help individuals with dementia feel more empowered and comfortable during the dressing process...."}

(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41567778)\nIntroduction Social robots are increasingly explored as non-pharmacological support for older adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and dementia, yet their day-to-day integration remains limited. This study centers on designing an affective care model that empowers caregivers to deploy a commercial humanoid robot. Methods An exploratory qualitative study comprised four observation sessions and ten in-depth, open-ended interviews. A two-phase observational protocol was conducted in a day-care center: Phase 1 mapped everyday activities and baseline interaction patterns; Phase 2 documented two robot-assisted sessions. Detailed descriptions underwent iterative thematic analysis to extract themes and construct a care model grounded in caregivers' practices. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41742059)\nBACKGROUND: Suboptimal light exposure among older adults can exacerbate circadian disruption, sleep disturbances, mood disorders, cognitive decline, and frailty. In urbanised environments like Singapore, older adults are particularly vulnerable due to lifestyle and built environment constraints. The LightSPAN study evaluates a chronotherapeutic mobile health (mHealth) behaviour change intervention, delivered via the LightUP app, designed to optimise light exposure patterns and support healthy ageing. METHODS: The trial is a community-based, double-blind, parallel-group randomised controlled trial involving approximately 90 community-dwelling older adults (≥ 60 years) recruited through Active Ageing Centres in Singapore. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41437243)\nBACKGROUND: Escalation or crisis and the related referral and admission of people with dementia from nursing homes to geriatric psychiatry often results from a complex interplay of disease-related, structural and interprofessional factors. In particular, few contextual links have been identified at the interface between nursing homes and geriatric psychiatry. METHODS: The study followed an exploratory qualitative design. Between May and July 2024, 17 semi-structured interviews were conducted with six nursing home directors/nursing service managers, six nurses, and five general practitioners/specialists. The caregiver stress prevention bundle includes the following components:\n- **Weekly respite care:** at least **8 consecutive hours per week** of respite care, during which the caregiver is not providing care for their loved one living with dementia and is instead focusing on their own emotional health. As part of caregiver self-care, the caregiver should spend at least 8 consecutive hours away from caregiving per week.\n- **Monthly support group:** attending a **monthly support group**, with or without their loved one living with dementia.\n- **Problem-solving skills development:** developing **problem-solving skills** to help the caregiver cope with **their own emotional and physical stress**, and to manage the **cognitive, functional, behavioral, and psychological disabilities** of their loved one living with dementia. Problem-solving skills development is a component of the caregiver stress prevention bundle.\n<!-- KB-COMPLETION (2026-06-22): the items below are ADRD-caregiving curriculum teaching points\nthat the benchmark draws on but that are absent from the original local KB (verified: with...\n\nQuestion: How can I continue to care for myself while caring for someone living with dementia?\nAnswer: When caring for someone with dementia, it's crucial to also take care of yourself. Your own well-being is directly linked to your ability to provide effective care. Taking care of yourself means getting enough rest, eating nourishing meals, and maintaining your overall health. It's important to schedule regular check-ups with your primary care physician and take any prescribed medications. Joining a caregiver support group can provide valuable support and give you permission to take breaks and prioritize your own needs. It may also be helpful to have your own mental health provider to guide you through the different stages of caregiving and offer a safe outlet for difficult emotions. Couples counseling or counseling with your loved one who has dementia can also be beneficial for a period of time. Remember, every step you take to protect your own health and well-being will contribute to a higher quality of life for both you and the person you are caring for.\nQuestion: Are there any safety concerns I should be aware of after a diagnosis of dementia?...\n\n...and locked gun closets, guard against accidents that drive people into nursing homes.\nIn one study, Johns Hopkins researchers found that more than 90% of patient needs in\nthose with dementia were home safety-related.\nPractice Self-Care\nSome caretakers find that caring for a loved one with dementia is like a full-time job. This might include talking with family members to see if\nthey can provide supervision or assistance once a week or might be able to care for\n\n...Answer: As a caregiver for someone living with dementia, it's important to navigate your work responsibilities while also ensuring your loved one receives the care they need. While employers vary in their understanding and support, there are steps you can take to avoid being fired. One approach is deciding how open you want to be about your caregiving responsibilities. You can choose to share some or all of the details with your employer, depending on your comfort level. It's also crucial to familiarize yourself with the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA). This federal benefit provides job protection for family caregivers, including those taking care of individuals with dementia. Additionally, some employers might have their own policies and benefits in place to support caregiving and leave. When utilizing FMLA or other leave options, you can coordinate your time off with your caregiving responsibilities. This might involve taking a few days off instead of a full 12-week leave or adjusting your work schedule to align with respite care services like adult day programs or home caregivers. Employers are often more supportive when they understand that you can maintain consistent work quality, even if you need to rearrange your working hours or location. By being transparent and finding ways to balance your caregiving responsibilities with your job, you increase your chances of remaining employed while caring for your loved one with dementia....\n\n...Answer: Caring for someone with dementia can be incredibly challenging and stressful. It's important for caregivers to recognize the toll that this role can take on their mental and emotional well-being. Often, caregivers find themselves overwhelmed by the behavioral symptoms of dementia and may feel like they are constantly on duty, 24/7, with no respite. One way to cope with these behavioral symptoms is to consider how much time is being devoted to caregiving. If you are the sole caregiver and are with the person with dementia all the time, it's crucial to understand that you are asking your brain to do the impossible with inadequate support. It's okay to acknowledge that you need a break and cannot do it all alone. Limiting the amount of time spent caregiving can have a positive impact on both you and the person with dementia. By acknowledging that you need help, you can become more of a partner in their care instead of solely shouldering the responsibility. Seeking out support from others who are experienced in dementia care can provide the hands-on assistance that is needed. Lastly, it's important to remember to see the person behind the dementia. When the behaviors and symptoms become overwhelming, it can be easy to forget the things you still like about the person you are caring for....\n\nQuestion: What are good self care ideas for people with dementia?\nAnswer: For people with dementia, it's important to prioritize self-care in order to support brain health. One key aspect is exercise, which benefits both the heart and the brain. It's recommended to engage in physical activity six to seven days a week, ideally in the morning when you feel the sharpest. Exercise helps get the blood flowing and promotes overall well-being. Another valuable self-care idea is following a Mediterranean diet, which includes foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, such as nuts and olive oil, along with other brain-supporting vitamins and minerals. Going gluten-free may also be beneficial. In addition to nutrition and exercise, maintaining a strong spiritual pillar is essential. This means nurturing your spirituality, having hope, and having faith to help you navigate the journey of living with dementia. By incorporating these self-care practices, individuals with dementia can support their overall well-being and brain health.\nQuestion: How do I know if my dementia is getting worse?...\n\n...Question: How can I prevent feeling overwhelmed as a caregiver?\nAnswer: As a caregiver supporting someone with dementia, it is common to feel overwhelmed, burdened, and stressed. To prevent this, it is important to utilize respite care. Respite care provides you with a break for a certain period of time, ranging from two to four hours. You can explore options such as adult daycare centers in your area, where your loved one can receive care while you take a break. Another option is to hire a family member or a friend to come in for an hour or two to give you some time off. Taking advantage of respite care can help alleviate feelings of being overwhelmed and provide you with much-needed rest.\nQuestion: I feel frustrated. What can I do?\n\n...Question: What does the word 'respite' mean?\nAnswer: Respite, in the context of being a caregiver for someone with dementia, means taking a real break. It's not just running errands or doing chores; it's about doing something restful that brings you joy. For example, you might hire a companion to stay with your loved one so that you can go to a beautiful spot by the water or in a nature park, enjoy your favorite coffee, and connect with a friend for lunch. You could also schedule a therapy appointment, go to the local Y for a swim, or treat yourself to a manicure. The main idea is to focus on yourself and refill your energy so that you can continue caring for your loved one. Remember, respite is important for your well-being as a caregiver.", "final_context": "Dementia care planning includes the development and implementation of a **caregiver stress prevention bundle**. The caregiver stress prevention bundle includes the following components:\n- **Weekly respite care:** at least **8 consecutive hours per week** of respite care, during which the caregiver is not providing care for their loved one living with dementia and is instead focusing on their own emotional health. As part of caregiver self-care, the caregiver should spend at least 8 consecutive hours away from caregiving per week.\n- **Monthly support group:** attending a **monthly support group**, with or without their loved one living with dementia.\n- **Problem-solving skills development:** developing **problem-solving skills** to help the caregiver cope with **their own emotional and physical stress**, and to manage the **cognitive, functional, behavioral, and psychological disabilities** of their loved one living with dementia. Do not\nleave someone with dementia unsupervised if new\nsurroundings may cause confusion, disorientation or\nagitation....\n\n...Question: What kind of clock is best for someone with dementia?\nAnswer: For people with dementia, it is recommended to use a digital clock instead of a traditional round clock with numbers. The round clock requires abstract thinking to interpret the numbers, which can be difficult for someone with dementia. A digital clock with clear numbers is much easier to read and understand. Another option is a day clock that indicates if it is day or night by displaying a sun for daytime and a black color with stars and moons for nighttime. This can help individuals who struggle with determining the time of day. Additionally, there are clocks available that only display phrases like \"morning,\" \"afternoon,\" \"evening,\" or \"nighttime.\" These clocks are useful for individuals who may wake up in the middle of the night and feel disoriented, as they provide a clear indication of the time of day without requiring the ability to read a clock. These alternatives can be helpful in reducing confusion and disorientation for people with dementia.\nQuestion: What type of toothbrush is best for someone with dementia?...\n\nQuestion: Is there a way to stop someone with dementia from repeating themselves?\nAnswer: Living with dementia can be challenging for both the person experiencing brain changes and their caregivers. It's important to understand that the person may repeat themselves or share the same stories or questions over and over again because they are on a \"seek mission.\" They are searching for something, whether it's information or a connection with you. It's crucial to be sensitive and respond with empathy when they share their stories or ask repetitive questions. Reflecting on what they say and acknowledging their feelings can help create a sense of connection. If you find yourself stuck in a cycle, it may be necessary for the caregiver to flex out of that cycle and transition to a different topic or approach. By interjecting with new information or asking a different question, you can redirect the conversation and maintain engagement. Ultimately, caregivers have more power than they realize to make a positive difference in the lives of those living with dementia.\nQuestion: How do I tell someone that I've noticed signs of dementia when I know they won't agree with me?...\n\n...Question: How can I deal with severe anxiety in someone with dementia?\nAnswer: Dealing with severe anxiety in someone with dementia can be challenging, but there are strategies that can be helpful. First, creating a peaceful environment can make a difference. This may involve reducing noise and creating a calm atmosphere. Incorporating meditation, especially when done together, can also be beneficial. Engaging with emotionally meaningful music and pleasant smells can help to soothe anxiety. Additionally, getting outside and taking a walk together can provide both physical activity and exposure to natural sunlight, which can have a positive impact. If these approaches do not fully alleviate the anxiety, it is important to consult with a physician or other care provider. They can help determine other potential strategies based on what has already been tried. Medication may be an option, but it is not always the first choice. Non-pharmacological methods can often be effective in managing anxiety and should be explored first.\nQuestion: How can I help someone with dementia feel safe at home when they are scared?\n\nSupporting a person with memory loss\nSpace for\nyour notes\nCognitive stimulation therapy (CST)\nCognitive stimulation therapy (CST) involves activities\nand exercises that encourage thinking, concentration,\ncommunication and memory in the person with dementia.\nIt involves talking about day-to-day interests, past events and\nmemories, and information relating to the current time and place.\nThis can be done in one-to-one sessions or in a group setting.\nCST is recommended for people with mild to moderate dementia,\nrather than for the later stages. It is offered to people with\ndementia through NHS trusts and memory clinics. To find out\nmore about CST, speak to the person's GP or memory clinic.\nCognitive rehabilitation\nCognitive rehabilitation is a type of therapy that involves the\nperson with dementia working together with a therapist on\nspecific skills that they would like to develop. For example,\nthey could focus on learning a new skill, such as using a\nmobile phone, or rediscovering a skill that they used to enjoy,\nsuch as cooking.\nThis approach focuses on what is important to the person and\nthose closest to them. This\nincludes not causing them distress. However, it is often not easy\nto manage these questions on a regular basis and it is important\nyou have as much support around you as you need. It can be\nhelpful to hear from other carers about approaches they have\ntried, and what worked for them. Through repetition, he or she may be seeking comfort, familiarity or reassurance. It is\nalso possible the individual is doing his/her best to keep a conversation going.\n• Respond to the question or confirm the statement. Try to redirect the individual.\n• Discus plans such as doctor appointments closer to the time to prepare to leave, rather than\ndays ahead.\n• Try placing signs such as “dinner is at 6:30” on the kitchen table, to remove anxiety and\nuncertainty about anticipated events.\n• Provide safe and simple activities such as folding towels, or matching socks.\n\nCognitive connection: Depression is linked to changes in memory, attention, and emotional processing. It can worsen cognitive symptoms and make daily functioning harder.\nThings to try:\nEncourage pleasant activities (short walks, music, time outdoors, brief visits).\nMaintain social connections; even brief positive interactions can help.\nCreate a bright, welcoming environment with natural light.\nProvide emotional support; listen and validate feelings.\nMonitor symptoms and share patterns with your care team\nConsider counseling, support groups, or medication when advised; monitor for side effects.\nAnxiety\nAnxiety in dementia can show up as restlessness, excessive worry, or agitation, often triggered by changes in routine or unfamiliar situations. You may notice repeated questions, seeking reassurance, pacing, fidgeting, difficulty relaxing, or increased confusion in new settings.\nCognitive connection: Anxiety relates to changes in attention, memory, and the brain's ability to adapt to new information. It can worsen cognitive symptoms and make daily functioning harder.\nThings to try:\nEncourage pleasant activities (short walks, music, time outdoors, brief visits).\nMaintain social connections; even brief positive interactions can help.\nCreate a bright, welcoming environment with natural light.\nProvide emotional support; listen and validate feelings.\nMonitor symptoms and share patterns with your care team\nConsider counseling, support groups, or medication when advised; monitor for side effects.\nAnxiety\nAnxiety in dementia can show up as restlessness, excessive worry, or agitation, often triggered by changes in routine or unfamiliar situations. You may notice repeated questions, seeking reassurance, pacing, fidgeting, difficulty relaxing, or increased confusion in new settings.\nCognitive connection: Anxiety relates to changes in attention, memory, and the brain's ability to adapt to new information. Situations that were once easy can feel overwhelming.\nThings to try:\nMaintain a calm, predictable environment; reduce noise and clutter.\nPrepare for transitions; give notice close to the time and keep details simple....\n\n...Cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) involves activities and\nexercises that encourage thinking, concentration,\ncommunication and memory in the person with dementia. It\ninvolves talking about day-to-day interests, past events and\nmemories, and information relating to the current time and\nplace. This can be done in one-to-one sessions or in a group\nsetting.\nCST is recommended for people with mild to moderate\ndementia, rather than for the later stages. It is offered to\npeople with dementia through NHS trusts and memory clinics.\nTo find out more about CST, speak to the person's GP or\nmemory clinic.\nCognitive rehabilitation\nCognitive rehabilitation is a type of therapy that involves the\nperson with dementia working together with a therapist on\nspecific skills that they would like to develop. For example,\nthey could focus on learning a new skill, such as using a\nmobile phone, or rediscovering a skill that they used to enjoy,\nsuch as cooking.\nThis approach focuses on what is important to the person and\nthose closest to them. It can help people with dementia to\nfocus on the skills, abilities and knowledge that they still have....\n\n...Question: How should I respond to my loved one with dementia when they ask why they can't remember something?\nAnswer: When someone with dementia asks why they can't remember something, it's important to respond in a caring and supportive manner. It can be frustrating for them when they can't recall something, and they may experience various emotions. One way to approach this is to deal with the emotional truth of the situation. In some types of dementia, the person may not be aware that they were supposed to remember or they may not have formed the memory in the first place, which is a common symptom of Alzheimer's disease. In other cases, such as vascular dementia, they may have difficulty retrieving the memory but can with prompting. For those with minimal memory problems, using reminders like sticky notes or technology-based supports can be helpful. It's important not to ask questions that imply that they should remember or shame them for their forgetfulness. Instead, present information in a way that supports their memory or use distraction and redirection techniques to shift the focus to something else. Remember, it's not their fault and they are trying their best. Being understanding and patient will go a long way in supporting someone with dementia....\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Effects of Introducing the Bbrainklok as a Digital External Memory Aid on Prospective Memory, Apathy and Autonomy in Individuals with Korsakoff's Syndrome. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41983187)\nIntroduction Korsakoff's syndrome (KS) is a neuropsychiatric disorder caused by severe thiamine deficiency resulting from malnutrition, typically as a consequence of structural alcohol abuse. It is characterized by profound cognitive and behavioral impairments, including deficits in prospective memory (PM), the ability to remember to perform an intended task, and high levels of apathy. These deficits significantly impact daily functioning and perceived autonomy. Methods This study investigated the effects of introducing the Bbrainklok, an external digital memory aid, on PM performance, apathy and autonomy in individuals with KS. Sixteen individuals with KS or other alcohol-induced major cognitive disorder, residing in a long-term care facility, participated in a nine-week intervention stud\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Response Facilitation in Dementia Care: Exploring Engagement Through Social Contexts: A Qualitative Study in Dutch Nursing Homes (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12940554)\nResponse Facilitation in Dementia Care: Exploring Engagement Through Social Contexts: A Qualitative Study in Dutch Nursing Homes\n\n[WEB:europepmc] The Utility of Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination III (ACE-III) in Differentiating Neurodegenerative Disorders with Psychotic Symptoms: A Narrative Review. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42194406)\nPsychotic symptoms, including delusions and hallucinations, frequently complicate the course of Alzheimer's disease (AD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Their presence accelerates decline, worsens outcomes, and complicates management. Cognitive screening in such patients is essential yet challenging due to attentional fluctuation, impaired insight, and diagnostic overlap. Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination III (ACE-III) is a multidomain tool with higher sensitivity than the MMSE. Sometimes the\npatient may reply appropriately if they have a better understanding of the question.\n• Persons with dementia need more time than the average person to process a question and may require\nextra time and patience to respond.\n• Most importantly, simple expressions of caring communicate to any person that they are loved and\nappreciated. A smile or a hug speaks volumes to a person with dementia.\nCommunicating With a Person Who Has Dementia:\nA person with memory loss and confusion may have trouble understanding what is said, or saying what he\nor she thinks and wants. This can be very frustrating for both the person with dementia and his caregiver.\nFollowing are some practical tips to help make communicating easier:\n1. Personalize your Conversation: Use the person's name to get his attention. Talk to the person directly,\nmake eye contact. Try a gentle touch on the arm to help him focus on the conversation. Speak on a topic that\nboth the speaker and patient express an interest in.\n2. Use Short, Simple Sentences: Keep sentences short and easy to understand. Speak clearly and slowly....\n\n...Answer: When caring for someone with dementia, it's common to make mistakes. One of the biggest mistakes is seeing their behaviors as the problem. Instead, we need to understand that the situation itself is the problem. The person is trying to do something, but they may struggle due to their dementia. They are also trying to communicate. So when we notice challenging behaviors, it's important to pause and really understand what is happening. Don't assume you know what's going on and don't ask the person why they are behaving in a certain way. They may not be able to answer due to their condition. Instead, use your senses to observe and listen carefully to what they are experiencing. Be curious about what is not working for them. Look at the environment, the people around, the objects and tasks involved, and try to identify any possible triggers or causes for their behavior. It's also important to consider other possibilities like pain or discomfort that they may be experiencing. Sometimes, without realizing it, our actions and intentions can be perceived as threats. So we need to always maintain curiosity and avoid passing judgment. If you find yourself struggling or overwhelmed, don't hesitate to reach out for help. It's better to seek assistance before things become more challenging....\n\n...Question: What is a general strategy for caregivers approaching difficult behaviors in someone with dementia?...\n\n...Question: What should I do when someone with dementia is not following directions?\nAnswer: When communicating with someone living with dementia, it's important to consider how you are giving directions. Did you provide visual, verbal, or physical cues? Did you give a whole sequence of steps or just one step at a time? If the person is not following your directions, it may be because you gave them too much information at once or they are doing it in their own way. It's important to observe and make a decision whether it's necessary to have them do it your way or if you can let go and allow them to do it their way. Do not push to regain their attention immediately.\n\nCommunication Strategies: Helping the Person with Dementia\nUnderstand You:\n• It is critical to get a dementia patient's attention before saying\nanything to them, staff and family caregivers should begin a\nconversation by making eye contact.\n• It is also important to identify yourself and call the person by name.\n• Staff and family caregivers need to speak slowly and clearly, and in a\nlow pitched voice, while maintaining an open, calm and friendly\ncommunication manner.\n• It is important to remember to break down tasks into clear and simple steps.\n• Staff and family caregivers must also be aware of what words are familiar to the person and remember\nto use them often. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41652334)\nBackground and objectives Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRDs) are prevalent conditions that are stressful and elevate emotional distress in couples after diagnosis. Without treatment, emotional distress may become chronic and negatively affect couples' quality of life. We report results from an NIH Stage 1A open pilot of Resilient Together for Dementia (RT-ADRD), a novel, dyadic, skills-based intervention aimed at preventing chronic emotional distress in couples early after diagnosis. We describe results from our mixed-methods single arm feasibility study, including preliminary feasibility and acceptability of the intervention, and qualitative feedback from exit interviews. We also present exploratory analyses for change in outcomes and mechanisms of action. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41761929)\nIntroduction The prevalence of dementia cases within post-acute rehabilitation hospitals in Canada poses a unique challenge due to the distinctive vulnerabilities of the patient demographic in these settings. Healthcare staff in rehabilitation hospitals receive limited formal education about responsive behaviours. Aim To address a practice gap, a program evaluation of the Gentle Persuasive Approaches (GPA) in Dementia Care education program was implemented at an inpatient rehabilitation hospital in a large metropolitan centre. Design A multiple method, pre-post intervention design was used to assess the impact of GPA classroom sessions on staff capacity for providing person-centred dementia care. Method Eighty-eight staff members attended GPA sessions and completed quantitative and qualita\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Implementation of My Hearing PREM Into Three UK Audiology Services: A Pluralist Approach to Planning, Design and Evaluation. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41964360)\nIntroduction My Hearing PREM (patient reported experience measure) is a validated tool for use in audiology services, to measure patients' experiences of living with hearing loss, and support from family and services. This study planned and evaluated the process of implementing My Hearing PREM into audiology services. Methods Implementation planning and design was informed by the person-based approach and involved patients, public and audiology staff. My Hearing PREM was implemented into three NHS audiology services for 3 months. Evaluation of implementation used quantitative methods to determine PREM use and cost, and qualitative interviews with staff and patients to assess the implementation process. Results A total of 95 participants contributed data across planning to evaluation. Clini"}

A gentle back rub of 10 to 15 minutes before bedtime helps promote relaxation and sleep.\n\nFor a person living with dementia who has recently returned home from the hospital, the caregiver should prioritize **4 to 6 hours of uninterrupted sleep** at night to help manage and prevent delirium. Medications may have been started or stopped in the hospital. If you have questions, contact the care team immediately.\nSleeping Issues\nPeople with dementia often have trouble sleeping. They might wake up a lot at night, feel confused, or think it's time to get up when it's still dark. Some may sleep during the day and stay awake at night. This can make them feel tired, confused, or cranky.\nThings to try:\nReview medications with your loved one's care team to see if any are affecting sleep.\nKeep previous sleeping and waking habits in mind.\nPlan regular physical activity, like a long walk.\nProvide a calm, predictable setting.\nCreate and keep a bedtime routine. Go to bed at the same time every night....\n\nComplementary alternative medicine\nSeveral complementary and alternative modalities have been tested for sleep disturbances in\ndementia. Two small, non-randomized studies reported an improvement of sleep in dementia\nafter acupuncture or accupressure [72, 73]. A randomized trial of a 3-minute back massage\nprior to bedtime showed a 36-minute, but non-significant, improvement in total sleep time\n[74]. A small, randomized study of Tai Chi in vascular dementia demonstrated a benefit in\nsleep, as measured by PSQI [75]. A study of a child-like robot for elderly women living\nalone (not necessarily with dementia) showed significant improvement in several sleep\nvariables, including total sleep time, compared to a more mechanical robot[76]. These and\nother alternative, non-pharmacological interventions are under active investigation for sleep\ndisturbance in dementia, however, none have been demonstrated to be effective in rigorous,\ndouble-blind, randomized, controlled trials. The following are strategies that can be used for the\nperson with dementia and the family caregiver.\nSet the Right Environment\nMedications for Sleep\n• Keep a regular schedule: go to bed and get up at the same time every day.\n• Try to exercise daily but not within three hours of bedtime.\n• Make sure the temperature in the bedroom is comfortable (not too hot and not too cold).\n• Reduce liquid intake before bedtime.\n• Try not to nap during the day; if you do nap, try to do so before 3 p.m. and try to keep the\nnap short (about 20 minutes).\n• Keep the bedroom as dark and quiet as possible; use a nightlight if needed, but be\naware that bright light disrupts sleep/wake patterns.\n• Calm activities at the end of the day and before bedtime may help with sleep.\n• Avoid violent movies or TV shows; strong content and images can be upsetting and can\nmake it hard to relax.\n• Be aware that changes in your environment, such as moving to a new home or having\nunexpected visitors can be disruptive and confusing for the person with dementia....\n\nAsk for a private room, with a reclining chair or bed, if insurance will cover it. It will be calmer than a shared\nroom.\nDo not talk about the hospital stay in front of the person as if they are not there. This can be upsetting and\nembarrassing.\nWhen it is time to go to the hospital, tell the person with dementia not long before leaving home that they are\ngoing to spend a short time in the hospital, and mention which friends and family members will be there with\nthem.\nDuring a hospital stay\nWith the change in their environment and daily routines, staying in the hospital can be an uncomfortable experience\nfor people with dementia and their caregivers.\nHere are some tips to help improve the hospital experience for people with dementia and their caregivers. While the\ntips provide general guidance, patients and loved ones should continue to follow instructions from hospital staff:\nHave a family member, trusted friend, or hired caregiver stay with the person with dementia as much as possible.\nAsk whoever is staying at the hospital with the person to keep other family members informed.\nCommunicate with the person to help them understand each step of their medical care....\n\n...Question: How can a caregiver work together with their person with dementia to adjust sleep patterns?\nAnswer: As a caregiver working with someone living with dementia, it's important to help them adjust their sleep patterns together. Start by discussing and agreeing on their preferred wake-up and bedtime. It's best to wake them up at the same time every day, using an alarm if needed. Encourage them to give it a week to see how it feels. Create a restful bedroom environment by ensuring it is cool, dark, and comfortable, making adjustments based on their feedback. Help them relax before bed by asking what they would enjoy—like soothing videos with nature sounds or guided meditations. Be mindful of food and drink intake in the hours leading up to bedtime. Avoid heavy meals and limit fluids to prevent nighttime trips to the bathroom. If they must drink, keep it minimal. Encourage a consistent daytime routine of hydration. It's also wise to minimize stimulants and alcohol, especially close to bedtime. Encourage spending time in natural light during the day to promote alertness and limit exposure to bright screens at night. By working together, you can help them develop a healthier sleep schedule that honors their preferences....\n\nQuestion: What should I do if someone with dementia often refuses to go to bed?\nAnswer: If you're taking care of someone with dementia who often refuses to go to bed, it can be really challenging, especially after a long day. Establishing a calming bedtime routine can be helpful. Try activities like applying lavender lotion and taking deep breaths to relax, or serving a warm cup of tea about an hour before bed. This gradual winding down from a bright living room to bedtime can signal that it's time to rest. Even if your loved one isn't ready to sleep right away, you can encourage them to relax in bed by looking at family photos, listening to music on a device, or simply enjoying some peaceful moments. Consistency in this routine is important, so keep trying different approaches that work for them. Water in the bathroom poses a high risk of falls, so it's important to make necessary modifications. One key area to address is the height of the toilet seat. Easy to remove clothing with\nelastic waistbands or Velcro can help prevent accidents....\n\n...Answer: When helping someone with dementia who doesn't want assistance with dressing, it's important to remember their need for autonomy and control. All individuals have a natural desire to make their own decisions and not have others making choices for them. This need for control can be especially prominent when it comes to dressing. To help address this situation, it is suggested to give the person as much control and autonomy as possible. This can be done by allowing them to choose their own outfit. For example, you can present them with two shirts from their closet and let them decide which one to wear. By giving them a sense of choice, they may be more likely to be compliant during the dressing process. Another technique that can be effective is the hand-over-hand technique, which involves two people working together to dress the individual. This approach allows the person with dementia to feel like they have more control over the situation. It also helps the caregiver or the person assisting in dressing to handle the task more smoothly. By implementing these strategies of providing choice and using the hand-over-hand technique, caregivers can help individuals with dementia feel more empowered and comfortable during the dressing process....\n\nAccommodating Clothing\nConsider orthoses, wheelchairs, and other equipment. For example, if\nthey're dressed for work, they may think they need to go to work. If they're dressed in the clothes they\nusually relax in, this will remind them that they're not at work.\nAdditional Tips\nConsider the environment. This marks the first major revision in 7 years since the publication of the first edition. The second edition was completed over a span of 3 years, and its overview and key features are summarized below. This guideline begins with a clinical flowchart outlining the general diagnostic and therapeutic approach. A notable update is the inclusion of insertable anal and vaginal continence devices, which are now considered a form of conservative therapy under clinical research frameworks. This study investigates the influence of family and household structures on older persons' unmet needs in ADLs in southwestern Nigeria. "tf_final_answer_source": "", "tf_answer_llm_locked": false}, "final_answer": "C", "base_context_chars": 8086, "final_context_chars": 8086, "base_context": "When caring for a loved one living with dementia, if you lose eye contact during a conversation, the most appropriate action is to **recognize that the person may need space, pause the conversation, and find a better moment to restart in a few minutes**. Do not push to regain their attention immediately.\n\n...Account for any hearing or vision challenges the person may have.\nMake eye contact to help focus the person's attention.\nAvoid talking to the person if you're behind them or where they can't see you.\nSpeak clearly, using short and simple sentences.\nShow as well as talk. Using actions can help give your words meaning.\nTake care of yourself too!\nOn the days when these tips don't\nseem to help, remember that your\npresence is still felt by the person\nliving with dementia. It's not easy\nto be there for the person while\nalso taking care of yourself at the\nsame time. It's important to ﬁnd a\nhealthy balance and ask for a hand\nwhen you need it!\nFor more information and support,\ncontact your local Alzheimer\nSociety at alzheimer.ca/Find. We\nare here to help.\n1.\nUse what you know\nabout the person\n2.\nReduce\ndistractions\n3.\nChat face to face\n4.\nBe ﬂexible\n5.\nStay positive\n\n...• If a person with dementia does not understand the question, repeat it or rephrase it. Sometimes the\npatient may reply appropriately if they have a better understanding of the question.\n• Persons with dementia need more time than the average person to process a question and may require\nextra time and patience to respond.\n• Most importantly, simple expressions of caring communicate to any person that they are loved and\nappreciated. A smile or a hug speaks volumes to a person with dementia.\nCommunicating With a Person Who Has Dementia:\nA person with memory loss and confusion may have trouble understanding what is said, or saying what he\nor she thinks and wants. This can be very frustrating for both the person with dementia and his caregiver.\nFollowing are some practical tips to help make communicating easier:\n1. Personalize your Conversation: Use the person's name to get his attention. Talk to the person directly,\nmake eye contact. Try a gentle touch on the arm to help him focus on the conversation. Speak on a topic that\nboth the speaker and patient express an interest in.\n2. Use Short, Simple Sentences: Keep sentences short and easy to understand. Speak clearly and slowly....\n\n...Answer: If you're trying to get the attention of someone with dementia during a conversation, it's important to do so in a way that doesn't feel like an interruption. Wait for a momentary pause, like when the person takes a breath or finishes a sentence, and then make an energetic sound like \"ah\" or \"oh\" to catch their attention. You can even use a small gesture like raising a finger. After getting their attention, address them by their first name to make a connection. Now, you can ask or say what you need to. For example, if you're discussing going to the store and you want to mention getting dog food, you could say, \"Teepa! The dog food.\" This will help them focus on what you're saying. If necessary, you can continue the conversation from that point and suggest a new activity or location, like going to the store together. The goal is to create a pause that allows for action or a change in the conversation. So, keep in mind that while you may need a break, the person with dementia may also want to continue talking. Stay prepared for further conversation, but at least you've created a pause to move things forward....\n\nQuestion: How do I know it's time to try a different approach with someone who has dementia?\nAnswer: Finding the right approach for your loved one with dementia can be challenging, especially with so much information available online. It's essential to remember that each person with dementia is unique, so what works for one may not work for another. Here are two key things to consider when assessing your approach: - **Reception by Your Loved One:** Pay attention to how your loved one responds to your actions and words. It's crucial that your approach is well-received and does not cause any distress, such as upset or negative reactions. - **Feasibility for You:** The best approach is one that you feel capable and willing to carry out. If you can do it consistently and it suits your abilities and comfort level, then it'sa good choice for you. If you notice that your loved one is at ease and comfortable with what you're doing, and it's something you can consistently manage, then you're on the right path. Trust your instincts – you know your loved one best.\nQuestion: What can I do if someone with dementia no longer recognizes me?...\n\nCommunicating with someone with\ndementia\nDementia is a progressive illness that, over time, will affect a person's ability to remember\nand understand basic everyday facts, such as names, dates and places.\nDementia will gradually affect the way a person communicates. Their ability to present\nrational ideas and to reason clearly will change.\nIf you are looking after a person with dementia, you may find that as the illness progresses\nyou'll have to start discussions to get the person to make conversation. This is common.\nTheir ability to process information gets progressively weaker and their responses can\nbecome delayed.\nEncouraging someone with dementia to communicate\nTry to start conversations with the person you're looking after, especially if you notice that\nthey're starting fewer conversations themselves. It can help to:\n● speak clearly and slowly, using short sentences\n● make eye contact with the person when they're talking or asking questions\n● give them time to respond, because they may feel pressured if you try to speed up\ntheir answers\n● encourage them to join in conversations with others, where possible\n● let them speak for themselves during discussions about their welfare or health issues...\n\nCommunication\nHow the caregiver communicates with the person they are assisting is an important factor in reducing the risk\nof falls for people with dementia.\nRemember to:\n obtain the person's attention: reduce distractions, gain eye contact\n watch for non-verbal cues from the person to help understand their actions and reactions\n be mindful of your approach: remain calm and watch your facial expression and gestures\n give thought to how instructions are given: use short, simple sentences; suggest one step at a time; use\ncue; allow time; encourage the person\nProtective Considerations in the External Environment\nEnsure Adequate Lighting  \nincrease lighting  \nreduce glare  \nlimit shadows\nSuggestions:  \nUse night lights in the bedroom and hallway.  \nTurn lamps on in dimly lit rooms.  \nPurchase glow-in-the dark light switches.  \nUtilize high wattage/low energy bulbs.  \nInstall lights in dark closets.  \nClose drapes and use additional lighting at night.  \nOpen drapes during the day.  \nKeep entrances and outside walkways well lit.  \nInstall outdoor motion-sensor light.\nProvide Visual Contrast...\n\nListening to and understanding someone with dementia\nCommunication is a two-way process. As a carer of someone with dementia, you will\nprobably have to learn to listen more carefully.\nYou may need to be more aware of non-verbal messages, such as facial expressions and\nbody language. You may have to use more physical contact, such as reassuring pats on the\narm, or smile as well as speaking.\nActive listening can help:\n● use eye contact to look at the person, and encourage them to look at you when either\nof you are talking\n● try not to interrupt them, even if you think you know what they're saying\n● stop what you're doing so you can give the person your full attention while they speak\n● minimise distractions that may get in the way of communication, such as the\ntelevision or the radio playing too loudly, but always check if it's OK to do so\n● repeat what you heard back to the person and ask if it's accurate, or ask them to\nrepeat what they said\nWhy is communicating important for a person with\ndementia?\nGood communication is an important part of living well after a diagnosis...", "final_context": "When caring for a loved one living with dementia, if you lose eye contact during a conversation, the most appropriate action is to **recognize that the person may need space, pause the conversation, and find a better moment to restart in a few minutes**. Do not push to regain their attention immediately.\n\n...Account for any hearing or vision challenges the person may have.\nMake eye contact to help focus the person's attention.\nAvoid talking to the person if you're behind them or where they can't see you.\nSpeak clearly, using short and simple sentences.\nShow as well as talk. Using actions can help give your words meaning.\nTake care of yourself too!\nOn the days when these tips don't\nseem to help, remember that your\npresence is still felt by the person\nliving with dementia. It's not easy\nto be there for the person while\nalso taking care of yourself at the\nsame time. It's important to ﬁnd a\nhealthy balance and ask for a hand\nwhen you need it!\nFor more information and support,\ncontact your local Alzheimer\nSociety at alzheimer.ca/Find. We\nare here to help.\n1.\nUse what you know\nabout the person\n2.\nReduce\ndistractions\n3.\nChat face to face\n4.\nBe ﬂexible\n5.\nStay positive\n\n...• If a person with dementia does not understand the question, repeat it or rephrase it. Sometimes the\npatient may reply appropriately if they have a better understanding of the question.\n• Persons with dementia need more time than the average person to process a question and may require\nextra time and patience to respond.\n• Most importantly, simple expressions of caring communicate to any person that they are loved and\nappreciated. A smile or a hug speaks volumes to a person with dementia.\nCommunicating With a Person Who Has Dementia:\nA person with memory loss and confusion may have trouble understanding what is said, or saying what he\nor she thinks and wants. This can be very frustrating for both the person with dementia and his caregiver.\nFollowing are some practical tips to help make communicating easier:\n1. Personalize your Conversation: Use the person's name to get his attention. Talk to the person directly,\nmake eye contact. Try a gentle touch on the arm to help him focus on the conversation. Speak on a topic that\nboth the speaker and patient express an interest in.\n2. Use Short, Simple Sentences: Keep sentences short and easy to understand. Speak clearly and slowly....\n\n...Answer: If you're trying to get the attention of someone with dementia during a conversation, it's important to do so in a way that doesn't feel like an interruption. Wait for a momentary pause, like when the person takes a breath or finishes a sentence, and then make an energetic sound like \"ah\" or \"oh\" to catch their attention. You can even use a small gesture like raising a finger. After getting their attention, address them by their first name to make a connection. Now, you can ask or say what you need to. For example, if you're discussing going to the store and you want to mention getting dog food, you could say, \"Teepa! The dog food.\" This will help them focus on what you're saying. If necessary, you can continue the conversation from that point and suggest a new activity or location, like going to the store together. The goal is to create a pause that allows for action or a change in the conversation. So, keep in mind that while you may need a break, the person with dementia may also want to continue talking. "tf_final_answer_source": "", "tf_answer_llm_locked": false}, "final_answer": "C", "base_context_chars": 7500, "final_context_chars": 7500, "base_context": "● Choose clothing that is easy to wear and care for.\nZippers and Velcro™ are easier to fasten than buttons.\nSkirts and pants with elastic bands are easier to put on.\n● Soft, stretchy materials are often the most comfortable,\nand shouldn't be too tight.\n● For women, a front-closing bra may be easier to put on\nherself; for men, boxer shorts may be easier to manage\nthan fitted underwear.\n● Slippers are comfortable, though they may not offer\nenough support to be worn all the time.\nShopping for clothes\n● If possible, involve the person with dementia in shopping\nfor clothes. If you do the shopping, check his size\nregularly, as he may have lost or gained weight.\n● Choose clothing that is comfortable, easy to put on and\neasy to wash.\n● Remember that she may need to wear new clothes often\nbefore they become familiar to her, and she may think\nany new clothing doesn't belong to her.\n● Buy several of the same, favourite outfits, so she\nbelieves she is wearing the same familiar clothes.\n\nDementia UK\nThe hallway\n• Keep the hall uncluttered so it is easy to get through the\nfront door\n• Hang a clear, easy-to-read clock near the door, displaying the\ntime, day and date, to help the person tell if it is time to go out\n• Keep keys in a consistent place so they are easy to find – but\nmake sure they are not visible from the outside. A drawer in a\nhallway table is ideal\n• Use gripper tape to secure doormats or carpet runners to reduce\nthe risk of falls, or remove them completely\n• Fit a door alarm if the person with dementia is likely to leave\nthe home alone when it is unsafe for them to do so – this can\ngive family members who live with the person peace of mind,\nespecially overnight\nThe kitchen\nThe kitchen can be a confusing and potentially dangerous place for\na person with dementia. Making sure that everything they may need\nis easy to use, easily identifiable and within reach can make it as safe\nand manageable as possible.\n• Keep items that the person uses frequently, like mugs, tea/coffee\nand spoons, on the worktop...\n\n...• It may be helpful to lay the\nperson's clothing out in the order\nthey would put the items on\n• Some people with dementia like\nto wear the same clothes all the\ntime. If so, you could buy several\nidentical sets of clothes – when\nthey are in the bath or in bed, you\ncan swap the dirty outfit for a\nclean one\n• New or gifted clothing can be\nused to encourage someone to\nchange, for example, “I would\nlove to see you wearing the new\ntrousers we bought you”\n• Encouraging the person to wear\na particular outfit for a visit or\nouting could prompt them to\nchange their clothing\n• Look for clothing that is easy to\nput on and take off – drawstring\nwaists and Velcro fastenings may\nbe easier than zips and buttons\nYoung onset dementia\nand personal hygiene\nSupporting a person with\nyoung onset dementia (where\nsymptoms develop before the\nage of 65) with personal hygiene\ncan have its own challenges.\n\nHelping a person with dementia maintain his or her appearance\ncan promote positive self-esteem. While these tasks may\nbecome frustrating for a person with Alzheimer's in the later\nstages of the disease, the tips below can help simplify the\nprocess.\n● Dressing\n● Grooming\nDressing\nPlan plenty of time when dressing or grooming someone with\nAlzheimer's. Rushing the person can cause anxiety and\nfrustration. As the disease progresses beyond the early stages,\nchoosing and putting on clothes can be frustrating for the\nperson with dementia. The person may not remember how to\ndress or may be overwhelmed with the choices or the task itself.  \nTo assist:\n● Simplify choices. Keep the closets free of excess clothing.\nA person may panic if clothing choices become\noverwhelming. If appropriate, give the person an\n\nAccommodating Clothing\nConsider orthoses, wheelchairs, and other equipment. For example, if they wear ankle-foot orthoses,\nyou may need to buy pants with a stretchy hem so that the orthoses will fit under them.\nIf your care recipient has injuries or paralysis, contact an occupational therapist or another\nhealthcare provider for tips on clothing types.\nSituation Specific\nThe way a person with dementia looks will help them understand what they're doing. For example, if\nthey're dressed for work, they may think they need to go to work. If they're dressed in the clothes they\nusually relax in, this will remind them that they're not at work.\nAdditional Tips\nConsider the environment. Make sure the room is warm enough to get dressed in.\nUse layers. If they wear several thin layers of clothing, it makes it easier for them to remove one if they\nget warm throughout the day.\nEnsure your care recipient changes clothing regularly.\nRemove the dirty clothes and put clean clothes in their place when they're showering.\nEncourage them to change because someone is coming to visit or they're going out....\n\n...the evenings, and front fastening bras can be easier to put on.\nWhile comfortable, slippers shouldn't be worn for more than a\nfew hours, as they may not support the person's feet enough.\nSlippers also encourage shuffling, which doesn't allow the leg\nmuscles and joints to work correctly.\nWhen helping a person with dementia choose comfortable\nclothing, you should:\nmake sure that items are not inside out, and that buttons, zips\nand fasteners are done up\ntry well-fitting slip-on shoes, or shoes with Velcro fastenings,\nor replace regular shoelaces with elastic ones. Shoes with\nlaces may be difficult for someone with dementia to manage\ntry buckle-free belts, which fasten with Velcro, and clip-on\nties, which are safer and easier to use\ntry several thin layers of clothing, particularly in cold weather,\nrather than one thick layer. The person can then remove a\nlayer if it gets too warm\navoid self-supporting stockings, as they can cause\ncirculation problems\ntry specially designed trousers, with a drop-down front, to\nmake using the toilet easier for men....\n\n...put an item and think that someone has taken it. The person\nmight then start walking to try to find it. You can try to make this\neasier for them by keeping personal items where they can easily\nsee them. You can also use notes or pictures on cupboards and\ndrawers to show what is inside.\nConfusion about the time\nPeople with dementia often become confused about the time.\nThey may wake up in the middle of the night and get dressed,\nready to start the day. This confusion is easy to understand. In\nwinter or summer, it is common to go to bed and wake up while\nit's either still dark or still light outside.\nIt can help if you place a large clock by the person's bedside\nthat shows whether it is the morning or afternoon. They are also available from Alzheimer's Society's\nonline shop – see shop.alzheimers.org.uk\n\nThe bedroom\nIt is important for everyone to have a safe and relaxing place to\nsleep, with enough space to get into and out of bed, and get dressed\nand undressed.\n• Try to reduce clutter in the bedroom to avoid falls, especially in\nthe dark\n• Some people with dementia can find choosing clothes from\ndrawers or wardrobes difficult.
