The following are strategies that can be used for the\nperson with dementia and the family caregiver.\nSet the Right Environment\nMedications for Sleep\n• Keep a regular schedule: go to bed and get up at the same time every day.\n• Try to exercise daily but not within three hours of bedtime.\n• Make sure the temperature in the bedroom is comfortable (not too hot and not too cold).\n• Reduce liquid intake before bedtime.\n• Try not to nap during the day; if you do nap, try to do so before 3 p.m. and try to keep the\nnap short (about 20 minutes).\n• Keep the bedroom as dark and quiet as possible; use a nightlight if needed, but be\naware that bright light disrupts sleep/wake patterns.\n• Calm activities at the end of the day and before bedtime may help with sleep.\n• Avoid violent movies or TV shows; strong content and images can be upsetting and can\nmake it hard to relax.\n• Be aware that changes in your environment, such as moving to a new home or having\nunexpected visitors can be disruptive and confusing for the person with dementia....\n\n...Answer: To help prevent delirium when your loved one is in the hospital, there are a few steps you can take. First, inform the doctors, nurses, and staff that your family member has cognitive impairments and express your concern about delirium. Ask them about their preventative strategies and how they plan to address the issue. You can also supplement their efforts by reducing noise in the room. If there are unnecessary alarms or bells that can be moved to a nurse's station or elsewhere, it can help create a more peaceful environment. This is important because excessive noise can disrupt sleep patterns and contribute to confusion. Additionally, if possible, try to secure a single room for your loved one rather than having them share with other patients. Sharing a room can lead to disturbances that may trigger confusion. If they must share, try to ensure that they are placed near a window. Natural light can help establish proper daytime and nighttime cues. Furthermore, it is important to advocate for your loved one's mobility. If they are capable, encourage them to sit in a chair or go for walks instead of spending all day in bed. This is because beds are primarily for sleeping, and being active during the day can help maintain a healthy sleep-wake cycle....\n\n...Help them feel calmer. Bring personal items. Sit with them when you can. Offer warm milk or a gentle back rub before bedtime.\nGetting up and walking as soon as possible has been shown to prevent and reduce the duration of delirium. Take your loved one on walks as permitted by their care team.\nWhen you come home from the hospital, make sure they are taking the right medications, in the right dose, at the right time. Medications may have been started or stopped in the hospital. If you have questions, contact the care team immediately.\nSleeping Issues\nPeople with dementia often have trouble sleeping. They might wake up a lot at night, feel confused, or think it's time to get up when it's still dark. Some may sleep during the day and stay awake at night. This can make them feel tired, confused, or cranky.\nThings to try:\nReview medications with your loved one's care team to see if any are affecting sleep.\nKeep previous sleeping and waking habits in mind.\nPlan regular physical activity, like a long walk.\nProvide a calm, predictable setting.\nCreate and keep a bedtime routine. Go to bed at the same time every night....\n\n...Question: How can a caregiver work together with their person with dementia to adjust sleep patterns?\nAnswer: As a caregiver working with someone living with dementia, it's important to help them adjust their sleep patterns together. Start by discussing and agreeing on their preferred wake-up and bedtime. It's best to wake them up at the same time every day, using an alarm if needed. Encourage them to give it a week to see how it feels. Create a restful bedroom environment by ensuring it is cool, dark, and comfortable, making adjustments based on their feedback. Help them relax before bed by asking what they would enjoy—like soothing videos with nature sounds or guided meditations. Be mindful of food and drink intake in the hours leading up to bedtime. Avoid heavy meals and limit fluids to prevent nighttime trips to the bathroom. If they must drink, keep it minimal. Encourage a consistent daytime routine of hydration. It's also wise to minimize stimulants and alcohol, especially close to bedtime. Encourage spending time in natural light during the day to promote alertness and limit exposure to bright screens at night. Medications may have been started or stopped in the hospital. If you have questions, contact the care team immediately.\nSleeping Issues\nPeople with dementia often have trouble sleeping. They might wake up a lot at night, feel confused, or think it's time to get up when it's still dark. Some may sleep during the day and stay awake at night. This can make them feel tired, confused, or cranky.\nThings to try:\nReview medications with your loved one's care team to see if any are affecting sleep.\nKeep previous sleeping and waking habits in mind.\nPlan regular physical activity, like a long walk.\nProvide a calm, predictable setting.\nCreate and keep a bedtime routine. Go to bed at the same time every night....\n\n...Question: How can a caregiver work together with their person with dementia to adjust sleep patterns?\nAnswer: As a caregiver working with someone living with dementia, it's important to help them adjust their sleep patterns together. Start by discussing and agreeing on their preferred wake-up and bedtime. It's best to wake them up at the same time every day, using an alarm if needed. Encourage them to give it a week to see how it feels. Create a restful bedroom environment by ensuring it is cool, dark, and comfortable, making adjustments based on their feedback. Help them relax before bed by asking what they would enjoy—like soothing videos with nature sounds or guided meditations. Be mindful of food and drink intake in the hours leading up to bedtime. Avoid heavy meals and limit fluids to prevent nighttime trips to the bathroom. If they must drink, keep it minimal. Encourage a consistent daytime routine of hydration. It's also wise to minimize stimulants and alcohol, especially close to bedtime. Encourage spending time in natural light during the day to promote alertness and limit exposure to bright screens at night. By working together, you can help them develop a healthier sleep schedule that honors their preferences...."}

(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41998681)\nArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in medical contexts, from clinical decision-support systems to patient-facing chatbots. While existing ethical debates focus on AI's moral or legal personhood, little attention has been given to how such systems affect human personal identity. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40271974)\nA majority of persons living with dementia rely on informal family and friend caregivers. There is currently no cure for dementia, with the condition having a significant impact on people's independence and quality of life (QoL). There are things\nyou can do to reduce your risk of dementia, like:\nBeing physically active\nBeing socially active\nEating a healthy diet\nManaging stress\nLimiting smoking & drinking\nWearing a helmet if biking, skiing, etc.\nDementia & Alzhiemer's Are NOT The Same Thing\nDementia is a general term that describes a set of symptoms affecting brain function. Alzheimer's\ndisease is just one type of dementia. There are also other types of dementias, like lewy body, vascular,\nfrontotemporal, and mixed dementias. A specific dementia diagnosis tells you more about what you\ncan expect.\nPeople Can Have A Meaningful Life With Dementia\nA dementia diagnosis doesn't mean life is over. Although abilities may change, it's still possible to live a\nmeaningful life. Below are some ways you can help your care recipient do this:\nEncourage them to participate in activities that are important or special to them. It is not a natural part of the ageing process.\nThere are different types of dementia, but the most\ncommon form is Alzheimer's disease.\nDementia is progressive, which means it begins with\nmild symptoms that get worse over time. Different\ntypes of dementia tend to affect people in different\nways, especially in the early stages.\n\n...known cause, treatment path, and progression.\nDementia is a\nnatural part of\naging.\nDementia is caused by\ndamage to brain cells.\nWhile dementia mainly affects older adults, not all\ndevelop it. For\nmore information on the different types, check out\nour Dementia Essentials toolkit.\nAlzheimer's disease\nand dementia are\nthe same.\nAlzheimer's disease is a\ntype of dementia.\nAlzheimer's is a specific disease with symptoms that\naffect memory and cognitive abilities.\nProgression\nMyth\nFact\nExplanation\n\nOne common misbelief about memory loss is that it always means you or a loved one has\ndementia. With aging, brain capacity typically grows, although there may be some slowing of processing and changes in executive function. Despite these shifts, memory, concepts, and overall cognitive ability tend to improve as one ages. An analogy compares a young person's knowledge to a small library and an older individual's to a vast collection, requiring more time to access information. Healthy living and absence of specific genetic disorders can support cognitive health well into later years. In contrast, dementia results from genetic, environmental, or lifestyle factors, causing cognitive decline that may begin 20-30 years before symptoms appear. Dementia, occurring in one's fifties, sixties, or seventies, significantly impacts daily tasks like driving and cooking. It is crucial to differentiate between normal aging and dementia, understanding that the two are not synonymous.\nQuestion: What do you hope people will take away from your film Pedacito de Carne?...\n\n...Question: Are memory problems part of normal aging?\nAnswer: As we get older, it's normal for our memory to change. These changes are a natural part of healthy aging and don't mean that we have a brain disease. We might forget a name and then remember it later, or forget where something happened and then recall it later. These types of memory lapses are common and expected as we age. However, it's important to understand that these changes are different from cognitive decline or dementia. One positive aspect of aging is the accumulation of wisdom. So, while our memories may not work as well as we want them to, it doesn't necessarily mean something is wrong. It's normal for our brains to change as we age, and some degree of memory change is a normal part of getting older. As we age, our brains undergo certain changes that can affect our memory and cognitive abilities to varying degrees. Many individuals report concerns about their memory or difficulty finding the right words as they get older. However, it is essential to distinguish between normal aging and a brain-based dementing illness like Alzheimer's. One way to differentiate these symptoms is through time. Degenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, progress and worsen over time. If an individual has experienced occasional slips in memory or word-finding difficulties that have remained relatively stable for several years, it is unlikely to be a progressive degenerative disease. Another factor to consider is the presence of other elements that may be affecting cognitive performance. For example, individuals who have been high performers but deprived of quality sleep may experience cognitive decline. In such cases, improving sleep habits or addressing sleep disorders can lead to cognitive improvement. Healthcare professionals also take the patient's complaints seriously. They often conduct cognitive testing and additional laboratory or imaging tests to assess if the structural and functional aspects of the brain are within normal limits. However, having a parent with dementia does not mean you will automatically develop it too. Dementia can result from many factors, including genetics, diet, environmental exposure, and blood pressure management over time. Here are some key points to consider: - **Genetics and Family History**: While genetics can play a role, it is not the only factor that determines whether you will get dementia. - **Lifestyle Choices Matter**: Your diet, how you manage blood pressure, and other environmental influences over your lifetime significantly contribute to your risk. - **Action Steps**: There are many proactive measures you can take, even starting a few years before a parent showed signs of dementia. Ultimately, just because a family member has dementia does not mean you are destined to get it. It is possible to avoid some risk\nfactors, while others cannot be controlled.\nThis factsheet describes the risk factors for the two most common types\nof dementia – Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia. It is written\nfor anyone who wants to know more about what increases a person's\nchances of getting dementia.\nFor advice on how to lower your chances of developing dementia, see\nbooklet 35, Dementia: reducing your risk.\n\nOverview Of The Different Kinds Of Dementia\nRead this article to learn a general summary of the 5 most common types of dementia.\nDementia is an umbrella term–it's not a diagnosis on its own. Finding out what kind of dementia your\ncare recipient has is important, it can help them understand underlying causes, know what to expect,\nand find suitable treatment.There are many types of dementia, but the following are the most common:\nAlzheimer's Disease\nThis is the most common type of irreversible dementia. It's known for symptoms of memory loss\naffecting daily life, like getting lost, asking repeated questions, or forgetting recent events. It's also\nknown for changes in judgment, reasoning, movement, mood, behavior, ability to do tasks, sleep, and\nmore.\nVascular Dementia\nVascular dementia is caused by poor or blocked blood supply to the brain, often resulting from a\nstroke, many small strokes, or cardiovascular problems. Although symptoms look very similar to\nAlzheimer's, it may progress in a step-like manner as the person continues to have small strokes,\nwhereas Alzheimer's tends to progress more consistently.\nLewy Body Dementia..."}

At the beginning, there is a preclinical phase where no one is aware of it. Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles build up silently in the brain. As the disease progresses, people start to notice changes in their ability to function. The first stage is called subjective cognitive decline, when individuals are aware that something is wrong but still perform normally on tests. In the next stage, mild cognitive impairment, day-to-day tasks become more difficult. This includes activities like making coffee, handling money, or balancing a checkbook. As the disease continues, it starts to impact basic activities of daily living such as eating, dressing, and toileting. In most cases, dementia is caused by Alzheimer's disease. Thankfully, there are several different treatment options available for Alzheimer's. The first type of treatment that is usually used is medication that helps to increase the levels of a chemical called acetylcholine. This can include medications like Donepezil (Aricept), Rivastigmine (Exelon), and Galantamine. These medications work by boosting up the levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Another medication that can be helpful is called Memantine (Namenda). This medication works by modulating two other chemicals in the brain, glutamate and dopamine. It can be especially helpful for individuals who are becoming apathetic and lack energy and motivation. Memantine is typically used in people with moderate to severe stages of Alzheimer's who are experiencing these difficulties. Lastly, for Alzheimer's, there is a new class of medications that can remove amyloid plaques from the brain and slow down the progression of the disease. These medications are still relatively new, but they show promise in treating Alzheimer's. It's important to note that these treatments are specifically for Alzheimer's, which is the most common cause of dementia....\n\n...Many Black (65%), Asian (63%), Native (61%) and Hispanic\nAmericans (60%) also thought that a cure was likely on the\nhorizon. The results must be interpreted in conjunction with other patient clinical information.\nThe risks associated with the Lumipulse G pTau217/ß-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio are mainly the possibility of false positive and false negative test results.\nFalse positive results, in conjunction with other clinical information, could lead to an inappropriate diagnosis of, and unnecessary treatment for, Alzheimer's disease. This could lead to psychological distress, delay in receiving a correct diagnosis as well as expense and the risk for side effects from unnecessary treatment.\nFalse negative results could result in additional unnecessary diagnostic tests and potential delay in effective treatment. Importantly, the Lumipulse G pTau217/ß-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio is not intended as a screening or stand-alone diagnostic test and other clinical evaluations or additional tests should be used for determining treatment options....\n\nMedications for Memory, Cognition and Dementia-Related Behaviors\nAlthough current medications cannot cure Alzheimer's, two U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved treatments address the underlying biology. Other medications may help lessen symptoms, such as memory loss and confusion.\nFDA-approved drugs for Alzheimer's\nThe FDA has approved medications that fall into two categories: drugs that change disease progression in people living with early Alzheimer's disease, and drugs that may temporarily mitigate some symptoms of Alzheimer's dementia.\nWhen considering any treatment, it is important to have a conversation with a health care professional to determine whether it is appropriate. A clinician who is experienced in using these types of medications should monitor people who are taking them and ensure that the recommended guidelines are strictly observed.\nDrugs that change disease progression\nDrugs in this category slow disease progression by going after the underlying biology of the disease process. They aim to slow the decline of memory and thinking, as well as function, in people living with Alzheimer's disease.\nAmyloid-targeting approaches...\n\n...When medications are indicated, the general advice is to:\nIt is important to see your doctor regularly while taking these medications. As the disease\nprogresses and symptoms change, the medications or doses may need to change, or the\nmedications might stop working or need to be stopped. Please consult with your doctors before\nmaking any changes to your medications and tell them about all medications you are taking,\nincluding prescription, non-prescription, vitamins, supplements and herbals.\nOverview of Medications for People with Cognitive\nImpairment\nCurrent medications can't cure Alzheimer's disease or other dementias, but they might be able to\nslow it down and make it easier to live with. They may relieve symptoms related to memory,\n• Start at a low dose and then increase slowly based on the patient's response in order to\nmaximize benefits and minimize side effects.\n• Avoid medications that may worsen memory and thinking or increase confusion, since\npeople with cognitive problems may be particularly sensitive to the effects of certain medications.\n• Avoid drug interactions that may interfere with medications used to treat cognitive problems.\n• Make one medication change at a time to understand its effect.\n\nMedications for Memory, Cognition\nand Dementia-Related Behaviors  \nAlthough current medications cannot cure Alzheimer's, two U.S. Food and\nDrug Administration (FDA)-approved treatments address the underlying\nbiology. Other medications may help lessen symptoms, such as memory loss\nand confusion.\n● FDA-approved drugs for Alzheimer's\n● Participate in clinical studies\n● Treatments at a glance\nFDA-approved drugs for Alzheimer's\nThe FDA has approved medications that fall into two categories: drugs that\nchange disease progression in people living with early Alzheimer's disease,\nand drugs that may temporarily mitigate some symptoms of Alzheimer's\ndementia.  \nWhen considering any treatment, it is important to have a conversation with a\nhealth care professional to determine whether it is appropriate. A clinician who\nis experienced in using these types of medications should monitor people who\nare taking them and ensure that the recommended guidelines are strictly\nobserved.\nDrugs that change disease progression\nDrugs in this category slow disease progression by going after the underlying\nbiology of the disease process. They aim to slow the decline of memory and\nthinking, as well as function, in people living with Alzheimer's disease....\n\n...Answer: The best treatment for dementia depends on what is causing it. In most cases, dementia is caused by Alzheimer's disease. Thankfully, there are several different treatment options available for Alzheimer's. The first type of treatment that is usually used is medication that helps to increase the levels of a chemical called acetylcholine. This can include medications like Donepezil (Aricept), Rivastigmine (Exelon), and Galantamine. These medications work by boosting up the levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Another medication that can be helpful is called Memantine (Namenda). This medication works by modulating two other chemicals in the brain, glutamate and dopamine. It can be especially helpful for individuals who are becoming apathetic and lack energy and motivation. Memantine is typically used in people with moderate to severe stages of Alzheimer's who are experiencing these difficulties. Lastly, for Alzheimer's, there is a new class of medications that can remove amyloid plaques from the brain and slow down the progression of the disease. These medications are still relatively new, but they show promise in treating Alzheimer's. It's important to note that these treatments are specifically for Alzheimer's, which is the most common cause of dementia....\n\n...Many Black (65%), Asian (63%), Native (61%) and Hispanic\nAmericans (60%) also thought that a cure was likely on the\nhorizon. White Americans were the least hopeful, with\n43% believing a cure for Alzheimer's disease was plausible in\nthis timeframe.\nA Path Forward: Facilitating the Future of\nAlzheimer's Detection, Diagnosis and Treatment\nThe 2025 Alzheimer's Disease Facts and Figures Special\nReport underscores the need to strengthen early\ndetection and diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease for more\nAmericans. Possible steps include:\n• Continuing research to discover, validate and advance\nbiomarker testing modalities.\n• Establishing clinical practice guidelines to assist with\ndetection and diagnosis and to ensure that evaluation\nand treatment are grounded in actionable evidence.\nFIGURE 25\nInterest in Options for Managing and\nTreating Alzheimer's Disease\nMedications\nthat lessen\nsymptoms\nMedications\nthat slow\nprogression\nEducation\nand support\nfor lifestyle\nchanges\nCounseling\nand\npsychotherapy\nCommunity\nresources,\nincluding\nsupport\ngroups\n100%\n80%\n60%\n40%\n20%\n47%...\n\n...if medication is needed. It may also help to have the person's eyesight\nor hearing checked.  \nThe first line of treatment for the behavioral symptoms of Alzheimer's is\nnon-drug approaches, but if these strategies fail and symptoms are\nsevere, medication may be appropriate. While antipsychotic\nmedications can be effective in some situations, they are associated\nwith an increased risk of stroke and death in older adults with dementia"}

This supports the statement that burnout in caregivers increases the risk of patients moving into institutional care.", "tf_support_injected": true, "tf_nli_label_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_confidence_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_citations_post_completion": [], "tf_nli_explanation_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_label_hop2": "", "tf_nli_confidence_hop2": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_hop2": null, "tf_nli_citations_hop2": [], "tf_nli_explanation_hop2": "", "tf_support_top_spans_hop2": [], "tf_support_top_scores_hop2": [], "tf_final_nli_label_used": "SUPPORTED", "tf_final_answer_source": "NLI_PRE", "tf_answer_llm_locked": true}, "final_answer": "Yes", "base_context_chars": 9722, "final_context_chars": 10005, "base_context": "...Answer: Leaving a loved one with dementia in a facility is not abandoning your duties as a caregiver. In fact, there are many situations where it is in the best interest of both the person with dementia and the caregiver to consider an alternative living environment. One of the main reasons is safety. If the person is prone to falls, constantly trying to leave, or engaging in dangerous behaviors like turning on the stove, it becomes crucial to place them in an environment that can ensure their safety. Sometimes, the decision to move to a facility is also driven by emotional factors. Caregivers can become overwhelmed and burnt out after a long period of providing care. They may need the help and support of a team of professionals, which is not possible when they are the sole caregiver at home. Caring for someone with dementia can be exhausting, and it is important to recognize when it is no longer feasible to continue alone. The decision to move a loved one into residential care is unique for every family, and only you can determine the right time. However, I strongly encourage you to work with healthcare professionals, friends, and family to identify red flags and establish a plan. It is heartbreaking when caregivers reach a breaking point and need to find a facility urgently without prior preparations....\n\nOf the 5.8 million people in the United States living with Alzheimer's disease and other\ntypes of dementia, the majority live in their own homes over the course of their\nillness—even in those in more advanced stages and at end-of life.\nAnd home care isn't always easier — meeting the complex and ever-changing care\nneeds for people with dementia can be challenging and caregiving often falls on the\nshoulders of family members and friends. And while caregiving can be rewarding,\ncaregivers can burn out and experience greater health problems themselves, physical\nand emotional burden, as well as financial strains from lost time at work or from paying\nout of pocket for care or services, experts warn.\n“The care of dementia is actually the care of two people: the person with the illness and\nthe person taking care of them,” says Johns Hopkins geriatric psychiatrist Deirdre\nJohnston, M.D. But when Johnston and a team of researchers studied more than 600\nBaltimore residents with dementia and their caregivers, they found a staggering 97% to\n99% of both groups had unmet dementia-related care needs....\n\n...Answer: As a caregiver for someone with dementia, you may find yourself facing tough decisions about whether or not to break a promise you made to never put them in a nursing home or long-term care. It's important to remember that everyone's journey with dementia is different, and what may have seemed like the right decision at the time may no longer be feasible or safe as the disease progresses. It's okay to reassess and revisit your plans as needed. Instead of holding yourself rigidly to a promise, consider the benefits and drawbacks of keeping the person in the community or at home versus moving them to a nursing home. Think about their safety, the level of care they require, and your own well-being. It's natural for circumstances to change, and it's important to prioritize what is best for both the person with dementia and yourself as their caregiver. In life, things don't always go according to plan. We may have envisioned a certain retirement age or future, but circumstances can alter our course. Similarly, as a caregiver, it's crucial to be adaptable and approach decisions with an open mind. Educate yourself about the progression of dementia, stay informed, and regularly reassess your decisions and plans. Set aside time every six months or annually to review and adjust your caregiving strategies as necessary....\n\n...Answer: There is a common misconception that nursing homes are bad for people living with dementia, but in many cases, it can actually be the best decision for both the individual with dementia and their family members. The hesitation around nursing homes often stems from stigma and the cultural belief that we should be able to handle everything ourselves. But it's important to recognize that nursing homes are simply one option among many. There are certain circumstances where nursing home care may be very appropriate. For example, if physically caring for the person with dementia puts their safety or yours at risk, if they are prone to wandering or are at risk of falls, if they have a complex medication schedule that is difficult to manage, or if there is no identified primary caregiver available. In these situations, a nursing home can provide 24-hour supervision and ensure the person's safety. Many family members who have made the decision to move their loved ones into a long-term care facility have expressed surprise at how beneficial it has been. There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible....\n\n...What makes burnout different from normal stress is that the stress is not being released through healthy coping mechanisms. As a result, burnout inhibits your ability to effectively manage the demands of caregiving. This is especially concerning in the context of dementia, a degenerative and terminal condition. Caregiver burnout not only impacts the caregiver's well-being but also hinders their ability to provide quality care for their loved one. It is important to recognize the signs of burnout and take steps to prevent or address it. Caregivers' health and well-being matter, both for their own sake and for the sake of the person they are caring for....\n\ndependence on family carers or community nursing services to\nassist with medicines management. Self‐report and informant\nreport on ability to safely managing medication may be helpful\nbut can be unreliable or prone to bias. Measures of cognitive\nfunction are useful but may lack sensitivity and specificity.\nDirect observation, using a structured, standardised\nperformance‐based tool, may help to determine whether a\nperson is able to manage their medicines and identify barriers to\nadherence such as inability to open medicine packaging.\nGillespie et al.\n(2014)31\nTo explore published literature that describes what is known about\nthe role of informal caregivers as they manage medications for\nolder adults and/or people living with dementia residing in the\ncommunity.\n10 articles reviewed\nNarrative review.\nThe role of informal caregiver is complex and often made more\ndifficult because of increasing medication regimen complexities,\naspects of the relationship between the caregiver and the care\nrecipient, health care system practices, and a lack of information\nand/or training available to the informal caregiver, especially\nwhen caring for people living with dementia.\n(Continues)\nTABLE 3\n(Continued)\nLIM AND SHARMEEN\n\n...Answer: If you're wondering how to determine if someone with dementia is no longer safe in their current living environment, there are a few things to consider. First, it's important to understand that people with dementia can continue living in their own homes, rely on someone else's home, or move to a formal care facility like a nursing home or assisted living. The key is to assess what the person needs in order to stay safe in their day-to-day life. Think about basic daily tasks such as eating, using the restroom, and knowing what to do in an emergency. Can the person with dementia do these things on their own? If not, is there someone who can help them? It's crucial to evaluate both the person with dementia and their surroundings. For example, would they know how to react in a home invasion or fire? Can they distinguish spoiled food from fresh food? Are they vulnerable to scams? As a caregiver, you may start noticing signs of unsafety when you run errands or spend time away from home. Perhaps you return to find something unusual or potentially dangerous has occurred, like the person wandering away and not remembering their way back. These are red flags that intervention is needed to prevent emergencies. Assess the areas where help is necessary and consider whether the person is currently receiving that support or if more is required....\n\nHowever, some individuals vulnerable to poor health outcomes may self-select into the\ncaregiver role, and high distress levels and attendant morbidity could partially be explained\nby personal or family variables not related to the caregiving experience per se.12 Caregivers\nwho have negative beliefs about their ability to cope and those who feel trapped in their role\nhave higher rates of morbidity, and depressive symptoms, and they turn to\ninstitutionalization of the patient more quickly.13\nWHY IS CAREGIVING STRESSFUL?\nFor dementia caregivers the strongest predictor of caregiver burden, depressive symptoms,\nand physical health issues are primary stressors, such as the patient's behavior problems,\nincluding day and nighttime wandering, emotional outbursts, and inappropriate\nbehavior.14,15 However, the type of dementia and the type of behavioral problems most\nclosely associated with it may play a role in caregiver distress as well.16,17 Dementia\ncaregivers experience more burden when caregiving intensity is higher and when they\nexperience fewer perceived benefits or uplifts. However, I strongly encourage you to work with healthcare professionals, friends, and family to identify red flags and establish a plan. It is heartbreaking when caregivers reach a breaking point and need to find a facility urgently without prior preparations....\n\nOf the 5.8 million people in the United States living with Alzheimer's disease and other\ntypes of dementia, the majority live in their own homes over the course of their\nillness—even in those in more advanced stages and at end-of life.\nAnd home care isn't always easier — meeting the complex and ever-changing care\nneeds for people with dementia can be challenging and caregiving often falls on the\nshoulders of family members and friends. And while caregiving can be rewarding,\ncaregivers can burn out and experience greater health problems themselves, physical\nand emotional burden, as well as financial strains from lost time at work or from paying\nout of pocket for care or services, experts warn.\n“The care of dementia is actually the care of two people: the person with the illness and\nthe person taking care of them,” says Johns Hopkins geriatric psychiatrist Deirdre\nJohnston, M.D. But when Johnston and a team of researchers studied more than 600\nBaltimore residents with dementia and their caregivers, they found a staggering 97% to\n99% of both groups had unmet dementia-related care needs....\n\n...Answer: As a caregiver for someone with dementia, you may find yourself facing tough decisions about whether or not to break a promise you made to never put them in a nursing home or long-term care. It's important to remember that everyone's journey with dementia is different, and what may have seemed like the right decision at the time may no longer be feasible or safe as the disease progresses. It's okay to reassess and revisit your plans as needed. Instead of holding yourself rigidly to a promise, consider the benefits and drawbacks of keeping the person in the community or at home versus moving them to a nursing home. Think about their safety, the level of care they require, and your own well-being. It's natural for circumstances to change, and it's important to prioritize what is best for both the person with dementia and yourself as their caregiver. In life, things don't always go according to plan. We may have envisioned a certain retirement age or future, but circumstances can alter our course. Similarly, as a caregiver, it's crucial to be adaptable and approach decisions with an open mind. Educate yourself about the progression of dementia, stay informed, and regularly reassess your decisions and plans. Set aside time every six months or annually to review and adjust your caregiving strategies as necessary....\n\n...Answer: There is a common misconception that nursing homes are bad for people living with dementia, but in many cases, it can actually be the best decision for both the individual with dementia and their family members. The hesitation around nursing homes often stems from stigma and the cultural belief that we should be able to handle everything ourselves. But it's important to recognize that nursing homes are simply one option among many. There are certain circumstances where nursing home care may be very appropriate. For example, if physically caring for the person with dementia puts their safety or yours at risk, if they are prone to wandering or are at risk of falls, if they have a complex medication schedule that is difficult to manage, or if there is no identified primary caregiver available. In these situations, a nursing home can provide 24-hour supervision and ensure the person's safety. Many family members who have made the decision to move their loved ones into a long-term care facility have expressed surprise at how beneficial it has been. There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible....\n\n...What makes burnout different from normal stress is that the stress is not being released through healthy coping mechanisms. As a result, burnout inhibits your ability to effectively manage the demands of caregiving. This is especially concerning in the context of dementia, a degenerative and terminal condition. Caregiver burnout not only impacts the caregiver's well-being but also hinders their ability to provide quality care for their loved one. It is important to recognize the signs of burnout and take steps to prevent or address it. Caregivers' health and well-being matter, both for their own sake and for the sake of the person they are caring for....\n\ndependence on family carers or community nursing services to\nassist with medicines management. Self‐report and informant\nreport on ability to safely managing medication may be helpful\nbut can be unreliable or prone to bias. Measures of cognitive\nfunction are useful but may lack sensitivity and specificity.\nDirect observation, using a structured, standardised\nperformance‐based tool, may help to determine whether a\nperson is able to manage their medicines and identify barriers to\nadherence such as inability to open medicine packaging.\nGillespie et al.\n(2014)31\nTo explore published literature that describes what is known about\nthe role of informal caregivers as they manage medications for\nolder adults and/or people living with dementia residing in the\ncommunity.\n10 articles reviewed\nNarrative review.\nThe role of informal caregiver is complex and often made more\ndifficult because of increasing medication regimen complexities,\naspects of the relationship between the caregiver and the care\nrecipient, health care system practices, and a lack of information\nand/or training available to the informal caregiver, especially\nwhen caring for people living with dementia.\n(Continues)\nTABLE 3\n(Continued)\nLIM AND SHARMEEN\n\n...Answer: If you're wondering how to determine if someone with dementia is no longer safe in their current living environment, there are a few things to consider. First, it's important to understand that people with dementia can continue living in their own homes, rely on someone else's home, or move to a formal care facility like a nursing home or assisted living. The key is to assess what the person needs in order to stay safe in their day-to-day life. Think about basic daily tasks such as eating, using the restroom, and knowing what to do in an emergency. Can the person with dementia do these things on their own? If not, is there someone who can help them? It's crucial to evaluate both the person with dementia and their surroundings. For example, would they know how to react in a home invasion or fire? Can they distinguish spoiled food from fresh food? Are they vulnerable to scams? As a caregiver, you may start noticing signs of unsafety when you run errands or spend time away from home. Perhaps you return to find something unusual or potentially dangerous has occurred, like the person wandering away and not remembering their way back. These are red flags that intervention is needed to prevent emergencies. Assess the areas where help is necessary and consider whether the person is currently receiving that support or if more is required....\n\nHowever, some individuals vulnerable to poor health outcomes may self-select into the\ncaregiver role, and high distress levels and attendant morbidity could partially be explained\nby personal or family variables not related to the caregiving experience per se.12 Caregivers\nwho have negative beliefs about their ability to cope and those who feel trapped in their role\nhave higher rates of morbidity, and depressive symptoms, and they turn to\ninstitutionalization of the patient more quickly.13\nWHY IS CAREGIVING STRESSFUL?\nFor dementia caregivers the strongest predictor of caregiver burden, depressive symptoms,\nand physical health issues are primary stressors, such as the patient's behavior problems,\nincluding day and nighttime wandering, emotional outbursts, and inappropriate\nbehavior.14,15 However, the type of dementia and the type of behavioral problems most\nclosely associated with it may play a role in caregiver distress as well.16,17 Dementia\ncaregivers experience more burden when caregiving intensity is higher and when they\nexperience fewer perceived benefits or uplifts. Interestingly, although patient physical\nimpairments increase burden for caregivers of nondemented patients, this is rarely the case\nfor dementia caregivers.14..."}

These findings are important because caregivers who are isolated\nand lonely tend to feel more burden than those who feel socially connected (Sung et al., 2023),\nwhile caregivers who perceive that they have adequate social support are better able to cope\nwith challenges, manage stress, and provide care (Lai & Thomson, 2018)....\n\nAmong the reasons shared by caregivers for providing\nassistance to a person with Alzheimer's or another\ndementia are the desire to keep a family member or friend\nat home (65%), close proximity to the person with dementia\n(48%), and the caregiver's perceived obligation to the\nperson with dementia (38%).A10 In addition, caregivers often\nindicate love and a sense of duty when describing what\nmotivates them to assume care responsibilities for a\nrelative or friend living with dementia.508\nOne-third of people living with dementia have received\nhelp from family members at least two years prior to a\npositive dementia screen from a health care provider.509\nIndividuals with dementia living in the community are\nmore likely than older adults without dementia to rely on\nmultiple unpaid caregivers (often family members); 30% of\nolder adults with dementia rely on three or more unpaid\ncaregivers, whereas 23% of older adults without dementia\ndo so.510 Only a small percentage (8%) of older adults with\ndementia do not receive help from family members or\nother informal care providers. Of these individuals, nearly\nhalf live alone, perhaps making it more difficult to ask for...\n\nCaregiving\nBurden and Stress\n• Compared with caregivers of people without\ndementia, caregivers of those with dementia indicate\nmore substantial emotional, financial and physical\ndifficulties.516, 574\n• Fifty-nine percent of family caregivers of people with\nAlzheimer's or other dementias rated the emotional\nstress of caregiving as high or very high (Figure 12).A10\n• Spousal dementia caregivers are more likely than\nnon-spousal dementia caregivers to experience\nincreased burden over time. This increased burden\nalso occurs when the person with dementia develops\nbehavioral changes and decreased functional ability.610\n• Many people with dementia have co-occurring\nchronic conditions, such as hypertension or arthritis,\nwhich may complicate caregiving. For example, a\nnational study found that caregivers of people with\ndementia who had a diagnosis of diabetes or\nosteoporosis were 2.6 and 2.3 times more likely,\nrespectively, to report emotional difficulties with care\ncompared with caregivers of people with dementia\nwho did not have these co-occurring conditions.611..."}

It can be frustrating for them when they can't recall something, and they may experience various emotions. One way to approach this is to deal with the emotional truth of the situation. In some types of dementia, the person may not be aware that they were supposed to remember or they may not have formed the memory in the first place, which is a common symptom of Alzheimer's disease. In other cases, such as vascular dementia, they may have difficulty retrieving the memory but can with prompting. For those with minimal memory problems, using reminders like sticky notes or technology-based supports can be helpful. It's important not to ask questions that imply that they should remember or shame them for their forgetfulness. Instead, present information in a way that supports their memory or use distraction and redirection techniques to shift the focus to something else. Remember, it's not their fault and they are trying their best. Being understanding and patient will go a long way in supporting someone with dementia....\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\n...A person with dementia might become more aware of the\nchanges they are experiencing.\nThey may be unable to continue with hobbies and tasks\nthey enjoy.\nThe person may have seen, heard or thought of something\nwhich has caused anxiety, but which they cannot remember\nor explain.\nThey may be responding to hallucinations and how\nthey interpret what they see – see factsheet 527, Changes\nin perception.\nIf the person feels anxious and needs to walk, go with them if\npossible. Try to encourage them to tell you why they are feeling\nthis way. Reassure them, for example by holding their hand if\nappropriate. If they are\nwalking too fast, try to keep pace with them and gradually go\nslower to encourage them to slow down too. However, it's important to approach this with empathy and understanding. Firstly, not all of these memories are necessarily fabricated. Sometimes, clients share historical events that only a few family members knew about, so it's possible that what may seem made up is actually true. Secondly, it's important to remember that dementia affects the person's cognitive abilities and their brain. This supports the statement that patients with dementia cannot control much of their behavior as the disease progresses.", "tf_support_injected": true, "tf_nli_label_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_confidence_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_citations_post_completion": [], "tf_nli_explanation_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_label_hop2": "", "tf_nli_confidence_hop2": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_hop2": null, "tf_nli_citations_hop2": [], "tf_nli_explanation_hop2": "", "tf_support_top_spans_hop2": [], "tf_support_top_scores_hop2": [], "tf_final_nli_label_used": "SUPPORTED", "tf_final_answer_source": "NLI_PRE", "tf_answer_llm_locked": true}, "final_answer": "Yes", "base_context_chars": 9052, "final_context_chars": 10120, "base_context": "...Question: Is the person with dementia doing things on purpose to make me upset?\nAnswer: Living with someone who has dementia can be challenging, especially when it feels like their actions are intentional and aimed at upsetting you. However, it's important to understand that individuals with dementia do not have the mental capacity to purposefully cause distress. While it may feel like their behavior is intentional, it is not. It can be difficult to navigate these emotions, but having a support group, whether it's family, friends, or a support network, is crucial. It's essential to have someone you can talk to and vent your frustrations. Remember, as the disease progresses, you will likely realize that their actions were not intentional. In the meantime, it's important to find strategies and support to help you cope with the challenges on a day-to-day basis.\nQuestion: How can you deal with someone with dementia always getting fixated on one subject?...\n\nMany people with dementia become confused and disorientated at times. This may lead to\nthem believing things that are not true – known as ‘false beliefs' or ‘delusions'. Our dementia\nspecialist Admiral Nurses explain why this might happen, and how you can help the person\nyou care for.\nCollapse all\nWhat are false beliefs and delusions?\nEveryone has different personal beliefs. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\n...of medications.41 Lastly, we are relying on self-report of\nmedication responsibilities and abilities and did not\ndirectly observe behaviors.\nCONCLUSION\nIn conclusion, individuals with MCI and mild dementia\nmanage their medications independently, often until a\nmistake is observed and caregivers subsequently assume\nmedication-related responsibilities. Among individuals\nwith moderate dementia, caregivers manage the majority\nof medication responsibilities, but many cannot directly\nobserve intake. As a trusted third party, clinicians can\ninitiate conversations about transitioning medication\nduties from older adults with dementia to family caregivers as their memory loss progresses. Clinicians can\nDYADIC MANAGEMENT OF MULTIDRUG REGIMENS\n15325415, 2024, 10, Downloaded from Wiley Online Library on [27/05/2025]. See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License\n\na sudden change in someone's behaviour or thinking, or if they appear more confused\nthan usual, make an urgent appointment with their GP.\nSigns of false beliefs and delusions\nSigns of false beliefs and delusions in people with dementia include:\n● claiming that someone is stealing from them or trying to harm them\n● hiding possessions to keep them safe\n● phoning the police frequently\n● refusing to open the door or answer the phone\n● talking in whispers, and saying things such as: “They can hear us”\n● trying to carry out activities they used to do, like going to school or work\n● mistaking people's identities\n● believing they're in a different place\n● reliving past traumas or events\nIt's important to remember that sometimes, the claims the person with dementia is\nmaking may be true, and someone could be stealing from them or taking advantage of\ntheir vulnerability. This needs to be carefully checked before you conclude that what\nthey are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. The frequency of aggression tends to increase as the disease progresses. Understanding the triggers for this behavior is crucial in managing it effectively. Disorientation can trigger agitation and aggression, even when individuals are in their own homes. Changes in the surroundings or the feeling of not being at home anymore can contribute to this behavior. Personal care activities, such as bathing or dressing, can also provoke frustration and aggression. In some cases, aggression can be a manifestation of underlying depression that individuals with Alzheimer's find difficult to express. It is important to note that aggression can also indicate pain or other medical conditions. Surprisingly, even constipation can be a potential cause. Table 21A13 shows the\naverage per-person Medicare payments for seven specific\nmedical conditions among beneficiaries who have\nAlzheimer's or other dementias and beneficiaries who do\nUse and Costs of Health Care Services by State\nSubstantial geographic variation exists in health care\nutilization and Medicare payments by individuals with...\n\nCaregiving\nCreated from data from the National Alliance for Caregiving in Partnership with the Alzheimer's Association.518\ndementia expenses and/or provided care for someone\nwith dementia at least once a month in the prior year)\nrevealed that 48% cut back on other spending and 43%\ncut back on savings due to the out-of-pocket costs of\nproviding help to someone with dementia.598 Due to care\nresponsibilities, close to 4 in 10 care contributors\nindicated that the “food they bought just didn't last, and\nthey didn't have money to get more,” and 3 in 10 ate less\nbecause of care-related costs.598\nOne in five caregivers of people with Alzheimer's or\nother dementias (22%) report problems dealing with\na bank or credit union when helping to manage the\nfinances of people living with dementia, compared with\n9% of caregivers of people without dementia.518\nEffects of Stress and Other Caregiving Factors on\nPeople with Dementia\nResearch has documented the effects of caregiver stress\non people with dementia and their use of health care\nservices. For example, distress on the part of family...\n\n...explanation for the spike in health care costs in the year\nimmediately before and the year immediately after\ndiagnosis of Alzheimer's or another dementia relates to\ndelays in timely diagnosis. One group of researchers\nfound that individuals with cognitive decline who\nobtained care from a specialist (that is, a neurologist,\npsychiatrist or geriatrician) had a shorter time to\ndiagnosis of Alzheimer's disease.969 Additionally,\nindividuals diagnosed with cognitive impairment by a\nspecialist had lower Medicare costs in the year after\nreceiving a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia than those\ndiagnosed by a non-specialist.\nImpact of Alzheimer's and Other Dementias on\nthe Use and Costs of Health Care in People with\nCoexisting Medical Conditions\nNearly 9 out of 10 Medicare beneficiaries with Alzheimer's\ndisease or other dementias have at least one other chronic\ncondition.485 Additionally, they are more likely than those\nwithout dementia to have other chronic conditions.485\nOverall, 2.7 times more Medicare beneficiaries with\nAlzheimer's or other dementias have four or more chronic\nconditions (excluding Alzheimer's disease and other...\n\n...These findings indicate that the new blood test can reliably predict the presence or absence of amyloid pathology associated with Alzheimer's disease at the time of the test in patients who are cognitively impaired. The test is intended for patients presenting at a specialized care setting with signs and symptoms of cognitive decline. The results must be interpreted in conjunction with other patient clinical information.\nThe risks associated with the Lumipulse G pTau217/ß-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio are mainly the possibility of false positive and false negative test results.\nFalse positive results, in conjunction with other clinical information, could lead to an inappropriate diagnosis of, and unnecessary treatment for, Alzheimer's disease. This could lead to psychological distress, delay in receiving a correct diagnosis as well as expense and the risk for side effects from unnecessary treatment.\nFalse negative results could result in additional unnecessary diagnostic tests and potential delay in effective treatment. Importantly, the Lumipulse G pTau217/ß-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio is not intended as a screening or stand-alone diagnostic test and other clinical evaluations or additional tests should be used for determining treatment options....\n\nsupervision and personal care as the disease progresses.\nAs the person with dementia's symptoms worsen,\ncaregivers can experience increased emotional stress and\ndepression; neglect of their own health due to caregiving\npriorities;590, 591 new or exacerbated health problems; and\ndepleted income and finances due in part to disruptions\nin employment and paying for health care or other\nservices for both themselves and the person living\nwith dementia.592-599\nCaregiver Emotional and Social Well-Being\nThe intimacy, shared experiences and memories that\nare often part of the relationship between a caregiver\nand person living with dementia may be threatened due\nto memory loss, functional impairment and psychiatric/\nbehavioral disturbances that can accompany the\nprogression of dementia. In the National Poll on Healthy\nAging, however, 45% of caregivers of people with\ndementia indicated that providing help to someone with\ncognitive impairment was very rewarding.522 In the\nNational Study of Caregiving, greater satisfaction from\ndementia caregiving was associated with more emotional\nsupport from family members and friends.600 Although\ncaregivers report positive feelings about caregiving,...\n\n...Question: Does stress cause Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Stress does not appear to be a major factor in causing Alzheimer's disease. The main contributors to the disease are the build-up of two proteins, amyloid and tau. Other risk factors, such as midlife hypertension, smoking, high cholesterol, and diabetes, seem to affect the blood vessels and have a greater impact on developing Alzheimer's than stress. However, stress can still affect the brain, particularly the hippocampus, which is important for memory. The stress hormone cortisol can have negative effects on this area of the brain. While stress may not play a significant role in the build-up of amyloid and tau, more research is needed for a clearer understanding.\nQuestion: How is mental health related to brain health?..."}

BPSD constitute a major component of\nthe dementia syndrome irrespective of its subtype. They are as clinically relevant as cognitive symptoms as they strongly correlate with the degree of functional and cognitive\nimpairment. Moreover, over 60% of participants presented with a chief complaint of\nbehavioral symptoms, which was more frequent than memory complaints [11]. "/Users/minjie/Desktop/code/rag_adrd/code/logs/20260729_132038/critic/ADRD_TF_016.md", "tf_support_top_spans": ["Taking a strengths-based, personcentered and sustainable approach can ensure that the needs of people living with dementia\nand their caregivers are served long term. ...collaborative, primary care-based models that bring\ntogether different members of the health care and\ncommunity-based workforces to care for people and their\ncaregivers across the Alzheimer's disease continuum.894, 895\nThese collaborative models have been associated with a\nrange of benefits, including reduced behavioral symptoms,\nimproved function and quality of life, decreased caregiver\nburden, and lower health care costs related to\nhospitalizations, emergency department visits and other\noutpatient visits.895-897\nAs one example of collaborative dementia care, the\nAlzheimer's and Dementia Care Program is a health\nsystems-based model in which nurse practitioners with\nextensive training in dementia care, known as dementia\ncare specialists (DCSs), co-manage care with PCPs and\ncommunity-based partners.", "It is important to consider a person's preferences and\nstrengths when deciding what might be the best fit for them. (550) Those who were more...\n\nQuestion: What is delirium?\nAnswer: Delirium is a common problem for individuals with cognitive impairments, such as dementia. It is characterized by fluctuations in alertness or arousal, which refers to how awake and attentive a person is to their surroundings and themselves. When someone experiences delirium, they may be confused and unaware of their location or the activities they are engaged in. Sometimes, they may even attribute themselves to the wrong place or task. This state of confusion is usually temporary, lasting from a few minutes to several days or even weeks as the person recovers. Delirium is an important issue to be aware of when caring for someone with cognitive impairments.\nQuestion: What is an elder law attorney?...\n\n...Question: Are people with dementia higher risk for surgery?\nAnswer: People with dementia, such as Alzheimer's disease, may be at a higher risk for developing delirium after surgery. Delirium is a state where people have problems with attention and confusion caused by a medical event or condition. Anesthesia and surgery can sometimes trigger delirium in individuals with dementia. However, if someone with dementia needs to have an operation, it is still possible for them to undergo it safely. There are steps that can be taken to lessen the risk of delirium, as we know that people with Alzheimer's disease are not only more prone to delirium but also may experience a faster progression of cognitive symptoms after an episode of delirium. In this case, prevention is vital, and specific measures can be implemented to try and prevent delirium after surgery.\nQuestion: Are there any recommended medications for congestion in someone with dementia?...\n\n...Question: What are the most common reasons for someone with dementia to go to the emergency room?\nAnswer: People with dementia often visit the emergency room for common issues like cough, shortness of breath, stomach problems, pain, and skin rashes. They may also go due to sudden confusion, known as delirium, which is more common in dementia patients. Falls are another reason, raising challenges in determining the cause, any injuries, and preventing future falls. Those living in care facilities can be sent to the emergency room by staff. Clear communication is crucial to ensure information transfer between facility staff and emergency healthcare providers for effective treatment. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41892502)\nBackground:  Delirium is a frequent and serious complication in elderly patients with hip fractures and is associated with adverse outcomes. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41716318)\nBackground Postoperative dysphagia is increasingly recognized as a common but underdiagnosed complication in older adults undergoing hip fracture surgery, and is associated with adverse outcomes such as aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, prolonged hospitalization, and delayed rehabilitation. However, evidence regarding its reported incidence and influencing factors remains fragmented and heterogeneous. Objective This scoping review aimed to map the existing evidence on the incidence, assessment methods, and factors associated with postoperative dysphagia in older adults undergoing hip fracture surgery, and to identify knowledge gaps relevant to perioperative management and rehabilitation. Therefore, it is crucial to use anticholinergic medications carefully and monitor their effects closely in patients with dementia.\nQuestion: At what stage of dementia does incontinence occur?\nAnswer: Incontinence, or the inability to control urination or bowel movements, is a common occurrence for patients with dementia. While it typically occurs in the moderate to severe stages of dementia, it can also happen earlier on. The timing of incontinence varies from patient to patient.\nQuestion: What are the different types of incontinence?\n\n07.010\n150. In addition\nto neurodegenerative processes, several factors, such as chronic\nor acute pain (e.g., arthritis), sleep disturbances, sensory\nimpairment, acute medical illness (e.g., infections, respiratory\ndiseases, urinary retention, renal failure), or metabolic changes\n(38),\ngenerate\nagitated\nbehavior.\nPsychological\nfactors,\ndepression, or psychological distress may also be involved\n(39). Sundowning, the ensuing agitation upon the dimming of\nnatural light as happens in the evening, is another predisposing\ncondition for agitation (40). Moreover, acute onset of agitation\ncan be triggered by changes in medication regimens or\ndrug side eﬀects (e.g., with antipsychotics or anticholinergic\ndrugs) (40).\nHospitalization is another well-known trigger of agitation\neither alone or as a manifestation of hyperkinetic delirium in\npeople with dementia (41).\nFinally, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2...\n\n...Question: What is the effect of anticholinergic medications in FTD?\nAnswer: Anticholinergic medications block a brain chemical called acetylcholine, which can be useful in some situations like inducing sleep or controlling involuntary movements. However, in frontotemporal dementia and other types of dementia, these medications typically worsen symptoms. They can cause excessive sedation, confusion, lethargy, slowed cognition, hallucinations, and delusions. It's best to avoid anticholinergic drugs whenever possible. Some medications, like Benadryl, have hidden anticholinergic effects that may lead to confusion. It's important to consult your doctor or pharmacist about the potential effects of medications if you have concerns.\nQuestion: Should Namenda (memantine) be used in people who have FTD?\n\n...inflammation and infection, such as pneumonia, can interfere\nwith brain function and cause delirium. Some people with\ndelirium will have hallucinations. Delirium is a medical emergency\n– for more information see page 1.\nHallucinations are a rare side effect of many medications. The\nmedicines for Parkinson's disease can often trigger hallucinations.\nSpeak to your GP before making any changes to medication.\nSome people with worsening vision start to see things that aren't\nthere (visual hallucinations) because of their deteriorating sight\nand not from any other condition, such as dementia or a mental\nhealth problem. This is called Charles Bonnet syndrome.\nHow does a person experience\nhallucinations?\nSome people with dementia will have hallucinations in different\nsenses – for example:\nauditory hallucinations – hearing things that aren't there,\nlike voices or footsteps\nolfactory hallucinations – smelling things that aren't there,\nsuch as smoke or perfume\ntactile hallucinations – physically feeling things that aren't\nthere, such as being kissed or insects crawling over their skin\ngustatory hallucinations – tasting things that aren't there,...\n\nTrade-off\nbetween\nbenefits and\nharms\nAt the time of diagnosis\nThe committee agreed that although the evidence they had seen was in\nrelation to a generally older aged population, there should be little\ndifference for people living with dementia. Although the effects of\nanticholinergic burden may differ by population, the specific drugs that\ncause the largest anticholinergic burden are likely to remain the same. It\nnoted that there may be implications for community prescribers to assess\ncognition before prescribing medications, in order to recognise that some\ndrugs may affect anticholinergic burden.\nThe committee agreed that, at the time of considering a diagnosis of\ndementia, it would be appropriate to reduce the level of anticholinergic\ndrugs being used, if possible alternatives were available, in order to rule\nout potential false diagnoses, and a ‘consider' recommendation was made\non this point.\nThe committee agreed that, whilst many of the classes of drugs with high\nanticholinergic activity were understood widely by clinicians, there were\nother individual drugs where the high level of anticholinergic activity was...\n\n...emergency. You should make an urgent appointment with the GP\nor call the NHS 111 telephone service. Delirium can be triggered\nby an untreated health condition. Most of the causes of delirium\nare treatable, such as constipation, dehydration or infections.\nDelirium can cause people to have hallucinations or delusions,\nbecome confused, drowsy, or distressed. For more information\ngo to alzheimers.org.uk/delirium\nWhat is perception?\nInformation from the sense organs, for example the eyes or\nears, travels to the brain. The brain processes this information,\nto understand it. The brain then analyses it alongside other\ninformation already in the brain, such as thoughts and memories\nand their associated emotions. Then the person becomes aware\nof what has been sensed (perceived).\nMy 93-yearold mother has\nbeen having\nfalse memories.\nNo matter what\nevidence is shown\nto her to prove\nthat what she is\nclaiming never\nhappened, she\nwill not back down\nand begins to get\nangry.\nFamily member\nof a person with\ndementia"}

However, there are medications that can help with these delusions. Delusions are a part of a group of symptoms called psychosis, and to treat this, we use a class of medications called antipsychotics. It's important to note that antipsychotics do come with risks, so it's crucial to balance the risks and benefits. If the delusions are extremely distressing, such as having a false belief that someone is coming to harm you, then the potential benefits of medication may outweigh the risks. However, it's important to only use antipsychotics for psychosis and not for other symptoms of dementia. In cases of delusions and hallucinations, it can be helpful to consult a geriatric psychiatry nurse practitioner or a dementia specialist provider. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42131829)\nSleep is a complex process thought to be regulated by both a circadian system closely tied to ambient light and a homeostatic process characterized by increasing pressure to sleep commensurate with increasing duration of wakefulness. Critical illness is often a complex, multi-system physiological insult characterized by high levels of stress hormones and inflammatory biomarkers as well as pain and anxiety which negatively impacts sleep. Sleep loss may potentiate physiological disturbances and is increasingly being linked to poor ICU outcomes. The current gold standard for improving the sleep of ICU patients is to bundle multiple non-pharmacologic interventions; medication should only be prescribed for sleep when those measures failed to produce the desired results. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42191189)\nObjectives This study aimed to identify potential significant statistical associations between the development of delirium, medication and several other patient-specific factors across a 10-year retrospective longitudinal real-world dataset. Design A retrospective, population-based cohort study. Setting The National University Hospital of Iceland. Participants All patients≥18 years hospitalised between 2010 and 2020. Primary and secondary outcome measures The primary outcome was a diagnosis of delirium within 2 years of a patient filling a prescription for a specific medication. The exposure was pre-admission medication use or a pre-existing condition. Secondary outcomes included mortality, length of hospital stay, readmission rate and frequency of additional delirium diagnosis. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42065220)\nHip fractures represent a time-critical, systemic condition in older adults, characterised by frailty, multimorbidity, inflammation, immobility, pain, and high risk of medical complications and mortality. While population ageing is expected to drive a continued rise in absolute hip fracture numbers, contemporary evidence demonstrates declining age-standardised incidence in many high-income countries, highlighting the importance of optimising perioperative care pathways to mitigate morbidity and mortality. Contemporary evidence consistently supports early surgical management, typically within 24-48 h, provided reversible medical issues are addressed in parallel rather than through prolonged preoperative workup. In addition, it is essential to monitor the health of people discharged from\nhospital with delirium. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41547868)\nBackground Compound paracetamol and amantadine hydrochloride capsules are commonly used over-the-counter medications at the primary care level. The primary component, amantadine, is excreted via the kidneys and poses a risk of accumulation in older patients, while chlorphenamine may increase the risk of delirium. This study examines the relationship between this medication and abnormal behavior by presenting case studies of two older patients and discussing clinical management strategies. Case presentation Case 1 involved a 78-year-old Chinese male with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 87 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , who developed visual hallucinations, delirium, and balance disturbances after five consecutive days of medication. He scored 8 on the Nursing Delirium Screening Scale. S\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Blonanserin transdermal patch for treating delirium: A case series. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42124932)\nAim Antipsychotics are commonly recommended for the treatment of delirium; however, alternative options are warranted due to the limitations of oral and injectable formulations. The blonanserin (BNS) transdermal patch may improve treatment adherence; however, evidence regarding its efficacy in managing delirium remains limited. Methods This retrospective case series describes 51 cases of delirium managed with BNS patches at Kyoto University Hospital between January 2020 and June 2022. The effectiveness of the BNS patch for delirium, the rationale for its selection, and the associated adverse events were retrospectively evaluated using electronic medical records. This term is used interchangeably with aberrant motor behavior and encompasses a range of\nactivities such as wandering away from home; repetitive, purposeless behaviors; social inappropriate activities including those\nassociatedwithdisinhibition(tendencytodisregardsocialandcultural norms and not restrain inner feelings, such as sexual drives).\nAccording to Cohen-Mansﬁeld (1999) four distinct categories of\nagitation are: (1) physically non-aggressive behavior; (2) verbally\nnon-aggressive behavior; (3) physically aggressive behavior; and\n(4) verbally aggressive behavior.\nCIRCADIAN RHYTHMS\nSleeppatternchangesmayoccurasaconsequenceof normalaging,\nbut are particularly prevalent in individuals with dementia. If they don't have the language skills to communicate what they\nneed, they may communicate through their behaviors. Agitation and aggression\ncan be a sign of an emotional or physical need.\nWhy Does This Happen?\n\nCoping With Agitation, Aggression, and\nSundowning in Alzheimer's Disease\nEspañol\nPeople with Alzheimer's disease may become agitated or\naggressive as the disease gets worse. Agitation means that\na person is restless and worried, and they aren't able to\nsettle down. Agitated people may pace a lot, not be able to\nsleep, or act aggressively toward others. They may verbally\nlash out or try to hit or hurt someone. When these problems\nstart to happen or worsen in the late afternoon or early\nevening, it's called sundowning. On this page, learn about\nthe causes of agitation, aggression, and sundowning and\nhow to manage them.\nCauses of agitation and aggression\nMost of the time, agitation and aggression happen for a\nreason. When they happen, try to find the cause, then talk\nwith a health care provider about possible solutions. Causes\nof agitation and aggression can include:\n\n...do something they previously could. Or they may feel a general\nsense of agitation but not know why.\nAgitation can take many forms. For example, a person who is\nagitated may be irritable, restless and keep fidgeting. They may\nwalk up and down, move objects, fixate on tasks such as tidying,\nor try to leave the house. For more information, see factsheet 501\nWalking and dementia.\nAggressive behaviour\nA person with dementia may behave in aggressive ways.\nAggressive behaviour can be:\nverbal – for example, swearing, screaming, shouting or\nmaking threats\nphysical – for example, hitting, pinching, scratching,\nhair-pulling or biting.\nFor more information, see factsheet 509 Aggressive behaviour.\n\nAggressive behaviors may be verbal or physical. They can\noccur suddenly, with no apparent reason, or result from a\nfrustrating situation. While aggression can be hard to cope with,\nunderstanding that the person with Alzheimer's or dementia is\nnot acting this way on purpose can help.\n● Causes\n● How to respond\nCauses\nAggression can be caused by many factors including physical\ndiscomfort, environmental factors and poor communication.
