If they don't have the language skills to communicate what they\nneed, they may communicate through their behaviors. Agitation and aggression\ncan be a sign of an emotional or physical need.\nWhy Does This Happen?\n\nCoping With Agitation, Aggression, and\nSundowning in Alzheimer's Disease\nEspañol\nPeople with Alzheimer's disease may become agitated or\naggressive as the disease gets worse. Agitation means that\na person is restless and worried, and they aren't able to\nsettle down. Agitated people may pace a lot, not be able to\nsleep, or act aggressively toward others. They may verbally\nlash out or try to hit or hurt someone. When these problems\nstart to happen or worsen in the late afternoon or early\nevening, it's called sundowning. On this page, learn about\nthe causes of agitation, aggression, and sundowning and\nhow to manage them.\nCauses of agitation and aggression\nMost of the time, agitation and aggression happen for a\nreason. When they happen, try to find the cause, then talk\nwith a health care provider about possible solutions. Causes\nof agitation and aggression can include:\n\n...do something they previously could. Or they may feel a general\nsense of agitation but not know why.\nAgitation can take many forms. For example, a person who is\nagitated may be irritable, restless and keep fidgeting. They may\nwalk up and down, move objects, fixate on tasks such as tidying,\nor try to leave the house. For more information, see factsheet 501\nWalking and dementia.\nAggressive behaviour\nA person with dementia may behave in aggressive ways.\nAggressive behaviour can be:\nverbal – for example, swearing, screaming, shouting or\nmaking threats\nphysical – for example, hitting, pinching, scratching,\nhair-pulling or biting.\nFor more information, see factsheet 509 Aggressive behaviour.\n\nAggressive behaviors may be verbal or physical. They can\noccur suddenly, with no apparent reason, or result from a\nfrustrating situation. While aggression can be hard to cope with,\nunderstanding that the person with Alzheimer's or dementia is\nnot acting this way on purpose can help.\n● Causes\n● How to respond\nCauses\nAggression can be caused by many factors including physical\ndiscomfort, environmental factors and poor communication. If\nthe person with Alzheimer's is aggressive, consider what might\nbe contributing to the change in behavior.\nPhysical discomfort\n● Is the person able to let you know that he or she is\nexperiencing physical pain? It is not uncommon for\npersons with Alzheimer's or other dementias to have\nurinary tract or other infections. Due to their loss of\ncognitive function, they are unable to articulate or identify\nthe cause of physical discomfort and, therefore, may\nexpress it through physical aggression.\n● Is the person tired because of inadequate rest or sleep?\n● Is the person hungry or thirsty?"}

This supports the statement that people with Alzheimer's disease suffer from a wide range of behavioral and psychological symptoms.", "tf_support_injected": true, "tf_nli_label_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_confidence_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_citations_post_completion": [], "tf_nli_explanation_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_label_hop2": "", "tf_nli_confidence_hop2": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_hop2": null, "tf_nli_citations_hop2": [], "tf_nli_explanation_hop2": "", "tf_support_top_spans_hop2": [], "tf_support_top_scores_hop2": [], "tf_final_nli_label_used": "SUPPORTED", "tf_final_answer_source": "NLI_PRE", "tf_answer_llm_locked": true}, "final_answer": "Yes", "base_context_chars": 8384, "final_context_chars": 9590, "base_context": "In the past, people experiencing apathy had to present with signs that affected\nat least two out of three domains—behavior/cognition, emotion, and social\ninteraction—over a period of four weeks. These domains have been updated to\ninclude anhedonia (decreased interest in things you used to enjoy), decreased\ninitiative, and decreased motivation.2\nOther symptoms associated with apathy include:2  \nImpaired concentration  \nReduced libido (sexual drive)  \nFatigue\nApathy is a common symptom of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.\nPeople with depression may also experience apathy or similar symptoms.3\nApathy vs. Depression\nApathy can be a common symptom of depression, but you do not need to be\ndepressed to experience apathy. Like depression, you might experience it later\nin life. Apathy can be difficult to diagnose in older adults because apathy and\ndepression have similar presentations among this population.3\nApathy and depression share some symptoms, but there are a few key\ndifferences.\nCommon Characteristics of Apathy and Depression\nApathy\nDepression\n\nSymptoms of depression\nIdentifying depression in someone with Alzheimer's can be\ndifficult, since dementia can cause some of the same\nsymptoms. Examples of symptoms common to both depression\nand dementia include:\n● Apathy\n● Loss of interest in activities and hobbies\n● Social withdrawal\n● Isolation\n● Trouble concentrating\n● Impaired thinking\nIn addition, the cognitive impairment experienced by people\nwith Alzheimer's often makes it difficult for them to articulate\ntheir sadness, hopelessness, guilt and other feelings associated\nwith depression.\nDepression in Alzheimer's doesn't always look like depression\nin people without Alzheimer's. Here are some ways that\ndepression in a person with Alzheimer's may be different:\n● May be less severe\n● May not last as long and symptoms may come and go\n● The person with Alzheimer's may be less likely to talk\nabout or attempt suicide\nAs a caregiver, if you see signs of depression, discuss them\nwith the primary doctor of the person with dementia. Proper\n\n...Some of these symptoms overlap with those of depression,\nsuch as losing interest in things and lacking energy. This is\nwhy it can be hard to know whether a person has depression\nor apathy, even for a doctor. The main difference between\nthe two conditions is that depression involves more negative\nfeelings, such as sadness or guilt (see ‘Symptoms of depression'\non page 3).\nA person with apathy may not be worried by their symptoms.\nHowever, it can reduce their quality of life if they are less able to\ndo things that are enjoyable or fulfilling.\nApathy can also put a strain on family and friends who are trying\nto help and support them. It can be hard to care for someone\nevery day who doesn't seem to mind what happens to them, or\nthose around them. The Dementia Support Forum is an online\nplace for families, friends and carers of people with dementia\nto share experiences. Visit forum.alzheimers.org.uk or call our\nDementia Support Line on 0333 150 3456.\nI don't worry\nabout it, just…\nsit here. That's all\nyou can do. She...\n\nremain stable across a 31-month period (Selbæk and Engedal,\n2012).\nThe debate about the deﬁnition of the several psychiatric\nand behavioral symptoms in dementia continues as a number\nof symptoms (apathy, sleep, and eating disturbances) have not\nbeen grouped consistently across studies. Particularly, the relation\nbetween apathy (highly prevalent in dementia) and the “mood”\nsub-syndrome remains unclear. However, a multi-faceted approach involving lifestyle changes like exercise, mental activities, and a healthy diet is seen as more effective for Alzheimer's. Focusing on just one aspect may not yield the same benefits as combining several strategies. Ongoing clinical trials by the FINGER network are investigating the impacts of these multi-pronged interventions on dementia. Results from these studies are anticipated in the near future, offering hope for more effective treatment approaches for individuals living with dementia.\nQuestion: Why should someone see a speech therapist for dementia?\n\nBrain Exercises and Dementia\nMedically Reviewed by Christopher Melinosky, MD on December 03, 2024 Written by Annie Stuart\n3 min read\nCan you help your brain stay healthy as you age by doing things that challenge your mind?\nCould that also help you avoid memory loss, or even prevent or delay dementia such as\nAlzheimer's?\nScientists need to do more research to find out for sure. But a number of studies show there are\nbenefits to staying mentally active.\nHere's what we know about the impact of exercising your brain.\nCan brain exercises help delay memory loss or dementia?\nWhen people keep their minds active, their thinking skills are less likely to decline, medical\nresearch shows. So games, puzzles, and other types of brain training may help slow memory\nloss and other mental problems.\nOne study involved more than 2,800 adults 65 and older. They went to up to 10 hour-long braintraining sessions for 5 to 6 weeks. The sessions focused on tactics for these skills:\nMemory\nReasoning\nSpeed of processing information\nPeople who took the training showed improvement in these skills that lasted for at least 5 years....\n\n...Neither education nor brain exercises are a sure way to prevent Alzheimer's. But they may help\ndelay symptoms and keep the mind working better for longer.\nSources\nUpdate History\nPrint\nView privacy policy, copyright and trust info\nSave\nNEXT ARTICLE\nSudden Memory Loss: Causes, Symptoms, and Treatment  \nAlzheimers\n\nQuestion: Can Alzheimer's disease be prevented?\nAnswer: Prevention of Alzheimer's disease specifically is not yet possible, as we still do not fully understand how to prevent the accumulation of amyloid plaques and tau protein tangles in the brain. However, there is evidence that a healthy lifestyle can delay or prevent the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, which is ultimately what we call a dementia syndrome. Maintaining a healthy lifestyle involves eating a well-balanced diet, getting regular aerobic exercise that increases blood flow to the brain, and ensuring you get enough sleep, including both light, deep, and REM sleep. Managing other chronic conditions, such as diabetes or high blood pressure, is also important for brain health. It's not just physical health that plays a role, but social engagement is also beneficial. Engaging in healthy activities with people you enjoy spending time with can have positive effects on your brain. While activities like crossword puzzles and Sudoku may improve specific cognitive skills, they don't necessarily transfer to real-life tasks. So while it's good to keep your brain active, it's important to have a holistic approach to brain health.\nQuestion: How can primary care doctors help me prevent dementia and keep my brain healthy?...\n\n...Answer: The amount of exercise you should do to optimize your brain health varies, but there are some guidelines that can help. Studies show that engaging in a moderate amount of aerobic exercise for at least 30 minutes, five days a week, or some form of resistance training, can be beneficial. The term \"moderate\" means more than just a leisurely stroll - it should be a brisk walk as if you're in a hurry. These types of exercise have been found to be correlated with a reduced risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. On the other hand, being sedentary can increase your risk of developing Alzheimer's. For example, the presence of a gene variant called APOE4, which is known to increase the risk of Alzheimer's, can lead to a smaller hippocampus, the part of the brain essential for forming new memories. However, engaging in regular exercise can help prevent this decrease in hippocampus size, even for individuals with this gene variant. So, the bottom line is that being sedentary is a risk factor for Alzheimer's, while regular physical activity can help reduce that risk. Although there is no exact formula, incorporating moderate aerobic exercise or resistance training into your routine can be beneficial for your brain health....\n\n...Answer: Exercise has a significant impact on brain health, particularly in relation to reducing the risk of developing dementia. Numerous studies have shown that aerobic exercise and strength training, especially for the lower extremities, can lower the risk of Alzheimer's by 40 to 60%. If there was a pill that could achieve these results, everyone would take it. The recommended amount of exercise is approximately 30 minutes of aerobic exercise, like brisk walking, four to five times a week. Being sedentary is detrimental to brain health, as it can lead to shrinkage of the hippocampus. The brain requires a significant amount of energy, with 20% of the body's energy devoted to its functioning, despite comprising only 2% of body mass. This energy comes from the blood supply, which delivers oxygen and glucose to the brain. If there is a compromise in blood flow, the brain cells may not function optimally, making them vulnerable to dementia in the future. The exact mechanisms by which exercise benefits brain health are not fully understood, but research suggests that maintaining good heart health and a healthy vasculature is crucial. Exercise helps shuttle glucose into the brain cells, supporting their optimal function. Therefore, exercise is a vital component in promoting brain health and reducing the risk of dementia....\n\n...Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2017;72(6):733-739.\n145. If there is a compromise in blood flow, the brain cells may not function optimally, making them vulnerable to dementia in the future. The exact mechanisms by which exercise benefits brain health are not fully understood, but research suggests that maintaining good heart health and a healthy vasculature is crucial. Exercise helps shuttle glucose into the brain cells, supporting their optimal function. Therefore, exercise is a vital component in promoting brain health and reducing the risk of dementia....\n\n...Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2017;72(6):733-739.\n145. Does brain training help?\nOne study found that exercising the mind delayed declines in thinking skills. After people started\nhaving Alzheimer's symptoms, though, mental decline sped up in those who kept their minds\nengaged. It's possible that being mentally active bolstered the brain at first, so symptoms didn't\nshow up until later.\nThe silver lining here? People who regularly challenge their minds may spend a shorter part of\ntheir lives in a state of decline, even if they do get Alzheimer's.\nWhat kinds of brain exercises should I do?\nThat may vary from person to person. But the main idea seems to be keeping your brain active\nand challenged. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42337959)\nAlzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder driven by intersecting pathological processes. Persistent attrition in AD drug-development pipelines highlights the limited clinical impact of single-target therapies and has increased interest in multi-target approaches acting on shared biological hubs. Although recent strategies extend beyond amyloid-centered interventions, much of the evidence supporting multifunctional compounds remains preclinical or shows heterogeneous outcomes in advanced clinical stages. This narrative review examines drug candidates that have entered Phase III clinical trials in the last decade, with emphasis on emerging multitarget pharmacotherapies such as muscarinic M1 receptor agonists, dual M1/sigma-1 receptor (σ1R) agonists, and dual σ1R\n\n[WEB:europepmc] The word Dementia should be retired. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42286130)\nThe word Dementia should be retired.\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Evolving national dementia policies in the OECD: Prevention, diagnosis, and care. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42222904)\nDementia incurs yearly costs of nearly 1.3 trillion US dollars worldwide, projected to rise significantly in the coming decades due to population aging. This policy review provides an overview of the latest national dementia strategies, diagnostic guidelines, and treatment guidelines across 38 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries. Our findings suggest that national dementia policies increasingly emphasize prevention through modifiable risk factors, early diagnosis, and non-pharmacological treatment approaches, progressing toward more coordinated care pathways. Clinical guidelines have evolved to incorporate new research evidence and practices in dementia diagnostics and treatment over the past decade. In Alzheimer's, the brain's neurons...\n\n...Question: How long do people with dementia live?\nAnswer: Dementia is a condition where a person has cognitive impairment, including severe memory loss that affects their daily life. There are different causes of dementia, with Alzheimer's disease being the most common. Other forms include dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia. Some forms of dementia progress quickly, such as Jakob-Creutzfeldt disease, which can lead to death in a matter of months. However, for most cases, like Alzheimer's disease, the progression is much slower. The time between diagnosis and passing away can range from six to 11 years. In some cases, the progression is even slower, while in others it may be faster. We have some understanding of why this variation occurs in different individuals, but it is difficult to determine someone's prognosis accurately. The best approach is to observe the person over time to gauge the trajectory of their condition. Our goal is to slow down the progression of dementia, allowing individuals to live long and meaningful lives despite the challenges it poses.\nQuestion: At what stage of dementia do behavioral symptoms usually start?...\n\n...Answer: When embarking on the journey of caring for someone with dementia, it's important to understand that it can be a long and challenging road. This journey can stretch out for many years, even with rare forms of dementia like frontotemporal dementia. Life expectancy can range from two to 20 years. I often refer to this experience as a marathon because it requires endurance and strength. Unfortunately, physicians are not always equipped to provide the support and guidance needed in this journey. They may give a diagnosis and focus solely on treating symptoms, leaving caregivers feeling uncertain and adrift. In the beginning, it is crucial to educate yourself about the disease. This learning process starts as soon as the diagnosis is given. Attend classes, seek knowledge, and become familiar with all aspects of the disease. Remember, you are not alone. Millions of people are going through the same journey and connecting with others who understand can be invaluable. Surround yourself with individuals who can provide support and guidance. These fellow caregivers will offer practical advice and empathetic understanding that doctors may not provide. Take care of yourself, too. Organize your paperwork, build a support network, and prioritize self-care. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...Question: What should I do if a person living with dementia is angry?\nAnswer: Responding to anger in someone with dementia can be challenging, but understanding the reasons behind it can help. In many cases, anger is linked to delusions or hallucinations where the person believes someone is stealing from them or has harmed them. Correcting these false beliefs can often alleviate the anger. If the anger persists without an apparent cause, it's essential to uncover the root of their frustration. For example, when a person with dementia is placed in a long-term care facility, they may become angry with their family members. In these situations, healthcare providers often advise families to redirect the blame onto themselves. This way, the person with dementia may eventually forget their anger towards their family. When environmental interventions fail to alleviate the anger, medication may be considered. Mood stabilizers or antidepressants can sometimes help manage anger or address underlying depression contributing to the anger. However, it's crucial to understand the context surrounding the anger before considering medication. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41795663)\nIntroduction Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPSs) are common in dementia, but their patterns in preclinical stages remain unclear. This study identified NPS clusters and associated health factors in a geriatric clinical population. Methods We analyzed 1234 participants from the Italian GERIatric COgnitive evaluation memory clinic cohort with Neuropsychiatric Inventory data. Clusters were derived using machine learning (K-means, Elbow method) separately for dementia and dementia-free groups. Associations were assessed via multinomial logistic regression. Results In the overall cohort, four NPS clusters emerged: minimal NPS, depression-anxiety-apathy, depression-anxiety, and delusions-agitation-irritability. Cluster profiles differed between the dementia and dementia-free groups. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41743052)\nIntroduction Agitation is a common and burdensome symptom in people with dementia, particularly when compounded by impaired communication, making early detection and effective management difficult. Wearable sensor technologies may offer a promising avenue for supporting real-time behavioral monitoring and personalized care in this context. Objective This study aims to examine the current clinical and technological capabilities of wearable sensor systems for detecting and managing agitation in persons with dementia, to assess whether these technologies can effectively support personalized care. Additionally, it seeks to identify key challenges and opportunities in applying human-centered design principles and tailored interventions to improve outcomes for both patients and caregivers. It's important to give them one activity at a time and break it down into simple steps. Folding towels, vacuuming, sweeping, watering the garden or indoor plants, and taking care of a pet are all examples of tasks that can be done with one or two steps. Reminders may be necessary, but it's better to focus on one activity at a time instead of overwhelming them with a long list of tasks. By providing guidance and support, individuals with dementia can still feel a sense of independence and accomplishment around the house.\nQuestion: Should I keep traditions alive when someone has dementia?...\n\n...A person with dementia may enjoy an outing, even if they do not remember where they\nhave been. What is important is that the moment is enjoyed, even though the\nexperience may be soon forgotten.\nSimple and unhurried activities are best. Give the time and space necessary to allow\nthe person to do as much as possible. Focus on one thing at a time. Communicate one\ninstruction at a time. Break down activities into simple, manageable steps.\nPrepare a safe working area\nPeople with dementia often have difficulty with visual perception and coordination.\nEnsure that surfaces are uncluttered, with few distractions and as little noise as\npossible. Good lighting (without glare), seating preferences and correct work heights are\nalso important. Use plastic containers to help avoid breakages.\nDon't allow activities to reinforce inadequacy or increase stress. Levels of ability can\nchange from day to day. Activities can be adapted and tried another time if they were\nnot successful or enjoyable the first time.\nUse times that suit the person's best level of functioning\n\nbreak down the tasks into simple steps and go one at a time  \nexplain each step using simple, respectful language  \noffer clear questions with limited options, like “Would you like to\nhave a bath or a shower?” or “Would you like to have your bath\nnow or before bed?”  \nlay out the equipment for the task in the order that they'll be\nused: for a shower, lay out the soap, face washer, towel and then\nclean clothes.\nWashing, baths and\nshowers\nBathing can be a particularly tricky task for someone living with\ndementia. They might:  \nfeel embarrassed about undressing in front of someone else,\nparticularly if they're experiencing incontinence  \nfind the room too hot or cold, too bright or dark  \nfeel water temperature and the sensation of running water\ndifferently than they used to  \nfeel scared: of falls, deep water, the intense physical sensations\ninvolved, or something else.\nThese are some things you can try.\n\nQuestion: What are some easy activities for someone with dementia?\nAnswer: When it comes to engaging someone who is living with dementia, it's important to choose activities that are simple and easy. Even basic tasks like doing laundry or making a sandwich can be too complicated for someone with moderate to late stage dementia. These tasks require a lot of mental effort and can become overwhelming. Instead, it's helpful to think about activities that are one or two steps and can provide a break for the caregiver. For example, listening to music can be a soothing and enjoyable activity. Stringing beads onto a string or sorting items like silverware can also be engaging and not too challenging. Folding towels is another great activity that can give a sense of purpose and accomplishment. For instance, one person I work with has their spouse put already clean towels into the dryer for a quick spin, and then they work together to fold them. This allows the caregiver to feel helpful and involved in the household tasks. These activities provide both mental stimulation and a sense of meaning for individuals living with dementia. They also allow caregivers to have a few minutes of respite to attend to their own needs.\nQuestion: What kind of music should I play for someone with dementia?...\n\n...OR\nSevere Dementia\nWhen dementia has progressed to the point that a person may not remember people they love and has difficulty with talking, eating, walking, and other basic activities, this is known as severe dementia. At this stage, your loved one is fully dependent on others for all activities of daily living, including personal care and mobility. We should focus on keeping the person comfortable and happy. A care partner steps in as a decision maker on their behalf, ensuring that their needs and preferences are respected.\nIntroduction\nCaring for someone with moderate to severe dementia can be meaningful and challenging. At this stage, your loved one needs help with many daily tasks. They may still enjoy familiar faces, favorite music, or simple routines, but memory, judgment, and communication are more limited. Over time, the skills we learn as teenagers and adults (like cooking, shopping, handling money, or using the phone) and even some skills learned in early childhood (like bathing, dressing, eating, or toileting) can require full assistance. Your role as a care partner is to support comfort, safety, and dignity each day — with guidance from your care team and the practical ideas below.\nGoals...\n\n...bowls with a contrasting color place mat. Avoid patterned dishes,\ntablecloths and place mats.\n● Check the food temperature. A person living with dementia might not be\nable to tell if something is too hot to eat or drink. Always test the\ntemperature of foods and beverages before serving.\n● Offer one food item at a time. The person may be unable to decide\namong the foods on his or her plate. Serve only one or two items at a\ntime. For example, serve mashed potatoes followed by the main entree.\n● Be flexible with food preferences. It is possible the person may suddenly\ndevelop certain food preferences or reject foods he or she may have\nliked in the past.\n● Allow plenty of time to eat. Keep in mind that it can take an hour or more\nfor\nthe person to finish.\n● Eat together. Break down activities into simple, manageable steps.\n\n\nCITATIONS:\n- SPAN 0\n- SPAN 1\n- SPAN 2\n=== END TOP EVIDENCE (TF) ===\n\nQuestion: What are some simple activities someone with dementia can do to help around the house?\nAnswer: People living with dementia can still contribute to household tasks and activities. It's important to give them one activity at a time and break it down into simple steps. Folding towels, vacuuming, sweeping, watering the garden or indoor plants, and taking care of a pet are all examples of tasks that can be done with one or two steps. Reminders may be necessary, but it's better to focus on one activity at a time instead of overwhelming them with a long list of tasks. By providing guidance and support, individuals with dementia can still feel a sense of independence and accomplishment around the house.\nQuestion: Should I keep traditions alive when someone has dementia?...\n\n...A person with dementia may enjoy an outing, even if they do not remember where they\nhave been. What is important is that the moment is enjoyed, even though the\nexperience may be soon forgotten.\nSimple and unhurried activities are best. Give the time and space necessary to allow\nthe person to do as much as possible. Focus on one thing at a time. Communicate one\ninstruction at a time. Break down activities into simple, manageable steps.\nPrepare a safe working area\nPeople with dementia often have difficulty with visual perception and coordination.\nEnsure that surfaces are uncluttered, with few distractions and as little noise as\npossible. Good lighting (without glare), seating preferences and correct work heights are\nalso important. Use plastic containers to help avoid breakages.\nDon't allow activities to reinforce inadequacy or increase stress. Levels of ability can\nchange from day to day. Activities can be adapted and tried another time if they were\nnot successful or enjoyable the first time.\nUse times that suit the person's best level of functioning\n\nbreak down the tasks into simple steps and go one at a time  \nexplain each step using simple, respectful language  \noffer clear questions with limited options, like “Would you like to\nhave a bath or a shower?” or “Would you like to have your bath\nnow or before bed?”  \nlay out the equipment for the task in the order that they'll be\nused: for a shower, lay out the soap, face washer, towel and then\nclean clothes.\nWashing, baths and\nshowers\nBathing can be a particularly tricky task for someone living with\ndementia. They might:  \nfeel embarrassed about undressing in front of someone else,\nparticularly if they're experiencing incontinence  \nfind the room too hot or cold, too bright or dark  \nfeel water temperature and the sensation of running water\ndifferently than they used to  \nfeel scared: of falls, deep water, the intense physical sensations\ninvolved, or something else.\nThese are some things you can try.\n\nQuestion: What are some easy activities for someone with dementia?\nAnswer: When it comes to engaging someone who is living with dementia, it's important to choose activities that are simple and easy. Even basic tasks like doing laundry or making a sandwich can be too complicated for someone with moderate to late stage dementia. These tasks require a lot of mental effort and can become overwhelming. Instead, it's helpful to think about activities that are one or two steps and can provide a break for the caregiver. For example, listening to music can be a soothing and enjoyable activity. Stringing beads onto a string or sorting items like silverware can also be engaging and not too challenging. Folding towels is another great activity that can give a sense of purpose and accomplishment. For instance, one person I work with has their spouse put already clean towels into the dryer for a quick spin, and then they work together to fold them. This allows the caregiver to feel helpful and involved in the household tasks. These activities provide both mental stimulation and a sense of meaning for individuals living with dementia. They also allow caregivers to have a few minutes of respite to attend to their own needs.\nQuestion: What kind of music should I play for someone with dementia?...\n\n...OR\nSevere Dementia\nWhen dementia has progressed to the point that a person may not remember people they love and has difficulty with talking, eating, walking, and other basic activities, this is known as severe dementia. At this stage, your loved one is fully dependent on others for all activities of daily living, including personal care and mobility. We should focus on keeping the person comfortable and happy. A care partner steps in as a decision maker on their behalf, ensuring that their needs and preferences are respected.\nIntroduction\nCaring for someone with moderate to severe dementia can be meaningful and challenging. At this stage, your loved one needs help with many daily tasks. They may still enjoy familiar faces, favorite music, or simple routines, but memory, judgment, and communication are more limited. Over time, the skills we learn as teenagers and adults (like cooking, shopping, handling money, or using the phone) and even some skills learned in early childhood (like bathing, dressing, eating, or toileting) can require full assistance. This behavior is known as \"shadowing,\" and it involves the person positioning themselves behind you and occasionally touching you. They may also ask repetitive questions or say the same things over and over again. It's important to understand that they are not doing this on purpose, but rather because they see you as someone they trust to guide them and keep them safe. However, if this behavior continues, it can be tiring and frustrating for you as the caregiver. To address this issue, it may be helpful to introduce a third person into the situation who can take on some of the caregiving responsibilities. This person should be someone the person with dementia can trust and who understands where to go and what to do. By building this triad early on, you can provide the person with dementia with another person to follow and rely on, giving you the opportunity to take a break and have your own needs met. If necessary, you may need to seek help from a volunteer, a family member, or even hire someone to give you some respite time. And while caregiving can be rewarding,\ncaregivers can burn out and experience greater health problems themselves, physical\nand emotional burden, as well as financial strains from lost time at work or from paying\nout of pocket for care or services, experts warn.\n“The care of dementia is actually the care of two people: the person with the illness and\nthe person taking care of them,” says Johns Hopkins geriatric psychiatrist Deirdre\nJohnston, M.D. But when Johnston and a team of researchers studied more than 600\nBaltimore residents with dementia and their caregivers, they found a staggering 97% to\n99% of both groups had unmet dementia-related care needs....\n\n...Answer: If you have someone living with dementia who is constantly following you, it can be overwhelming and make it difficult to have any time alone, even to go to the bathroom. This behavior is known as \"shadowing,\" and it involves the person positioning themselves behind you and occasionally touching you. They may also ask repetitive questions or say the same things over and over again. It's important to understand that they are not doing this on purpose, but rather because they see you as someone they trust to guide them and keep them safe. However, if this behavior continues, it can be tiring and frustrating for you as the caregiver. To address this issue, it may be helpful to introduce a third person into the situation who can take on some of the caregiving responsibilities. This person should be someone the person with dementia can trust and who understands where to go and what to do. By building this triad early on, you can provide the person with dementia with another person to follow and rely on, giving you the opportunity to take a break and have your own needs met. If necessary, you may need to seek help from a volunteer, a family member, or even hire someone to give you some respite time. Remember, it's important to care for yourself so that you can continue to care for your loved one with dementia....\n\n...OR\nSevere Dementia\nWhen dementia has progressed to the point that a person may not remember people they love and has difficulty with talking, eating, walking, and other basic activities, this is known as severe dementia. At this stage, your loved one is fully dependent on others for all activities of daily living, including personal care and mobility. We should focus on keeping the person comfortable and happy. A care partner steps in as a decision maker on their behalf, ensuring that their needs and preferences are respected.\nIntroduction\nCaring for someone with moderate to severe dementia can be meaningful and challenging. At this stage, your loved one needs help with many daily tasks. They may still enjoy familiar faces, favorite music, or simple routines, but memory, judgment, and communication are more limited. Over time, the skills we learn as teenagers and adults (like cooking, shopping, handling money, or using the phone) and even some skills learned in early childhood (like bathing, dressing, eating, or toileting) can require full assistance. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42333920)\nUse of technology is widespread in healthcare, and although much has been written about innovative technology in support of older adults, little research focuses on whether technology facilitates person-centeredness-the ability to serve individuals' interest, values, goals, and needs. This structured narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the multidimensional impact of dementia caregiving on the physical, psychological, cognitive, social, and financial health of spousal caregivers. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36834069)\nIntroduction Today, antiretroviral therapy (ART) is effectively used as a lifelong therapy to treat people living with HIV (PLWH) to suppress viral replication. Moreover, PLWH need an adequate care strategy in an interprofessional, networked setting of health care professionals from different disciplines. HIV/AIDS poses challenges to both patients and health care professionals within the framework of care due to frequent visits to physicians, avoidable hospitalizations, comorbidities, complications, and the resulting polypharmacy. The concepts of integrated care (IC) represent sustainable approaches to solving the complex care situation of PLWH. First, it's important to understand that confusion is a common symptom of dementia. So, it's essential to figure out what the confusion is related to. Can you talk through it or work through it with them? If not, and you've already tried different strategies, phrases, and ideas, there are other things you can do. Keeping the person as active as possible during the day can help. Encourage them to walk, socialize, or even attend an adult day program. Staying active during the day can make them tired at night and may help reduce confusion. Additionally, it's important to regulate day and night for individuals with dementia. Let them see the sun during the day and close the blinds at night, helping them differentiate between day and night. This simple routine can often help with the confusion they experience.\nQuestion: How do I encourage a person with dementia to get out of bed after they wake up?...\n\n...around specific topics.\nJoin Now\n● Encourage the person living with dementia to get plenty of rest.\n● Schedule activities such as doctor appointments, trips and bathing in\nthe morning or early afternoon hours when the person living with\ndementia is more alert.\n● Encourage a regular routine of waking up, eating meals and going to\nbed.\n● When possible, spend time outside in the sunlight during the day.\n● Make notes about what happens before sundowning events and try to\nidentify triggers.\n\n...they are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. You\ncould say something like: “The thought that someone has stolen your purse\nmust be very distressing. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...Answer: If someone living with dementia is repeatedly getting up at night, it's important to approach the situation with curiosity. This behavior could be a new pattern, and it's worth exploring why it's happening. First, determine if it's waking you up or if you're already awake and noticing their restlessness. Sometimes, people with dementia may go to bed early and naturally wake up after a few hours to use the bathroom. However, if they are consistently not getting deep sleep or having difficulty staying in bed, there may be an unmet need that needs to be addressed. It could be hunger, thirst, lack of daytime activity, nighttime stress or distress, difficulty with urination or bowel movements, respiratory issues like sleep apnea, discomfort from conditions like arthritis or restless leg syndrome, or feeling disoriented or unfamiliar in their surroundings. It's crucial to examine our own reactions to this behavior and ensure that we're not unintentionally making it harder for them to rest and go back to sleep. Be curious about the underlying causes and discuss them with someone who can provide guidance. A1\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Structural MRI in frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease: stage-dependent atrophy patterns. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42082780)\nDifferentiating Alzheimer's disease (AD) from frontotemporal dementia (FTD) remains a major clinical challenge, particularly in early disease stages when phenotypic overlap is common and in later stages when cortical degeneration becomes widespread. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides a widely available, non-invasive framework for assessing region-specific brain atrophy patterns associated with these disorders. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on MRI-based approaches for distinguishing FTD from AD across disease stages. FTD, particularly the behavioral variant, is characterized by early and prominent degeneration of frontal and anterior temporal networks, frequently with hemispheric asymmetry and early behavioral change, including apathy as a core feature\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Longevity and cognitive resilience in a Colombian family carrying the &lt;i&gt;APOE&lt;/i&gt; ε2 variant. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42244184)\nAPOE  is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Despite global efforts to promote resilience, delay cognitive decline, and slow aging,  APOE  ε2, one of the most robust resilience-associated variants, remains relatively underexplored in translational research. Exceptional longevity offers a window into cognitive trajectories. We present clinical, cognitive and neuroimaging data from five  APOE  ε2/ε3 siblings aged 94-105. Cognition ranged from normal to mild dementia. MRI showed less atrophy than expected for advanced age, and FDG-PET revealed preserved metabolism. Findings demonstrate  APOE  ε2-associated resilience in the oldest-old and offer insight into mechanisms of exceptional cognitive aging with potential translational relevance.\n\n[WEB:europepmc] A Severe Symptomatic Case of Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities After Donanemab Infusion. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42311735)\nAmyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) are known complications of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody therapy for Alzheimer's disease. Although many cases are asymptomatic, severe presentations can mimic stroke or toxic encephalopathy. This case highlights a rare presentation of ARIA with myoclonic movements and acute encephalopathy following donanemab infusion. We report a 75-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease who developed acute confusion, hallucinations, and involuntary movements one day after her sixth donanemab infusion. Stroke workup was negative. MRI demonstrated findings consistent with both ARIA-E and ARIA-H. She was treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, followed by an oral prednisone taper, which resulted in gradual neurological improvement. Clinicians mu\n\n...Question: What are the more rare causes of dementia?\nAnswer: There are several rare types of dementia that fall into three categories. The first category includes chronic traumatic encephalopathy and other disorders that can be caused by repetitive head impacts. This can occur from things like concussions and similar injuries. The second category is made up of disorders that resemble Alzheimer's disease. These include primary age-related tauopathy (PART) and limbic predominant age-related TDP43 encephalopathy (LATE). We usually refer to PART and LATE to make it easier. The third category consists of disorders that affect a person's ability to move well. This includes progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), cortical basal degeneration (CBD), and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). So, in summary, the rare types of dementia can be grouped into those caused by repetitive head impacts, Alzheimer's disease lookalikes, and disorders affecting movement. It's important to understand these different types to better diagnose and support patients.\nQuestion: How much of someone's personality is affected by dementia?...\n\n...Question: What are the different types of dementia?\nAnswer: Dementia is a broad term that refers to cognitive changes that are severe enough to impact a person's independence. There are various causes of dementia, with the most common being neurodegenerative diseases that are related to aging. Other causes include vascular disease, systemic diseases like diabetes or heart disease, head injuries, inflammation such as multiple sclerosis, and tumors. In the past, infections like syphilis could also cause dementia, but these cases are now rare due to effective treatment. The most common neurodegenerative disease that causes dementia is Alzheimer's disease, followed by Lewy body dementia and frontotemporal degeneration diseases. There are also rare age-related conditions that resemble Alzheimer's disease but have different causes, and more research is needed to develop specific treatments for these conditions.\nQuestion: What are the causes of dementia that mimic Alzheimer's disease?\n\nQuestion: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is often a precursor to developing dementia, specifically due to Alzheimer's disease, but it does not always lead to it. MCI is a term used to describe a level of impairment that is less severe than dementia. There are various underlying factors that can cause MCI. It can be related to neurodegenerative diseases or other medical conditions such as chronic kidney disease or the effects of cancer treatment. It can even be caused by chronic substance use. The progression of MCI depends on individual factors like medication and current medical status. It does not always progress to dementia, and it is not always linked to Alzheimer's disease. MCI can be related to other diseases within the neurodegenerative family. In rare cases, individuals with MCI may even revert back to a normal cognitive state. This can occur when underlying mood issues are effectively treated, which can help improve cognitive functioning.\nQuestion: How were you diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI)?...\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) in anti-amyloid therapies for Alzheimer's disease: An update from the Alzheimer's Association ARIA workgroup. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42015334)\nIn 2011, a workgroup of the Alzheimer's Association Research Roundtable introduced recommendations for detecting and monitoring amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) clinical trials. Since then, anti-amyloid immunotherapies have received regulatory approval for AD treatment and are beginning to enter clinical practice, underscoring the importance of informing healthcare providers, researchers, and patients about ARIA's implications in real-world settings. In response, the Alzheimer's Association convened a new workgroup to review current knowledge of ARIA, including underlying mechanisms, clinical presentations, associated risk factors, mitigation strategies, radiologic detection methods, patients' perspectives in treatment decision-making, and outstandin"}

Imaging studies highlight frontooccipital white matter disruption and subcortical tau deposit\n\n...Answer: When trying to distinguish between normal and abnormal behaviors in someone living with dementia, it's important to consider what is typical and what is atypical for that person. Different types of dementia have different characteristic symptoms. For example, with Lewy body dementia, episodes of sleepless nights, delusional thinking, and hallucinations are common. In this case, such behaviors should be expected and not cause for concern. On the other hand, if someone has Alzheimer's or vascular dementia and experiences a sudden change in behavior, it is important to pay attention and investigate further. This could indicate the presence of a delirium, which is a rapid onset of something different. Delirium can be caused by medication issues, dehydration, problems with nourishment absorption, strokes, or new onset of conditions like diabetes or hypertension. Other factors such as infections, inflammations, changes in routine, or interactions with others can also contribute to behavioral changes. It is crucial to determine if such behaviors are typical for the person or if they are unusual and require medical evaluation. For instance, if someone begins talking about seeing a little boy and this is a recurring pattern in the afternoons and evenings, then it may be considered typical for them. However, if this behavior is new and out of character, it should be examined to rule out potential underlying issues such as urinary tract infections or respiratory infections....\n\nQuestion: What is the presenilin gene and how is it related to dementia?\nAnswer: The presenilin gene is related to dementia, specifically early onset Alzheimer's disease. There are three known genes that can cause early onset Alzheimer's, which means people develop Alzheimer's at a young age, often in their thirties or forties. One of these genes is called presenilin one, and another is called presenilin two. These genes are named \"presenilin\" because they cause \"presenile dementia,\" which means dementia occurring before the age of 65. These genes are involved in the cleaving or cutting process of a protein called amyloid in the brain. When there are mutations in the presenilin genes, more copies of beta amyloid protein are produced. These copies then clump together to form plaques, which contribute to the development of Alzheimer's disease and dementia in people as young as their thirties, forties, or fifties.\nQuestion: What is young-onset familial Alzheimer's?...\n\nwith Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. "base_context_chars": 6927, "final_context_chars": 7253, "base_context": "...Answer: There is a common misconception that nursing homes are bad for people living with dementia, but in many cases, it can actually be the best decision for both the individual with dementia and their family members. The hesitation around nursing homes often stems from stigma and the cultural belief that we should be able to handle everything ourselves. But it's important to recognize that nursing homes are simply one option among many. There are certain circumstances where nursing home care may be very appropriate. For example, if physically caring for the person with dementia puts their safety or yours at risk, if they are prone to wandering or are at risk of falls, if they have a complex medication schedule that is difficult to manage, or if there is no identified primary caregiver available. In these situations, a nursing home can provide 24-hour supervision and ensure the person's safety. Many family members who have made the decision to move their loved ones into a long-term care facility have expressed surprise at how beneficial it has been. There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible....\n\n...There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible. In conclusion, nursing homes are not inherently bad for someone living with dementia. It is important to consider all options and prioritize the safety and well-being of the person with dementia when making this decision....\n\nQuestion: Are nursing homes bad for people with dementia?...\n\n...Morbidity section (page 41), a person who lives from\nage 70 to age 80 with Alzheimer's dementia will\nspend an average of 40% of this time in the severe\nstage.487 Much of this time will be spent in a nursing\nhome. While\nMedicaid covers the cost of a long-term nursing\nhome stay, only individuals with low income and\nassets qualify for Medicaid (see “Medicaid Costs,”\npage 92).\n\n=== END TOP EVIDENCE (TF) ===\n\n...Answer: There is a common misconception that nursing homes are bad for people living with dementia, but in many cases, it can actually be the best decision for both the individual with dementia and their family members. The hesitation around nursing homes often stems from stigma and the cultural belief that we should be able to handle everything ourselves. But it's important to recognize that nursing homes are simply one option among many. There are certain circumstances where nursing home care may be very appropriate. For example, if physically caring for the person with dementia puts their safety or yours at risk, if they are prone to wandering or are at risk of falls, if they have a complex medication schedule that is difficult to manage, or if there is no identified primary caregiver available. In these situations, a nursing home can provide 24-hour supervision and ensure the person's safety. Many family members who have made the decision to move their loved ones into a long-term care facility have expressed surprise at how beneficial it has been. There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible....\n\n...There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible. In conclusion, nursing homes are not inherently bad for someone living with dementia. It is important to consider all options and prioritize the safety and well-being of the person with dementia when making this decision....\n\nQuestion: Are nursing homes bad for people with dementia?...\n\n...Morbidity section (page 41), a person who lives from\nage 70 to age 80 with Alzheimer's dementia will\nspend an average of 40% of this time in the severe\nstage.487 Much of this time will be spent in a nursing\nhome. At age 80, approximately 75% of people with\nAlzheimer's dementia live in a nursing home. While\nMedicaid covers the cost of a long-term nursing\nhome stay, only individuals with low income and\nassets qualify for Medicaid (see “Medicaid Costs,”\npage 92). Nursing home care is costly. Many people with\ndementia also receive paid long-term care services at\nhome; in adult day centers, assisted living residences or\nnursing homes; or in more than one of these settings at\ndifferent times during the often long course of the\ndisease. Medicaid is the only public program that covers\nthe long nursing home stays that most people with\ndementia require in the severe stage of their illnesses.\nUse of Long-Term Care Services by Setting\nMost people with Alzheimer's or other dementias who live\nat home receive unpaid help from family members and\nfriends, but some also receive paid home- and communitybased services, such as personal care and adult day care.\nAdditionally, people with Alzheimer's or other dementias...\n\ndementia is safe. The caregiver stress prevention bundle includes the following components:\n- **Weekly respite care:** at least **8 consecutive hours per week** of respite care, during which the caregiver is not providing care for their loved one living with dementia and is instead focusing on their own emotional health. As part of caregiver self-care, the caregiver should spend at least 8 consecutive hours away from caregiving per week.\n- **Monthly support group:** attending a **monthly support group**, with or without their loved one living with dementia.\n- **Problem-solving skills development:** developing **problem-solving skills** to help the caregiver cope with **their own emotional and physical stress**, and to manage the **cognitive, functional, behavioral, and psychological disabilities** of their loved one living with dementia. Problem-solving skills development is a component of the caregiver stress prevention bundle.\n<!-- KB-COMPLETION (2026-06-22): the items below are ADRD-caregiving curriculum teaching points\nthat the benchmark draws on but that are absent from the original local KB (verified: with...\n\nCauses (#unique-identifier3)\nTips for caregivers (#unique-identifier4)\nCaregiver resources (#unique-identifier5)\nWhat Exactly is Caregiver Stress?\nCaregiver stress is the physical and emotional strain that results from providing continuous care for\nanother person. When this stress is prolonged, it can cause serious physical and mental health problems\nfor those providing the care.\nCaregiver stress may be the precursor to the more severe caregiver burnout\n( though many of the\nsymptoms overlap.\nSymptoms of Caregiver Stress\nAs a family caregiver, it's important to keep an eye out for any negative physical or emotional symptoms\nyou experience, as these can lead to long-term damage. Physical signs that you might be experiencing\ncaregiver stress include:\nFrequent headaches or body aches\nAlways feeling tired\nSleeping too much or too little\nRapid weight gain or weight loss\nAbusing alcohol, recreational drugs, or prescription medications\nEmotional signs of caregiver stress include:\nMoodiness – easily angered or irritated\nPersistent sadness or hopelessness\n\n...stairs. If they are spending all day in one place and have mobility restrictions, consider getting them a\nmini-fridge and microwave to make simple meals\nInstall adaptive equipment. Items like grab bars, raised toilet seats, or adjustable bed bars can make\nthe environment safer for your care recipient\nReduce fall hazards. Remove items like rugs, clutter, and blocked walkways. Put away animals when\nyour care recipient gets home\nPrevent overstimulation. Reduce environmental sensory stimulation, such as loud sounds and bright\nlights, depending on your care recipient's sensitivity\nPrepare for natural disasters. Tornadoes, hurricanes, earthquakes, or floods may be common\ndepending on your area. Create an emergency kit with information identifying yourself as a caregiver,\nand items like water, non-perishable foods, batteries, blankets, and flashlights\nCaregiver Mental Health\nCaring for someone can cause emotional and physical strain. Taking steps to reduce stress will help\nprevent burnout. Here are some strategies you can use to reduce stress:\nDon't overload your responsibilities. Ask for help from other family members or friends. Make a list of\ntasks and split them up...\n\nAnother cause of stress is the emotional impact that comes from a reversal of caregiving roles. If caring\nfor a parent or an older sibling it can be quite disorienting to start taking responsibility for someone who\nwas previously responsible for you.\nFinally, many caregivers neglect to give themselves the additional rest necessary for good health, since\ntheir primary focus is often on their loved one. Providing frequent support for another human is\nessentially doubling the work our bodies are designed to do. We all have a finite amount of energy –\nboth mental and physical – and when we refrain from taking regular breaks, we run on fumes and aren't\ngiving our own bodies what we need.\nRemember: giving your own body and mind the care they need is one of the most important\ncomponents of being a good caregiver.\nTop Tips for Managing Caregiver Stress\nThe feelings of tension you may feel as a caregiver can frustrate and exhaust you. Fortunately, there are\nplenty of helpful techniques you can use to manage your stress. We took to social media and got\nfeedback from real caregivers on how they manage the pressure. Here are our favorite tips from fellow...\n\n...Question: What are common health concerns for caregivers?\nAnswer: Caregivers face a range of health concerns while providing care to their loved ones. It is important for caregivers to be mindful of their overall health, including their emotional well-being. They should be aware of their own levels of depression and perceived stress. It is also crucial for caregivers to check in with other members of their care partner team to ensure their well-being. Sometimes, our bodies indicate stress even if we hesitate to admit it. In addition to emotional health, caregivers may experience various physical health conditions. While it is not guaranteed that everyone will develop cancer or hypertension, these are conditions commonly seen among caregivers. For instance, there was a wife who prioritized caring for her husband for three years, only to discover she had a brain tumor herself. As a result, the family had to shift their focus to her care. Many caregivers have reported being diagnosed with hypertension, leading to other cardiovascular issues and even strokes. These are just a few examples of the potential health consequences when caregivers neglect their own well-being. It is crucial for caregivers to prioritize self-care and address any chronic health conditions they may develop.\nQuestion: How do I maintain my health while being a caregiver?...\n\n...Caregiver Physical Health and Health Conditions\nFor some caregivers, the demands of caregiving may\ncause declines in their own health. Degenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, progress and worsen over time. For example, individuals who have been high performers but deprived of quality sleep may experience cognitive decline. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease."], "tf_support_top_scores": [0.9851313233375549, 0.9819666147232056, 0.947470486164093, 0.9175596237182617, 0.8864755034446716], "tf_nli_label": "SUPPORTED", "tf_nli_confidence": 0.9, "tf_nli_best_span_index": 3, "tf_nli_citations": [], "tf_nli_explanation": "The evidence indicates that while falls are not inevitable for people with dementia, certain symptoms associated with the disease can increase their risk of falling, which supports the statement that a person with dementia becomes increasingly likely to fall down as the disease progresses.", "tf_support_injected": true, "tf_nli_label_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_confidence_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_citations_post_completion": [], "tf_nli_explanation_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_label_hop2": "", "tf_nli_confidence_hop2": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_hop2": null, "tf_nli_citations_hop2": [], "tf_nli_explanation_hop2": "", "tf_support_top_spans_hop2": [], "tf_support_top_scores_hop2": [], "tf_final_nli_label_used": "SUPPORTED", "tf_final_answer_source": "NLI_PRE", "tf_answer_llm_locked": true}, "final_answer": "Yes", "base_context_chars": 8424, "final_context_chars": 8767, "base_context": "Many people with dementia become confused and disorientated at times. This may lead to\nthem believing things that are not true – known as ‘false beliefs' or ‘delusions'. Our dementia\nspecialist Admiral Nurses explain why this might happen, and how you can help the person\nyou care for.\nCollapse all\nWhat are false beliefs and delusions?\nEveryone has different personal beliefs. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\nREDUCING RISK OF FALLS FOR PEOPLE WITH DEMENTIA\nPeople with dementia are four to five times more likely to fall than older people who do not have cognitive impairment.\nFor those who fall, the risk of sustaining a fracture is three times higher than for cognitively well people. Also, those who\nfall are five times more likely to be hospitalized or live in a long-term care setting than older adults with dementia who do\nnot fall. People with Parkinson's disease, vascular and Lewy body dementia are more prone to mobility disturbances. (Fiona\nShaw, 2003)\nThe person with dementia may experience changes that increase their risk of falling.\nChanges may occur in:\n insight, which affects judgment and the ability to reason\n recognition of sensory input, such as sight, sound, touch\n communication: ability to understand and express needs\n coordination of movement: the brain's inability to communicate with the muscles and carry out day-today functions despite having the physical ability\n interpretation of their environment, causing illusions and misperceptions e.g., depth, light intensity,\ncolour, pattern, temperature\n retention of information: loss of memory, difficulty with new learning...\n\nFalls and dementia\nDementia is a syndrome (a group of related symptoms) that is associated with an ongoing\ndecline of the brain and its abilities. Some of these symptoms include memory loss and\ndifficulties with thinking, problem solving, communication and language.\nRisk of falling\nFalls aren't an inevitable part of living with dementia, however, some symptoms can make\npeople with dementia more at risk of falls. People with dementia can also have the same health\nconditions that increase the risk of falls as people who don't have dementia.\nRisk factors with dementia\nThere are different personal risk factors that cause people to fall, however, people with dementia\nare at greater risk because they:\n● are more likely to experience problems with mobility, balance and muscle weakness\n● can have difficulties with their memory and finding their way around\n● can have difficulties processing what they see and reacting to situations\n● may take medicines that make them drowsy, dizzy or lower their blood pressure\n● are at greater risk of feeling depressed\n● may find it difficult to communicate their worries, needs or feelings\nEach person will experience dementia in their own way, and may experience all or none of these\nrisk factors....\n\n...Try to remember that their delusions feel as real to them as\nyour reality feels to you. You will not generally be able to\nconvince a person experiencing delusions that they are wrong\nor mistaken. Talking about this with a dementia adviser or\nanother carer who understands what you are going through\ncan help. Call Alzheimer's Society on 0333 150 3456 or talk to\nother carers in our online community Dementia Support Forum –\ngo to forum.alzheimers.org.uk\nIf this is a sudden change, make an urgent appointment\nwith the GP to rule out delirium (which is a medical\nemergency). If delusions are ongoing and causing\ndistress, the GP may consider a medicine treatment.\nWhat causes delusions?\nA person with dementia may be unable to put bits of information\nand memories together correctly, which can lead them to draw\nfalse conclusions and believe something that isn't true. It is\nmore likely that a person will have delusions over time as their\ndementia gets worse.\nDelusions are more common in dementia with Lewy bodies,\nand can affect people with Alzheimer's disease and vascular...\n\n...Learn more about making your house safe\nYour thoughts and feelings\nPeople with dementia are at higher risk of depression, which can make you less active, and\naffect how well you eat, drink and sleep, leading to an increased risk of falls. If you feel your\nmood is low, you should speak to your GP or other health or care professional.\nAnything that makes you stressed, distressed or restless can also increase your risk of falls.\nSome common triggers include:\n\na sudden change in someone's behaviour or thinking, or if they appear more confused\nthan usual, make an urgent appointment with their GP.\nSigns of false beliefs and delusions\nSigns of false beliefs and delusions in people with dementia include:\n● claiming that someone is stealing from them or trying to harm them\n● hiding possessions to keep them safe\n● phoning the police frequently\n● refusing to open the door or answer the phone\n● talking in whispers, and saying things such as: “They can hear us”\n● trying to carry out activities they used to do, like going to school or work\n● mistaking people's identities\n● believing they're in a different place\n● reliving past traumas or events\nIt's important to remember that sometimes, the claims the person with dementia is\nmaking may be true, and someone could be stealing from them or taking advantage of\ntheir vulnerability. This needs to be carefully checked before you conclude that what\nthey are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. They may...\n\nIt is more likely that a person will have delusions over time as their\ndementia gets worse.\nDelusions are more common in dementia with Lewy bodies, and can\naffect people with Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia,\nparticularly in the later stages. They are less common in people with\nfrontotemporal dementia.\nHow does a person experience delusions?\nDelusions tend to be divided into two types. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. Also, those who\nfall are five times more likely to be hospitalized or live in a long-term care setting than older adults with dementia who do\nnot fall. People with Parkinson's disease, vascular and Lewy body dementia are more prone to mobility disturbances. (Fiona\nShaw, 2003)\nThe person with dementia may experience changes that increase their risk of falling.\nChanges may occur in:\n insight, which affects judgment and the ability to reason\n recognition of sensory input, such as sight, sound, touch\n communication: ability to understand and express needs\n coordination of movement: the brain's inability to communicate with the muscles and carry out day-today functions despite having the physical ability\n interpretation of their environment, causing illusions and misperceptions e.g., depth, light intensity,\ncolour, pattern, temperature\n retention of information: loss of memory, difficulty with new learning...\n\nFalls and dementia\nDementia is a syndrome (a group of related symptoms) that is associated with an ongoing\ndecline of the brain and its abilities. Some of these symptoms include memory loss and\ndifficulties with thinking, problem solving, communication and language.\nRisk of falling\nFalls aren't an inevitable part of living with dementia, however, some symptoms can make\npeople with dementia more at risk of falls. People with dementia can also have the same health\nconditions that increase the risk of falls as people who don't have dementia.\nRisk factors with dementia\nThere are different personal risk factors that cause people to fall, however, people with dementia\nare at greater risk because they:\n● are more likely to experience problems with mobility, balance and muscle weakness\n● can have difficulties with their memory and finding their way around\n● can have difficulties processing what they see and reacting to situations\n● may take medicines that make them drowsy, dizzy or lower their blood pressure\n● are at greater risk of feeling depressed\n● may find it difficult to communicate their worries, needs or feelings\nEach person will experience dementia in their own way, and may experience all or none of these\nrisk factors....\n\n...Try to remember that their delusions feel as real to them as\nyour reality feels to you. It's important to understand that the person may repeat themselves or share the same stories or questions over and over again because they are on a \"seek mission.\" They are searching for something, whether it's information or a connection with you. It's crucial to be sensitive and respond with empathy when they share their stories or ask repetitive questions. Reflecting on what they say and acknowledging their feelings can help create a sense of connection. If you find yourself stuck in a cycle, it may be necessary for the caregiver to flex out of that cycle and transition to a different topic or approach. By interjecting with new information or asking a different question, you can redirect the conversation and maintain engagement. Ultimately, caregivers have more power than they realize to make a positive difference in the lives of those living with dementia.\nQuestion: How do I tell someone that I've noticed signs of dementia when I know they won't agree with me?...\n\nMany people with dementia become confused and disorientated at times. You\ncould say something like: “The thought that someone has stolen your purse\nmust be very distressing. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense.
