They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\n...Answer: People with Alzheimer's disease often experience changes in their language abilities. One common difficulty is finding the right words to express themselves. They may know what they want to say but struggle to come up with the specific word. This issue tends to be more noticeable in the early stages of the disease. Repeating oneself is another common language change in Alzheimer's. People may ask the same question or say the same thing repeatedly without realizing it. Family members often notice this repetition. Comprehending and processing information can also be challenging for someone with Alzheimer's. It may become difficult to grasp and remember multiple steps or pieces of information given at once. Remembering the last part of the conversation might be easier, while earlier information may be forgotten. As the disease progresses, these language difficulties may worsen. The person may struggle to remember even simple steps or find it harder to come up with words. Repetition of words or phrases may increase as well. In the later stages of Alzheimer's, communication abilities may decline further, and the person may eventually lose the ability to speak. However, it is important to note that the preservation of language and communication abilities can vary among individuals throughout the disease process....\n\nQuestion: Is it okay to lie to my loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: It is understandable to have questions about how to communicate with a loved one who has dementia. Sometimes, people with dementia may believe in things that aren't true. For example, they may think a deceased person is still alive. In such situations, it can be helpful to use what I call \"therapeutic fiblets.\" These fiblets are not lies but rather responses that keep the person calm and safe. For instance, if your loved one says they want to visit their deceased mother, you can respond by saying that you will plan a trip. The key is to find a response that doesn't allow them to argue or become upset. It's important to understand that using therapeutic fiblets is not deceitful but rather a way to ensure their well-being and your own sanity. Instead of reminding them of the truth, which may only lead to frustration for both of you, it's better to focus on making them feel secure. So remember, when necessary, use therapeutic fiblets to create a positive and supportive environment for your loved one with dementia....\n\n...Answer: Having dementia can greatly change a person's experience of the world. According to\nthese authors, repetitive questions were predicted by higher\nMMSE score, poorer immediate recall on word list learning,\nand female gender, while repetitive statements/stories were\npredicted by more severe dysexecutiveness and younger age.\nRepetitive speech is hypothesized to be a result of compromised memory or executive function.45 Those who have poor\nimmediate recall are more likely to repeat questions, whereas\npatients with more advanced executive dysfunctions are more\nlikely to repeat statements and stories.46 However, while memory impairment is present in all patients with AD, repetitive\nquestioning behavior is not. Kishimoto et al47 found that\npatients with AD with higher score of repetitive questioning\ntend to show higher relative cerebral blood flow in the left pericallosal region; no sex differences were detected. This needs to be carefully checked before you conclude that what\nthey are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. The RBs\nare reported in 60% of the patients with AD and were not\nassociated with gender, age of onset, or MMSE score.40 Verbal\nrepetition is a common complaint in AD and can include\nrepeating phrases, words, questions or actions, and telling the\nstory multiple times in the same conversation.41 There are 3\nphenomenologically distinct types of verbal repetition above\nthe single word or morpheme level: repetitive questions, stories\nor perseverative narratives, and statements.42 The prevalence\nof repetitive questions ranges from 31%31 to 67.4%,32 90%,43\nand 91%.26 Cullen et al44 performed a finding in which 87%\nof the persons having AD presented with RBs: questions were...\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Study protocol for a randomized controlled trial assessing clinical efficacy of digital cognitive rehabilitation for preclinical and mild clinical stages of alzheimer's disease continuum: the MI-RICORDO project. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41219714)\nBackground Early or preclinical stages of AD continuum may benefit from lifestyle interventions and cognitive rehabilitation strategies that can delay or prevent progression to dementia. In this context, digital health technologies offer a disruptive potential to expand access to cognitive rehabilitation and meet the increasing demand for early interventions. This study protocol outlines a randomized controlled trial (RCT) designed to evaluate the efficacy and efficiency of a personalized, multidomain digital cognitive rehabilitation approach compared to conventional paper-and-pencil therapy. A secondary objective is to investigate the structural and functional neuroplasticity mechanisms associated with both interventions, using advanced magnetic resonance imaging techniques. Methods The s\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Optimizing the physical activity intervention for older adults with mild cognitive impairment: a factorial randomized trial. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38774280)\nBackground Physical activity (PA) intervention is one of the most effective interventions to promote cognitive function of older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). However, the level of PA remains low. Based on the two core interventions (X-CircuiT and health education), this study aimed to examine the effect of three implementation strategies (viz., role modeling, goal-setting, and reminding) on the PA level among older adults with MCI using the multiphase optimization strategy (MOST). Methods Participants were randomized into one of eight conditions in a factorial design involving three factors with two levels: (i) role modeling (on vs. off); (ii) goal-setting (on vs. off); and (iii) reminding (on vs. off). The primary outcome was PA level at 12 weeks. The secondary outcomes we\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Nurse leaders' perspective on heat-related challenges and work-organizational interventions in inpatient care settings in Germany: A qualitative descriptive study. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42063585)\nBackground In Germany, rising heat-related mortality and hospital admissions are posing significant challenges to healthcare systems. Nurses working in inpatient care facilities are particularly vulnerable because of heat stress. Objective This qualitative descriptive study explores the impact of heat waves on nurses and their work environment in inpatient care facilities. It examines existing interventions to mitigate heat stress and identify areas for improvement. The study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with nurse leaders from inpatient care facilities, including hospitals and long-term care facilities in Saxony, Germany. Methods Forty-eight nurse leaders from varied roles and facilities were interviewed (September 2022-June 2023). Qualitative analysis identified key the\n\n...of their stereotypic behaviors, and the third patient showed\nnoticeable improvement with some residual movements after\n8 weeks of treatment. Helvink and Holroyd7 observed 5 cases\nof elderly patients with cognitive impairment (2 patients with\nAD, 2 with vascular dementia, and 1 with dementia due to alcoholism) exhibiting repetitive and stereotypic behaviors who\nwere treated successfully with buspirone. It is possible that,\nas a 5-HT1A antagonist, buspirone works through a serotonergic mechanism to decrease these behaviors. It is interesting that\ntreatment studies of stereotypies in people with FTD have\nshown that trazodone, an antidepressant, is effective in reducing such behavior, particularly in patients with clinical symptoms of depression.44 Whether the association between\ndepressive symptoms and repetitive actions is causal or coincident remains to be clarified. Rockwood et al57 reported reduction in verbal repetition in patients with AD after treatment\nCipriani et al.\n\nwith galantamine. In another study, it was found that verbal\nrepetition often improved in patients with AD treated with\ndonepezil and that improvement usually occurred in people\nwho also improved in other domains.58\nConclusion\nBehavior change is a widespread consequence of neurodegenerative diseases. Among the clinical features of dementia\ndescribed in the literature, repetitive and stereotypic behaviors\nare common; these symptoms correlate with a reduced caregiver quality of life, thereby affecting the care of elderly persons manifesting them. The neural substrates involved remain\nunclear, but traditionally, the basal ganglia and the frontal–\nstriatal circuits have been a candidate for explaining RBs.\nSterotypic behavior is more common in FTD than in AD.\nCurrently, very little is known about treatment; a number of\nquestions remain unresolved and further studies are needed to\ndetermine the specific phenomena.\nDeclaration of Conflicting Interests\nThe authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to\nthe research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.\nFunding\nThe authors received no financial support for the research, authorship,\nand/or publication of this article.\nReferences...\n\nAuthor (Year)\nStudy aim/s\nSample\nData Collection\nMethods and Analysis\nMain Findings\nArlt et al.\n(2008)23\nTo identify factors associated with adherence to medication in\npatients with cognitive impairment or dementia, and to discuss\nstrategies for improvement of non‐adherence.\nLiterature published in PubMed\n(1987‐2007)\nReview of quantitative\nand qualitative\nstudies\nStrategies for facilitating medication adherence in patients with\ndementia include prescribing as few medicines as possible,\ntailoring dose regimens to personal habits, and coordinating all\ndrug dosing schedules as much as possible. Technological\nsolutions (automated computer‐based reminding aids, online\nmedication monitoring and telemonitoring) may be helpful for\npeople with mild dementia but it is important to consider actual\nuse. When to introduce assistance with medication\nmanagement should take into account the person's\nindependence and safety aspects especially with medicines with\na narrow therapeutic range. Individual's cognitive status, mood,\nlevel of self‐efficacy, and particular living situation should also\nbe considered. No evidence‐based recommendations currently\nexist.\nCampbell et al....\n\n...22: 23–33.\n18. Serrani Azcurra DJ. This could happen if they get up in the night and are at risk of falling or if they become disoriented and start rummaging around. If their sleep-wake cycle is off and they are awake during the night, getting dressed and ready for the day, then they would need care overnight. However, if someone with dementia is able to sleep through the night without getting up, they may not need 24-hour care unless their sleep pattern becomes disrupted. It is important to assess the specific needs of the individual with dementia to determine if 24-hour care is necessary.\nQuestion: What are the options for daytime and nighttime support at home?\n\n...There may come a time when the person living with Alzheimer's\ndisease or dementia will need more care than can be provided\nat home. As the disease progresses into the\n\n...Question: When will I need 24 hour supervision for the person with dementia?\nAnswer: Deciding when to transition to 24-hour care for a loved one with dementia can be a difficult and emotional process. One important trigger is when your loved one starts wandering at night or engaging in behaviors that put themselves at risk during certain hours of the day. It may be challenging for you to handle these situations, especially during the early hours of the morning. Your loved one may try to hide their dementia symptoms by presenting a higher functioning persona, leading you to believe they can handle themselves throughout the day. However, it is crucial to recognize that their behaviors may mask their true level of functioning. While there is no set rule for when to seek 24-hour care, it is wise to start investigating this option as soon as possible. Signs that might raise alarm bells include wandering and confusion when interacting with appliances. It is essential to balance providing supervision yourself and seeking professional care, especially during periods when you cannot be there. Underestimating the level of supervision your loved one needs can lead to unfortunate situations. It is important to acknowledge and accept the need for 24/7 caregiving, even though it may be challenging and require a personal commitment....\n\nAdvanced Or Late-Stage Dementia\nIn this stage of dementia, the person you care for will have symptoms that are more severe than in\nprevious stages. These symptoms will have a big impact on their daily functioning. Examples of these\nsymptoms include:\nIncreased problems with communication, like not talking much (or at all) or not making sense when\ntalking\nChallenges with simple physical tasks, like eating, swallowing, or sitting up\nRelying on others for daily tasks, like going to the bathroom, personal care, and dressing\nDifficulty responding to their environment, and may keep their eyes closed\nHow Caregivers Can Support:\nPeople with advanced or late-stage dementia will eventually need 24-hour care. This could mean\nmoving the person to a long-term care community or bringing more help into the home. The goal of\nthis stage is to maintain and enhance the person's quality of life. You can help by:\nReferring back to advance planning documents. If they arranged a living will, you can help ensure\ntheir wishes are upheld by making sure anyone involved knows about it....\n\n...Answer: In the context of Dementia, when comparing in-home care to a facility, there are several factors to consider. In-home care can be more expensive if a person requires round-the-clock supervision, but often individuals with dementia do not need constant supervision. They may just need a little extra help. In-home care can be tailored to the specific needs of the patient. For instance, if they require care throughout the day and night, a caregiver can be hired to be there 24 hours a day. Alternatively, if they only need assistance for a few hours a day, the care can be adjusted accordingly. On the other hand, in a facility, individuals receive support 24 hours a day. However, it's important to note that different types of facilities offer varying levels of assistance. In an assisted living facility, there may be minimal help during nighttime and evening hours. In contrast, a nursing facility will have nurses available on staff around the clock. Ultimately, the decision between in-home care and a facility depends on the individual's specific needs, the level of supervision required, and the available resources. It is important to consider all these factors to determine the most suitable option for someone with dementia.\n\n...Perhaps you return to find something unusual or potentially dangerous has occurred, like the person wandering away and not remembering their way back. These are red flags that intervention is needed to prevent emergencies. Assess the areas where help is necessary and consider whether the person is currently receiving that support or if more is required. This might involve bringing in outside help or relocating to a place that offers the required assistance. Keep in mind that eventually, all individuals with dementia will require around-the-clock care. The timing will vary for each person, so it's crucial to pay attention to the warning signs and clues that indicate when that time is approaching. If you wouldn't feel comfortable leaving your loved one alone at home for a day, that may indicate they are no longer safe without added care and supervision. Remember, early intervention is key to ensuring the person's safety and well-being....\n\n...Answer: There is a common misconception that nursing homes are bad for people living with dementia, but in many cases, it can actually be the best decision for both the individual with dementia and their family members. The hesitation around nursing homes often stems from stigma and the cultural belief that we should be able to handle everything ourselves. But it's important to recognize that nursing homes are simply one option among many. There are certain circumstances where nursing home care may be very appropriate. For example, if physically caring for the person with dementia puts their safety or yours at risk, if they are prone to wandering or are at risk of falls, if they have a complex medication schedule that is difficult to manage, or if there is no identified primary caregiver available. In these situations, a nursing home can provide 24-hour supervision and ensure the person's safety. Many family members who have made the decision to move their loved ones into a long-term care facility have expressed surprise at how beneficial it has been. There may be a temporary regression in the person's condition following the move, as adjusting to a new environment can be challenging for someone with cognitive decline. However, by working closely with the facility staff and ensuring they understand the person's preferences, interests, and life story, the transition can be made as smooth as possible....\n\n...Additional building safety features, like locked exits to manage wandering\nSpecial therapies, like music, art, and reminiscence therapy\nSpecialized staff training & 24-hour supervision\nNursing Home Or Long-Term Care\nThese facilities provide 24-hour care and medical treatment, as well as more nursing and personal care\nthan what is offered in assisted living. (153) A study of 1,189,090 participants\nfound high LDL (>3mmol/l) was associated with an increased risk of dementia, HR 1.33, 1.26-1.41.(47) Higher\nbaseline LDL-C in a large cohort from UK general practice cohort (n=1,853,954) followed up for a median of 7.4...\n\n...One specific gene called APOE, or apolipoprotein E, has a particular form called APOE4 that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This means that individuals who have this gene have a small increase in their risk of developing the disease. It's comparable to having a gene that raises your cholesterol a little, which doesn't guarantee heart attacks or strokes but does increase the chance of them occurring. APOE is considered a risk factor gene, and it contributes to Alzheimer's disease in a larger number of cases compared to early-onset Alzheimer's. So, to summarize, early-onset Alzheimer's affects only 1% of cases and is caused by an autosomal dominant gene, while the APOE gene is a risk factor gene that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. These are the two main genetic causes of Alzheimer's....\n\n...Answer: Dementia is a complex medical condition, particularly when it comes to the genetics of Alzheimer's disease. In about 1% of cases, Alzheimer's disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. This means that if you have a specific gene, your chances of developing the disease are nearly 100%. These families are easily identified because the disease usually starts before the age of 60, and sometimes even earlier. On the other hand, the more common form of Alzheimer's disease is late onset Alzheimer's disease, which occurs after the age of 60 or 65. In this case, there are genes that slightly increase the risk of developing the disease, but the increase is minimal. So if you have a sibling with Alzheimer's disease, your own risk only goes up a little bit. To put it into perspective, having a family member with heart troubles increases your own risk of developing heart disease to some extent. But if you have good cholesterol levels, normal blood pressure, don't have diabetes, and don't smoke, that one factor alone only raises your risk of heart disease slightly. The same sort of math applies to the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. In conclusion, while having a sibling with Alzheimer's disease may slightly increase your risk, it is important to focus on maintaining a healthy lifestyle and managing other risk factors to reduce your overall chances of developing the disease....\n\n...baseline LDL-C in a large cohort from UK general practice cohort (n=1,853,954) followed up for a median of 7.4\nyears, was similarly associated with higher risk of all cause dementia (RR 1.05, 1.03–1.06 per SD increase in LDLC, 1.01 mmol/L or 39 mg/dL increase). This means that individuals who have this gene have a small increase in their risk of developing the disease. It's comparable to having a gene that raises your cholesterol a little, which doesn't guarantee heart attacks or strokes but does increase the chance of them occurring. APOE is considered a risk factor gene, and it contributes to Alzheimer's disease in a larger number of cases compared to early-onset Alzheimer's. So, to summarize, early-onset Alzheimer's affects only 1% of cases and is caused by an autosomal dominant gene, while the APOE gene is a risk factor gene that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. These are the two main genetic causes of Alzheimer's....\n\n...Answer: Dementia is a complex medical condition, particularly when it comes to the genetics of Alzheimer's disease. In about 1% of cases, Alzheimer's disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. This means that if you have a specific gene, your chances of developing the disease are nearly 100%. These families are easily identified because the disease usually starts before the age of 60, and sometimes even earlier. On the other hand, the more common form of Alzheimer's disease is late onset Alzheimer's disease, which occurs after the age of 60 or 65. In this case, there are genes that slightly increase the risk of developing the disease, but the increase is minimal. So if you have a sibling with Alzheimer's disease, your own risk only goes up a little bit. To put it into perspective, having a family member with heart troubles increases your own risk of developing heart disease to some extent. But if you have good cholesterol levels, normal blood pressure, don't have diabetes, and don't smoke, that one factor alone only raises your risk of heart disease slightly. The same sort of math applies to the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. One of the key signs is cognitive fluctuations, or changes in awareness. This can manifest in different ways, such as confusion and impaired speech. Another common symptom is difficulty waking up or feeling groggy in the morning. People with Lewy body dementia may take a long time to fully wake up and become alert. Changes in movement are also typical, similar to Parkinson's disease. These can include shaking or tremors that happen not only at rest but also when moving the hands. Unlike Parkinson's, these tremors do not respond well to medication. Other symptoms can include trouble swallowing, balance problems, and an extreme sensitivity to medications and chemicals. Behavioral, mood, and cognitive changes, including memory deficits, can also be present. Loss of smell can be an early sign of Lewy body dementia. People may experience a decreased sense of taste or smell before other symptoms appear. One defining symptom is called REM sleep behavior disorder, where people act out their dreams while asleep. This can occur many years before other symptoms develop. It's important to stay aware of these symptoms and seek medical attention if they are noticed. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. When imaging studies,\ncerebrospinal fluid analysis or other tests show that the\nbrain changes are caused by Alzheimer's disease,\nindividuals are said to have dementia due to Alzheimer's\ndisease or Alzheimer's dementia.\nAlzheimer's disease is progressive, meaning the brain...\n\n...Answer: Dementia is not a disease, but rather a syndrome. A syndrome is a collection of symptoms that occur together. In the case of dementia, a person must have impairments in at least two cognitive domains. These domains might include memory and executive function, which is the ability to plan and carry out tasks that involve multiple steps, or language difficulties such as finding words or using the right words. The symptoms of dementia are caused by an underlying disease or changes in the brain. For example, Alzheimer's disease is a common cause of dementia. If someone has dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, we would say they have dementia caused by Alzheimer's disease. Other diseases or degenerative changes in the brain, such as frontotemporal dementia or Lewy bodies, can also cause dementia. Frontotemporal dementia affects the frontal lobe of the brain, while Lewy bodies can cause impairments in executive function and early-onset psychosis. It's important to note that aging is not a disease, and dementia is more common as we get older. Age itself is not the cause of dementia, but rather an underlying disease is. Understanding the specific underlying cause of dementia allows for a more targeted treatment plan....\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Neural and motor mechanisms of handwriting: from healthy aging to neurodegenerative disorders. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41952872)\nHandwriting is a complex cognitive and motor skill supported by a distributed brain network involving cortical, subcortical, and cerebellar regions responsible for planning, execution, and sensorimotor integration. Beyond its communicative role, handwriting provides biologically meaningful information about brain function and motor control, serving as a sensitive marker of both normal and pathological changes. Age-related alterations, such as reduced fine motor precision, impaired sensory feedback, and cognitive slowing, contribute to the progressive decline in handwriting fluency and legibility. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40587504)\nBackground The prevalence of Alzheimer's disease (AD) continues to rise as the aging population increases, and the resulting cognitive decline severely affects patients' quality of life. However, the public's understanding of AD is markedly insufficient, which limits the effectiveness of early prevention and treatment. This study conducted a cross-sectional survey to assess the level of knowledge about AD among adult residents in Jiulongpo District, Chongqing, as well as their attitudes towards people with dementia, providing a basis for formulating targeted intervention strategies. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted in Jiulongpo, Chongqing, China, from September to October 2024. The self-reported questionnaire for participants included three parts: demographic information, the\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Assessing Alzheimer's disease knowledge in the Syrian population using the ADKS: A cross-sectional study. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41189255)\nAlzheimer disease (AD), a leading neurodegenerative disorder, disproportionately affects women and presents increasing global socioeconomic challenges. Despite growing identification of modifiable risk factors, public knowledge about AD's causes and progression remains limited in many regions. This study assesses AD knowledge among Syrian adults using the Alzheimer Disease Knowledge Scale (ADKS) and examines demographic correlations. This study evaluates the level of AD knowledge in the Syrian population and identify demographic factors associated with knowledge levels. A cross-sectional study was conducted from June to August 2024 using the validated Arabic version of the ADKS. The questionnaire (30 true/false items across 7 domains) was distributed electronically to Syrian adults (≥18 ye\n\n...Question: Can Lewy Body dementia cause twitches and tremors?\nAnswer: Lewy body dementia can indeed lead to twitches and tremors. It stems from a misbehaving protein known as alpha synuclein, akin to the protein implicated in Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's presents with tremors and shaking as central features. There exists a considerable similarity between Parkinson's and Lewy body disease, often resulting in shared symptoms. Therefore, it's not unusual for individuals with Lewy body dementia to experience motor or movement issues, including tremors. Usually, these tremors materialize when the body is at rest. This stands in contrast to action tremors which surface when engaged in activities like holding a cup of coffee, where the hand exhibits involuntary movements.\nQuestion: What are the other symptoms do I need to think about after a Lewy body dementia diagnosis?...\n\nthat aren't there, known as visual hallucinations. Symptoms also include\nproblems with focus and attention. Other signs include uncoordinated or\nslow movement, tremors, and stiffness, known as parkinsonism.\n● Frontotemporal dementia. This is a group of diseases characterized by\nthe breakdown of nerve cells and their connections in the frontal and\ntemporal lobes of the brain. These areas are associated with personality,\nbehavior and language. Common symptoms affect behavior, personality,\nthinking, judgment, language and movement.\n● Mixed dementia. Autopsy studies of the brains of people age 80 and older\nwho had dementia indicate that many had a combination of several causes.\nPeople with mixed dementia can have Alzheimer's disease, vascular\ndementia and Lewy body dementia. Studies are ongoing to determine how\nhaving mixed dementia affects symptoms and treatments.\nOther disorders linked to dementia\n● Huntington's disease. Huntington's disease is caused by a genetic\nchange. The disease causes certain nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord\nto waste away. Symptoms include a decline in thinking skills, known as\ncognitive skills. Symptoms usually appear around age 30 or 40....\n\n...defining features of the clinical syndrome, behavioral symptoms are extremely common, affecting\nup to 90% of patients. Behavioral symptoms in AD can be difficult to manage and may require a\ncombination of non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches. The latter is complicated\nby FDA “black-box warnings” for the medication classes most often used to target these\nsymptoms, and currently there are initiatives in place to limit their use. In this review, we describe\ncommon behavioral symptoms of AD—with a particular focus on the challenging symptoms of\n“agitation” and “irritability”—and discuss evidence-based approaches to their management.\nUltimately, multidimensional approaches tailored to the patient and their environment are\nrecommended, and evidence-based practices should be used when available.\nKeywords\nAlzheimer's disease; Neuropsychiatric symptoms; Pharmacological approaches; Nonpharmacological approaches; Black-box warning\nIntroduction\nMore than five million Americans suffer from Alzheimer's Disease (AD), and by 2050 this\nnumber is expected to triple [1]. Published online in JAMA Internal\nMedicine, the study is the first large-scale analysis of people's ability to manage their money before and after a\ndementia diagnosis.\nCommon symptoms of dementia, including memory\nand cognitive limitations, can lead people with\ndementia to have trouble handling money and\npaying bills, so repeated financial mistakes can be\nan early sign of the disease. The researchers analyzed information\nfrom 1999 to 2018 on more than 81,000 Medicare\nbeneficiaries, about a third of whom were diagnosed...\n\n...Keep a medication chart or checklist in a visible location.\nHave a caregiver or nurse oversee medication administration.\nUse medication management apps or devices with locking features.\nAbility to Handle Finances\nHandling money and paying bills may now be overwhelming, with mistakes or confusion about financial statements. This is often due to changes in attention, organization, and number skills. Watch for signs like unpaid bills, unusual purchases, giving money away inappropriately, or confusion about bank statements or financial transactions. Once someone has been diagnosed with mild dementia, even if they believe they are handling finances correctly (and they may be), it is always worth taking a second look and intervening to make sure that errors are not being made.\nThings to try:\nSet up automatic bill payments and direct deposit.\nLimit access to checkbooks and credit cards.\nAssign a trusted family member as financial power of attorney.\nMonitor accounts for unusual activity.\nUse joint bank accounts or assign a trusted family member as financial power of attorney.\nReview bank statements together regularly.\nUse a simple budgeting worksheet or app.\nConsult with a financial advisor experienced in elder care for additional safeguards.\nMood and Emotion\nDepression/Anxiety\n\nMENU\nShare:   \nAn official website of the United States government Here's how you know\nShare this infographic about steps to\ntake after a dementia diagnosis.\nManaging Money Problems for People With\nDementia\nEspañol\nPeople with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia\noften have problems managing their money. Research\nshows that money problems may be one of the first\nnoticeable signs of the disease.\nEarly on, a person with dementia may be able to perform\nbasic tasks, such as paying bills, but they are likely to\nhave problems with more complicated tasks, such as\nbalancing a bank account. As the disease gets worse, the\nperson may try to hide financial problems to protect their\nindependence. Or the person may not realize that they\nare losing the ability to handle money matters.\nSigns of money problems\nLook for signs of money problems such as trouble\ncounting change, paying for a purchase, calculating a tip,\nbalancing a checkbook, or understanding a bank\nstatement. The person may be afraid or worried when\nthey talk about money. You may also find:\nUnopened and unpaid bills\nLots of new purchases on a credit card bill...\n\nThings to try:\nUse a pill organizer with compartments for each day and time.\nSet alarms or phone reminders for medication times.\nArrange for pharmacy blister packs or pre-filled trays.\nSupervise or assist with medication administration as needed.\nKeep a medication chart or checklist in a visible location.\nHave a caregiver or nurse oversee medication administration.\nUse medication management apps or devices with locking features.\nAbility to Handle Finances\nHandling money and paying bills may now be overwhelming, with mistakes or confusion about financial statements. This is often due to changes in attention, organization, and number skills. Watch for signs like unpaid bills, unusual purchases, giving money away inappropriately, or confusion about bank statements or financial transactions. Once someone has been diagnosed with mild dementia, even if they believe they are handling finances correctly (and they may be), it is always worth taking a second look and intervening to make sure that errors are not being made.\nThings to try:\nSet up automatic bill payments and direct deposit.\nLimit access to checkbooks and credit cards.\nAssign a trusted family member as financial power of attorney.\nMonitor accounts for unusual activity....\n\n20 Experiences of money management and financial abuse in the context of dementia\n3.1.2 Common problems that arise with managing money\nWe asked people with dementia whether they had difficulties managing their finances, and\nwhat tasks they were finding difficult. Of those surveyed, 76% experienced some difficulties\nin managing their money, with common problem areas including:\n• shopping for things you need: 60%\n• paying bills: 55%\n• dealing with the bank: 76%\n• making plans for the future: 40%.\nIn both the survey and focus groups, people with dementia described how their symptoms\naffected their ability to manage money. Being able to process information was viewed as\ncentral to handling money effectively; this can become increasingly difficult with dementia.\nThe common problems people reported included difficulty with recognising letters and\nsymbols, or confusing numbers and letters. This made several tasks more difficult. For\nexample, filling in forms to pay bills, reading bills and bank statements, and monitoring\nspending. As these individuals reported, all of these tasks are essential for planning and\nkeeping track of financial transactions, and where money is being spent:...\n\n...Alzheimer's Association does, however, define three stages of Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's\ndisease dementia is the most common type of dementia. Some of the symptoms in these three\nstages are the same as symptoms for many of the forms of dementia.\nEarly-stage Alzheimer's disease (mild)\nPeople in the mild stage of Alzheimer's disease are still able to function on their own. They may\nstill drive, go to work and socialize. Some changes are happening that may or may not be\nnoticed by the person with Alzheimer's disease, but may be noticeable by close friends and\nfamily members.\nDifficulties may include:\n● Trouble remembering a person's name after being introduced.\n● Losing or misplacing multiple objects.\n● Having a hard time coming up with the right word consistently.\n● Trouble planning, organizing, managing or completing tasks.\n● Consistently forgetting what you just read.\nMiddle-stage Alzheimer's disease (moderate)\nPeople in the middle stage of Alzheimer's disease can be in this stage for many years. They can\ntake part in everyday activities with help. Symptoms are more obvious.\n\n...Question: What's the difference between dementia and Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Dementia and Alzheimer's disease are related but different terms. Dementia refers to cognitive difficulties, such as memory problems, that are significant enough to impact daily tasks like paying bills or cooking. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, but there are other causes, such as dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia, and vascular dementia. Some people may have changes in their brain associated with Alzheimer's disease, like the buildup of proteins called amyloid and tau, but they may not have enough cognitive impairment to meet the criteria for dementia. In these cases, it may be referred to as mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease. Executive function comprises the higher-level\ncognitive skills used to control and coordinate other\ncognitive abilities and behaviors.46 Declines in executive\nfunction can play out as difficulty planning, organizing\nand carrying out tasks, as well as poor judgment, socially\ninappropriate behavior, and inability to understand how\none's behavior or choices affect others.47 Impaired\nexecutive function not only makes it challenging for\nindividuals with Alzheimer's dementia to manage\nfinances, but may also make them especially vulnerable\nto financial abuse and scams because their ability to\ndiscern between well-intentioned and ill-intentioned\nbehavior and language in others may be diminished. Once someone has been diagnosed with mild dementia, even if they believe they are handling finances correctly (and they may be), it is always worth taking a second look and intervening to make sure that errors are not being made.\nThings to try:\nSet up automatic bill payments and direct deposit.\nLimit access to checkbooks and credit cards.\nAssign a trusted family member as financial power of attorney.\nMonitor accounts for unusual activity.\nUse joint bank accounts or assign a trusted family member as financial power of attorney.\nReview bank statements together regularly.\nUse a simple budgeting worksheet or app.\nConsult with a financial advisor experienced in elder care for additional safeguards.\nMood and Emotion\nDepression/Anxiety\n\nMENU\nShare:   \nAn official website of the United States government Here's how you know\nShare this infographic about steps to\ntake after a dementia diagnosis.\nManaging Money Problems for People With\nDementia\nEspañol\nPeople with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia\noften have problems managing their money. Research\nshows that money problems may be one of the first\nnoticeable signs of the disease.\nEarly on, a person with dementia may be able to perform\nbasic tasks, such as paying bills, but they are likely to\nhave problems with more complicated tasks, such as\nbalancing a bank account. As the disease gets worse, the\nperson may try to hide financial problems to protect their\nindependence. Or the person may not realize that they\nare losing the ability to handle money matters.\nSigns of money problems\nLook for signs of money problems such as trouble\ncounting change, paying for a purchase, calculating a tip,\nbalancing a checkbook, or understanding a bank\nstatement. The person may be afraid or worried when\nthey talk about money. You may also find:\nUnopened and unpaid bills\nLots of new purchases on a credit card bill...\n\nThings to try:\nUse a pill organizer with compartments for each day and time.\nSet alarms or phone reminders for medication times.\nArrange for pharmacy blister packs or pre-filled trays.\nSupervise or assist with medication administration as needed.\nKeep a medication chart or checklist in a visible location.\nHave a caregiver or nurse oversee medication administration.\nUse medication management apps or devices with locking features.\nAbility to Handle Finances\nHandling money and paying bills may now be overwhelming, with mistakes or confusion about financial statements. This is often due to changes in attention, organization, and number skills. Watch for signs like unpaid bills, unusual purchases, giving money away inappropriately, or confusion about bank statements or financial transactions. Once someone has been diagnosed with mild dementia, even if they believe they are handling finances correctly (and they may be), it is always worth taking a second look and intervening to make sure that errors are not being made.\nThings to try:\nSet up automatic bill payments and direct deposit.\nLimit access to checkbooks and credit cards.\nAssign a trusted family member as financial power of attorney.\nMonitor accounts for unusual activity....\n\n20 Experiences of money management and financial abuse in the context of dementia\n3.1.2 Common problems that arise with managing money\nWe asked people with dementia whether they had difficulties managing their finances, and\nwhat tasks they were finding difficult. Of those surveyed, 76% experienced some difficulties\nin managing their money, with common problem areas including:\n• shopping for things you need: 60%\n• paying bills: 55%\n• dealing with the bank: 76%\n• making plans for the future: 40%.\nIn both the survey and focus groups, people with dementia described how their symptoms\naffected their ability to manage money. Being able to process information was viewed as\ncentral to handling money effectively; this can become increasingly difficult with dementia.\nThe common problems people reported included difficulty with recognising letters and\nsymbols, or confusing numbers and letters. This made several tasks more difficult. For\nexample, filling in forms to pay bills, reading bills and bank statements, and monitoring\nspending. As these individuals reported, all of these tasks are essential for planning and\nkeeping track of financial transactions, and where money is being spent:...\n\n...Alzheimer's Association does, however, define three stages of Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's\ndisease dementia is the most common type of dementia. Some of the symptoms in these three\nstages are the same as symptoms for many of the forms of dementia.\nEarly-stage Alzheimer's disease (mild)\nPeople in the mild stage of Alzheimer's disease are still able to function on their own. They may\nstill drive, go to work and socialize. Some changes are happening that may or may not be\nnoticed by the person with Alzheimer's disease, but may be noticeable by close friends and\nfamily members.\nDifficulties may include:\n● Trouble remembering a person's name after being introduced.\n● Losing or misplacing multiple objects.\n● Having a hard time coming up with the right word consistently.\n● Trouble planning, organizing, managing or completing tasks.\n● Consistently forgetting what you just read.\nMiddle-stage Alzheimer's disease (moderate)\nPeople in the middle stage of Alzheimer's disease can be in this stage for many years. They can\ntake part in everyday activities with help. Symptoms are more obvious.\n\n...Question: What's the difference between dementia and Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Dementia and Alzheimer's disease are related but different terms. Dementia refers to cognitive difficulties, such as memory problems, that are significant enough to impact daily tasks like paying bills or cooking. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, but there are other causes, such as dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia, and vascular dementia. Some people may have changes in their brain associated with Alzheimer's disease, like the buildup of proteins called amyloid and tau, but they may not have enough cognitive impairment to meet the criteria for dementia. In these cases, it may be referred to as mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease. However, it's important to note that there is debate in the field about whether these individuals should be considered to have Alzheimer's disease.\nQuestion: What are the most important first steps after an Alzheimer's diagnosis?...\n\n...9 and 11, respectively).\nAn example of a subtle change is difficulty making\nsound financial decisions. The U.S. Social Security\nAdministration notes that people living with dementia\nare at an especially high risk of becoming victims of\nfraud and financial abuse.45 This may be because\nhandling finances is a particularly complex cognitive\nactivity made even harder by declines in executive\nfunction. Executive function comprises the higher-level\ncognitive skills used to control and coordinate other\ncognitive abilities and behaviors.46 Declines in executive\nfunction can play out as difficulty planning, organizing\nand carrying out tasks, as well as poor judgment, socially\ninappropriate behavior, and inability to understand how\none's behavior or choices affect others.47 Impaired\nexecutive function not only makes it challenging for\nindividuals with Alzheimer's dementia to manage\nfinances, but may also make them especially vulnerable\nto financial abuse and scams because their ability to\ndiscern between well-intentioned and ill-intentioned\nbehavior and language in others may be diminished. As\nthe underlying disease progresses, these changes can\nbecome more pronounced, leading to difficulties with\ntasks needed for independent living, such as paying bills...."}

This behavior is a common symptom of dementia known as a paranoid delusion, where they feel mistrust towards you or others, often focusing their frustrations on their primary caregiver. Here are some steps to consider: - Understand that these accusations stem from their confusion and loss due to dementia, which makes them feel vulnerable and insecure. Their wallet symbolizes their identity and wellbeing, and when it's lost, they may feel robbed of those qualities. - Approach the situation with compassion. Acknowledge their feelings, saying something like, “I'm sorry you feel that way. Losing your wallet must be really frustrating.” This can help alleviate some of their anxiety. - Try to redirect their focus by engaging them in distraction techniques, such as having a phone call with someone else to shift their attention away from the missing wallet. If their paranoia continues, consult a healthcare professional about medication to help ease their fears. Remember, it's essential to remain patient and supportive as they navigate this difficult time....\n\nOverview\nHallucinations and delusions are symptoms of Alzheimer's\ndisease and other dementias. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...Answer: Distinguishing between disease progression and other factors that may contribute to the decline in a dementia patient can be challenging. To navigate this, it is advisable to make changes to the patient's care one at a time. This allows for a better understanding of whether a particular intervention is helpful or detrimental. If there is a medication that could potentially worsen cognition, it may be worth exploring the option of safely discontinuing that medication. However, it is important to note that sometimes the disease itself is progressing, and the medication may actually be providing some benefit. In such cases, it can be more difficult to recognize the positive impact of the medication amid the overall decline. In general, dementia typically progresses at a relatively consistent pace, with some minor fluctuations of acceleration or deceleration. It is uncommon for the disease to manifest noticeable changes within a matter of days or weeks. Therefore, if there is a specific change that occurs over a short period of time, it can be helpful to investigate whether a triggering factor, such as a medication, may be responsible. However, it is essential to acknowledge that dementia is a complex condition, and variations in its progression can occur naturally. This poses a challenge for both families and healthcare professionals in determining whether a change is due to a medication or simply the intrinsic nature of the disease itself....\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\nSupporting a person with memory loss\nSpace for\nyour notes\nForgetting upcoming events\nPeople with dementia may forget upcoming events, such\nas medical appointments, visits and anniversaries. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42113830)\nThe shortage of healthcare professionals increasingly challenges the provision of care for institutionalised older adults. This study investigates healthcare professionals' expectations regarding the added value of social robots in daily care, as their perspective is adamant for implementation of these robots but not yet fully investigated. Two consecutive focus group sessions were conducted across three nursing homes with 24 healthcare professionals. The first session focused on identifying potential ways in which social robots could add value for both staff and residents. After sharing suggestions across all groups, the second session facilitated cross-validation and in-depth discussion of practical implications. Data were analysed using qualitative thematic analysis. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42146027)\nBehavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are prevalent in up to 90% of people with dementia. Management of BPSD often includes non-pharmacological approaches, supplemented by psychotropic medications when necessary. However, these medications can lead to adverse reactions, including extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). This report describes the case of an older adult presenting with BPSD secondary to vascular dementia. The management of the BPSD included various psychotropic and antipsychotic medications, which led to the development of orofacial dyskinesias. These drugs are called immunotherapy drugs and work by removing harmful proteins from the brain and preventing cell death. While they are not completely potent, studies have shown that they can help people maintain their cognition and function for about seven to ten months longer than those who do not take the drugs. However, it is important to note that these medications do come with side effects. The main side effects are brain bleeding and brain swelling, but it is important to understand that these complications only occur in about 40% of people who take the drugs. Furthermore, most people who do experience these side effects do not have any symptoms. Only about 20% of those who have changes on their MRI will experience symptoms such as headaches, nausea, confusion, or difficulty moving or seeing. These symptoms can be severe and may require hospitalization and treatment with anti-inflammatory drugs. It is important to consider these side effects, especially if you are already taking blood thinners or have a high risk of stroke, as these new Alzheimer's therapies should not be taken together with clot-busting medications. It is believed that the brain requires a steady blood flow to function properly, and this blood flow naturally decreases with age. High blood pressure, especially if not well managed over a long period of time, can restrict blood flow to the brain. This can potentially lead to inflammation, stroke, or a transient ischemic attack (TIA), all of which can contribute to cognitive symptoms later in life. While high blood pressure alone is not the sole cause of vascular dementia, it can play a significant role in its development, as well as other forms of dementia, like Lewy body disease. Additionally, high blood pressure adds on to other factors that contribute to the development of dementia over time. It is important for individuals with high blood pressure to work with their healthcare providers to manage their blood pressure effectively, as this may help reduce the risk of developing dementia.\nQuestion: How are heart and brain health interrelated?...\n\ncognition over both groups. Cognitive function was not related to group allocation or to weight loss. Overall\ntighter control of diabetes, but not very low blood sugar, or weight loss without improved diabetic control may\nattenuate the risk and be a way of decreasing dementia.\nHypertension and its trajectory\nOur commission has previously discussed the evidence that midlife hypertension increases the risk for all-cause\ndementia, AD and vascular dementia, but that nearer the time of dementia people's BP tends to fall.(2) Blood\npressure across the lifecourse rises in western societies, with evidence of rises associated with socioeconomic\ncircumstance. A systematic review of longitudinal studies estimated that BP first rises then starts to decrease 5\nyears prior to dementia diagnosis while weight falls around 10 years before diagnosis.(185) However, an\nindividual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis finds that high blood pressure may continue to be a risk in older\nage(186) but some people who are developing dementia have a lower blood pressure and therefore the picture\nis mixed. These meta-analyses do not cover blood pressure variability but a cohort study (n=2234, ≥ 65 years)...\n\n...Learn more about the risk factors you can control and use these tips to help you reduce\nyour risk of dementia:\nWhat's the risk?\nWhat can you do to reduce the risk?\nHigh blood pressure\nPeople who have consistent high blood\npressure (hypertension) in mid-life (ages\n45 to 65) are more likely to develop dementia\ncompared to those with normal blood pressure.\nHigh blood pressure can increase the risk of\ndeveloping dementia, particularly vascular\ndementia, because of its effect on the heart, the\narteries, and blood circulation.\n• Be physically active.\n• Eat a healthy diet that is low in fat.\n• Reduce your sodium and salt intake.\n• Monitor your blood pressure regularly.\n• Find healthy ways to manage your stress.\n• If your doctor has suggested taking medication for\nhypertension or high cholesterol, take it as directed.\n\n...may increase a person's risk of dementia. There are many possible\nreasons. For example, an unhealthy diet increases the risk of high blood\npressure which is a risk factor for dementia (see page 10). Ideally a\nperson should eat lots of fruits and vegetables, wholegrain cereals, fish,\nlow-fat dairy, beans and pulses, and not too much red or processed\nmeats like sausages, ham or bacon. Too much salt (more than a\nteaspoon per day) is also linked with higher risk of dementia.\nn\nnToo much alcohol – Regularly drinking above the recommended\namounts of alcohol exposes the brain to high levels of toxic substances\nthat can damage nerve cells over time. The recommended amount\nof alcohol per week is 14 units, ideally spread over at least three days\nrather than all at once. Drinking very high levels of alcohol over a long\nperiod of time also increases a person's risk of Korsakoff's syndrome\nand alcohol-related brain damage, which increases the risk of dementia.\nFor more information see factsheet 438, What is alcohol-related brain\ndamage (ARBD)?\n\n...physical inactivity, diabetes, social isolation, excessive alcohol consumption, air pollution, smoking, obesity,\ntraumatic brain injury, depression).(2) We discussed mechanisms for these 12 risk factors which indicated that\nrisk at any age might be reduced.\nHere we update the evidence and consider other potential risk factors. We use a lifecourse approach to\nunderstand how to reduce risk or prevent dementia, as many risks operate at different timepoints in the\nlifespan. For example, obesity and high blood pressure (BP) represent risk factors in mid-life, often with earlier\nlife origins, but in late-life may reduce if people are developing mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia.\n\n...This is because vascular dementia is directly caused by problems with\nblood supply to the brain (see factsheet 402, What is vascular dementia?).\nHowever, CVD risk factors can also increase a person's risk of developing\nAlzheimer's disease.\nMany people can avoid these CVD risk factors and there are many\norganisations who can provide support with this. For more information see\nbooklet 35, Dementia: reducing your risk and ‘Other useful organisations'\non page 15.\n\nHere we update the evidence and consider other potential risk factors. We use a lifecourse approach to\nunderstand how to reduce risk or prevent dementia, as many risks operate at different timepoints in the\nlifespan. For example, obesity and high blood pressure (BP) represent risk factors in mid-life, often with earlier\nlife origins, but in late-life may reduce if people are developing mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia.\n(12-14) As before, we look for risk factors with high-quality, consistent, dose respondent, validly measured\nevidence, which precedes dementia and remain when measured a decade or more before onset. We only\ninclude those with convincing evidence, while acknowledging there are likely to be other risk and protective\nfactors. The commissioners met and discussed the evidence and what to include and set out our discussions and\n\n...Answer: Dementia is a complex medical condition, particularly when it comes to the genetics of Alzheimer's disease. In about 1% of cases, Alzheimer's disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. This means that if you have a specific gene, your chances of developing the disease are nearly 100%. These families are easily identified because the disease usually starts before the age of 60, and sometimes even earlier. On the other hand, the more common form of Alzheimer's disease is late onset Alzheimer's disease, which occurs after the age of 60 or 65. In this case, there are genes that slightly increase the risk of developing the disease, but the increase is minimal. High blood pressure can increase the risk of\ndeveloping dementia, particularly vascular\ndementia, because of its effect on the heart, the\narteries, and blood circulation.\n\n=== END TOP EVIDENCE (TF) ===\n\n...Question: Can high blood pressure make someone more likely to develop dementia?\nAnswer: Dementia is a complex syndrome that can be caused by various diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease. It is believed that the brain requires a steady blood flow to function properly, and this blood flow naturally decreases with age. High blood pressure, especially if not well managed over a long period of time, can restrict blood flow to the brain. This can potentially lead to inflammation, stroke, or a transient ischemic attack (TIA), all of which can contribute to cognitive symptoms later in life. While high blood pressure alone is not the sole cause of vascular dementia, it can play a significant role in its development, as well as other forms of dementia, like Lewy body disease. Additionally, high blood pressure adds on to other factors that contribute to the development of dementia over time. It is important for individuals with high blood pressure to work with their healthcare providers to manage their blood pressure effectively, as this may help reduce the risk of developing dementia.\nQuestion: How are heart and brain health interrelated?...\n\ncognition over both groups. Cognitive function was not related to group allocation or to weight loss. Overall\ntighter control of diabetes, but not very low blood sugar, or weight loss without improved diabetic control may\nattenuate the risk and be a way of decreasing dementia.\nHypertension and its trajectory\nOur commission has previously discussed the evidence that midlife hypertension increases the risk for all-cause\ndementia, AD and vascular dementia, but that nearer the time of dementia people's BP tends to fall.(2) Blood\npressure across the lifecourse rises in western societies, with evidence of rises associated with socioeconomic\ncircumstance. A systematic review of longitudinal studies estimated that BP first rises then starts to decrease 5\nyears prior to dementia diagnosis while weight falls around 10 years before diagnosis.(185) However, an\nindividual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis finds that high blood pressure may continue to be a risk in older\nage(186) but some people who are developing dementia have a lower blood pressure and therefore the picture\nis mixed. These meta-analyses do not cover blood pressure variability but a cohort study (n=2234, ≥ 65 years)...\n\n...Learn more about the risk factors you can control and use these tips to help you reduce\nyour risk of dementia:\nWhat's the risk?\nWhat can you do to reduce the risk?\nHigh blood pressure\nPeople who have consistent high blood\npressure (hypertension) in mid-life (ages\n45 to 65) are more likely to develop dementia\ncompared to those with normal blood pressure.\nHigh blood pressure can increase the risk of\ndeveloping dementia, particularly vascular\ndementia, because of its effect on the heart, the\narteries, and blood circulation.\n• Be physically active.\n• Eat a healthy diet that is low in fat.\n• Reduce your sodium and salt intake.\n• Monitor your blood pressure regularly.\n• Find healthy ways to manage your stress.\n• If your doctor has suggested taking medication for\nhypertension or high cholesterol, take it as directed.\n\n...may increase a person's risk of dementia. There are many possible\nreasons. For example, an unhealthy diet increases the risk of high blood\npressure which is a risk factor for dementia (see page 10). Ideally a\nperson should eat lots of fruits and vegetables, wholegrain cereals, fish,\nlow-fat dairy, beans and pulses, and not too much red or processed\nmeats like sausages, ham or bacon. Too much salt (more than a\nteaspoon per day) is also linked with higher risk of dementia.\nn\nnToo much alcohol – Regularly drinking above the recommended\namounts of alcohol exposes the brain to high levels of toxic substances\nthat can damage nerve cells over time. The recommended amount\nof alcohol per week is 14 units, ideally spread over at least three days\nrather than all at once. Drinking very high levels of alcohol over a long\nperiod of time also increases a person's risk of Korsakoff's syndrome\nand alcohol-related brain damage, which increases the risk of dementia.\nFor more information see factsheet 438, What is alcohol-related brain\ndamage (ARBD)?\n\n...physical inactivity, diabetes, social isolation, excessive alcohol consumption, air pollution, smoking, obesity,\ntraumatic brain injury, depression).(2) We discussed mechanisms for these 12 risk factors which indicated that\nrisk at any age might be reduced.\nHere we update the evidence and consider other potential risk factors. We use a lifecourse approach to\nunderstand how to reduce risk or prevent dementia, as many risks operate at different timepoints in the\nlifespan. For example, obesity and high blood pressure (BP) represent risk factors in mid-life, often with earlier\nlife origins, but in late-life may reduce if people are developing mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia.\n\n...This is because vascular dementia is directly caused by problems with\nblood supply to the brain (see factsheet 402, What is vascular dementia?).\nHowever, CVD risk factors can also increase a person's risk of developing\nAlzheimer's disease.\nMany people can avoid these CVD risk factors and there are many\norganisations who can provide support with this. We only\ninclude those with convincing evidence, while acknowledging there are likely to be other risk and protective\nfactors. There are two ways in which genes can play a role in the development of Alzheimer's disease. The first way is through early-onset Alzheimer's disease, which occurs in about 1% of cases. This form of the disease appears before the age of 60 and sometimes even as early as the thirties or forties. In families with early-onset Alzheimer's, the condition is what we call autosomal dominant. This means that if someone inherits the gene related to this form of Alzheimer's, they have a very high chance of developing the disease, close to 100%. The risk of inheriting the gene from a parent who has the gene is 50/50 for each child in these families. The second way in which genes contribute to Alzheimer's disease is as risk factors. One specific gene called APOE, or apolipoprotein E, has a particular form called APOE4 that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This means that individuals who have this gene have a small increase in their risk of developing the disease. It's comparable to having a gene that raises your cholesterol a little, which doesn't guarantee heart attacks or strokes but does increase the chance of them occurring....\n\n...Answer: Dementia is a complex medical condition, particularly when it comes to the genetics of Alzheimer's disease. In about 1% of cases, Alzheimer's disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. This means that if you have a specific gene, your chances of developing the disease are nearly 100%. These families are easily identified because the disease usually starts before the age of 60, and sometimes even earlier. On the other hand, the more common form of Alzheimer's disease is late onset Alzheimer's disease, which occurs after the age of 60 or 65. In this case, there are genes that slightly increase the risk of developing the disease, but the increase is minimal. However, there are certain genes that can cause Alzheimer's, the most common being the APOE4 allele. This gene is present in about a quarter of the population, but in about half of people with Alzheimer's disease. Having this gene generally lowers the age of onset by about three to four years. For example, someone who would have gotten Alzheimer's at age 80 may develop it in their late seventies if they have the APOE4 allele. If they have two copies of the gene, they may develop it even earlier, in their early seventies. In addition to the APOE4 allele, there are some rarer genetic causes of Alzheimer's. These involve mutations in the Alzheimer's precursor protein, which is responsible for making amyloid. When amyloid is produced in excessive amounts, it can form clumps called plaques that damage and eventually kill brain cells. Two other mutations, called presenilin-1 and presenilin-2, are involved in the splicing or cutting of the amyloid protein. Individuals with these gene mutations can develop Alzheimer's as early as their thirties, with the more common age of onset being in their forties or fifties....\n\n...alone is not sufficient to cause Alzheimer's dementia.83\nGenetics\nResearchers have found variants of many genes that\nincrease or decrease the risk of Alzheimer's disease.\nAt least 75 genetic variants are associated with an\nincreased risk of Alzheimer's.84 Of the many genes that\nincrease risk, APOE-e4 has the strongest impact on risk\nof late-onset Alzheimer's dementia. Driving requires many cognitive abilities, and as dementia progresses, it can become more challenging. Your healthcare team can perform assessments to determine if it is still appropriate for you or your loved one to drive. When cognitive abilities start to change, driving should be one of the first things to consider altering. Physical changes, such as decreased mobility or slower reaction times, can also affect driving ability. Regular assessment by your care team and communication with your caregiver are essential for ensuring safe driving. It's important to note that driving restrictions may vary. Some individuals may choose to limit driving during certain times, like at night, or under specific weather conditions, such as rain or fog. Different levels of restrictions can be self-imposed or involve additional support to help with transportation needs. Driving challenges related to physical and sensory changes, coordination, and abstract reasoning can impact judgment while on the road. Wandering while driving is a concern, but there are measures you can take to ensure safety, such as using an air tag or another tracking device for the vehicle. Knowing that your family is aware of your whereabouts can provide confidence and peace of mind for everyone involved. Overall, regular assessment, communication, and exploring alternative modes of transportation are key to ensuring safety on the road for individuals with dementia....\n\n...different approaches to assessing fitness-to-drive, there is currently no nationwide standardized testing\nto determine when someone with dementia is no longer safe to drive a motor vehicle. Since judgment and decision-making might be affected, it's important to assess and address safety in certain areas. One crucial aspect is driving. Speaking with your doctor about your driving ability and regularly engaging in driving assessments can help determine if you are safe to drive. If you are a caregiver and have concerns about your loved one's driving safety, it's likely they shouldn't be driving. Poor decision-making and impulsiveness can also indicate they are not safe to drive, even without an assessment. It's important to consider the safety of yourself, passengers, and the community. Likewise, if you have guns, weapons, power tools, or other dangerous items at home, it may be wise to entrust them to a trusted family member or friend for safekeeping. Additionally, collect chemicals, paints, and other potentially harmful substances and store them securely to prevent accidental misuse. This review looked for evidence of existing interventions to enhance care in situations regarding low awareness, and considered their utility, feasibility and acceptability when delivering personalised care. However, there are different medications available that can help manage its symptoms. The first type of medication can turn back the clock on dementia symptoms, making them similar to how they were six to 12 months ago. However, it's important to note that these medications cannot stop or change the rate at which dementia progresses. Recently, a new class of medications has been developed that can slow down the progression of dementia. These medications are not in pill form, but are given through an intravenous infusion. Patients would need to visit an infusion center at a clinic or hospital either every two weeks or every month to receive the infusion. This treatment can help remove some of the Alzheimer's plaques in the brain, which in turn slows down the progression of the disease. While dementia cannot currently be cured, ongoing research is being conducted to see if these infusions can be used to prevent dementia from occurring in the first place. This is particularly exciting for patients in the early stages of Alzheimer's. We can now extend their period of mild symptoms and hopefully keep them from advancing to more severe stages.
