This is because memories from a long time ago have undergone a process called consolidation. Consolidation makes memories more robust and easy to access. On the other hand, recent memories are still in a fragile state and can disappear quickly. This is why individuals with memory loss may struggle more with short-term memory. They may have trouble remembering what they ate for dinner the night before, but they can easily recall where they went to college, where they met their spouse, or when their child was born. These distant memories have been consolidated and reinforced through repeated conversations and recollections. Short-term memory poses a bigger challenge for people experiencing cognitive decline.\nQuestion: What is the difference between a disease and a syndrome?\n\n...Question: How can I help someone with dementia remember things from the past?\nAnswer: If you're trying to help someone with dementia remember things from the past, there are a few strategies you can try. People with dementia often have better memories of the past than recent events. One approach is to start reminiscing with them and discussing things from the past. You can talk about family vacations, special events, or memorable moments. If they don't remember, you can show them photographs or create a visual representation to help trigger their memories. Sharing stories and asking questions about specific events may also help bring up memories. It's important to remember that there isn'ta guaranteed way to help them remember, but these techniques can be helpful. For recent events, taking photographs and showing them later can also be effective, as it provides a visual reminder. By using these strategies, you can support your loved one with dementia in recalling moments from their past and creating meaningful connections.\nQuestion: How do I stop or prevent resentment from someone with dementia?...\n\n...Question: Why can I remember things from long ago, but I can't remember what happened 5 minutes ago?\nAnswer: People often wonder why they can remember things from a long time ago but struggle to recall recent events. This is a common question, especially among those with Alzheimer's. One of the main symptoms of Alzheimer's dementia is poor short-term memory. This means we have difficulty remembering things that happened just a few minutes ago. It's like our minds rapidly forget information. Alzheimer's primarily affects our short-term memory, but our long-term memory can stay intact for a long time. That's why memories from our childhood, for example, tend to stick with us. On the other hand, we may quickly forget what someone said to us just a few minutes ago. [Learn more about Alzheimer's dementia here](url)\nQuestion: Will I ever get back to talking and thinking like I used to?...\n\nSupporting a person with memory loss\nSpace for\nyour notes\nOlder memories – which have been recalled or spoken\nabout more often – are more firmly established than newer\nmemories. This means that a person with dementia may forget\nrecent events but still be able to recall detailed memories\nfrom earlier life.\nIn the same way, people with dementia may still be able to\nremember things that they have repeated many times in their life,\nsuch as a route to school. This also includes skills that involved a\nlot of practice, like playing a musical instrument or driving.\nPeople with dementia may also be able to remember more\nemotional events, such as weddings or birthday parties.\nThis is because memory also has an emotional aspect to it.\nThis emotional memory is usually affected much later on\nin dementia.\nThis means that a person with dementia may remember how\nthey feel about an event even if they have forgotten the details\nof it. For example, they may not remember where they went\non holiday or that a friend came to visit, but they may still feel\nhappy about it after.\nThis emotional memory can be triggered by senses, such as...\n\n...Question: Why is understanding the difference between short term and long term memories important?\nAnswer: Understanding the difference between short-term memories and long-term memories is important, especially in the context of Alzheimer's disease. In Alzheimer's, short-term memories are usually affected first, meaning that individuals may have difficulty recalling recent events, such as things that happened a few hours, days, or weeks ago. On the other hand, long-term memories, which refer to events that occurred many years ago, are often preserved. People with Alzheimer's disease may have no trouble remembering things that happened 30, 40, or even 50 years ago. This is a typical pattern observed in Alzheimer's disease. So, if you or someone you care for is experiencing difficulty with recent memories but can easily recall events from decades ago, it could be a sign of Alzheimer's disease. It is crucial to recognize these patterns as it can help in early detection and management of the condition.\nQuestion: Does dementia progression ever plateau or stop?\n\n...Question: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to dementia?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a condition where someone has cognitive changes or deficits when tested but is still able to manage their daily life independently, although they might need some reminders or extra notes. MCI has a cause, but it's often unclear what that cause is. Dementia, on the other hand, is a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms. MCI can be grouped into two categories: amnestic and non-amnestic. Amnestic MCI is often related to Alzheimer's disease, which is a progressive illness. With the use of biomarker testing, such as measuring amyloid protein, we can now better identify people with MCI due to Alzheimer's disease who are likely to progress. However, not all individuals with MCI will progress to dementia. Some may never progress or may have a delayed progression. It's important to focus on optimizing brain health by getting enough sleep, following a nutritious diet, engaging in physical exercise, and managing conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes. By taking these steps, it's possible to delay or prevent the progression to dementia. While it's not inevitable, the likelihood of progression should still be considered.\n\nQuestion: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is often a precursor to developing dementia, specifically due to Alzheimer's disease, but it does not always lead to it. MCI is a term used to describe a level of impairment that is less severe than dementia. There are various underlying factors that can cause MCI. It can be related to neurodegenerative diseases or other medical conditions such as chronic kidney disease or the effects of cancer treatment. It can even be caused by chronic substance use. The progression of MCI depends on individual factors like medication and current medical status. It does not always progress to dementia, and it is not always linked to Alzheimer's disease. MCI can be related to other diseases within the neurodegenerative family. In rare cases, individuals with MCI may even revert back to a normal cognitive state. This can occur when underlying mood issues are effectively treated, which can help improve cognitive functioning.\nQuestion: How were you diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI)?...\n\n...the patient and informant may differ substantially from the clinician's\nsense of those words. It is crucial to recognize these patterns as it can help in early detection and management of the condition.\nQuestion: Does dementia progression ever plateau or stop?\n\n...Question: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to dementia?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a condition where someone has cognitive changes or deficits when tested but is still able to manage their daily life independently, although they might need some reminders or extra notes. MCI has a cause, but it's often unclear what that cause is. Dementia, on the other hand, is a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms. MCI can be grouped into two categories: amnestic and non-amnestic. Amnestic MCI is often related to Alzheimer's disease, which is a progressive illness. With the use of biomarker testing, such as measuring amyloid protein, we can now better identify people with MCI due to Alzheimer's disease who are likely to progress. However, not all individuals with MCI will progress to dementia. Some may never progress or may have a delayed progression. It's important to focus on optimizing brain health by getting enough sleep, following a nutritious diet, engaging in physical exercise, and managing conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes. By taking these steps, it's possible to delay or prevent the progression to dementia. While it's not inevitable, the likelihood of progression should still be considered.\n\nQuestion: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is often a precursor to developing dementia, specifically due to Alzheimer's disease, but it does not always lead to it. MCI is a term used to describe a level of impairment that is less severe than dementia. There are various underlying factors that can cause MCI. It can be related to neurodegenerative diseases or other medical conditions such as chronic kidney disease or the effects of cancer treatment. It can even be caused by chronic substance use. The progression of MCI depends on individual factors like medication and current medical status. It does not always progress to dementia, and it is not always linked to Alzheimer's disease. MCI can be related to other diseases within the neurodegenerative family. In rare cases, individuals with MCI may even revert back to a normal cognitive state. This can occur when underlying mood issues are effectively treated, which can help improve cognitive functioning.\nQuestion: How were you diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI)?...\n\n...the patient and informant may differ substantially from the clinician's\nsense of those words. The clinician must therefore encourage the\npatient or informant to elaborate by giving specific examples. The loss\nof episodic memory that occurs in typical MCI or dementia due to AD\ninvolvesdifficultieswithlearningandrecallingnewlyacquiredinformation and recent life events. Sometimes patients or informants may use\nthe term “memory loss” when referring to word-finding difficulty, inattention, loss of geographic orientation, or loss of the ability to perform\nstep-by-step tasks. It can be very challenging to distinguish the early\nstages of cognitive decline due to neurodegenerative disease from\nnormal aging. It is important to skillfully communicate that changes\nwhich may be common in individuals with advancing age are not always"}

For those of us who experience it at an earlier stage in life, memory is rarely the main issue. There are other symptoms that can be even more challenging, such as extreme fatigue and problems with executive functioning. Executive functioning includes things like processing information, sequencing tasks, and doing things in a specific order without skipping steps. It's important to recognize that focusing only on memory loss oversimplifies the experience of living with dementia. While memory has affected me to some degree since my diagnosis, it is not my primary concern. Each person's journey with dementia is unique, even if we have the same disease. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\nOne common misbelief about memory loss is that it always means you or a loved one has\ndementia. One key way to do this is to avoid arguing with them. People with dementia have a different perspective than ours, and it's easy for us as caregivers to become frustrated when they act in ways that seem irrational to us. We might try to correct them and bring them back to our reality, but this approach doesn't work. It's called reality orientation, and it involves constantly correcting the person and telling them what is real. Instead, a better approach is called validation therapy. This means validating the person's perspective, even if it's different from ours. If they believe something that we know is not true, there's no need to argue or correct them. By accepting their perspective and not arguing, we can help keep them relatively happy.\nQuestion: Can antipsychotics make dementia worse?...\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\n...Question: What do I do when someone with dementia is at home, but they are asking to go home?\nAnswer: When a loved one with dementia insists on going home when they are already at home, it can be confusing. It's important to understand that they may not recognize their current surroundings due to the effects of the condition. Acknowledging their feelings and perceptions is key. You can try adapting to their needs by considering if changing the environment or engaging with different people could help. Providing familiar objects or activities might also offer comfort. Sometimes, a change of scenery or simply listening to their concerns can make a difference. Remember, their memory challenges can make them feel disoriented, so being patient and supportive is crucial. Instead of arguing, try to understand their reality and work together to find solutions that help them feel safe and connected.\nQuestion: What is the impact of saying You don't remember? to someone with dementia?...\n\n...Question: What can I do if someone with dementia no longer recognizes me?\nAnswer: One of the most feared symptoms of Alzheimer's and dementia is when a loved one no longer recognizes you. It can be heartbreaking for both the patient and the caregiver. However, it's important to note that not everyone with dementia will experience this symptom, and it typically occurs in the late stages of the disease. If you find yourself in this situation, my recommendation is to join with them in the moment. For example, if they ask where someone is, instead of arguing or trying to remind them of who you are, simply respond by saying that person will be back soon and suggest doing something together, like getting a cup of coffee. By acknowledging their reality and diverting their attention, you may find that the issue of recognition resolves itself. It's important to remember that these symptoms can come and go. However, if the confusion is sudden or accompanied by other symptoms, such as increased confusion throughout the day, it may be wise to consult a doctor, as there could be another underlying issue, such as delirium or infection.\nQuestion: How can I help my person with dementia when they are obsessively worrying about their finances?...\n\n...another relative's home or a care facility.\n• Listen to an interesting podcast from NPR's Radiolab program about Capgras Syndrome.\n• People with dementia are at risk of being victims of fraud and robbery. It is important to\ninvestigate these complaints to see if it really is a delusion.\n• Often, the person has misplaced their things and they need someone to calmly assist them\nin finding them.\n• Remember the person is not doing this on purpose; try not to take it personally.\n• Avoid arguing with the person; it is generally better to just try to help resolve the issue.\n• If you are unable to find the item, apologize to the person for their loss. Offer to try to\nreplace it.\n• Help the person organize and store their things in places that are intuitive for them. Create\nvisual cues that help the person locate things\n• Purchase backups for things that are frequently misplaced like glasses, a wallet, purses and\nkeys.\n• If the person lives in a care facility, use iron-on labels to put their name on clothing, shoes\nand other personal items.\n5/1/25, 11:44 AM...\n\n...As the illness progresses, older memories are easier to retrieve than more recent memories.1 This\nmeans people living with dementia may use past memories to help understand their current world.\nBecause of this, care partners may not fully understand or interpret the person's words, actions or\ngestures immediately.\nRemember, the reality of the person living with dementia is authentic to them even if it differs from\nwhat you are experiencing. It is important to respect their reality. This might mean going along with a\nstory they are telling you that seems unreal to you.2\nSupporting a person to live well with dementia\nFor people living with dementia to maintain a sense of well-being, they need to live in a supportive\nsocial environment, where they are accepted, respected, have meaningful relationships and are\nsupported to grow.\nThere are many ways to create a supportive environment:\n•\nGet to know the person and show them respect (e.g., greet the person by name, use eye\ncontact, actively communicate with and listen to the person).\n•\nConnect with the person rather than correcting them. Share a moment with the person even if\ntheir reality or perception of the moment is different from yours own.\n•...\n\n...Question: Why would someone with dementia start making up memories?\nAnswer: It's common for individuals with dementia to share memories that may seem made up or farfetched. However, it's important to approach this with empathy and understanding. Firstly, not all of these memories are necessarily fabricated. Sometimes, clients share historical events that only a few family members knew about, so it's possible that what may seem made up is actually true. Secondly, it's important to remember that dementia affects the person's cognitive abilities and their brain. They may be sharing their perspective and memories the best way they can, given their condition. It's not accurate or fair to label them as intentionally making things up or lying. Instead, we should approach their memories with empathy and respect, understanding that they are trying to communicate based on their own unique experience. It's crucial to create a supportive environment where they feel heard and validated. If you have any concerns or questions about your loved one's memories, it's always a good idea to consult with a healthcare professional who specializes in dementia care.\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\n\nQuestion: How do I resolve arguments with someone who has dementia?\nAnswer: Resolving arguments with someone with dementia can be quite challenging. These arguments often stem from a difference in perception of reality, rather than a difference of opinion about something like food preferences. Decision-making is affected by a person's working memory, which allows them to process and manipulate information by linking it to the past and applying it to the future. However, dementia can cause gaps in the ability to do this effectively. This explains why trying to argue or logically come to an agreement with someone with dementia is usually unsuccessful. In addition to these cognitive challenges, discussing their diagnosis can also trigger emotional reactions or denial. Instead of arguing, a more helpful approach is to make decisions on their behalf while acting in their best interest. It can be beneficial to keep some details behind a curtain and only share the most important information. This is not to keep things a secret, but rather a therapeutic intervention to prevent confusion and promote better care. It's important for caregivers to recognize the toll that this role can take on their mental and emotional well-being. Often, caregivers find themselves overwhelmed by the behavioral symptoms of dementia and may feel like they are constantly on duty, 24/7, with no respite. One way to cope with these behavioral symptoms is to consider how much time is being devoted to caregiving. If you are the sole caregiver and are with the person with dementia all the time, it's crucial to understand that you are asking your brain to do the impossible with inadequate support. It's okay to acknowledge that you need a break and cannot do it all alone. Limiting the amount of time spent caregiving can have a positive impact on both you and the person with dementia. By acknowledging that you need help, you can become more of a partner in their care instead of solely shouldering the responsibility. Seeking out support from others who are experienced in dementia care can provide the hands-on assistance that is needed. Lastly, it's important to remember to see the person behind the dementia. When the behaviors and symptoms become overwhelming, it can be easy to forget the things you still like about the person you are caring for....\n\n...Answer: When it comes to caring for a loved one with dementia, figuring out how to divide up responsibilities among family members can be challenging. These decisions can often lead to tension and strain relationships. That's why it's crucial to have open and honest discussions before making any decisions. First, it's important to understand that caregiving involves a wide range of tasks. It includes things like providing medication, assisting with personal care, driving to appointments, preparing meals, managing household chores, handling paperwork, and dealing with legal and financial matters. To start, sit down with your family and create a list of all the tasks that need to be done. Then, determine who will be responsible for each task. Remember that being responsible doesn't always mean physically doing the task yourself. It could mean hiring someone to help or taking turns among family members. For example, if you need someone to do your loved one's taxes, decide whether you or a sibling will take care of it or if it's better to hire an accountant. Additionally, consider tasks that require round-the-clock care. If no one in the family is available to stay overnight on weekends, you may need to hire someone for that specific task. The key is to be honest about the many responsibilities that come with caring for your loved one....\n\nIntroduction and background 13\n1.2.4 Dementia and mental capacity\nIt is important to recognise that a diagnosis of dementia does not necessarily mean\nindividuals can no longer make decisions for themselves. People with dementia lose this\ncapacity over time, with variation between individuals. Furthermore, earlier diagnosis and\nnew treatments are helping people to retain mental capacity for longer.\nAs in any other area, all practical steps must be taken to help an individual participate in\nfinancial decision-making. Even if the person with dementia can no longer make complex\ndecisions, they may be able to make day-to-day decisions. Once the person begins to lose\ncapacity to make decisions about financial matters, the carer or family should be fully\ninvolved in decisions about their welfare and treatment. The use of advocates may also be\nnecessary. For those without carers, there are local and national systems that help people\nwhen they are no longer able to manage their money.\nThe Mental Capacity Act 2005 must underpin the decision-making and advanced\nplanning process. The Act foremost assumes that all individuals have the capacity to make\ndecisions for themselves unless otherwise determined. It provides a statutory framework...\n\n...Answer: As a caregiver for someone with dementia, you may find yourself facing tough decisions about whether or not to break a promise you made to never put them in a nursing home or long-term care. It's important to remember that everyone's journey with dementia is different, and what may have seemed like the right decision at the time may no longer be feasible or safe as the disease progresses. It's okay to reassess and revisit your plans as needed. Instead of holding yourself rigidly to a promise, consider the benefits and drawbacks of keeping the person in the community or at home versus moving them to a nursing home. Think about their safety, the level of care they require, and your own well-being. It's natural for circumstances to change, and it's important to prioritize what is best for both the person with dementia and yourself as their caregiver. In life, things don't always go according to plan. We may have envisioned a certain retirement age or future, but circumstances can alter our course. Similarly, as a caregiver, it's crucial to be adaptable and approach decisions with an open mind. Educate yourself about the progression of dementia, stay informed, and regularly reassess your decisions and plans. Set aside time every six months or annually to review and adjust your caregiving strategies as necessary....\n\ntheir stories or memories are shared, it is as if he or she gives one handle of the bag to the\nlistener. However, in the case of the person with dementia, in the beginning he or she can share\ntheir sack filled with stories, but as the disease progresses, not only does he or she give one\nhandle over to the listener, but he or she then gives the other one as well. A spiritual crisis for\npersons with dementia is, “who will carry my story, when I am no longer able to do so?”\nOne of the sad things about our society is that we don't fully understand how to\ncommunicate with or empathize with persons who have cognitive impairments. To have a\nfamily member who has dementia is often referred to as “the long good - bye.” Another way to\ntalk about it is in terms of anticipatory grief. If the task of the caregiver and family member is to\nsay good - by, then too often we externalize and distance ourselves from the source of the pain....\n\n...Answer: Leaving a loved one with dementia in a facility is not abandoning your duties as a caregiver. In fact, there are many situations where it is in the best interest of both the person with dementia and the caregiver to consider an alternative living environment. One of the main reasons is safety. If the person is prone to falls, constantly trying to leave, or engaging in dangerous behaviors like turning on the stove, it becomes crucial to place them in an environment that can ensure their safety. Sometimes, the decision to move to a facility is also driven by emotional factors. Caregivers can become overwhelmed and burnt out after a long period of providing care. They may need the help and support of a team of professionals, which is not possible when they are the sole caregiver at home. Caring for someone with dementia can be exhausting, and it is important to recognize when it is no longer feasible to continue alone. The decision to move a loved one into residential care is unique for every family, and only you can determine the right time. However, I strongly encourage you to work with healthcare professionals, friends, and family to identify red flags and establish a plan. It is heartbreaking when caregivers reach a breaking point and need to find a facility urgently without prior preparations....\n\n...Question: Should I comply with the wishes of someone with dementia who wants to keep the diagnosis a secret?\nAnswer: When a loved one with dementia wishes to keep their diagnosis a secret, it's important to consider the underlying reasons behind this desire. People often want to protect others or themselves from worry or feelings of inadequacy. As a caregiver, it's important to have open discussions with the person with dementia, assuring them that they are not alone and that you will be there to support them throughout their journey. It's also important to acknowledge that some relationships may be lost along the way, and to focus on nurturing those who will provide long-term support. While it may be initially okay to keep the diagnosis a secret, it's crucial to assess when maintaining the secret becomes more burdensome and isolating than seeking support. At that point, it may be necessary to go against the person's wishes and involve others in their care. Always approach these conversations delicately and prioritize the best interests of both the person with dementia and yourself as a caregiver.\nQuestion: What should I say when someone with dementia worries if other people know that they have dementia?...\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. The strain of balancing\ncaregiving responsibilities with their own personal needs, work, and social\nobligations can take a heavy toll on caregivers' mental health. The daily stress\nof caregiving for dementia can lead to feelings of exhaustion, anxiety, and\neven depression.\nThe Emotional Toll of Caring for a Loved One with\nDementia\nEmotional strain is a significant issue for family caregivers. Watching a loved\none slowly lose their memories, identity, and independence is a\nheart-wrenching experience. Many caregivers feel overwhelmed by the\nchanges in their family member, which can lead to feelings of sadness,\nfrustration, and helplessness."}

A syndrome is a collection of symptoms that occur together. In the case of dementia, a person must have impairments in at least two cognitive domains. These domains might include memory and executive function, which is the ability to plan and carry out tasks that involve multiple steps, or language difficulties such as finding words or using the right words. The symptoms of dementia are caused by an underlying disease or changes in the brain. For example, Alzheimer's disease is a common cause of dementia. If someone has dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, we would say they have dementia caused by Alzheimer's disease. Other diseases or degenerative changes in the brain, such as frontotemporal dementia or Lewy bodies, can also cause dementia. Frontotemporal dementia affects the frontal lobe of the brain, while Lewy bodies can cause impairments in executive function and early-onset psychosis. It's important to note that aging is not a disease, and dementia is more common as we get older. Age itself is not the cause of dementia, but rather an underlying disease is. Understanding the specific underlying cause of dementia allows for a more targeted treatment plan....\n\nDementia Facts Vs. Myths\nExplore common misconceptions about dementia and differentiate between the facts and myths.\nAs a caregiver of someone with dementia, you know that there'sa lot for people to misunderstand or\nmisinterpret about it. Whether it's an inaccurate statement made on a TV show or an assumption\nmade by a family member, these myths can easily influence the way we understand and perceive a\nperson with dementia. In this article, we'll review some of the most common myths and the facts\nbehind them, so you and others can better understand your care recipient and provide more\nempathetic and effective care.\nExploring Common Misconceptions\nArticle\n9 Minutes\nDementia Defined\nMyth\nFact\nExplanation\nDementia is a\ndisease.\nDementia is a syndrome\n(not a specific disease).\nSyndrome: a group of symptoms that don't have a\nknown cause, treatment path, or progression.\nDisease: a group of symptoms that typically have a\nknown cause, treatment path, and progression.\nDementia is a\nnatural part of\naging.\nDementia is caused by\ndamage to brain cells....\n\n...Question: Can a dementia diagnosis be incorrect?\nAnswer: Yes, a dementia diagnosis can be incorrect. It's important to understand that dementia is not a specific disease itself, but rather a term used to describe a functional status involving cognitive impairments. There are different levels of cognitive impairments, which range from subjective cognitive impairment (when there are impairments but they don't affect daily life) to mild cognitive impairment (where activities of daily living may be affected but not instrumental activities like driving or managing finances) to major neurocognitive impairment or dementia (where both activities of daily living and instrumental activities are impacted). Determining the specific cause of the functional impairment, such as Alzheimer's, Lewy body disease, frontal temporal lobe dementia, or vascular dementia, can be challenging. Sometimes, a person may initially be diagnosed with one condition, like Alzheimer's, only to later discover that they actually have a different underlying cause of their cognitive impairments. It is through ongoing evaluation and the gathering of more information that a more accurate diagnosis can be made.\nQuestion: My loved one was just diagnosed with dementia. Now what?...\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\n...Answer: Getting a diagnosis of dementia can be a challenging and frustrating process. Dementia is not a disease, but a syndrome caused by an underlying condition such as Alzheimer's disease, vascular disease, Lewy body disease, or frontotemporal degeneration. To begin the diagnosis process, individuals should share their concerns about cognitive decline with their primary care provider. This can be done by the person experiencing the symptoms or by someone close to them who has observed changes in their thinking or behavior. It's important for the primary care team to be receptive and open to these concerns. The next step is to measure the symptoms. There are various tests and surveys that assess cognition, behavior, and daily functioning. Neuropsychiatric tests can be done using a computer or with a tester using paper, pencil, or digital devices. These tests provide detailed measurements of thinking ability. An MRI may also be taken to examine the brain for signs of shrinkage or changes that indicate the cause of the dementia syndrome. In addition, a physical exam will be conducted, although physical changes may not be evident in dementia cases. Reflexes and certain movements may be checked. Symptoms\nmay include memory loss and difficulties with thinking, problem-solving or language, severe enough to reduce a\nperson's ability to perform everyday activities. A person with dementia may also experience changes in mood or\nbehaviour. These dementia symptoms are irreversible, which means that any loss of abilities cannot come back.\nDementia is not a specific disease. Many diseases can cause dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, vascular\ndementia, Lewy Body disease, frontotemporal dementia and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. These conditions can\nhave similar and overlapping symptoms.\nThere is currently no cure for dementia. However, there are treatment options and lifestyle choices that may slow\nit down. Most people who have these kinds of thoughts\ndon't act on them, but some do. This is why depression should\nbe taken very seriously. It should not be dismissed as a person\njust feeling ‘a bit down'.\nDementia increases the risk of suicide, particularly during the\nfirst few months after a dementia diagnosis. Younger people\nand those with a history of mental health problems are also at\nhigher risk.\nThe charity Samaritans has useful information on what to do if\nyou're worried about someone. See ‘Other useful organisations'\non page 22.\n\nDepression\nWhat is depression?\nEveryone feels sad or low sometimes, but these feelings usually pass. Depression (also\ncalled major depression, major depressive disorder, or clinical depression) is different. It\ncan cause severe symptoms that affect how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily\nactivities, such as sleeping, eating, or working.\nDepression can affect anyone regardless of age, sex, race or ethnicity, income, culture,\nor education. Research suggests that genetic, biological, environmental, and\npsychological factors play a role in the disorder.\nWomen are diagnosed with depression more often than men, but men can also be\ndepressed. Because men may be less likely to recognize, talk about, and seek help for\ntheir negative feelings, they are at greater risk of their depression symptoms being\nundiagnosed and undertreated.\nIn addition, depression can co-occur with other mental disorders or chronic illnesses,\nsuch as diabetes, cancer, heart disease, and chronic pain. Depression can make these\nconditions worse and vice versa. Sometimes, medications taken for an illness cause\nside effects that contribute to depression symptoms as well.\nWhat are the different types of depression?...\n\nSupporting a person with dementia who has depression, anxiety or apathy\nSpace for\nyour notes\nTreatment for depression\nTreatments for depression vary depending on how long a person\nhas had it and how severe it is. If they have mild depression,\nthey may be offered a support group or self-help (activities\nand strategies they can work through themselves). If they have\nmore severe or persistent depression, their GP or mental health\nprofessional may prescribe an antidepressant medicine as well\nas referring them for a talking therapy (see ‘Talking therapies'\non page 16).\nThe symptoms of dementia, such as problems with memory\nand thinking, can make it harder to treat depression. To have the\nmost benefit, talking therapies often need a person to have most\nof their mental abilities working well. Even so, they can still be\neffective and worth trying.\nMany people find that talking with a professional counsellor or\ntherapist can be helpful in making sense of their thoughts and\nfeelings, particularly during the earlier stage of the condition.\nSupport groups can also sometimes help. They give people\na chance to talk to others who are going through a similar...\n\n...low but can be irritable, angry, or anxious. Disturbed\nbiological rhythms in sleep, appetite and energy are\ncommon and patients may be negative, hopeless or\neven nihilistic. Ideas of worthlessness, guilt and selfharm also occur. Overall cognitive ability may decline\nsignificantly due to the depression alone. Attributing\ncognitive impairment to the dementia or the\ndepressive disorder may be difficult until an adequate\ntrial of treatment for depression has occurred.4\nSome signs of dementia may strongly resemble those\nof a major depression such as social withdrawal,\nlack of interest in self or others, low initiative and\npoor motivation. The diagnosis of the depression\nmay be made more difficult when the dementia has\nnot been recognised before. Certain medications and some\nmedical conditions can cause the same symptoms as\ndepression. A doctor can rule out these possibilities by doing a\nmedical exam and lab tests.\nIf depression is left untreated, it can lead to emotional and\nphysical problems. It can also affect the quality of care you're\nable to provide the person with Alzheimer's or dementia.\nTreatment\nDepression can be effectively treated. And the earlier treatment\nbegins, the earlier you'll feel better. Treatment commonly\ninvolves a combination of medication, therapy and support.\nMedication\nFeeling better takes time. There is currently no\ncure for dementia. However, there are treatment options and brain healthy lifestyle choices that may slow it\ndown and can lead to an improved quality-of-life. Brain healthy lifestyle choices can also reduce your risk of\ndeveloping dementia.\nWhat are risk factors?\nRisk factors are aspects of your lifestyle, environment and genetic background that increase the likelihood\nof getting a disease. Risk factors on their own are not causes of a disease. Rather, risk factors represent an\nincreased chance, but not a certainty, that dementia will develop....\n\nQuestion: How do you treat depression in people recently diagnosed with dementia?\nAnswer: If someone with dementia is also experiencing depression, there are different treatment options depending on the severity of the depression. If it'sa true diagnosis of depression, medication and therapy are recommended. The level of depression can range from mild to severe. If the person is having suicidal thoughts, it's important to seek immediate help. But if the depression is more on the milder side, it may be a result of struggling with the diagnosis and not knowing what to do. In these cases, seeing a healthcare professional is still recommended to address the depressive symptoms. The healthcare provider, along with the person diagnosed with dementia and their trusted family members, can discuss and come up with strategies for treatment. Generally, therapy and medication, such as antidepressants, can be effective for individuals with dementia who have recently been diagnosed with depression.\nQuestion: Should I comply with the wishes of someone with dementia who wants to keep the diagnosis a secret?...\n\n...The occurrence of depression occurring in people with MCI or dementia can lead to a\nnumber of negative outcomes. It\ncan cause severe symptoms that affect how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily\nactivities, such as sleeping, eating, or working.\nDepression can affect anyone regardless of age, sex, race or ethnicity, income, culture,\nor education. Research suggests that genetic, biological, environmental, and\npsychological factors play a role in the disorder.\nWomen are diagnosed with depression more often than men, but men can also be\ndepressed. Because men may be less likely to recognize, talk about, and seek help for\ntheir negative feelings, they are at greater risk of their depression symptoms being\nundiagnosed and undertreated.\nIn addition, depression can co-occur with other mental disorders or chronic illnesses,\nsuch as diabetes, cancer, heart disease, and chronic pain. Depression can make these\nconditions worse and vice versa. Sometimes, medications taken for an illness cause\nside effects that contribute to depression symptoms as well.\nWhat are the different types of depression?...\n\nSupporting a person with dementia who has depression, anxiety or apathy\nSpace for\nyour notes\nTreatment for depression\nTreatments for depression vary depending on how long a person\nhas had it and how severe it is. If they have mild depression,\nthey may be offered a support group or self-help (activities\nand strategies they can work through themselves). If they have\nmore severe or persistent depression, their GP or mental health\nprofessional may prescribe an antidepressant medicine as well\nas referring them for a talking therapy (see ‘Talking therapies'\non page 16).\nThe symptoms of dementia, such as problems with memory\nand thinking, can make it harder to treat depression. To have the\nmost benefit, talking therapies often need a person to have most\nof their mental abilities working well. Even so, they can still be\neffective and worth trying.\nMany people find that talking with a professional counsellor or\ntherapist can be helpful in making sense of their thoughts and\nfeelings, particularly during the earlier stage of the condition.\nSupport groups can also sometimes help. They give people\na chance to talk to others who are going through a similar...\n\n...low but can be irritable, angry, or anxious. Disturbed\nbiological rhythms in sleep, appetite and energy are\ncommon and patients may be negative, hopeless or\neven nihilistic. Ideas of worthlessness, guilt and selfharm also occur. Overall cognitive ability may decline\nsignificantly due to the depression alone. Attributing\ncognitive impairment to the dementia or the\ndepressive disorder may be difficult until an adequate\ntrial of treatment for depression has occurred.4\nSome signs of dementia may strongly resemble those\nof a major depression such as social withdrawal,\nlack of interest in self or others, low initiative and\npoor motivation. The diagnosis of the depression\nmay be made more difficult when the dementia has\nnot been recognised before. Apathy is a particularly\nconfounding sign for diagnosis, and specialist\n\n● Difficulty thinking or concentrating.\n● Changes in appetite and weight.\n● Physical symptoms that do not respond to treatment, such\nas headaches, digestive disorders and pain.\nSource: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and\nStatistical Manual of Mental Disorders\nSee your doctor\nIf you are concerned that you might be depressed, see your\ndoctor as soon as possible. Certain medications and some\nmedical conditions can cause the same symptoms as\ndepression. A doctor can rule out these possibilities by doing a\nmedical exam and lab tests.\nIf depression is left untreated, it can lead to emotional and\nphysical problems. It can also affect the quality of care you're\nable to provide the person with Alzheimer's or dementia.\nTreatment\nDepression can be effectively treated. And the earlier treatment\nbegins, the earlier you'll feel better. Treatment commonly\ninvolves a combination of medication, therapy and support.\nMedication\nFeeling better takes time. If you are prescribed an\nantidepressant, talk with your doctor about how long it will take\n\nRisk Factors\nIn this sheet you will find information about:\n• Risk factors for dementia\n• Strategies and lifestyle choices that can help you reduce your risk of developing dementia\nWhat is dementia?\nDementia is an overall term for a set of symptoms that is caused by disorders that affect a person's brain.\nSymptoms may include memory loss and changes in mood and behaviour, as well as difficulties with thinking\nor language that are severe enough to reduce a person's ability to perform everyday tasks.\nDementia is progressive, meaning that its symptoms gradually get worse over time. There is currently no\ncure for dementia. However, there are treatment options and brain healthy lifestyle choices that may slow it\ndown and can lead to an improved quality-of-life. Brain healthy lifestyle choices can also reduce your risk of\ndeveloping dementia.\nWhat are risk factors?\nRisk factors are aspects of your lifestyle, environment and genetic background that increase the likelihood\nof getting a disease. Risk factors on their own are not causes of a disease. Rather, risk factors represent an\nincreased chance, but not a certainty, that dementia will develop....\n\nQuestion: How do you treat depression in people recently diagnosed with dementia?\nAnswer: If someone with dementia is also experiencing depression, there are different treatment options depending on the severity of the depression. If it'sa true diagnosis of depression, medication and therapy are recommended. The level of depression can range from mild to severe. If the person is having suicidal thoughts, it's important to seek immediate help. But if the depression is more on the milder side, it may be a result of struggling with the diagnosis and not knowing what to do. In these cases, seeing a healthcare professional is still recommended to address the depressive symptoms. The healthcare provider, along with the person diagnosed with dementia and their trusted family members, can discuss and come up with strategies for treatment. Generally, therapy and medication, such as antidepressants, can be effective for individuals with dementia who have recently been diagnosed with depression.\nQuestion: Should I comply with the wishes of someone with dementia who wants to keep the diagnosis a secret?...\n\n...The occurrence of depression occurring in people with MCI or dementia can lead to a\nnumber of negative outcomes. For example, pre-existing depression has been identified as a\npredictor of, or risk factors for, subsequent dementia. One meta-analysis9 estimated that\npersons experiencing depression have approximately double the risk of developing dementia\nthan those without a prior history of depression, and more recent study findings concur 6, 10.\nDepression may also be a risk factor for progression from MCI to dementia. Several studies\nreport an association between baseline depressive symptoms in participants with MCI and\nlater progression to dementia 11–15.\nNIH Public Access\nAuthor Manuscript\nAnn Longterm Care. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2011 August 1."}

This supports the statement regarding high genetic susceptibility.", "tf_support_injected": true, "tf_nli_label_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_confidence_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_post_completion": null, "tf_nli_citations_post_completion": [], "tf_nli_explanation_post_completion": "", "tf_nli_label_hop2": "", "tf_nli_confidence_hop2": null, "tf_nli_best_span_index_hop2": null, "tf_nli_citations_hop2": [], "tf_nli_explanation_hop2": "", "tf_support_top_spans_hop2": [], "tf_support_top_scores_hop2": [], "tf_final_nli_label_used": "SUPPORTED", "tf_final_answer_source": "NLI_PRE", "tf_answer_llm_locked": true}, "final_answer": "Yes", "base_context_chars": 7373, "final_context_chars": 7731, "base_context": "...Answer: Alzheimer's disease, a condition that affects memory and thinking skills, can have genetic causes. There are two ways in which genes can play a role in the development of Alzheimer's disease. The first way is through early-onset Alzheimer's disease, which occurs in about 1% of cases. This form of the disease appears before the age of 60 and sometimes even as early as the thirties or forties. In families with early-onset Alzheimer's, the condition is what we call autosomal dominant. This means that if someone inherits the gene related to this form of Alzheimer's, they have a very high chance of developing the disease, close to 100%. The risk of inheriting the gene from a parent who has the gene is 50/50 for each child in these families. The second way in which genes contribute to Alzheimer's disease is as risk factors. One specific gene called APOE, or apolipoprotein E, has a particular form called APOE4 that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This means that individuals who have this gene have a small increase in their risk of developing the disease. It's comparable to having a gene that raises your cholesterol a little, which doesn't guarantee heart attacks or strokes but does increase the chance of them occurring....\n\n...One specific gene called APOE, or apolipoprotein E, has a particular form called APOE4 that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This means that individuals who have this gene have a small increase in their risk of developing the disease. It's comparable to having a gene that raises your cholesterol a little, which doesn't guarantee heart attacks or strokes but does increase the chance of them occurring. APOE is considered a risk factor gene, and it contributes to Alzheimer's disease in a larger number of cases compared to early-onset Alzheimer's. So, to summarize, early-onset Alzheimer's affects only 1% of cases and is caused by an autosomal dominant gene, while the APOE gene is a risk factor gene that slightly increases the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. These are the two main genetic causes of Alzheimer's....\n\n...Two other mutations, called presenilin-1 and presenilin-2, are involved in the splicing or cutting of the amyloid protein. The state of the\nscience for the term “Alzheimer's dementia”\nis dementia that has been confirmed to be\ndue to the brain changes of Alzheimer's\ndisease (see “Dementia or Alzheimer's\nDisease?” in the Overview, page 5);\nhowever, population-based prevalence\nstudies do not yet exist that have the data\nto provide an estimate of the prevalence of\nbiomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's dementia.\nWhen such estimates do become available,\nwe will report them, which could result in\ndifferences in reported prevalence (see\n“Prevalence Estimates” on page 32).\n\n...Question: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to dementia?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a condition where someone has cognitive changes or deficits when tested but is still able to manage their daily life independently, although they might need some reminders or extra notes. MCI has a cause, but it's often unclear what that cause is. Dementia, on the other hand, is a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms. MCI can be grouped into two categories: amnestic and non-amnestic. Amnestic MCI is often related to Alzheimer's disease, which is a progressive illness. With the use of biomarker testing, such as measuring amyloid protein, we can now better identify people with MCI due to Alzheimer's disease who are likely to progress. However, not all individuals with MCI will progress to dementia. Some may never progress or may have a delayed progression. It's important to focus on optimizing brain health by getting enough sleep, following a nutritious diet, engaging in physical exercise, and managing conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes. By taking these steps, it's possible to delay or prevent the progression to dementia. While it's not inevitable, the likelihood of progression should still be considered.\n\nQuestion: Are there any biomarkers for dementia?\nAnswer: This is an exciting time in the field of dementias because researchers are developing biomarkers for many of these conditions. The furthest progress has been made with Alzheimer's disease. Using special PET scans, doctors can now see the amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles that were originally identified by Dr. Alzheimer over a hundred years ago. Changes in these plaques and tangles can be detected in spinal fluid as well. New blood tests for amyloid and tau, two key proteins associated with Alzheimer's, are also being developed. For dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia, a marker called alpha-synuclein can be detected through a skin biopsy. In the case of vascular dementia, strokes can be seen on an MRI scan. Unfortunately, for disorders like behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia and chronic traumatic encephalopathy, there are currently no reliable biomarkers available. With the recent advent of biomarkers that\ndetect the brain changes believed to characterize\nAlzheimer's disease, it may now be possible to determine\nwhich individuals diagnosed with MCI have MCI due\nto Alzheimer's disease. The number and proportion of\nolder adults who have MCI due to Alzheimer's disease\nare currently difficult to estimate because they require\nstudies with both population-based prevalence measures\nof MCI and tests of Alzheimer's biomarkers, and this\nline of research is in its infancy. Furthermore, there is\nvariation across studies in both the threshold of cognitive\nimpairment required for an MCI diagnosis and the\nlevel of biomarker burden that defines the presence of\nAlzheimer's disease. Researchers in the fields of behavioral and cognitive neurology are actively working to find earlier methods to identify cognitive impairments related to biological factors. - For Alzheimer's, scientists focus on specific proteins, particularly amyloid and tau proteins. - Traditional approaches involve imaging techniques or analyzing protein levels through lumbar puncture. - Recently, blood tests that measure amyloid levels have been used in research settings, but they are not yet validated for everyday clinical use. The aim of this narrative review is to synthesize evidence on the association between the environment and cognition in older adults, integrating biological, environmental, and behavioral elements. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42170124)\nAlzheimer's dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which cognitive decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and functional dependence emerge from a long preclinical and prodromal phase. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42062916)\nBackground Cognitive decline stands as a significant factor contributing to disability and dependency among older adults. Multi-domain lifestyle (MDL) interventions are widely recognized for their effectiveness in preserving cognitive functioning in older adults with dementia. However, little is known about MDL interventions using technology-based approaches in older adults residing in assisted living facilities. This qualitative study aimed to explore both the perceived health benefits and challenges of using a mobile-based multidomain Silvia Program among older adults residing in assisted living facilities. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. Sometimes, clients share historical events that only a few family members knew about, so it's possible that what may seem made up is actually true. Secondly, it's important to remember that dementia affects the person's cognitive abilities and their brain. They may be sharing their perspective and memories the best way they can, given their condition. It's not accurate or fair to label them as intentionally making things up or lying. It's important to understand that these new relationships do not diminish the love and importance of your relationship with your loved one. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42260566)\nBackground Alzheimer's is a progressive disorder of the brain that gradually affects memory, personality, behaviour, identity, and interpersonal relationships, particularly among older adults. Alice Munro's novella \"The Bear Came Over the Mountain\" offers a compelling literary framework for exploring these impacts through narrative gerontology, a lens that emphasizes storytelling's role in shaping identity and relational bonds during ageing and illness. Method This study applies narrative gerontology to analyze Munro's depiction of Alzheimer's, focusing on the experiences of Fiona and Grant. Through detailed textual analysis, it examines the gerontological concept of \"we-narrative\" (shared relational identity) to understand how identity, memory loss, and relational dynamics evolve. In Sweden, national and regional frameworks such as Nära Vård (Good and Close Care) and the Sörmland Dementia Strategy promote autonomy, participation, and collaboration. Yet, their enactment unfolds within layered institutional systems characterized by multiple logics, documentation demands, and fragmented responsibilities, which often dilute the intent of person-centered policies. The study applied a policy enactment perspective to examine how person-centered and dementia-related policies are interpreted, negotiated, and translated into municipal homecare services. This journal is\nindexed on PubMed Central, MedLine, CAS, Scopus and the Elsevier\n\n...Question: What should I do if I am concerned about how our relationship as an LGBTQIA+ couple will be affected in a dementia care setting other than our home?\nAnswer: If you are in a relationship and are considering a location other than your private home for dementia care, it is important to think about a few key factors. Firstly, finding a care provider who has experience in dementia care and is knowledgeable about the challenges faced by LGBTQIA+ individuals is crucial. This is because there can be bias and prejudice towards minority groups, and it's important to have someone sensitive to these issues. Consider how bringing in outside help could impact your dynamic as a couple and your relationship. Think about how it might affect your physical, sensory, social, and daily intimacy, as well as the shared space you have. It may be helpful to discuss your routines and habits with potential care providers and assess if they can accommodate your needs. If not, you may want to consider seeking alternative resources or support to advocate for your rights. This is a serious conversation that may require involving healthcare providers and legal support to ensure both of your lives are impacted positively moving forward. The focus should be on creating a happy and engaging experience for them, rather than worrying about whether they're doing it \"right.\" So go ahead and play games with your loved one, even if they may not remember the rules or understand the game. The key is to provide them with a meaningful and enjoyable activity that brings them happiness and connection.\nQuestion: Is it a good idea to get a pet for someone with dementia?\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\n...Answer: When someone with dementia starts forgetting to follow the rules, like cutting in line or trying to get ahead, it's important to approach the situation with understanding and empathy. Recognize that they may have a perceived need or feel anxious about waiting in line. It's also important to check our own reactions and find ways to manage the situation calmly. One strategy is to have a companion card on hand. This card explains that the person you are with is experiencing changes in their brain, and apologizes in advance for any distress they may cause. The back of the card can provide information about where to find more resources and support. Alternatively, if it's safe and reasonable, you can try to find a solution together. For example, in the scenario presented, the narrator suggests getting in front of someone in line. It's important to communicate respectfully with others and explain the situation, without causing confrontation or distress. Sometimes, it may not be possible to stop the behavior, and in those moments it can be best to apologize and move on. It's important to remember that impulse control may be low for someone with dementia, and trying to reason or argue may not be productive. By offering understanding and finding ways to work together, we can help minimize challenges and maintain a positive experience for everyone involved....\n\n...Question: What should I do when someone with dementia is not following directions?\nAnswer: When communicating with someone living with dementia, it's important to consider how you are giving directions. Did you provide visual, verbal, or physical cues? Did you give a whole sequence of steps or just one step at a time? If the person is not following your directions, it may be because you gave them too much information at once or they are doing it in their own way. It's important to observe and make a decision whether it's necessary to have them do it your way or if you can let go and allow them to do it their way. In the example, Teepa is initially confused when asked to put on the shirt, but once it is clearly explained, she understands. It'sa reminder that it's not just about getting the shirt on, but about how we communicate in all aspects of caregiving. Remember to slow down and adjust your pace to accommodate the person with dementia, as everyone follows directions differently.\nQuestion: How do I deal with anger from someone with dementia because I can't understand them?...\n\nQuestion: Is it okay to lie to my loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: It is understandable to have questions about how to communicate with a loved one who has dementia. Sometimes, people with dementia may believe in things that aren't true. For example, they may think a deceased person is still alive. In such situations, it can be helpful to use what I call \"therapeutic fiblets.\" These fiblets are not lies but rather responses that keep the person calm and safe. For instance, if your loved one says they want to visit their deceased mother, you can respond by saying that you will plan a trip. The key is to find a response that doesn't allow them to argue or become upset. It's important to understand that using therapeutic fiblets is not deceitful but rather a way to ensure their well-being and your own sanity. Instead of reminding them of the truth, which may only lead to frustration for both of you, it's better to focus on making them feel secure. So remember, when necessary, use therapeutic fiblets to create a positive and supportive environment for your loved one with dementia....\n\n...Question: Why would someone with dementia start making up memories?\nAnswer: It's common for individuals with dementia to share memories that may seem made up or farfetched. However, it's important to approach this with empathy and understanding. Firstly, not all of these memories are necessarily fabricated. Sometimes, clients share historical events that only a few family members knew about, so it's possible that what may seem made up is actually true. Secondly, it's important to remember that dementia affects the person's cognitive abilities and their brain. They may be sharing their perspective and memories the best way they can, given their condition. It's not accurate or fair to label them as intentionally making things up or lying. Instead, we should approach their memories with empathy and respect, understanding that they are trying to communicate based on their own unique experience. It's crucial to create a supportive environment where they feel heard and validated. If you have any concerns or questions about your loved one's memories, it's always a good idea to consult with a healthcare professional who specializes in dementia care.\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\n\n...Question: How do I avoid lying to someone with dementia?\nAnswer: Avoiding lying to someone with dementia can be a challenging task. While honesty and transparency are generally valued in our society, the nature of dementia can make it difficult for individuals to understand logic and reasoning. In such cases, bending the truth or engaging in therapeutic fibbing can be a more compassionate and loving approach. It is important to remember that accepting this can be easier for some people than others. However, the benefits to the person with dementia often outweigh the potential drawbacks. While it may require some internal reflection on how one can live with lying to someone they care about, it is crucial to prioritize the well-being and best interests of the person with dementia. Reminding ourselves that we love them and are acting in their best interest can help us come to terms with this difficult decision. Ultimately, making these choices with compassion and love can support the overall care and comfort of individuals with dementia.\nQuestion: How do I deal with someone with dementia yelling at me?...\n\nQuestion: How can I include someone with advanced dementia in activities?\nAnswer: People with advanced dementia can still participate in activities that bring them joy and improve their overall well-being. It's important for us, as caregivers, to let go of our expectations about how these activities should look. Even if someone with dementia doesn't follow the rules or seems to be doing something that doesn't make sense, it's okay. What matters is if they are enjoying themselves. Let them read a book upside down or hold cards the wrong way. Even coloring outside the lines is fine. You can also introduce new activities that they haven't tried before. Remember to tap into their past and bring activities they used to enjoy into their current life. For example, if they were a golfer, they may enjoy looking at golf magazines, watching golf on TV, or playing a putting game at home. Don't underestimate the value of simply being in their presence while you engage in an activity. Pay attention to their non-verbal cues and, if they can still speak, ask for their feedback. Their calmness and enjoyment will guide you in providing meaningful activities.\nQuestion: How can holiday meals be made easier for people with dementia?...", "final_context": "...Question: What do I do if someone with dementia wants to play a game but doesn't remember the rules?\nAnswer: If you have a loved one with dementia who wants to play games but can't remember how to play them, that's totally okay.
