This is actually a common occurrence. When visitors come to see the person with dementia, it can be exciting and new for them. This unique experience can make them appear sharper and more engaged. On the other hand, you, the person who spends the most time with them, often see them at their worst and when they need the most help. You may also be a constant reminder of the things they can no longer do and the potential dangers they face. This can lead to them appearing more impaired and dependent on you. It's important to understand that if your loved one seems better around others, it doesn't mean they are faking it or trying to deceive you. People with dementia can have good and bad moments, and it's especially common for them to appear much better in unfamiliar situations, like when friends or family members who don't visit often come by. This phenomenon can also be noticed when they are talking on the phone with others. In conclusion, the presence of others may bring out the best in individuals with dementia, while you may witness their struggles more frequently as their primary caregiver. Remember that their behavior can vary depending on the circumstances, and it is not intentional or deceptive....\n\nQuestion: Is it okay to lie to my loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: It is understandable to have questions about how to communicate with a loved one who has dementia. Sometimes, people with dementia may believe in things that aren't true. For example, they may think a deceased person is still alive. In such situations, it can be helpful to use what I call \"therapeutic fiblets.\" These fiblets are not lies but rather responses that keep the person calm and safe. For instance, if your loved one says they want to visit their deceased mother, you can respond by saying that you will plan a trip. The key is to find a response that doesn't allow them to argue or become upset. It's important to understand that using therapeutic fiblets is not deceitful but rather a way to ensure their well-being and your own sanity. Instead of reminding them of the truth, which may only lead to frustration for both of you, it's better to focus on making them feel secure. So remember, when necessary, use therapeutic fiblets to create a positive and supportive environment for your loved one with dementia....\n\nCommunicating with someone with\ndementia\nDementia is a progressive illness that, over time, will affect a person's ability to remember\nand understand basic everyday facts, such as names, dates and places.\nDementia will gradually affect the way a person communicates. Their ability to present\nrational ideas and to reason clearly will change.\nIf you are looking after a person with dementia, you may find that as the illness progresses\nyou'll have to start discussions to get the person to make conversation. This is common.\nTheir ability to process information gets progressively weaker and their responses can\nbecome delayed.\nEncouraging someone with dementia to communicate\nTry to start conversations with the person you're looking after, especially if you notice that\nthey're starting fewer conversations themselves. It can help to:\n● speak clearly and slowly, using short sentences\n● make eye contact with the person when they're talking or asking questions\n● give them time to respond, because they may feel pressured if you try to speed up\ntheir answers\n● encourage them to join in conversations with others, where possible\n● let them speak for themselves during discussions about their welfare or health issues...\n\n...Answer: If your loved one with dementia is speaking in a way that doesn't make sense, it can be frustrating and confusing for both of you. In some cases, the person may have reverted back to their first language, which you may not understand. In other cases, they may be putting together words in a way that doesn't form coherent sentences. When you try to understand what they're saying and can't, it can make them upset and in turn, make you upset as well. One thing to keep in mind is that if their immediate needs are taken care of and they're not in need of something urgent like using the restroom or being hungry or thirsty, they may simply be sharing something with you. In these situations, you can still engage in active listening skills without fully understanding their words. This can include nodding, smiling, and using affirming responses like \"uh-huh\" or \"okay.\" If the person with dementia continues to talk and seems content with the conversation, even if you don't understand what they're saying, it's best to allow them to express themselves. This is more likely to result in a positive interaction compared to constantly trying to understand them and getting frustrated. Remember, your non-verbal cues and how you respond communicate to them whether or not you understand, which can affect their emotions....\n\n...but semantic abilities are impaired. Conclusion:\nCommunication for people with dementia and with\npeople with dementia for all persons involved in\ncare (including family members, medical staff and\ntherapists, and members of the community) can\nbe very challenging. It is often necessary to adapt\nthe way of communication to avoid stress and\nnegative feelings in a person with dementia. As\nthe disease causing dementia progresses, communication problems are increasing as well. Many\ntimes caregivers and therapists are in situations\nwhere their communicative behavior (verbal, but\nalso nonverbal) needs to show support, compassion, care, and desire to help.\nKeywords: dementia, communication, communication diffi culties.\n1. INTRODUCTION\nThe increase of the average chronological\nage of the population is accompanied by specifi c psychopathology of that age, and consequently the interest of science for problems of\nelderly (1). Alzheimer's Disease International\nreports that at present it is estimated that 35\nmillion people worldwide have Alzheimer's or\nrelated dementia, and an increase in expected\nlife expectancy is expected to increase global\nprevalence to around 66 million by 2030 and...\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\n...Myth\nFact\nExplanation\nPeople with\ndementia can't\nunderstand others\nbecause of their\ncondition.\nPeople with dementia can\noften understand and engage\nin communication.\nWhile some forms of dementia can affect verbal\ncommunication, you can meet your care\nrecipient where they are by finding ways of\ncommunicating that work for them and their\ncurrent abilities. For example, you can use\ngestures or ask yes or no questions that they can\nnod or shake their heads to respond to.\n\n...might try the following suggestions:\n● Enhance communication. When talking with your loved one, maintain eye\ncontact. Speak slowly in simple sentences, and don't rush the response.\nPresent one idea or instruction at a time. Use gestures and cues, such as\npointing to objects.\n● Encourage exercise. The main benefits of exercise in people with\ndementia include improved strength, balance and cardiovascular health.\nExercise also might help with symptoms such as restlessness. Speak slowly in simple sentences, and don't rush the response.\n\n\nCITATIONS:\n- SPAN 2\n=== END TOP EVIDENCE (TF) ===\n\n...Answer: Sometimes, people with dementia may seem to be doing much better when they are around other people than when they are with you. This is actually a common occurrence. When visitors come to see the person with dementia, it can be exciting and new for them. This unique experience can make them appear sharper and more engaged. On the other hand, you, the person who spends the most time with them, often see them at their worst and when they need the most help. You may also be a constant reminder of the things they can no longer do and the potential dangers they face. This can lead to them appearing more impaired and dependent on you. It's important to understand that if your loved one seems better around others, it doesn't mean they are faking it or trying to deceive you. People with dementia can have good and bad moments, and it's especially common for them to appear much better in unfamiliar situations, like when friends or family members who don't visit often come by. This phenomenon can also be noticed when they are talking on the phone with others. In conclusion, the presence of others may bring out the best in individuals with dementia, while you may witness their struggles more frequently as their primary caregiver. Remember that their behavior can vary depending on the circumstances, and it is not intentional or deceptive....\n\nQuestion: Is it okay to lie to my loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: It is understandable to have questions about how to communicate with a loved one who has dementia. Sometimes, people with dementia may believe in things that aren't true. For example, they may think a deceased person is still alive. In such situations, it can be helpful to use what I call \"therapeutic fiblets.\" These fiblets are not lies but rather responses that keep the person calm and safe. For instance, if your loved one says they want to visit their deceased mother, you can respond by saying that you will plan a trip. The key is to find a response that doesn't allow them to argue or become upset. It's important to understand that using therapeutic fiblets is not deceitful but rather a way to ensure their well-being and your own sanity. Instead of reminding them of the truth, which may only lead to frustration for both of you, it's better to focus on making them feel secure. So remember, when necessary, use therapeutic fiblets to create a positive and supportive environment for your loved one with dementia....\n\nCommunicating with someone with\ndementia\nDementia is a progressive illness that, over time, will affect a person's ability to remember\nand understand basic everyday facts, such as names, dates and places.\nDementia will gradually affect the way a person communicates. Their ability to present\nrational ideas and to reason clearly will change.\nIf you are looking after a person with dementia, you may find that as the illness progresses\nyou'll have to start discussions to get the person to make conversation. This is common.\nTheir ability to process information gets progressively weaker and their responses can\nbecome delayed.\nEncouraging someone with dementia to communicate\nTry to start conversations with the person you're looking after, especially if you notice that\nthey're starting fewer conversations themselves. It can help to:\n● speak clearly and slowly, using short sentences\n● make eye contact with the person when they're talking or asking questions\n● give them time to respond, because they may feel pressured if you try to speed up\ntheir answers\n● encourage them to join in conversations with others, where possible\n● let them speak for themselves during discussions about their welfare or health issues...\n\n...Answer: If your loved one with dementia is speaking in a way that doesn't make sense, it can be frustrating and confusing for both of you. In some cases, the person may have reverted back to their first language, which you may not understand. In other cases, they may be putting together words in a way that doesn't form coherent sentences. When you try to understand what they're saying and can't, it can make them upset and in turn, make you upset as well. One thing to keep in mind is that if their immediate needs are taken care of and they're not in need of something urgent like using the restroom or being hungry or thirsty, they may simply be sharing something with you. In these situations, you can still engage in active listening skills without fully understanding their words. This can include nodding, smiling, and using affirming responses like \"uh-huh\" or \"okay.\" If the person with dementia continues to talk and seems content with the conversation, even if you don't understand what they're saying, it's best to allow them to express themselves. This is more likely to result in a positive interaction compared to constantly trying to understand them and getting frustrated. Remember, your non-verbal cues and how you respond communicate to them whether or not you understand, which can affect their emotions....\n\n...but semantic abilities are impaired. Conclusion:\nCommunication for people with dementia and with\npeople with dementia for all persons involved in\ncare (including family members, medical staff and\ntherapists, and members of the community) can\nbe very challenging. It is often necessary to adapt\nthe way of communication to avoid stress and\nnegative feelings in a person with dementia. As\nthe disease causing dementia progresses, communication problems are increasing as well. Many\ntimes caregivers and therapists are in situations\nwhere their communicative behavior (verbal, but\nalso nonverbal) needs to show support, compassion, care, and desire to help.\nKeywords: dementia, communication, communication diffi culties.\n1. INTRODUCTION\nThe increase of the average chronological\nage of the population is accompanied by specifi c psychopathology of that age, and consequently the interest of science for problems of\nelderly (1). Alzheimer's Disease International\nreports that at present it is estimated that 35\nmillion people worldwide have Alzheimer's or\nrelated dementia, and an increase in expected\nlife expectancy is expected to increase global\nprevalence to around 66 million by 2030 and...\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\n...Myth\nFact\nExplanation\nPeople with\ndementia can't\nunderstand others\nbecause of their\ncondition.\nPeople with dementia can\noften understand and engage\nin communication.\nWhile some forms of dementia can affect verbal\ncommunication, you can meet your care\nrecipient where they are by finding ways of\ncommunicating that work for them and their\ncurrent abilities. For example, you can use\ngestures or ask yes or no questions that they can\nnod or shake their heads to respond to.\n\n...might try the following suggestions:\n● Enhance communication. When talking with your loved one, maintain eye\ncontact. Speak slowly in simple sentences, and don't rush the response.\nPresent one idea or instruction at a time. Use gestures and cues, such as\npointing to objects.\n● Encourage exercise. The main benefits of exercise in people with\ndementia include improved strength, balance and cardiovascular health.\nExercise also might help with symptoms such as restlessness. There is\ngrowing evidence that exercise also protects the brain from dementia,\nespecially when combined with a healthy diet and treatment of risk factors\nfor cardiovascular disease.\nSome research also shows that physical activity might slow the progression"}

However, it's important to remember that their behavior may stem from a sensory experience rather than being sexual in nature. As the person in proximity, you need to take charge of the situation, but without making the person with dementia feel like they've done something wrong. It's also crucial to avoid causing distress or anger for them. In these situations, it's helpful to modify what you're doing and present them with alternative ways of being touched that are less intimate and distressing. You can also give simple directions and allow them time to process the information. It's important to prioritize safety and your own comfort while still meeting their needs. For example, when getting into a car and fastening a seatbelt, you can use the hand-under-hand technique to guide their movements. It's important to allow them to be wrong and not constantly correct them unless their safety is at risk. Reminding them of their diagnosis and their memory problems can make them feel worse and strain the relationship, so it's best to avoid doing so. It's also important to not let caregiving consume everything and neglect the personal relationship; take time to simply enjoy activities together without making it all about caregiving. Even though caregiving requires a lot of time and effort, find moments during the day to connect and be present without a focus on caregiving. Lastly, it's crucial to remember that the decline of the disease is not a reflection of how well you are caregiving. Despite doing everything recommended by doctors and experts, the dementia will progress and your loved one will decline. There is no right or wrong answer to this personal question. You should explore your own feelings and desires, and seek guidance from trusted sources like friends, faith partners, or social workers. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42359382)\nPurpose This study aimed to clarify and analyze the concept of Patient-Centered Communication (PCC) among home-based dementia caregivers. Although patient centered communication is recognized as a cornerstone of quality dementia care, its defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, and empirical referents remain poorly delineated in the context of home-based caregiving. Design A concept analysis using the Walker and Avant (2019) eight-step framework was employed to systematically examine the structure and meaning of PCC within home-based dementia care. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability and validity of the HSCP-KALLIS scale. Methods This methodological study was a subsequent phase of the HSCP-KALLIS scale development undertaken between 2022 and 2023, using an online survey approach with participants who were health and social care professionals. During this stage, caregivers may want to use\nsupport services, such as hospice care, which focus on\nproviding comfort and dignity at the end of life. Hospice can be\nof great benefit to people in the final stages of Alzheimer's and\nother dementias and their families.\n\n...Question: How do you safely and effectively address personal care issues for someone with dementia?\nAnswer: When it comes to supporting someone with dementia, self-care is important. It can be broken down into five steps: preparation, initiation, participation, evaluation, and then either continuing or making changes. First, you need to prepare yourself mentally and emotionally. Then, you initiate the interaction with the person with dementia. Encourage their participation in the activity or task. Afterward, evaluate how it went. If it went well, continue with the same approach. If not, you may need to make some adjustments. There are five areas where you can make changes: the location, the people involved, the items used, the timing, or even try a completely different activity. These are your \"five P's\" – the place, people, props, programming, and possibility. By following this process and being aware of what is and isn't working, you can find ways to better support the person with dementia. Remember, seeking permission and recognizing when something isn't working is crucial before proceeding.\nQuestion: Why might someone with dementia keep their eyes closed or look away?...\n\n...Question: What is a dementia touch point and how is it useful in dementia care?\nAnswer: A dementia touchpoint is a topic or activity that can be enjoyable and engaging for both the caregiver and the person with dementia. It can help make conversations more interesting and less repetitive. Instead of just talking about the weather or what's on TV, a touchpoint is something fun and interactive that you can discuss together. For example, you could have a plant in their room as a touchpoint. You can water the plant together, take photos of it, and compare how it's growing. You can also look at pictures of other plants and talk about ones you might want to have in the future. Another touchpoint could be a puzzle that you work on together. You can discuss the progress you've made, how well they're doing, and where you want to display the completed puzzle. The goal is to choose a topic or activity that you both enjoy and can talk about and interact with. It's important to make the conversation pleasant and avoid making it feel like an interrogation. So, I encourage you to try finding a fun touchpoint to engage with your loved one with dementia...."}

(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41804465)\nThe clinical overlap between behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and primary psychiatric disorders (PPD) often results in delayed and incorrect diagnoses. We performed a literature review of 16 studies to evaluate how neuropsychiatric, behavioral, and social cognitive symptoms can aid in distinguishing bvFTD from PPD during early clinical assessment. Our study revealed differences in symptom profile and trajectory in the two diseases. Apathy, disinhibition, and compulsions were more likely to progress in bvFTD, while often remaining stable or improving in PPD. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/39365656)\nBackground An estimated 6.7 million persons are living with dementia in the United States, a number expected to double by 2060. Persons experiencing moderate to severe dementia are 4 to 5 times more likely to fall than those without dementia, due to agitation and unsteady gait. Socially assistive robots fail to address the changing emotional states associated with agitation, and it is unclear how emotional states change, how they impact agitation and gait over time, and how social robots can best respond by showing empathy. Objective This study aims to design and validate a foundational model of emotional intelligence for empathetic patient-robot interaction that mitigates agitation among those at the highest risk: persons experiencing moderate to severe dementia. Methods A design science\n\nIn dementia caregiving, **the great majority of communication — about 90% — is nonverbal**, conveyed through facial expression, body language, posture, tone of voice, and touch rather than through words. Because roughly 90% of communication is nonverbal, caregivers should pay close attention to these cues.\n**People are usually not aware of the nonverbal messages they are sending.** Nonverbal communication is largely unconscious, so a caregiver's own facial expressions, posture, and tone may convey feelings — such as impatience, stress, or warmth — without the caregiver realizing it.\n**Once you learn how to look for nonverbal messages, you will better understand what a person living with dementia is trying to express.** As verbal ability declines, people living with dementia rely increasingly on nonverbal communication, so reading these cues reveals their needs and feelings.\n\n...A person with dementia may not express many emotions through their facial expression, particularly happiness or sadness. Activities or events that generally entertain them may create little to no response. The lack of motivation and the low energy levels may cause a lack of effort and planning in carrying out activities they usually like.\nIn the long term, apathy may affect a person's ability to maintain personal relationships, which in turn can increase isolation. When apathy is one of the first signs of dementia – especially when it appears before a formal diagnosis – friends and family members may become frustrated by their loved one's indifference, and not realize the underlying cause.\nTips for caregivers\nIf you're caring for someone with dementia, their lack of interest and unwillingness to engage in everyday life activities can be a source of distress.\nIt's common for family members and caregivers to feel overloaded with every minute of their loved one's life. Making some changes in how you approach caring for your loved one can promote their autonomy and independence.\nFor example, it is essential to minimize your loved one's weaknesses. Reassure and involve them in simple and rewarding activities to maintain their self-esteem....\n\n...Question: How do I deal with anger from someone with dementia because I can't understand them?\nAnswer: Dealing with anger in someone living with dementia can be challenging, but there are strategies to help diffuse the situation. It's important to remember that it's normal to feel frustrated and angry at times. One approach is to apologize and explain that you're having difficulty understanding what they're saying. By taking responsibility for the miscommunication, you might be able to avoid escalating the situation. You can also try mirroring their facial expressions to establish a connection and show that you're trying to understand. If possible, finding humor in the situation can help lighten the mood and ease tension. Additionally, it's okay to express your own emotions, such as crying, as it can sometimes elicit empathy and comfort from the person with dementia, especially if they are a parent. Remember, being a caregiver is challenging, and it's important to be compassionate with yourself.\n\nQuestion: How do I introduce a new caregiver to someone with dementia if it upsets them every time we mention it?\nAnswer: People with dementia can get upset when new caregivers are mentioned ahead of time because they can fixate on future events due to disorientation with time. To introduce a new caregiver without causing distress, it's recommended not to bring it up until the event is imminent. For instance, inform them on the day of the caregiver's arrival to avoid prolonged stress and anxiety. You can present it positively by mentioning that a great new caregiver is coming soon. By delaying the discussion until the last minute, you can lessen their anxiety and reduce repetitive questions. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41918798)\nIntroduction Supporting a person living with dementia involves multiple challenges, particularly when responding to changes in behaviour and psychological symptoms, which can be emotionally demanding for care partners. Despite this, limited research has examined how care partners in Latin America experience and respond to these symptoms. Therefore, this study aims to gain an understanding of how family care partners of persons living with dementia experience and cope with behavioural and psychological dementia symptoms (BPSD). Methods A qualitative study was carried out using semi-structured interviews with 17 family care partners of individuals with clinically confirmed dementia and BPSD, recruited from a private neurology clinic in Lima, Peru. It is important to respect their reality. This might mean going along with a\nstory they are telling you that seems unreal to you.2\nSupporting a person to live well with dementia\nFor people living with dementia to maintain a sense of well-being, they need to live in a supportive\nsocial environment, where they are accepted, respected, have meaningful relationships and are\nsupported to grow.\nThere are many ways to create a supportive environment:\n•\nGet to know the person and show them respect (e.g., greet the person by name, use eye\ncontact, actively communicate with and listen to the person).\n•\nConnect with the person rather than correcting them. Share a moment with the person even if\ntheir reality or perception of the moment is different from yours own.\n•...\n\nMany people with dementia become confused and disorientated at times. This may lead to\nthem believing things that are not true – known as ‘false beliefs' or ‘delusions'. Our dementia\nspecialist Admiral Nurses explain why this might happen, and how you can help the person\nyou care for.\nCollapse all\nWhat are false beliefs and delusions?\nEveryone has different personal beliefs. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\n...Question: Why are some people with dementia in denial about their diagnosis?\nAnswer: People with dementia may seem like they are in denial because they don't believe anything is wrong with them. However, this is not actually denial, but a condition called anosognosia. Anosognosia is a lack of awareness, which means that their brain is not able to understand that something is wrong with them. No matter how much evidence or convincing you try, they will not be able to comprehend that there is an issue with their brain. First, try to understand why they may be reluctant to eat. It could be that they are experiencing problems with their teeth or mouth, making it difficult to chew or swallow. As the disease progresses, these issues can become more common. You could also consider if there is an environmental overload that might be affecting their ability to focus on eating. For example, being in a busy dining room with lots of noise and activity could be overwhelming. In my own experience, I find it hard to engage in conversation or listen to someone while I'm eating. I need to solely focus on the activity. So it might be helpful to create a quiet and calm environment during meals. You could troubleshoot these potential issues and see if they make a difference. Additionally, if necessary, you may want to explore alternative ways of consuming food, such as drinking it in liquid or pureed form.\nQuestion: Is it possible for someone with dementia to forget to eat?\n\nQuestion: Is it possible for someone with dementia to forget to eat?\nAnswer: It is indeed possible for individuals with dementia to forget to eat. Many people with dementia often report feeling not hungry anymore. This lack of appetite can be exacerbated by memory and cognitive issues. As the disorder progresses, individuals may also lose track of time, making it even easier to forget to eat. In later stages of dementia, problem-solving abilities may deteriorate, making it difficult to figure out what to do about feeling hungry. Caregivers need to be attentive to whether their loved ones with dementia are taking care of their eating needs, such as getting themselves snacks or making sandwiches. It is important to speak with a physician or care team if there are concerns about a decreased motivation to eat or noticeable changes in eating habits.\nQuestion: Are there foods that slow the progression of dementia?...\n\n...Answer: People with dementia often experience changes in their eating patterns. Some individuals may eat more, particularly sweets, while others may lose their appetite. When assessing changes in eating habits, it's important to thoroughly evaluate the underlying causes. One reason for reduced food intake in people with dementia is the loss of cooking skills or the inability to follow recipes. Additionally, older adults, including those with dementia, may experience diminished taste and smell, which can affect their hunger levels. Altering the flavors and appearance of foods may make them more appealing. Some individuals with dementia may become overwhelmed by a regular plate of food they once enjoyed. Observing whether they fare better with finger foods or utensils can help determine their preferred method of eating. Physical difficulties in grasping utensils may require specialized utensils or finger-based eating. The dining environment, such as distractions or the presence of other people, can also affect eating. Pain or dental issues may contribute to reduced food intake, so it's crucial to be vigilant in observing any signs of discomfort. If the person with dementia experiences choking, it's important to consult their primary care doctor, who may recommend a swallowing evaluation. Communicating any observations or concerns to the healthcare provider is essential for the person's well-being....\n\n...Question: How can you tell when someone with dementia is close to death?\nAnswer: When it comes to determining if someone with dementia is approaching the end of their life, it can be a challenging task. However, there are a few signs that we can look out for. One common observation is a decrease in appetite or difficulty in eating. This may occur because the body is struggling to process nutrients, leading to a decreased desire or ability to eat. Another symptom that may arise is increased confusion or delirium as the individual nears the end of their life. Additionally, it is not uncommon for the person to sleep more, potentially spending most of their day sleeping. Nonetheless, it is important to note that evaluating the progression of dementia can be quite complicated. Therefore, it is crucial to have open conversations with healthcare providers or individuals who have been observing the person with dementia over a long period. This can provide a better understanding of the overall trajectory of the disease and help guide decisions and expectations.\nQuestion: How should I think about resuscitation (CPR and chest compressions) in someone who has severe dementia?...\n\nQuestion: What can a person with dementia do when they no longer recognize hunger and thirst cues?\nAnswer: For individuals with dementia who no longer recognize hunger or thirst cues, there are a few strategies that can be helpful. Firstly, instead of asking if they are hungry or thirsty, offer choices between different foods or beverages. This gives them a sense of control over their eating and drinking without focusing on the yes or no response. Establishing a meal and beverage schedule can also be beneficial, providing a structured routine for when to eat and drink, since relying on cues may no longer be effective. Leaving out easily accessible snacks like nuts or pretzels can increase the likelihood of them eating, and having visible glasses of water or cans of sparkling water throughout the house can remind them to drink. Lastly, inviting them to eat with you and showing them that you are eating or drinking can encourage them to do the same. Support and encouragement are crucial in ensuring they receive the necessary nutrition and hydration, especially when their cues are diminished. Regular check-ins, even remotely, can help ensure they are staying nourished and hydrated.\nQuestion: What is suggested if a person with dementia has changes in food preferences?...\n\nEating and drinking\nSpace for\nyour notes\n3 Poor appetite and\nstopping eating\nA person with dementia may lose interest in food. They may\nrefuse to eat it or spit it out. The person may become angry or\ndistressed, or behave in a challenging way during mealtimes.\nIf someone isn't eating enough, it can lead to weight loss and\nless muscle strength. They may also feel tired and weak. This can\nmake them frailer and less able to recover from infections\nor viruses.\nIf you're concerned about someone who continues to refuse to\neat, speak to a pharmacist or the GP.\nWhy someone with dementia might\nstop eating\nA person may lose interest in, or turn down, food and drink\nbecause of physical difficulties, such as problems with\nchewing and swallowing, or constipation. For more information\nsee ‘How dementia affects eating and drinking' on page 1.\nThere are other reasons why a person may stop eating.\nUnderstanding the reason can help you find appropriate\nsupport and solutions.\nDepression\nLoss of appetite can be a sign of depression, which is common\nin people with dementia. There are effective treatments for...\n\n...Question: What do I do if someone living with dementia is eating or chewing non-food items?\nAnswer: If the person living with dementia is starting to eat non-food items, such as napkins or Kleenex, it is important to determine the cause of this behavior. It could be a sensory need, where the person has a desire to do something with their mouth, or it could be a case of mistaken identity, where they are having difficulty identifying objects. If it is a case of mistaken identity, removing those non-food items from their reach can help. However, if it is a sensory need, finding safe alternatives for them to chew on, such as specially designed objects for adults with autism, may be helpful. The key is to understand the underlying cause of the distress and respond accordingly. Instead of reacting negatively, it is better to respond by offering a substitution. This could involve offering a tasty food item to redirect their attention from non-food items. By providing an alternative that can be safely consumed, you can help them focus on eating actual food rather than non-food items.\nQuestion: How can I include someone with more advanced dementia in family meals?...\n\n...they are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. Because roughly 90% of communication is nonverbal, caregivers should pay close attention to these cues.\n**People are usually not aware of the nonverbal messages they are sending.** Nonverbal communication is largely unconscious, so a caregiver's own facial expressions, posture, and tone may convey feelings — such as impatience, stress, or warmth — without the caregiver realizing it.\n**Once you learn how to look for nonverbal messages, you will better understand what a person living with dementia is trying to express.** As verbal ability declines, people living with dementia rely increasingly on nonverbal communication, so reading these cues reveals their needs and feelings.\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\nListening to and understanding someone with dementia\nCommunication is a two-way process. As a carer of someone with dementia, you will\nprobably have to learn to listen more carefully.\nYou may need to be more aware of non-verbal messages, such as facial expressions and\nbody language. First, you need to have a good understanding of the disease itself. This means learning about both the physical and emotional aspects of caring for someone with dementia. It's crucial to prioritize safety for both the person with dementia and yourself. This means making sure the environment is safe and secure and taking measures to prevent accidents or injuries. It's also important to prioritize your own mental well-being and find ways to cope with the challenges of caregiving. Rather than arguing or trying to convince the person with dementia against their desires, it's best to find ways to redirect their attention or provide alternatives that are safer or more suitable. For example, if they want to go skydiving, you could suggest going for ice cream instead. In order to effectively care for someone with dementia, it's important to understand their world and learn about their experiences and needs. Reading about dementia and joining support groups can provide valuable insights and strategies. Being an effective caregiver often requires a lot of repetition, so it's important to learn and prepare for the specific tasks involved in their care. Attending caregiver classes and seeking information from local agencies can be helpful resources. However, it's crucial to always keep the person with dementia at the center of your care and to respect their dignity and autonomy....\n\n...It's important to remember that impulse control may be low for someone with dementia, and trying to reason or argue may not be productive. By offering understanding and finding ways to work together, we can help minimize challenges and maintain a positive experience for everyone involved....\n\n...Answer: When someone with dementia is facing adversity, it is important for caregivers to provide support in a meaningful way. It can be difficult when loved ones try to offer comfort by pretending that everything will be fine and that the person will live forever, as this can feel isolating and unrealistic. Instead, caregivers should try to strike a balance between comforting and acknowledging the reality of the situation. For example, if someone is worried about a pet who is undergoing surgery, they may want their caregiver to be there with them in their anxiety and provide reassurance based on the facts. It is important for caregivers to understand that their role is not to simply cheerlead or offer false hope, but to genuinely be present and empathetic. Rather than standing at the top of a metaphorical rabbit hole and shouting encouragement, caregivers should be willing to jump into the hole with the person experiencing grief, anxiety, or sadness. By being there with them and providing support, caregivers can help them navigate through difficult emotions and find ways to cope. Every individual may have different needs when it comes to support, but genuine companionship and understanding are essential. So, caregivers should aim to provide empathy, comfort, and companionship when someone with dementia is facing adversity....\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\n...Question: How do you maximize happiness for your loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: When caring for a loved one with dementia, it's important to prioritize their happiness. One key way to do this is to avoid arguing with them. People with dementia have a different perspective than ours, and it's easy for us as caregivers to become frustrated when they act in ways that seem irrational to us. We might try to correct them and bring them back to our reality, but this approach doesn't work. It's called reality orientation, and it involves constantly correcting the person and telling them what is real. Instead, a better approach is called validation therapy. This means validating the person's perspective, even if it's different from ours. If they believe something that we know is not true, there's no need to argue or correct them. By accepting their perspective and not arguing, we can help keep them relatively happy.\nQuestion: Can antipsychotics make dementia worse?...\n\n...Attend carefully to what the person is saying and doing,\nto understand their reality. Acknowledge their worry, and\nexplain you will try to help. They are more likely to be gently\ndistracted, once they feel heard.\nNot contradicting their experience. They shouldn't be told\nwhat is or is not true in a confrontational manner. They may\nbecome frightened or upset.\nRemembering that emotional memories are often easier\nto retrieve. Staying open, calm and friendly can help the\nperson with dementia to associate a carer with positive\nemotions, even if they struggle to understand who you are\nin the present.\nRemaining calm. If a carer becomes frustrated that the person\nis struggling with the present, they should take themselves\nout of the situation until they feel calmer, perhaps making a\ndrink for them both to take some time out of the room.\nRemembering the positive difference they make to the\nperson with dementia. The person with dementia does not\nneed to fully understand your reality for them to feel happy,\nso continue to try and do what makes them feel content.\n\nLying In Dementia\nCaregiving\nLying In Dementia Caregiving\nAs a caregiver for a person with dementia, you may have faced situations where\ntelling the truth would cause more harm than withholding it. For example, if your\ncare recipient repeatedly asks where their long-deceased parent is, you'll likely\navoid telling them the truth to prevent them from re-experiencing feelings of grief\nand loss. Some caregivers lie to protect their care recipient's safety or well-being.\nIn these situations, “lying” to protect the person you care for may be beneficial to\nyou both.\nDid You Know?\nSome researchers refer to this strategy as “therapeutic lying” or\n“therapeutic fibbing” to reflect that refraining from telling the truth can\nbe beneficial to a care recipient with dementia in certain situations.\nCaregivers of people with dementia may often experience the dilemma of whether\nor not to modify the truth to their care recipient–even if they know they intend to\nhelp them. This is normal! Research talks about how there are different types of\nlies used in caregiving, different reasons that caregivers may use lies, and the pros...\n\nQuestion: Is it okay to lie to my loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: It is understandable to have questions about how to communicate with a loved one who has dementia. Sometimes, people with dementia may believe in things that aren't true. For example, they may think a deceased person is still alive. In such situations, it can be helpful to use what I call \"therapeutic fiblets.\" These fiblets are not lies but rather responses that keep the person calm and safe. For instance, if your loved one says they want to visit their deceased mother, you can respond by saying that you will plan a trip. The key is to find a response that doesn't allow them to argue or become upset. It's important to understand that using therapeutic fiblets is not deceitful but rather a way to ensure their well-being and your own sanity. Instead of reminding them of the truth, which may only lead to frustration for both of you, it's better to focus on making them feel secure. So remember, when necessary, use therapeutic fiblets to create a positive and supportive environment for your loved one with dementia....", "final_context": "...Answer: To be an effective caregiver for someone with dementia, there are several important things to keep in mind. Being an effective caregiver often requires a lot of repetition, so it's important to learn and prepare for the specific tasks involved in their care. Attending caregiver classes and seeking information from local agencies can be helpful resources. However, it's crucial to always keep the person with dementia at the center of your care and to respect their dignity and autonomy....\n\n...It's important to remember that impulse control may be low for someone with dementia, and trying to reason or argue may not be productive. By offering understanding and finding ways to work together, we can help minimize challenges and maintain a positive experience for everyone involved....\n\n...Answer: When someone with dementia is facing adversity, it is important for caregivers to provide support in a meaningful way. It can be difficult when loved ones try to offer comfort by pretending that everything will be fine and that the person will live forever, as this can feel isolating and unrealistic. Instead, caregivers should try to strike a balance between comforting and acknowledging the reality of the situation. For example, if someone is worried about a pet who is undergoing surgery, they may want their caregiver to be there with them in their anxiety and provide reassurance based on the facts. It is important for caregivers to understand that their role is not to simply cheerlead or offer false hope, but to genuinely be present and empathetic. Rather than standing at the top of a metaphorical rabbit hole and shouting encouragement, caregivers should be willing to jump into the hole with the person experiencing grief, anxiety, or sadness. By being there with them and providing support, caregivers can help them navigate through difficult emotions and find ways to cope. Every individual may have different needs when it comes to support, but genuine companionship and understanding are essential. So, caregivers should aim to provide empathy, comfort, and companionship when someone with dementia is facing adversity....\n\n...Answer: When dealing with behavioral symptoms of dementia, it's important to understand that your loved one may say hurtful things or accuse you of things that aren't true. It's crucial to remember that these behaviors are a result of the dementia and not a reflection of their true feelings towards you. The brain of someone with dementia is undergoing changes, causing them to lose control and have distorted perceptions of their world. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. For example, they may misplace something and accuse you of stealing it, even though it's not true. It's challenging, but it's important not to argue with or correct them because their experience of events is real to them. Questioning their reality or telling them they are wrong will only make them feel angry, confused, and disconnected. They may even feel ashamed for their behaviors and struggles. It's crucial to recognize that they don't have the same coping tools as before, and it's our responsibility to provide understanding and support. In some cases, they may simply say things that are incorrect, and it can be emotionally difficult to let them believe these things....\n\n...Question: How do you maximize happiness for your loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: When caring for a loved one with dementia, it's important to prioritize their happiness. One key way to do this is to avoid arguing with them. People with dementia have a different perspective than ours, and it's easy for us as caregivers to become frustrated when they act in ways that seem irrational to us. We might try to correct them and bring them back to our reality, but this approach doesn't work. It's called reality orientation, and it involves constantly correcting the person and telling them what is real. Instead, a better approach is called validation therapy. This means validating the person's perspective, even if it's different from ours. If they believe something that we know is not true, there's no need to argue or correct them. By accepting their perspective and not arguing, we can help keep them relatively happy.\nQuestion: Can antipsychotics make dementia worse?...\n\n...Attend carefully to what the person is saying and doing,\nto understand their reality. Acknowledge their worry, and\nexplain you will try to help. They are more likely to be gently\ndistracted, once they feel heard.\nNot contradicting their experience. They shouldn't be told\nwhat is or is not true in a confrontational manner. They may\nbecome frightened or upset.\nRemembering that emotional memories are often easier\nto retrieve. Staying open, calm and friendly can help the\nperson with dementia to associate a carer with positive\nemotions, even if they struggle to understand who you are\nin the present.\nRemaining calm. If a carer becomes frustrated that the person\nis struggling with the present, they should take themselves\nout of the situation until they feel calmer, perhaps making a\ndrink for them both to take some time out of the room.\nRemembering the positive difference they make to the\nperson with dementia. The person with dementia does not\nneed to fully understand your reality for them to feel happy,\nso continue to try and do what makes them feel content.\n\nLying In Dementia\nCaregiving\nLying In Dementia Caregiving\nAs a caregiver for a person with dementia, you may have faced situations where\ntelling the truth would cause more harm than withholding it. For example, if your\ncare recipient repeatedly asks where their long-deceased parent is, you'll likely\navoid telling them the truth to prevent them from re-experiencing feelings of grief\nand loss. Some caregivers lie to protect their care recipient's safety or well-being.\nIn these situations, “lying” to protect the person you care for may be beneficial to\nyou both.\nDid You Know?\nSome researchers refer to this strategy as “therapeutic lying” or\n“therapeutic fibbing” to reflect that refraining from telling the truth can\nbe beneficial to a care recipient with dementia in certain situations.\nCaregivers of people with dementia may often experience the dilemma of whether\nor not to modify the truth to their care recipient–even if they know they intend to\nhelp them. This is normal! Research talks about how there are different types of\nlies used in caregiving, different reasons that caregivers may use lies, and the pros...\n\nQuestion: Is it okay to lie to my loved one with dementia?\nAnswer: It is understandable to have questions about how to communicate with a loved one who has dementia. Sometimes, people with dementia may believe in things that aren't true. For example, they may think a deceased person is still alive. In such situations, it can be helpful to use what I call \"therapeutic fiblets.\" These fiblets are not lies but rather responses that keep the person calm and safe. For instance, if your loved one says they want to visit their deceased mother, you can respond by saying that you will plan a trip. The key is to find a response that doesn't allow them to argue or become upset. It's important to understand that using therapeutic fiblets is not deceitful but rather a way to ensure their well-being and your own sanity. Instead of reminding them of the truth, which may only lead to frustration for both of you, it's better to focus on making them feel secure. So remember, when necessary, use therapeutic fiblets to create a positive and supportive environment for your loved one with dementia...."}

Many people feel uneasy about being in such facilities and it can be challenging for us to hear this. Instead of immediately justifying their current situation or trying to explain why they need to be there, it is important to simply be present and listen to their feelings. Let them openly express their desire to go home. We often avoid this conversation because we know they have to stay in the care facility and it can also bring up feelings of guilt. However, when someone with dementia expresses their longing for home while in a long-term care facility, we can provide reassurance and comfort by acknowledging their emotions and asking about what they miss about their home. For example, if your\ncare recipient repeatedly asks where their long-deceased parent is, you'll likely\navoid telling them the truth to prevent them from re-experiencing feelings of grief\nand loss. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. For more information, see\nfactsheet 527 Changes in perception.\nAgitation including restlessness\nA person with dementia may become agitated suddenly because\nof a change or specific cause, such as noise or not being able to\ndo something they previously could. Or they may feel a general\nsense of agitation but not know why.\nAgitation can take many forms. For example, a person who is...\n\nChanges in perception\nSpace for\nyour notes\n4 Delusions\nDelusions (or strongly held false beliefs) are a common symptom\nfor a person with dementia. They can take the form of paranoia,\nwhich makes the person feel threatened, even if there is no\nor little reason to feel this way. Dementia can make a person\nsuspicious of the people around them. A person experiencing a\ndelusion may feel that they are being watched, or that someone\nis acting against them. They may jump to conclusions without\nmuch evidence. For example, if their neighbour has made a\nnasty comment about them once, they may believe that the\nneighbour is directing a hate campaign against them. Because\nof dementia, the person may no longer be able to moderate\nintense or wild thoughts.\nIf the person you care for has delusions, this can be very\ndifficult to cope with, especially if they are convinced that\nyou have done something wrong or are trying to harm them.\nTry to remember that their delusions feel as real to them as\nyour reality feels to you. You will not generally be able to\nconvince a person experiencing delusions that they are wrong...\n\nWhat are delusions?\nDelusions (or strongly held false beliefs) are a common symptom for a\nperson with dementia. They can take the form of paranoia, which makes\nthe person feel threatened, even if there is no or little reason to feel this\nway. Dementia can make a person suspicious of the people around\nthem.\nA person experiencing a delusion may feel that they are being watched,\nor that someone is acting against them. They may jump to conclusions\nwithout much evidence.\nFor example, if their neighbour has made a nasty comment about them\nonce, they may believe that the neighbour is directing a hate campaign\nagainst them. Because of dementia, the person may no longer be able to\nmoderate intense or wild thoughts.\nIf the person you care for has delusions, this can be very difficult to cope\nwith, especially if they are convinced that you have done something\nwrong or are trying to harm them. Try to remember that their delusions\nfeel as real to them as your reality feels to you. You will not generally be\nable to convince a person experiencing delusions that they are wrong or\nmistaken....\n\nLying In Dementia\nCaregiving\nLying In Dementia Caregiving\nAs a caregiver for a person with dementia, you may have faced situations where\ntelling the truth would cause more harm than withholding it. For example, if your\ncare recipient repeatedly asks where their long-deceased parent is, you'll likely\navoid telling them the truth to prevent them from re-experiencing feelings of grief\nand loss. Some caregivers lie to protect their care recipient's safety or well-being.\nIn these situations, “lying” to protect the person you care for may be beneficial to\nyou both.\nDid You Know?\nSome researchers refer to this strategy as “therapeutic lying” or\n“therapeutic fibbing” to reflect that refraining from telling the truth can\nbe beneficial to a care recipient with dementia in certain situations.\nCaregivers of people with dementia may often experience the dilemma of whether\nor not to modify the truth to their care recipient–even if they know they intend to\nhelp them. This is normal! Research talks about how there are different types of\nlies used in caregiving, different reasons that caregivers may use lies, and the pros...\n\nMany people with dementia become confused and disorientated at times. This may lead to\nthem believing things that are not true – known as ‘false beliefs' or ‘delusions'. Our dementia\nspecialist Admiral Nurses explain why this might happen, and how you can help the person\nyou care for.\nCollapse all\nWhat are false beliefs and delusions?\nEveryone has different personal beliefs. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\n...they are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. They may\nbecome angry or upset if you challenge them, which can make it hard to care for\nthem.\nHowever, there are ways to help a person who is experiencing false beliefs or\ndelusions.\n● try to explain what's happening without challenging or correcting them. You\ncould say something like: “The thought that someone has stolen your purse\nmust be very distressing. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...and the need for “hope” embodied in concrete\nactions (eg, taking a medication) must be weighed.\nKaasalainen et al.\n(2011), Canada25\nTo explore the personal\nexperiences related to\nmedication management of\npeople living with dementia\n(PLWD), their informal\ncaregivers and assisting\nhealth care professionals.\n57 English‐speaking participants\nthat included 20 informal\ncaregivers recruited\nthrough health care\nservices and Alzheimer's\nSociety, 11 PLWD,\nSemi‐structured individual\ninterviews using a grounded\ntheory approach.\nGrounded theory.\nManagement of medicines varied with the severity of\ndementia. Early stage dementia: medication\nmanagement characterised by patients' desire to\nmaintain independence, denial of issues or disease,\nand a refusal to take medications owing to feeling\nangry. Late‐stage dementia: older adults often refuse\nmedications due to delusional or suspicious thinking,\n(Continues)\nLIM AND SHARMEEN\n\nIt's also a good idea to arrange a medical check-up to rule out other physical or\nmental health problems, and to review any medication that may be causing false\nbeliefs and delusions.\nCan false beliefs and delusions be prevented?\nIt's not always possible to prevent false beliefs and delusions in a person with\ndementia, but these tips might help.\n● agree on places to keep important items like keys, handbag and wallet, so you\nknow where to look first if they think something has disappeared\n● keep spares of essentials that might get misplaced, such as glasses or keys\n● make sure they have regular eye and hearing tests – difficulties with sight or\nhearing can increase confusion\n● encourage them to eat and drink regularly\n● try to keep to a routine and limit changes to their environment\n● keep photographs of them and close family/friends at different life stages\naround the house, to help them recognise the time they're living in\nSources of support\nIt can be very upsetting if the person you care for is accusing you of something you\nhaven't done.\nOur Dementia Helpline provides free, confidential support. You can call 0800 888 6678..."}

It's important to understand that they are not doing this on purpose, but rather because they see you as someone they trust to guide them and keep them safe. However, if this behavior continues, it can be tiring and frustrating for you as the caregiver. To address this issue, it may be helpful to introduce a third person into the situation who can take on some of the caregiving responsibilities. This person should be someone the person with dementia can trust and who understands where to go and what to do. By building this triad early on, you can provide the person with dementia with another person to follow and rely on, giving you the opportunity to take a break and have your own needs met. If necessary, you may need to seek help from a volunteer, a family member, or even hire someone to give you some respite time. Remember, it's important to care for yourself so that you can continue to care for your loved one with dementia....\n\nQuestion: Is there a way to stop someone with dementia from repeating themselves?\nAnswer: Living with dementia can be challenging for both the person experiencing brain changes and their caregivers. It's important to understand that the person may repeat themselves or share the same stories or questions over and over again because they are on a \"seek mission.\" They are searching for something, whether it's information or a connection with you. It's crucial to be sensitive and respond with empathy when they share their stories or ask repetitive questions. Reflecting on what they say and acknowledging their feelings can help create a sense of connection. If you find yourself stuck in a cycle, it may be necessary for the caregiver to flex out of that cycle and transition to a different topic or approach. By interjecting with new information or asking a different question, you can redirect the conversation and maintain engagement. He or\nshe may become restless, causing a need to move around or\npace, or become upset in certain places or when focused on\nspecific details.\n● Possible causes\n● Tips to prevent agitation\n● How to respond\n● Medications for agitation\nPossible causes of agitation\nAnxiety and agitation may be caused by a number of different\nmedical conditions, medication interactions or by any\ncircumstances that worsen the person's ability to think.\nUltimately, the person with dementia is biologically experiencing\na profound loss of their ability to negotiate new information and\nstimulus. It is a direct result of the disease.\nSituations that may lead to agitation include:\n● Moving to a new residence or nursing home.\n● Changes in environment, such as travel, hospitalization or\nthe presence of houseguests.\n● Changes in caregiver arrangements.\n● Misperceived threats.\n● Fear and fatigue resulting from trying to make sense out of\na confusing world.\n\nAnxiety and Agitation  \nA person with Alzheimer's may feel anxious or agitated. He or she may\nbecome restless, causing a need to move around or pace, or become upset in\ncertain places or when focused on specific details.\n● Possible causes\n● Tips to prevent agitation\n● How to respond\n● Medications for agitation\nPossible causes of agitation\nAnxiety and agitation may be caused by a number of different medical\nconditions, medication interactions or by any circumstances that worsen the\nperson's ability to think. Ultimately, the person with dementia is biologically\nexperiencing a profound loss of their ability to negotiate new information and\nstimulus. It is a direct result of the disease.\nSituations that may lead to agitation include:\n● Moving to a new residence or nursing home.\n● Changes in environment, such as travel, hospitalization or the presence\nof houseguests.\n● Changes in caregiver arrangements.\n● Misperceived threats.\n● Fear and fatigue resulting from trying to make sense out of a confusing\nworld.\nTreating Behavioral Symptoms\nAnyone experiencing behavioral symptoms should receive a thorough\nmedical checkup, especially when symptoms appear suddenly. Treatment\n\nCan dementia cause aggressive behaviour?\nAs a person's dementia progresses, they may sometimes behave in ways\nthat are physically or verbally aggressive.\nThis can be very distressing for the person and for those around them.\nLooking at what causes this behaviour and being aware of the person's\nneeds can help to reduce this behaviour or make it easier to manage.\nAggressive behaviour may be:\n● verbal – for example, swearing, screaming, shouting or making\nthreats\n● physical – for example, hitting, pinching, scratching, hair-pulling,\nbiting or throwing things.\nSome people assume that aggressive behaviour is a symptom of\ndementia itself. This can be true, but it's more likely that there is another\ncause. It's important to see beyond the behaviour and think about what\nmay be causing it. Reasons for the person's behaviour could include:\n● difficulties to do with dementia – for example, memory loss,\nlanguage or orientation problems\n● their mental and physical health – for example, they may have pain\nor discomfort that they are unable to communicate\n● the amount and type of contact they have with another person or\nother people...\n\n...they are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. They may\nbecome angry or upset if you challenge them, which can make it hard to care for\nthem.\nHowever, there are ways to help a person who is experiencing false beliefs or\ndelusions.\n● try to explain what's happening without challenging or correcting them. You\ncould say something like: “The thought that someone has stolen your purse\nmust be very distressing. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...Question: Does everyone with dementia get upsetting behavioral symptoms?\nAnswer: Not everyone with dementia will experience behavioral and psychological symptoms such as anxiety, depression, agitation, and restlessness. However, it is quite common, with about 90% of people with dementia showing some form of these symptoms. It is important to note that there are individuals whose loved ones are happy, content, and unaffected by these symptoms. If you find yourself caring for someone who is like that, hearing about others' experiences in support groups might be scary and make you worry if you will face the same challenges. The truth is, it is not necessarily something you will have to deal with. Every situation is unique, and not everyone with dementia experiences these symptoms. However, it is true that symptoms like agitation, depression, anxiety, restlessness, and irritability, known as behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia, occur in up to 90% of dementia cases.\nQuestion: What are the behavioral symptoms of dementia?"}

While aggression can be hard to cope with,\nunderstanding that the person with Alzheimer's or dementia is\nnot acting this way on purpose can help.\n● Causes\n● How to respond\nCauses\nAggression can be caused by many factors including physical\ndiscomfort, environmental factors and poor communication. It is not uncommon for\npersons with Alzheimer's or other dementias to have\nurinary tract or other infections. Due to their loss of\ncognitive function, they are unable to articulate or identify\nthe cause of physical discomfort and, therefore, may\nexpress it through physical aggression.\n● Is the person tired because of inadequate rest or sleep?\n● Is the person hungry or thirsty?\n\nCan dementia cause aggressive behaviour?\nAs a person's dementia progresses, they may sometimes behave in ways\nthat are physically or verbally aggressive.\nThis can be very distressing for the person and for those around them.\nLooking at what causes this behaviour and being aware of the person's\nneeds can help to reduce this behaviour or make it easier to manage.\nAggressive behaviour may be:\n● verbal – for example, swearing, screaming, shouting or making\nthreats\n● physical – for example, hitting, pinching, scratching, hair-pulling,\nbiting or throwing things.\nSome people assume that aggressive behaviour is a symptom of\ndementia itself. Being aware may\nhelp you to better select or reduce activities.\n• Too much stimulation, such as exposure to crowds, loud noise, or unfamiliar\nplaces or events, may cause agitation or withdrawal.\n• Certain behaviors such as fidgeting, rocking, or pacing may reflect the person's\nattempt to cope with stress or tension. This can be challenging because their skin may be more fragile and it is easier to cause harm than we might think. Reacting to their aggression can trigger a physical response in you due to increased adrenaline and cortisol levels. To deal with physical aggression, it is crucial to acknowledge that what happened was a surprise to the person with dementia and made them feel threatened. Understand that their aggression is a fight response, as they seek to remove themselves from the situation. It is important to give them space and step back to avoid escalating the situation. One strategy is to avoid aggression altogether by modifying your approach. Instead of fixing something that may be bothering them, like straightening their clothes, engage with them positively and offer choices. By being observant and responsive to their distress, you can help de-escalate their emotions, allowing for problem-solving to take place. Remember, it is essential to provide understanding and empathy when dealing with physical aggression in someone with dementia....\n\nQuestion: What causes aggressive behavior in people with dementia?\nAnswer: Aggressive behavior in people with dementia, particularly Alzheimer's disease, can be a challenging issue for families. The frequency of aggression tends to increase as the disease progresses. Understanding the triggers for this behavior is crucial in managing it effectively. Disorientation can trigger agitation and aggression, even when individuals are in their own homes. Changes in the surroundings or the feeling of not being at home anymore can contribute to this behavior. Personal care activities, such as bathing or dressing, can also provoke frustration and aggression. In some cases, aggression can be a manifestation of underlying depression that individuals with Alzheimer's find difficult to express. It is important to note that aggression can also indicate pain or other medical conditions. Surprisingly, even constipation can be a potential cause. By identifying the factors or triggers that precede aggressive episodes, caregivers can better address and prevent such behavior.
