(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42015253)\nThe World Health Organization (WHO) recognises dementia as a public health priority. Currently, more than 55 million people live with dementia, and this figure is expected to almost triple to 139 million by 2050. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia, and there is still no cure. Despite the availability of symptomatic and first disease-modifying treatments, effective treatment remains limited. This makes it even more important to be aware that it is estimated that nearly half of all dementia cases could be prevented by eliminating 14 major risk factors. Consequently, the role of these modifiable risk factors has been the subject of research to inform effective preventive strategies. This narrative review summarises the current evidence on the prevention of cognitive decl\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Effects of a complex intervention on agitation and aggression in people living with dementia and mild cognitive impairment in shared-housing arrangements: results for a secondary outcome of the multicenter, cluster-randomized controlled DemWG study. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41580643)\nBackground Although some studies have suggested that homelike care environments can have beneficial effects on people living with dementia (PlwDs) and people living with mild cognitive impairment (PlwMCIs), studies on effects of a non-pharmacological, psychosocial intervention on behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSDs) in the setting of shared-housing arrangements (SHAs) are still lacking. Methods In the prospective, multicenter, mixed-methods, cluster-randomized controlled DemWG study, 97 SHAs comprising 341 PlwDs or PlwMCIs were randomly assigned to either the intervention group (IG) or control group (CG). (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41980837)\nObjective To raise awareness about the environmental impact of medications and provide practical opportunities to reduce this effect. Sources of information The  Planetary Health for Primary Care  resource. Main message Environmental harms and climate change are threats to human health, yet the health care system is responsible for 4.6% of greenhouse gas (GHG) pollution in Canada. Most of this pollution is generated upstream in the supply chain where products, including medications, are produced. In primary care, medications account for 61% of GHG pollution. Medications also have other impacts on the environment including contamination of air, water, and soil. The Evidence, Collaboration, Options, Review Rx (ECO-Rx) framework was designed to support appropriate use of medications through t\n\n[WEB:europepmc] Neuropsychiatric symptoms in mild cognitive impairment and early Alzheimer's disease: Clinical pattern and diagnostic implications. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41523330)\nBackground Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) are widely recognized for their hallmark cognitive deficits, typically characterized by progressive cognitive deterioration. However, neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS), including depression, apathy, anxiety, irritability, and sleep disturbances, are increasingly prevalent in the early stages of these conditions and significantly influence the disease trajectory and patient outcomes. Importantly, neuropsychiatric symptoms often precede overt memory loss by several years, with subtle mood and behavioral disturbances serving as early pre-diagnostic markers of an underlying Alzheimer's pathology. The precautions you take will depend on what is appropriate for the individual you are\ncaring for, as well as the features of the person's physical environment. For example, what will work\nfor someone who lives in a small town may not be suitable for someone in a large urban centre.\nKeep a diary of when and where the person tends to wander. Look for a pattern - this may give\nyou clues as to what is triggering the behaviour.\nKeep objects associated with the outdoors (car keys, jackets, shoes) out of the person's view.\nIf possible, re-locate door locks above eye level or where the person can't see them.\nTry disguising doors by decorating or covering them with posters, wall hangings or mirrors.\n5/27/25, 1:20 PM...\n\n...Answer: If you have a loved one with dementia who begins wandering, it's important to take it seriously and prioritize their safety. Not everyone with dementia wanders, but if they do, there are some steps you can take. First, try to prevent wandering by keeping them engaged with activities that interest them. This will help keep their activity level up and reduce the likelihood of wandering. Also, keep items like shoes out of their line of sight, as this can be a trigger for wanting to leave. You can also install a sound on the door that alerts you when it's opened, so you can quickly respond if they do wander. Letting neighbors know about the situation can also be helpful, as they can contact you if they see your loved one outside without supervision. It's also a good idea to inform the local authorities and provide them with a recent photo of your loved one. Consider using a tracking device that can be attached to something they always have with them, such as a wallet, keys, or shoelace. And if they have a cell phone, make sure location detection is on and use features like \"Find My Friend\" to keep track of their whereabouts. I hope these tips help, and I sincerely hope you never find yourself in this situation....\n\n...Answer: People with dementia may wander for various reasons. In the early stages, they might get lost while trying to go somewhere because they may have the wrong time or day in mind for their intended destination. For example, they might think they have an appointment or need to visit the dentist but remember the address of a previous dentist. This could simply be a misremembering. As the dementia progresses, individuals may not feel comfortable in their current surroundings and try to leave. This is known as elopement. Sometimes, they are not aimlessly wandering, but rather trying to reach a specific place, although they may be confused about the time, place, or situation. Later on, if people with dementia are not engaged in meaningful activities, or with loved ones, or if they cannot find something they are looking for, they may start looking for things on their own. They may rely on visual, auditory, and sensory cues to guide them. From an outside perspective, it may appear as though they are aimlessly wandering, but they are actually seeking something that they feel is missing or hidden. To help prevent wandering, it is important to understand what they may be seeking. Instead of getting upset when you find them, try to be curious and observe their behavior....\n\nWhether or not a person living with dementia wanders, it is a good idea to take proactive steps to\nunderstand this particular behaviour and reduce the risk of the person becoming lost.\nReasons for wandering\nFiguring out why a person living with dementia wanders can be difficult. Every person living with\ndementia is unique; however, there are some common reasons:\nThe person may be too hot or too cold.\nThe person may be agitated due to medication side-effects, too much noise, or other forms of\nover-stimulation.\nThey may be experiencing delusions and hallucinations due to dementia or medication sideeffects.\nThey may be in discomfort. For example, the person may be hungry, in pain, or may need to\nuse the toilet.\nThey may be bored and be seeking stimulation.\nThey may not have enough of an outlet for their energy.\nRestlessness or changing sleep patterns can lead to confusion between night and day.\nThey may be experiencing a common phenomenon called sundowning - read more about\nsundowning here.\nThe person may believe they need to leave the house in order to go to work, or take care of\ntheir children....\n\n...Question: Is there a home security system I should use to keep a person with dementia from wandering?\nAnswer: If you have a loved one with dementia who tends to wander, there are ways to keep them safe at home. It's important to focus on notification rather than trying to keep them confined. For example, using locks on exterior doors may be difficult for someone with advanced dementia to recognize. Instead, consider using security systems that provide notifications when a door is opened or closed. This could be a small beep, bells, a chime, or even a smart doorbell that notifies you through an app. This way, you can be aware if your loved one is trying to leave the house. Remember, it's crucial to balance safety with the person's ability to exit the home in case of emergencies. Engaging them in stimulating activities can also help redirect their urge to wander. The person with dementia may be scared and trying to make sense of their experiences without all the information. As a result, they might fill in the gaps with their own version of events that doesn't align with reality. They may...\n\n...Question: Why doesn't someone with dementia see that there is a problem?\nAnswer: Living with dementia can sometimes cause a person to have difficulty recognizing that there is a problem. This lack of self-awareness is called anosognosia. It is not intentional or a form of denial, but rather a result of changes in the brain caused by dementia. Just like young children, who are not initially self-aware, we develop this ability over time. We learn to be aware of our bodies, sensations, and the consequences of our actions. However, dementia affects the part of the brain responsible for self-awareness, making it challenging for individuals with dementia to recognize changes in their abilities. It can be tempting for caregivers to solely focus on the person with anosognosia, but it is important for them to also be aware of their own feelings and seek support to better understand the situation and how to cope with it. This may lead to\nthem believing things that are not true – known as ‘false beliefs' or ‘delusions'. Our dementia\nspecialist Admiral Nurses explain why this might happen, and how you can help the person\nyou care for.\nCollapse all\nWhat are false beliefs and delusions?\nEveryone has different personal beliefs. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\n...they are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. He or she may\nbecome restless, causing a need to move around or pace, or become upset in\ncertain places or when focused on specific details.\n● Possible causes\n● Tips to prevent agitation\n● How to respond\n● Medications for agitation\nPossible causes of agitation\nAnxiety and agitation may be caused by a number of different medical\nconditions, medication interactions or by any circumstances that worsen the\nperson's ability to think. Ultimately, the person with dementia is biologically\nexperiencing a profound loss of their ability to negotiate new information and\nstimulus. It is a direct result of the disease.\nSituations that may lead to agitation include:\n● Moving to a new residence or nursing home.\n● Changes in environment, such as travel, hospitalization or the presence\nof houseguests.\n● Changes in caregiver arrangements.\n● Misperceived threats.\n● Fear and fatigue resulting from trying to make sense out of a confusing\nworld.\nTreating Behavioral Symptoms\nAnyone experiencing behavioral symptoms should receive a thorough\nmedical checkup, especially when symptoms appear suddenly. Treatment\n\n• Recognize that the time of day may affect behavior. ‘Sundowning,' a behavior\nthat includes wandering, pacing, agitation or depressed mood occurs for many\nindividuals with dementia later in the day or early evening. Being aware may\nhelp you to better select or reduce activities.\n• Too much stimulation, such as exposure to crowds, loud noise, or unfamiliar\nplaces or events, may cause agitation or withdrawal.\n• Certain behaviors such as fidgeting, rocking, or pacing may reflect the person's\nattempt to cope with stress or tension. Try to redirect the individual's energy\ntoward manageable, supervised activities.\n• Restraining a person with dementia in response to agitation is NEVER advised.\nPhysical restraints disregard the individual's dignity and increase the level of\nagitation.\n• Community services such as adult day services can provide a structured\nenvironment for activities.\n• While a non-pharmacological approach is preferable, medication can have a\nsignificant role in reducing agitation. Medication should be used only under the\nsupervision of a physician. Unless monitored, adverse reactions can occur.\nRepetition...\n\nA person with Alzheimer's may feel anxious or agitated. He or\nshe may become restless, causing a need to move around or\npace, or become upset in certain places or when focused on\nspecific details.\n● Possible causes\n● Tips to prevent agitation\n● How to respond\n● Medications for agitation\nPossible causes of agitation\nAnxiety and agitation may be caused by a number of different\nmedical conditions, medication interactions or by any\ncircumstances that worsen the person's ability to think.\nUltimately, the person with dementia is biologically experiencing\na profound loss of their ability to negotiate new information and\nstimulus. It is a direct result of the disease.\nSituations that may lead to agitation include:\n● Moving to a new residence or nursing home.\n● Changes in environment, such as travel, hospitalization or\nthe presence of houseguests.\n● Changes in caregiver arrangements.\n● Misperceived threats.\n● Fear and fatigue resulting from trying to make sense out of\na confusing world.", "final_context": "It's also a good idea to arrange a medical check-up to rule out other physical or\nmental health problems, and to review any medication that may be causing false\nbeliefs and delusions.\nCan false beliefs and delusions be prevented?\nIt's not always possible to prevent false beliefs and delusions in a person with\ndementia, but these tips might help.\n● agree on places to keep important items like keys, handbag and wallet, so you\nknow where to look first if they think something has disappeared\n● keep spares of essentials that might get misplaced, such as glasses or keys\n● make sure they have regular eye and hearing tests – difficulties with sight or\nhearing can increase confusion\n● encourage them to eat and drink regularly\n● try to keep to a routine and limit changes to their environment\n● keep photographs of them and close family/friends at different life stages\naround the house, to help them recognise the time they're living in\nSources of support\nIt can be very upsetting if the person you care for is accusing you of something you\nhaven't done.\nOur Dementia Helpline provides free, confidential support. You can call 0800 888 6678...\n\nAll people with\ndementia decline\nat the same rate.\nThe progression of dementia\ncan vary greatly from person to\nperson.\nThe type of dementia, treatment, and a person's\noverall health are key factors in their progression.\nOnce diagnosed\nwith dementia, a\nperson will die\nquickly.\nDementia does not lead to\nimmediate death.\nThe amount of time a person can live with\ndementia depends on the type of dementia and\nother factors like age and health conditions.\nPeople can live with mild symptoms of dementia\nfor many years before their symptoms progress.\nThere is nothing I\ncan do to stop\nmemory loss or\ndementia.\nWhile some risk factors can't be\ncontrolled, lifestyle choices and\noverall health are changes a\nperson can make to reduce their\nrisk.\nAlcohol intake, blood pressure, cholesterol levels,\nand diabetes all affect the development of\ndementia.\nTreatment\nMyth\nFact\nExplanation\nDementia symptoms can\nbe reversed with\nmedications.\nThere is no current cure for\ndementia.\nThere are medications currently available to\nhelp slow the progression, but there is no cure....\n\nMany people with dementia become confused and disorientated at times. This may lead to\nthem believing things that are not true – known as ‘false beliefs' or ‘delusions'. Our dementia\nspecialist Admiral Nurses explain why this might happen, and how you can help the person\nyou care for.\nCollapse all\nWhat are false beliefs and delusions?\nEveryone has different personal beliefs. These include things like religious or political\nbeliefs, and beliefs that we have developed through our experiences and life lessons.\nAt times, many of us have beliefs that may not be true. For example, someone might\nbelieve their neighbour doesn't like them, even if there's no evidence. But we usually\nhave some control over our beliefs, so they don't have an undue influence on our\nlives.\nWhen someone has dementia, however, they may lose the ability to think logically\nabout whether their beliefs are true. These false beliefs, also called delusions, can\nbecome very powerful and upsetting.\nCommon false beliefs and delusions include:\n● thinking that someone is trying to steal from them\n● thinking that someone is trying to harm them\n● believing that their partner is being unfaithful...\n\n...they are saying is a false belief or delusion.\nHelping a person with false beliefs and delusions\nFalse beliefs and delusions feel very real to the person with dementia. They may\nbecome angry or upset if you challenge them, which can make it hard to care for\nthem.\nHowever, there are ways to help a person who is experiencing false beliefs or\ndelusions.\n● try to explain what's happening without challenging or correcting them. You\ncould say something like: “The thought that someone has stolen your purse\nmust be very distressing. Let's see if we can find it in case it was accidently\nmisplaced”\n● speak in a calm, reassuring way to ease their distress\n● try to involve the person in doing something they enjoy as a way of distracting\nthem\n● if these strategies are not working, try just ‘going along' with the person until\nthey're calmer and/or have moved onto a different topic\n\n...They may be a symptom of the physical changes in the brain\ncaused by dementia. A person may become agitated\nsuddenly because of a change or specific cause, such as\nincreased noise or not being able to do something they\npreviously could. Or they may feel a general sense of\nagitation but not know why.\nA person may feel restless as a side-effect of certain\nmedication (such as some antipsychotic medications). If you\nthink this is the case, ask the person's GP to check whether\ntheir prescription could be causing them to feel restless.\nThere is also a medical condition called ‘restless leg\nsyndrome' that gives people an overwhelming, irresistible\nHow to make a\ndementia fidget toy\nto ease restlessness\nRestlessness and agitation are common behaviours in people living with\ndementia. These behaviours can be difficult for others to understand, but\nfinding out the causes can help you to support the person.\nSee menu\nShop\nContact us\nSearch\n\nAnxiety and Agitation  \nA person with Alzheimer's may feel anxious or agitated. Because roughly 90% of communication is nonverbal, caregivers should pay close attention to these cues.\n**People are usually not aware of the nonverbal messages they are sending.** Nonverbal communication is largely unconscious, so a caregiver's own facial expressions, posture, and tone may convey feelings — such as impatience, stress, or warmth — without the caregiver realizing it.\n**Once you learn how to look for nonverbal messages, you will better understand what a person living with dementia is trying to express.** As verbal ability declines, people living with dementia rely increasingly on nonverbal communication, so reading these cues reveals their needs and feelings.\n\n**People living with dementia forget about 90% of new information within 1 to 5 minutes** of receiving it, because short-term memory is impaired. Caregivers should therefore repeat information, keep it simple, and not rely on the person retaining newly given details.\n**Emotionally spiced (emotionally expressive) nonverbal communication is effective in improving retention of new information** for people living with dementia. Pairing information with warm, emotionally meaningful nonverbal cues helps the information be remembered.\n\nUldall et al., 2012). Where feelings of frustration are expressed and behaviours arising from unmet\ncare needs are displayed, others may perceive these as challenging behaviour (Duxbury et al., 2013;\nHughes, 2013). Although expression by verbal means may be more limited, non-verbal communication can convey feelings, emotions and preferences (Ellis & Astell, 2017; Quinn et al., 2014).\nNon-verbal communication is often preserved in people with moderate-to-severe dementia, while\nthe desire and ability to communicate opinions and answer questions is maintained (Astell & Ellis,\n2006; Brandão et al., 2014; Clare et al., 2008a; Ellis & Astell, 2004; Moore & Hollett, 2003).\nDementia 21(4)\n\n...M¨ohler et al., 2018).\nInteractional techniques were considered essential when combined with more tangible methods.\nNon-verbal communication, such as facial expressions and body language, often allows contextualization of verbal communication (Downs & Collins, 2015). Previous research has shown that\nthe ability to express emotions and awareness may be preserved in individuals with moderate-tosevere dementia (Karger, 2018; Quinn et al., 2014). The importance of communicating using nonverbal techniques was commonly cited including reference to palliative care. However, interpreting\nwhat is being conveyed requires skill and effort (Clare et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2014; Downs & Collins,\n2015; Ellis & Astell, 2017; Quinn et al., 2014; Round et al., 2014) and links to the need for\nexperience, skill and conﬁdence or appropriate training for the less experienced.\nRegardless of the tools and techniques selected, ensuring the conversation and approach is\ncentred on individual need was a fundamental aspect of communication in this study. SLPs can also teach caregivers effective examples of\nnonverbal communication to maintain interpersonal closeness.\nLanzi et al.\nPerspect ASHA Spec Interest Groups. Caregivers should therefore repeat information, keep it simple, and not rely on the person retaining newly given details.\n**Emotionally spiced (emotionally expressive) nonverbal communication is effective in improving retention of new information** for people living with dementia. Pairing information with warm, emotionally meaningful nonverbal cues helps the information be remembered.\n\nQuestion: Why do some people with dementia lie?\nAnswer: People with dementia often say things that might not be true. This is because dementia affects their memory, especially in Alzheimer's disease. When they say things that are not true, it's not really lying in the traditional sense. They might actually believe what they are saying is the truth. Their poor memory causes them to fill in the gaps with what they think might have happened or what they truly believe happened. Another reason people with dementia might lie is because they are aware that something is wrong with their brain and they have memory problems. They try to cover it up and don't want others to realize they are having trouble with their thinking. To appear as if they don't have memory problems, they make up stories and facts. It's important to understand that the person with dementia is not intentionally trying to deceive or lie, but their condition affects their perception of reality.\nQuestion: Why would someone with dementia talk to themselves in the mirror?...\n\n...Question: Do people with dementia know they are forgetting things?\n\n...Answer: People living with dementia may have a strong urge to collect certain items. This is because there is a primitive part of our brain that desires and needs things. One reason for collecting is the fear of needing something in the future and not having it. So, individuals with dementia tend to stash and keep items that catch their attention. However, once collected, they may forget that they have them. It's more about the act of getting the item than actually keeping it. It's important to observe what someone with dementia collects as it can give insight into their preferences. They may be visually drawn to bright and shiny objects, items with many parts, or things like baby dolls, stuffed animals, coins, or napkins. Some may be attracted to items with auditory qualities or specific textures. The location of items can also play a role. To address this behavior in a helpful way, caregivers can substitute items that are likely to be collected and make them easily accessible. By doing this, individuals with dementia can continue collecting and experiencing a sense of value and purpose. It's important to note that the collected items may need to be hidden a bit so that the person can enjoy the process of finding them. Overall, understanding and supporting someone's collecting behavior can make their life more meaningful and less bothersome....\n\n...Question: Why can I remember things from long ago, but I can't remember what happened 5 minutes ago?\nAnswer: People often wonder why they can remember things from a long time ago but struggle to recall recent events. This is a common question, especially among those with Alzheimer's. One of the main symptoms of Alzheimer's dementia is poor short-term memory. This means we have difficulty remembering things that happened just a few minutes ago. It's like our minds rapidly forget information. Alzheimer's primarily affects our short-term memory, but our long-term memory can stay intact for a long time. That's why memories from our childhood, for example, tend to stick with us. On the other hand, we may quickly forget what someone said to us just a few minutes ago. [Learn more about Alzheimer's dementia here](url)\nQuestion: Will I ever get back to talking and thinking like I used to?...\n\nSupporting a person with memory loss\nSpace for\nyour notes\nLosing items\nPeople with dementia often lose items as a result of their memory\nloss. They may misplace common items, such as glasses or\nkeys, or put an item somewhere for safekeeping and then forget\nwhere it is. They may also leave items in unusual places – for\nexample, leaving the remote control in the bathroom, or tea\nbags in the fridge.\nIf the person thinks an item should be somewhere and it's not,\nthis may lead them to think that someone is hiding or stealing\nthings from them. This is a type of delusion. It can be difficult\nboth for the person and those around them. It can help to try\nsee things from their point of view. The person with dementia\nis trying to make sense of their reality and what is happening.\nFor more information on delusions, see factsheet 527, Changes\nin perception.\nIt is also important to note that there may be truth in what the\nperson is saying – don't dismiss it because they have dementia.\nHow you can help\nTry to keep items in places where the person is used to them...\n\nQuestion: Do people with dementia know they are forgetting things?\nAnswer: People with dementia may have different levels of awareness regarding their memory loss. Some individuals with dementia may not realize that they are forgetting things or that they need assistance. They may not even be aware of the difficulties they are facing. On the other hand, some people with dementia do recognize that something is wrong. They may have moments of realization when they forget something and acknowledge it when reminded. When someone with dementia has no memory of their forgetfulness, they may react defensively or not believe others when reminded of their lapses. Those who do remember their forgetfulness may feel sad, blame themselves, or become frustrated with their situation. It is important to understand that both reactions are possible in dementia, and it can vary from person to person.\nQuestion: What is a dementia touch point and how is it useful in dementia care?...\n\nSupporting a person with memory loss\nSpace for\nyour notes\n1 Memory loss and\ndementia\nIt is common for people with dementia to experience memory\nloss. This is because dementia is caused by damage to the brain,\nand this damage can affect areas of the brain involved in creating\nand retrieving memories.\nMemory loss can be a symptom of any type of dementia.\nFor people with Alzheimer's disease, it is often among the very\nfirst signs.\nMemory can be affected in different ways. These include:\nnot being able to create new memories – this means that\nrecent events are not ‘recorded' in the person's memory and\nso cannot be recalled later. For example, the person may\nforget a conversation they have just had.\ntaking longer to retrieve information – this means that,\neven though the person is still able to recall things, this takes\nthem much longer or they might need a prompt. For example,\nthey might need more time to find the name for an object.\nnot being able to retrieve information – this means that,\neven though the person may be able to create new memories,\nthey are not able to access them when needed. Although expression by verbal means may be more limited, non-verbal communication can convey feelings, emotions and preferences (Ellis & Astell, 2017; Quinn et al., 2014).\nNon-verbal communication is often preserved in people with moderate-to-severe dementia, while\nthe desire and ability to communicate opinions and answer questions is maintained (Astell & Ellis,\n2006; Brandão et al., 2014; Clare et al., 2008a; Ellis & Astell, 2004; Moore & Hollett, 2003).\nDementia 21(4)\n\n...or negative information with negative wording, those with MCI judged the sham\nmedications similarly to healthy counterparts. However, when positive information was\nframed using negative wording, or negative information with positive wording, adults with\nMCI were more influenced by the way the information was framed than were the healthy\nelders, responding more to the tone of the message than the information itself.11 This\nsuggests that how information is expressed when delivering it to cognitively impaired adults\nis critically important and may influence their health care decisions. Therefore, for health\ncare providers, understanding the communication profiles of people with MCI can help\nensure that they receive comprehensible diagnostic information, fully understand their\nmedical care options, and make well-considered treatment decisions, according to their\npersonal goals of care.\nTo our knowledge, there has been only a single topic that included communication deficits\nin older adults with mild cognitive impairment.12 The present systematic review focused\nexclusively on studies of participants with MCI, identified using standard diagnostic\ncriteria,1 excluding studies of subjects with dementia (unless included as a comparison\ngroup to MCI participants). This\nfinding occurs as a result of bilateral\nmedial temporal lobe (hippocampal)\ndamage, which severely impairs the\npatient's ability to learn new information. Today, researchers are\nlooking at potential risk factors present even earlier in...\n\nQuestion: Does mild cognitive impairment always lead to Alzheimer's disease?\nAnswer: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is often a precursor to developing dementia, specifically due to Alzheimer's disease, but it does not always lead to it. MCI is a term used to describe a level of impairment that is less severe than dementia. There are various underlying factors that can cause MCI. It can be related to neurodegenerative diseases or other medical conditions such as chronic kidney disease or the effects of cancer treatment. It can even be caused by chronic substance use. The progression of MCI depends on individual factors like medication and current medical status. It does not always progress to dementia, and it is not always linked to Alzheimer's disease. MCI can be related to other diseases within the neurodegenerative family. In rare cases, individuals with MCI may even revert back to a normal cognitive state. As part of caregiver self-care, the caregiver should spend at least 8 consecutive hours away from caregiving per week.\n- **Monthly support group:** attending a **monthly support group**, with or without their loved one living with dementia.\n- **Problem-solving skills development:** developing **problem-solving skills** to help the caregiver cope with **their own emotional and physical stress**, and to manage the **cognitive, functional, behavioral, and psychological disabilities** of their loved one living with dementia. Many caregivers feel overwhelmed by the\nchanges in their family member, which can lead to feelings of sadness,\nfrustration, and helplessness.\n\n...Answer: Leaving a loved one with dementia in a facility is not abandoning your duties as a caregiver. In fact, there are many situations where it is in the best interest of both the person with dementia and the caregiver to consider an alternative living environment. One of the main reasons is safety. If the person is prone to falls, constantly trying to leave, or engaging in dangerous behaviors like turning on the stove, it becomes crucial to place them in an environment that can ensure their safety. Sometimes, the decision to move to a facility is also driven by emotional factors. Caregivers can become overwhelmed and burnt out after a long period of providing care. They may need the help and support of a team of professionals, which is not possible when they are the sole caregiver at home. Caring for someone with dementia can be exhausting, and it is important to recognize when it is no longer feasible to continue alone. The decision to move a loved one into residential care is unique for every family, and only you can determine the right time. As part of caregiver self-care, the caregiver should spend at least 8 consecutive hours away from caregiving per week.\n- **Monthly support group:** attending a **monthly support group**, with or without their loved one living with dementia.\n- **Problem-solving skills development:** developing **problem-solving skills** to help the caregiver cope with **their own emotional and physical stress**, and to manage the **cognitive, functional, behavioral, and psychological disabilities** of their loved one living with dementia. It's important to schedule regular check-ups with your primary care physician and take any prescribed medications. Joining a caregiver support group can provide valuable support and give you permission to take breaks and prioritize your own needs. The second program is the online support groups, which provide a safe space for caregivers to connect with facilitators who have experience in Alzheimer's disease and caregiving. These support groups offer weekly and monthly support, helping caregivers reduce stress and learn caregiving strategies while also finding a sense of community. The caregiver lounges are offered regularly, providing consistent support. Some\nstudies suggest that distress remains unchanged...\n\n...Answer: When someone with dementia is facing adversity, it is important for caregivers to provide support in a meaningful way. It can be difficult when loved ones try to offer comfort by pretending that everything will be fine and that the person will live forever, as this can feel isolating and unrealistic. Instead, caregivers should try to strike a balance between comforting and acknowledging the reality of the situation. For example, if someone is worried about a pet who is undergoing surgery, they may want their caregiver to be there with them in their anxiety and provide reassurance based on the facts. It is important for caregivers to understand that their role is not to simply cheerlead or offer false hope, but to genuinely be present and empathetic. Rather than standing at the top of a metaphorical rabbit hole and shouting encouragement, caregivers should be willing to jump into the hole with the person experiencing grief, anxiety, or sadness. By being there with them and providing support, caregivers can help them navigate through difficult emotions and find ways to cope. Every individual may have different needs when it comes to support, but genuine companionship and understanding are essential. The caregiver stress prevention bundle includes the following components:\n- **Weekly respite care:** at least **8 consecutive hours per week** of respite care, during which the caregiver is not providing care for their loved one living with dementia and is instead focusing on their own emotional health. Some\nstudies suggest that distress remains unchanged...\n\n...Answer: When someone with dementia is facing adversity, it is important for caregivers to provide support in a meaningful way. It can be difficult when loved ones try to offer comfort by pretending that everything will be fine and that the person will live forever, as this can feel isolating and unrealistic. Instead, caregivers should try to strike a balance between comforting and acknowledging the reality of the situation. For example, if someone is worried about a pet who is undergoing surgery, they may want their caregiver to be there with them in their anxiety and provide reassurance based on the facts. It is important for caregivers to understand that their role is not to simply cheerlead or offer false hope, but to genuinely be present and empathetic. Rather than standing at the top of a metaphorical rabbit hole and shouting encouragement, caregivers should be willing to jump into the hole with the person experiencing grief, anxiety, or sadness. By being there with them and providing support, caregivers can help them navigate through difficult emotions and find ways to cope. Every individual may have different needs when it comes to support, but genuine companionship and understanding are essential.
